title: My Edinburgh fringe odyssey: ‘The nudity is expressive, shocking – sometimes harrowing’ | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: There are 3,649 shows at the fringe this year, but how many embody its spirit of radical experimentation? I took a journey through foam, lube and gore to find out ...
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: There are 3,649 shows at the fringe this year, but how many embody its spirit of radical experimentation? I took a journey through foam, lube and gore to find out ...
Content: Arifa Akbar hunts for out-there shows.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArifa Akbar hunts for out-there shows.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026My Edinburgh fringe odyssey: ‘The nudity is expressive, shocking – sometimes harrowing’There are 3,649 shows at the fringe this year, but how many embody its spirit of radical experimentation? I took a journey through foam, lube and gore to find out ...Arifa AkbarWed 19 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomewhere in Edinburgh,a man is drinking his own urine. Elsewhere, the story of a religious sect that commands its followers touse “butt plugs”plays out as a musical. In yet another room, a comedian sings the same songover and over for an hour.It is shows like these that have sustained the welcomingly weird and ungovernable lore of theEdinburgh festivalfringe. In recent years, though, the annual jamboree has been accused of becoming an increasingly commercially savvy entity. The radical experimentalism might just be intact, but does this now sit at the fringes of the fringe, rather than its centre?Francesca Moody, one of the festival’s superproducers, says that putting on a show here has become increasingly expensive. When she producedPhoebe Waller-Bridge’s stage version of Fleabagin 2013, it cost about £10,000. By 2019, when she co-producedRichard Gadd’s Baby Reindeer, it cost about £40,000. Putting on a one-person show now, she says, costs her closer to £100,000.The reasons for this, which have beenwell reported, include soaring accommodation costs, funding cuts and rising production costs. Some have argued that this might dial down the risky spirit on which the fringe was founded. The ethos was different when the financial risks were not as high, says Moody. “It was a space for messing around and building your craft, your sense of taste. As a producer or as an artist, you’re working out what your voice is, and doing that over a number of years.”Artists and producers may now want more out of it too: to be scouted for the big-time with a transfer to London or, the ultimate dream, a television series in the mould of Fleabag or Baby Reindeer. Some high-profile productions have lined up transfers before their shows debut at the fringe. The Australian writer-performer Hannah Reilly’s showRoleplay, about a woman who becomes a “slutfluencer” – which is also produced by Moody – already has a London transfer. As doesBigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It, featuring a clown duo who cause chaos in their town after faking Bigfoot sightings. Elsewhere, the musical Bliss, which turns the traditional fairytale story on its head, will travel to London with the backing of the entertainment company ATG.Moody believes the low-budget gems are still out there though. Comedian and fellow fringe veteran Rory Bremner agrees. Although he is a big name at the festival, with his latest show, Making an Impression, playing at the 1,000-seater McEwan Hall, he still likes to test out “work-in-development” material alongside new, unknown acts. “It’s an opportunity to try stuff that I’ve written in the last couple of days,” he says. These below-the-radar gigs take place in pubs or tents, sometimes containing as few as six people in the audience and often raising money for charity.View image in fullscreenSet for the big time? Xhloe and Natasha, the clown duo in Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMoody thinks small-scale, risk-taking work will find a home at the fringe because people are “hungry” for it. “There is always going to be a weird, idiosyncratic little show in a back room or basement that people discover at the fringe. It’s just about finding it.”So off I go on my very own theatrical odyssey to discover the “fringe of the fringe” and find an interactive act with a surprising degree of danger attached. Truthmachine plays out in an upstairs room of the city’s Quaker Meeting House and is produced by the Australian company Counterpilot. A maximum of 12 people at any one time sign up to a 30-minute participatory show with a lie detector test at its heart. If that exudes Jeremy Kyle vibes, it proves much more thoughtful and transgressive than the gimmick it first appears to be. We are seated before our own voting machines for a warm-up, in which people are selected at random, put under a spotlight and asked to state “yes” or “no” to questions that range from the conceptual (“has capitalism failed?”) to the icky (“have you ever touched yourself at night?”). It has an interrogatory feel, as exposing as a game of spin the bottle, but with strangers. I find myself wondering what might come next, and where the nearest exits are.There is no time to escape because, before you can say “polygraph machine”, one of us is chosen to be strapped up to one. It is hardly coercive – the lie detector test is the basis on which we have all convened – but I still grow edgy. A young woman is chosen and begins boldly answering questions that become more intimate while her heartbeat and other biological measurements are taken, giving us the probability of her telling a lie as a percentage. “Have you ever had a sexual dream about a family member?” she is asked. I feel everyone in the room wince. Then: “Have you had a sexual experience in public?” “Did you enjoy it?” “Was it your idea?” “Did you want to get caught?” There are existential inquiries too: “Do you think you will get what you want?” “Can everyone be forgiven?”Things have turned a shade Black Mirror, it seems. This is not so much a playful game of truth or dare as a carefully orchestrated experiment around group dynamics and exposure. What are we prepared to share? What will we hide from others? What brings up shame or social inadequacy? I am surprised by how relieved I am not to be the person strapped up to the biometric sensors, but also how much my discomfort tells me about myself.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Collins in Succubus, a one-woman horror comedy.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianI come out blinking into the daylight and head to Succubus, a one-woman horror show that features a trigger warning of cannibalism. A debut written and acted by burlesque performer Georgina Collins (AKA Strawberry Duvall), it was inspired partly by her experience with doctors dismissing her medical symptoms as “hormonal issues”. The play touches on medical misogyny but in dark, satirical ways, its social commentary as sharp-fanged as the female killer at its centre. Its conspicuously low-budget set design adds to its semblance of a B-movie feminist horror gore-fest, especially its props, which include a string of fake sausages representing human intestines.Succubus is performed at the 60-seater Dexter stage at the Underbelly and is packed on the day I attend. Directed by Grainne Robson, it is not just an imaginative take on the notion of the monstrous feminine but finely crafted in its writing. Emily Ritchie and Zara Jayant, former theatre publicists, are its producers. “When we started the company, there were so many artists whose only resort was to wait for the door to open. We thought: ‘Why not build the door ourselves?’” says Jayant. Succubus was financed on a profit-share model, its £6,500 budget raised through crowdfunding, a supper-club, a horror-themed film quiz night, a burlesque cabaret night and a raffle.View image in fullscreenCraig Manson as Bunny, an aspiring theatre starlet … and a serial killerPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe night show at Summerhall Arts is another horror, in the shape of Bunny! It is the name of Craig Manson’s drag alter ego, who emerges in a blond wig and off-the-shoulder gold dress with tufts of chest hair peeping from beneath. The self-produced show is gloriously scrappy but with a serious sting. Bunny is a struggling performer, desperate for a breakthrough after a decade of rejections and living in penury. In real life, Manson has been vocal about the state of arts funding in Scotland. In a blend of comedy and song, Bunny decides that the only way to correct the inequities is to kill off her competitors, beginning with an artistic director and graduating to famous actors and artists. It is fizzy entertainment, intelligently barbed.So is Mother, Maiden and Crone at the Bedlam theatre, a loose modern-day adaptation of Macbeth by an Edinburgh-based drag troupe. Shakespeare is occasionally winched into a plotline involving the drama of a gay bar (a hen do for a bride called McBride), with a violent denouement on a dancefloor involving fatal quantities of foam and lube.View image in fullscreenModern-day take on Macbeth … Mother, Maiden and Crone.Photograph: Lou Mccurdy @Loumacphotography/Loumac PhotographyThe show had a limited run in a hotel basement at last year’s fringe and has been financed through fundraisers. The auditorium is filled this year and I feel as if I have been let in on a thrilling local secret.The fringe is famed for discovering student talent, namely through the Edinburgh University group Footlights, but the show I plump for is off the beaten-track of university comedy societies. Moth And Dog Are Dying to Get Out is a play with enormous ambition, selected for the National student drama festival at Curve theatre, in Leicester, this spring. It features two teenage boys navigating same-sex desire for each other under the oppressive forces of homophobia, peer pressure and strong-man masculinity. Written by full-time student Aidan Monks and inspired by the writings of the poet Peter Scalpello, it stars Dylan Swain as Dog and Ben Stuart as Moth. They are schoolboys, one of whom has been “outed” as gay with a graphic image stuck on his locker (a photo of his “spread arsehole” from Grindr). It plays out in flashbacks and forwards, the narrative jagged yet emotionally tender. It is a heart-rending play, as lo-fi as Succubus in its production values but full of promise and led by two brave performances.There are other shows tucked away in studio spaces that encapsulate the spirit of experiment, such as Letícia Rodrigues’s autobiographical production about body size,116 Grams: A Play to Lose Weight, which shocks with its expressive, sometimes harrowing, nudity.Thank You, F**k You and I’m Sorry(was there ever a more fringe-appropriate title?), is in the studio space at C Arts and is an intense, sung-through requiem that mourns a dead father. There is an audience of three on the night I attend but Welsh performer Jonathan Powell (also known as Jonny Forever) powers on, playing violin and guitar alongside the vocals. It is entirely self-funded and deeply personal.The fringiest shows, I realise, are visible in plain sight if you look, and often nestling in the smaller spaces of established venues. Bunny! is in the modestly sized Anatomy lecture theatre at Summerhall. Another jewel of the festival is in an even smaller basement space in the venue, the former gents locker room at Summerhall.QFWFQ, with Los Angeles performer Gregory Nussen, directed by Hannah Pilkes, is an enormously accomplished riff on Italo Calvino’s novel, If on a Winter’s Night a Traveller, with its own postmodern stops and starts, direct addresses and reflections on the construction of story. It is a small but exquisitely formed creature of the festival, full of experimental energy, intelligent inquiry and, most of all, an exciting mix of mischief and danger. Nussen leads one audience member to the toilet, makes phone calls and tells stories on stories. They are a natural comic but switch to a gripping dramatic tone when they begin their stories of coming out as non-binary, going to Jewish summer camp and then on a tour of the concentration camps in Poland. Nussen arrives at Zionism, the genocide in Gaza, the brutality of Israel’s government before they interrupt themselves with another layer of story, another voice, which states that this is too dangerous a story to be aired.As the winner of the best solo show at the 2025 Hollywood Fringe, it is not exactly an Edinburgh festival fringe discovery, but it is an amazing find from a punter’s point of view, immaculately structured, surreal and labyrinthine. The invention and imagination makes me tingle. It is better than the work I’ve seen on bigger Edinburgh stages. The best of the fringe, found in this basement room, and stumbled across before noon. This is what the festival is all about.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Judi Dench has inspired a new decorating trend – and I oppose it with every fibre of my being | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: Reverse decluttering is here, prompting a shudder from me and my fellow neat freaks. Why would you want to be surrounded by mementos when you could be perfectly tidy?
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: Reverse decluttering is here, prompting a shudder from me and my fellow neat freaks. Why would you want to be surrounded by mementos when you could be perfectly tidy?
Content: The reverse decluttering trend gives credence to the idea that possessions can evoke pride.Photograph: Posed by model; Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe reverse decluttering trend gives credence to the idea that possessions can evoke pride.Photograph: Posed by model; Westend61/Getty ImagesOpinionHomesJudi Dench has inspired a new decorating trend – and I oppose it with every fibre of my beingPolly HudsonReverse decluttering is here, prompting a shudder from me and my fellow neat freaks. Why would you want to be surrounded by mementos when you could be perfectly tidy?Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTShareOlder doesn’t always mean wiser. Jo Whiley has spoken about a home hack she picked up from – clang! – Dame Judi Dench, and I’m afraid I’m opposed to it with every fibre of my being. Whiley is in a new phase – her four children are grownup – so she recently began the most satisfying project of all: a decluttering spree. Hard even to type those words without a shiver of anticipation. Trigger warning for fellow neat freaks, though: this anecdote does not end well.Whiley went to interview Dench for her RHS Roots podcast and found the actor’s house “packed with family photographs, children’s drawings and memories everywhere”. Mind-blowingly, she means this as a positive. “Seeing Judi’s reminded me that lived-in spaces are often the most beautiful because they reflect a lifetime of love, family and shared experiences,” she says. “I suddenly thought: ‘Why am I putting all these things away?’” As soon as I got home, I immediately put all the family photographs back out.” TLDR: I cleaned up and then I made it all messy again. Shudder.This sorry tale could be viewed as a recluttering, but instead it’s called reverse decluttering –and it’s a trend. Give me strength. It’s backed up by a review article fromCurrent Opinion in Psychology, which determined that – duh – some objects help to bring significant memories to mind.Another studyfound that possessions could evoke pride. What, more pride than tidiness? Nothing matters more than that. Decluttering is the heroin of housework – in its addictiveness, that is. In every other way, it’s the opposite of heroin – it will make your life better and you’ll never be sorry you tried it. I live to declutter. It cleanses not only your environment, but also your mind, body and soul. I’m prepared to keep a capsule collection of essential items – everything else is to be chucked out, sometimes while someone is still using it, if they pause for long enough. I’m like a snake, constantly shedding skin and donating it to the charity shop.Because fate has a sense of humour, I accidentally married a hoarder. The following sounds like hyperbole, but it’s completely true to say the man has never thrown anything away. If at any point since birth he was given or bought it, he still has it. He has every laptop he’s ever owned, even though all but the one he uses no longer work, which is why he begrudgingly replaced them. He has clothes from his schooldays, including a T-shirt that hasn’t fitted him for decades and resembles a cobweb because of the ratio of hole to material. If a member of his family ever touched it – even an individual he never met, even if it is ugly, broken, useless or all three – he intends to take it to his grave.He has a mustard cravat that also smells like mustard, despite many spins in the washing machine, which belonged to a great-great-aunt’s husband’s brother. You’d be amazed how few occasions call for a cravat, unless you assumed it was none at all. My husband is like a bird refusing to budge from its nest because it’s fiercely protecting eggs, but instead of eggs it’s nonfunctional laptops, antique T-shirts and a pungent cravat.Clearly, snakes and birds are not natural bedfellows, which is why our relationship is an endless argument about whether his items have been innocently mislaid (by him) or secretly disposed of (by me). If he hears about reverse decluttering, it’s all over for me. To continue the snake metaphor too far, I won’t have a leg to stand on. We recently had a lengthy, passionate debate over a stone; I won only on a technicality (he couldn’t name the beach it was from before the buzzer went). The route out of our house is a one-way street and there’s a no-returns policy. If he even tries to mess with the system, I’ll unhinge my jaw and swallow him whole.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsHomesOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Love You to Death review – is this all they asked the woman who faked her son’s illnesses?  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Lisa Hayden-Johnson was convicted of child cruelty, but she still insists that she didn’t do anything wrong – and barely gets a grilling about it. Her children, who speak for the first time in this documentary, deserve much more
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Lisa Hayden-Johnson was convicted of child cruelty, but she still insists that she didn’t do anything wrong – and barely gets a grilling about it. Her children, who speak for the first time in this documentary, deserve much more
Content: ‘Incomprehensible purposes’ … Lisa and her son Matthew.Photograph: Paul Levie/TNAView image in fullscreen‘Incomprehensible purposes’ … Lisa and her son Matthew.Photograph: Paul Levie/TNATV reviewTelevision & radioReviewLove You to Death review – is this all they asked the woman who faked her son’s illnesses?Lisa Hayden-Johnson was convicted of child cruelty, but she still insists that she didn’t do anything wrong – and barely gets a grilling about it. Her children, who speak for the first time in this documentary, deserve much moreLucy ManganWed 19 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s an increasingly common pattern emerging whereby documentary makers take a story that was run through the Outrage-A-Tron by the tabloids to produce headlines that warped public understanding (“Britain’s Worst/Most Evil/Most Deadly” and so on), then proceed to put back some of the lost nuance and present the more complicated original picture. Lucy Letby (“Britain’s Worst Child Killer”) has been the subject of at least two such films redressing the lost balance. Last week, the story of Rhianan Rudd (“Britain’s Youngest Terrorist”) was unpacked and its many sadder parts laid out for inspection inThe Schoolgirl Terrorist?In Love You to Death, it is the turn of Lisa Hayden-Johnson, who became known as “Britain’s Most Evil Mum” during her trial and conviction for child crueltyafter years spent fabricating her son Matthew’s apparent illnesses. He was put through more than 300 medical encounters, nine general anaesthetics, four operations by the age of nine, and endured many unnecessary constraints on his life, including using a wheelchair, feeding tube and oxygen tank, until Lisa was arrested when he was nine.Love You to Death interviews Lisa, Matthew and his older sister Laura – who has some memories of being “a trial run” for her mother’s fabrications but whose suffering is largely of the more indirect, but no less damaging, kind that comes with living in a household that revolves around an ill and disabled member, taking on caring responsibilities very young, then finding out that all of it existed only to serve another’s incomprehensible purposes.The documentary lays out the chronology first, from Matthew’s seven-week premature birth in 2001, through his early stays in hospital as Lisa insisted he was failing to thrive because he was allergic to so many foods. It goes on through his apparently accumulating conditions, his local fame as “the boy in the buggy” whom the community rallied to help, and Lisa’s insistence to their main clinician Dr Broomhall – not interviewed, though their local GP Dr Paul Johnson is – that Matthew be referred to Great Ormond Street for more thorough investigations. This was despite Broomhall’s reluctance and the increasing suspicions among ward staff that all was not well.View image in fullscreenLisa and Matthew at the Children of Courage Awards 2005.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyEventually Dr Stella Imong, who had many dealings with Matthew’s “quite demanding” mother on the ward and had noticed the increasing number of factors in his notes that weren’t quite tallying, confronted Dr Broomhall about the situation and the latter reported Lisa to the police. The working presumption was that Lisa was suffering from Munchausen’s syndrome by proxy (now known as fabricated or induced illness) and enjoying the attention gained by having a sick child.It is a glaring weakness of the programme that it does not probe further into the whys and wherefores of the medical establishment’s inertia here. Especially as GP Paul Johnson all but shuffles his feet in embarrassment as he describes how confrontation “before you’re sure” can damage doctors’ reputations and hurt anyone falsely accused of harming their child. There is also mention of nurses raising concerns much earlier than any were acted upon, and any astute viewer will surely have more questions than are answered. A film about medical ethics, arrogance, cowardice and self-protection could easily work here.But the emphasis is on Lisa and her enduring insistence – bar the occasional slight concessions – that she did nothing wrong. Matthew was ill, she says, and everything she did was to help him. The children have no contact with her now, which clearly upsets her, but there is no sign that she is willing – or perhaps able – to provide them with the acceptance of her condition and what she really did that they need to establish any kind of rapprochement. Another weakness is the lack of anything other than softball questions to Lisa. She is rarely pressed on any issue or incident and it feels like a dereliction of journalistic duty.Laura and Matthew talk about her with regret, mystification and – particularly in Laura’s case – a longing for her to accept responsibility for their suffering. They are a study in grace and compassion. They manage to see her as mentally ill rather than “evil”, despite their experience of life lived right on the border between those two states. They undoubtedly deserve better – from their mother, from the professionals involved with their childhoods, and this programme, which – though it valuably restores much of what the tabloids eschewed – fails on some of its own quite vital terms.Love You to Death is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionHealthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hogging weights, loud grunting and sweaty benches: 11 gym dos and don’ts from fitness experts | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Here’s what professionals have to say about good workout etiquette, from using equipment to being on your phone
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Here’s what professionals have to say about good workout etiquette, from using equipment to being on your phone
Content: ‘Respect the equipment, respect other people’s time and space, and respect the shared environment,’ says Mathew Forzaglia, a fitness professional.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Respect the equipment, respect other people’s time and space, and respect the shared environment,’ says Mathew Forzaglia, a fitness professional.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesWell actuallyHogging weights, loud grunting and sweaty benches: 11 gym dos and don’ts from fitness expertsHere’s what professionals have to say about good workout etiquette, from using equipment to being on your phoneMadeleine AggelerWed 19 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI like to think of myself as a fairly laid-back person. Other people’s behavior is not my business. There is one notable exception: my gym nemesis.He brings his computer to the gym and takes work conference calls at full volume. He has four to six pairs of dumbbells around him at all times – then doesn’t put them away. Intellectually I understand he is a fragile, flawed human like the rest of us, but in my gut I sometimes wonder if he arrived here from another galaxy.Life is full of unspoken rules, and the gym is no different. The heavy weights, sweaty people and mysterious machines can make it daunting to figure out how to behave. So we asked fitness experts for their thoughts on gym etiquette – their biggest pet peeves as well as the behaviors that might seem intimidating, but are actually fine.Good gym etiquette is less about following a long list of rules than it is simple respect, says Mathew Forzaglia, a fitness professional and educator. “Respect the equipment, respect other people’s time and space, and respect the shared environment,” he says.Gym no-nosDon’t leave a messWhether it’s leaving a bench covered in your sweat, or not re-racking weights after you use them, failing to clean and reset equipment after you use it is not only a hygiene issue, it’s potentially unsafe.Leaving out heavy plates or dumbbells “creates an accessibility issue for people who physically can’t move the weight someone else abandoned”, says Amanda Katz, a New York City-based personal trainer and run coach.As for wiping off your sweat, “it’s common courtesy and takes just a few seconds”, says Forzaglia. “No one wants to lie down on a bench covered in someone else’s sweat.”Don’t hoard equipmentIf you’re planning to do a complex circuit training routine that involves having access to six machines at once, save it for a home workout or tweak it to be more sequential.“You can’t claim the cable machineandthe leg pressandthree sets of dumbbells,” says Laura Girard, certified personal trainer, strength coach and founder of The Energy Academy in New York City. “Learn to share.”Don’t offer unsolicited adviceIt can feel intoxicating to think you know better than others. Spot someone across the gym doing deadlifts with what you think is bad form, and it might be tempting to go over and give them a few tips. Don’t.“Unless someone is in immediate danger, I don’t think it’s appropriate to offer coaching to strangers,” says Katz. Most of us are not fitness professionals, and even if we are, we don’t know why someone might be training the way they are. “There are countless reasons an exercise might look different than expected – from injury rehabilitation to a coach’s programming,” says Katz.Other people’s bodies and how they train them are not your business. “Never assume you know somebody’s goals or body better than they do,” says Girard.Don’t be loudWhether it’s playing your pump-up playlist sans headphones, grunting loudly through exercises – or, as I encountered in my gym just the other week, a man shouting “LET’S GO!” before every set of shoulder shrugs – being loud is not fair or pleasant for your fellow gym-goer.“Everyone deserves their own playlist and to not have their nervous system frayed by a random shout when they’re already doing something vulnerable and uncomfortable,” says Girard.Don’t scroll or talk on your phoneResting between sets is normal and fine – more on this later. But monopolizing a machine because you’re scrolling social media, answering emails or taking calls is not.“The gym is for training,” says Forzaglia. “If you need to catch up on your phone, step outside for a minute.”Don’t show up late to a group class“I understand that life happens and sometimes you’re running late,” says Jessie Diaz-Herrera, co-founder and fitness instructor at Power Plus Wellness in New York City. But walking into a class 15 or 20 minutes late can be extremely disruptive to other participants, and potentially present a safety issue “if the instructor has already gone through the warm-up or explained the movements”, she says.Gym OKsDo talk to peopleWhile unsolicited advice is never welcome, this doesn’t mean you have to completely ignore other people at the gym.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Most people at the gym are either also new, or love the gym and would be happy to chat your ear off,” says Girard. As long as you don’t interrupt someone in the middle of a set, Girard says it’s “totally OK to approach for a quick form check or help with equipment”. (But wait for a go-ahead or an invitation from them to strike up a longer conversation.)It’s also fine to politely ask someone how many sets they have left, or if you can work in between their sets, says Forzaglia.“Most experienced gym-goers appreciate respectful communication,” he says. “I’d much rather someone ask than stand around waiting or skip an exercise because they felt uncomfortable speaking up.”Do rest between setsAlthough you shouldn’t disappear into your phone for long stretches, resting on or around equipment for a minute or two between sets of exercise is normal and expected.“Rest is part of strength training and Hiit protocols, and most people understand that,” says Katz. “You don’t need to rush through your workout to look like you belong or keep your heart rate up unless it’s the intention of the session.”Do use whatever equipment you needThere is no hierarchy that gives one gym member a greater right to equipment than another, whether in terms of experience or ability.Very difficult and extremely cool: how to start doing pull-upsRead more“You are no less deserving of a squat rack because you’re only squatting the bar,” says Girard.Be a good neighbor and share space and equipment, Girard says, but don’t shut yourself out because you don’t think you’re advanced enough.Do record yourself if you want toRecording your workout is not inherently rude, says Diaz-Herrera. “A lot of people use videos to check their form, track their progress or create content,” she says. The important thing is to not intentionally film others.If you think you might be in someone’s video and don’t want to be, Diaz-Herrera says it’s absolutely OK to ask whether you appear in frame, and if they mind moving the camera or cropping you out. “That’s not being difficult or making a big deal out of it,” she says. “It’s just communicating and respecting each other’s space.”Do change gyms if you need toIf you don’t feel comfortable in a particular gym or fitness class, find another one.“Remember not every space is the right fit and that’s OK,” says Katz. “A welcoming environment can make all the difference, so give yourself an opportunity to try another gym, class or community until you find one where you feel supported.”And if the gym in general isn’t for you, that’s also fine.“You don’t need to go to the gym to make fitness part of your life,” says Girard. “The gym is just a space where equipment lives, and it’s totally optional.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyFitnessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 16: Manchester United | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans will be key to Michael Carrick’s chances of success over a full season and of healing the rift between club and fans
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans will be key to Michael Carrick’s chances of success over a full season and of healing the rift between club and fans
Content: Bruno Fernandes of Manchester United in action during a pre-season friendly match against Paris Saint-Germain. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesBruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans will be key to Michael Carrick’s chances of success over a full season and of healing the rift between club and fansByJamie JacksonWed 19 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:5th (NB: this is not necessarily Jamie Jackson’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:3rdProspectsThe information at the start of the close season was thatManchester Unitedplanned to trade for bargains rather than elite names and the major purchases so far this summer prove this to indeed be the case. Youri Tielemans is a 29-year-old who has been a professional for nearly half of his life and was bought, with no competition, for his £35m release clause from Aston Villa. The midfielder was followed by the £48m (+£2m) purchase of Andrey Santos, a 22-year-old with 11 league starts last season for Chelsea. The Brazilian states a preference for operating “deep, like a No 6” making him the direct replacement for his compatriot Casemiro, whose CV includes five Champions Leagues. United are also set to sign another midfielder in Carlos Baleba from Brighton for around £75m.Michael Carrick, going in to his first full season in charge, admits his squad needs more additions and a new left-back is on the radar. Lewis Hall is the prime target but Newcastle’s resistance to a sale means Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly had drawn interest. At the window’s commencement, Carrick wanted Elliot Anderson but this was unrealistic – he went to City for around £32m more than Tielemans’ and Santos’s combined fee. Confirmed as manager in May after guiding United to third, Carrick may rue Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s reluctance to invest the finances he generated by taking the club back into the Champions League and the 45-year-old may find himself engulfed in precisely what has plagued all of his predecessors in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era: a crisis of performances and results.Carrick also has to wrestle with the Marcus Rashford situation: the forward wants to leave, the club desires him off the wage bill, but can a suitor be found before 1 September? Oh and, Lisandro Martínez and Matthijs De Ligt, two frontline centre-backs, have only recently returned from injury.Graphic of Manchester United’s league finishesOff-field pictureIn early July United unveiled plans for theirproposed new 100,000-seater stadium, located about 350 metres north-west of Old Trafford, insisting this is a “sanity, not vanity project”. Behind the catchy line, however, is a club in the red to the sum of £1.3bn. Omar Berrada, United’s chief executive, declared in March that £2bn was the working cost of the stadium, which is projected to be completed in 2035. This seems optimistic – try doubling it, maybe.Owner-fan relationshipUntrusting, unhappy, annoyed, betrayed, toxic, broken, unmendable, etcetera: choose your pejorative when it comes to describing how most Manchester United fans feel about the Glazers. This has been the case regarding the six siblings, who are United’s majority owners, since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club in May 2013. Relations between fans and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s football department could also be rosier. Some are content due to last season’s third-place finish and the success of last summer’s buys – Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbuemo primarily. Others, though, are cheesed off about the current window’s business, the moving of season-ticket holders around the ground to free up seats for corporate packages, and therecent bid to eliminate toutsthat caused many genuine supporters to have to prove their innocence.The managerLike Ole Gunnar Solskjær before him, Carrick performed superbly in a caretaker capacity. The task now facing him is out-performing his former United team-mate and friend in the role of permanent manager, the Norwegian’s first full season in charge having ended in third place. Carrick’s prospects will be improved if by 1 September a left-back has been recruited. Given Arsenal, Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham have splashed far more cash than United on strengthening this summer, Carrick would no doubt take third – or any Champions League berth – if it was offered to him, albeit he is unlikely to admit as much.Star signingView image in fullscreenManchester United’s new midfield signing Youri Tielemans in action during a training session in Dublin.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesAfter being a major part of Aston Villa’s Europa League glory in May, and then captaining Belgium to the World Cup quarter-finals during the summer, Tielemans has been recruited to add drive, quality and a streetwisen touch to United’s midfield. His career shows a record of making the difference when required – he struck a memorable volley against Freiburg in Istanbul and powered in a long-range winner to claim the FA Cup for Leicester in 2021. There is no doubt about it – the son of Flemish Brabant is a big-game footballer.Stat attackManchester United led thePremier Leaguefor shots last season, with 596. Much will depend upon Bruno Fernandes if they are to repeat this feat. He created at least 89 chances more than any other member of the squad and only fell six shy of taking the most shots. Fernandes turns 32 in early September; can he outrun age for another season?Manchester United shots and chances graphicSet for a breakthroughShea Lacey, the quick-footed diminutive winger from Liverpool, made four appearances under three different managers last season. On 21 December, an 84th-minute debut in the 2-1 loss at Aston Villa under Ruben Amorim made him academy product No 256 to feature for United. Eighteen days later, entering again on 84 minutes in the 2-2 draw at Burnley, Lacey’s next cameo was for Darren Fletcher. Fast-forward four days and Lacey lasted only 27 minutes of United’s 2-1 defeat to Brighton in the FA Cup after being sent off late on, later apologising. The 19-year-old had to wait five months before making his next appearance for United, this time under Carrick, entering in the 62nd minute of the final-day 3-0 victory at Brighton. He is now very much part of the first-team squad and one to watch.World Cup impactWhen England needed to stymie Argentina’s second-half onslaught in last month’s World Cup semi-final, with Anthony Gordon having put them 1-0 up, Thomas Tuchel became passive. Off went Gordon and Declan Rice and on came Ezri Konza and Nico O’Reilly. England subsequently crumpled, going on to lose 2-1. If Tuchel had instead turned to Kobbie Mainoo, a ball-carrying midfielder who could retain possession and move England up the field, Argentina may well have been thwarted. As it turned out, Mainoo did not play a second of the tournament. “I was in contact with him quite a bit through the summer [as] I’ve been in that position myself and not played at a World Cup,” Carrick said.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Manchester UnitedPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Açaí, chipotle and gnocchi – and other words you are probably mispronouncing | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The English language can seem designed to trip us up, whether we’re greeting a colonel or travelling to Worcestershire. Here are some of the biggest stumbling blocks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The English language can seem designed to trip us up, whether we’re greeting a colonel or travelling to Worcestershire. Here are some of the biggest stumbling blocks
Content: Berry, berry hard to say … an açaí bowl with fresh fruits.Photograph: Alexander Spatari/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBerry, berry hard to say … an açaí bowl with fresh fruits.Photograph: Alexander Spatari/Getty ImagesPass notesLife and styleAçaí, chipotle and gnocchi – and other words you are probably mispronouncingThe English language can seem designed to trip us up, whether we’re greeting a colonel or travelling to Worcestershire. Here are some of the biggest stumbling blocksWed 19 Aug 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Açaí.Age:First imported to western countries from South America as freeze-dried pulp in the 1990s.Appearance:A small, dark-purple berry, or a purée made from them, commonly used in smoothies.Ithas bits coming off it.Sorry?There’s a sort of chin whisker hanging from the“c”and something weird is going on with the dot over the“i”.Those are accents, designed to help you pronounce the word correctly.They’re no help to me.That could explain why açaí is the most mispronounced word in the UK, often rendered in speech as “ack-eye” or “ah-sigh”.How should I be saying it?“Ah-sigh-ee”.Seriously?Açaí is just the tip of the iceberg. It tops a new list of 20 commonly mispronounced words.What are some others?Quinoa came fourth; gnocchi came fifth; chipotle was seventh.Are you sure this isn’t a list of Britain’s least-ordered menu items?Not all the words on the list are foods. Segue, often mispronounced “seeg” instead of “segway”, was second. Worcestershire came sixth.What? Knowing how to pronounce Worcestershireisthe only advantage Britons have over the rest of the world.Those days are over.Who came up with this list?It’s from a recent poll of 2,000 people commissioned by Škoda.Why would a Czech car company care how I pronounce chipotle?I think it is trying to make a point because Škoda is often mispronounced as “scoder” rather than “shkoda”. And, obviously, it’s a publicity thing.DoesŠkoda think it’s good publicity to humiliatea country?Beneath the confusion over imported foodstuffs and the never-ending debate about how to say gif, it does seem that an identity crisis is unfolding.What do you mean?People in Britain have forgotten that some of their peculiar pronunciations make English a nightmare for foreigners.Can you give me an example?The word colonel came 15th in the poll. Some British people think it’s pronounced as it is spelt, when it should be pronounced “kernel”, which isn’t how it is spelt.Ludicrous.Likewise, some of those polled mistakenly pronounced “squirrel” as a single-syllable word to rhyme with “girl”, instead of a two-syllable word that doesn’t rhyme with anything.I’m sure we can find something it rhymes with.Good luck with your search.I have one more, slightly embarrassing question…It’s pronounced “chi-poht-lay”.Do say:“There once was a man from Wirral/ who woke up in bed with a squirrel …”Don’t say:“Do you have any blueberries?”Explore more on these topicsLife and stylePass notesSpoken wordLinguisticsEnglish and creative writingLanguageShareReuse this content

title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy sacks senior aide amid Ukraine corruption crisis | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Presidential deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra dismissed day after former defence minister called for wartime election
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Presidential deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra dismissed day after former defence minister called for wartime election
Content: No official reason was given for the sacking of Iryna Mudra, a presidential deputy chief of staff.Photograph: Raj Valley/AlamyView image in fullscreenNo official reason was given for the sacking of Iryna Mudra, a presidential deputy chief of staff.Photograph: Raj Valley/AlamyUkraineVolodymyr Zelenskyy sacks senior aide amid Ukraine corruption crisisPresidential deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra dismissed day after former defence minister called for wartime electionDan Sabbaghin KyivWed 19 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has fired a senior aide amid a fresh corruption investigation – one day after a former defence minister warned the country was facing “a crisis of governance” andneeded to hold a wartime presidential election.Iryna Mudra, a presidential deputy chief of staff, was dismissed by decree after multiple reports in Ukrainian media that her house was being searched by officials investigating an alleged money-laundering scheme.Sacking turns former Zelenskyy loyalist into potent political opponentRead moreNo official reason was given for Mudra’s sacking as Zelenskyy sought to carry on as normal, despite Mykhailo Fedorov’s surprise call for an early presidential election in a video address released late on Tuesday.The president did not directly address the ousted minister’s accusations or his election demand in his initial public statements, though he did thank Ukraine’s parliament for voting to confirm Fedorov’s replacement, Yevhen Khmara, in the post.At the heart of Fedorov’s argument were accusations that corruption remained widespread under Zelenskyy and that the president had failed to get a grip. “Corruption is only a symptom. The main problem runs much deeper. We have a systemic crisis of governance,” Fedorov had said.View image in fullscreenMykhailo Fedorov has become the first major public figure to call for an election, effectively posing a direct challenge to the sitting president.Photograph: Efrem Lukatsky/APThe removal of Fedorov from his post in July triggered the mostsignificant street protests in Ukrainesince the war began.Fedorov is now considering visiting the US, possibly as soon as next week, in an apparent effort to win over American support. In the past, the US president, Donald Trump, has called for Ukraine to hold elections, though his comments were made at a time when his relationship with Zelenskyy was strained.Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Fedorov became the first major public figure to call for a presidential poll, effectively posing a direct challenge to the sitting president.“Can Russia effectively be given the right to dictate when Ukrainians can choose their government again? I am convinced that the answer is no,” Fedorov said in a nine-minute video address released on social media late on Tuesday.Zelenskyy’s term notionally expired in spring 2024, but an election during wartime is prohibited by the constitution, and had anyway been considered by most Ukrainians to be impractical and potentially divisive while Russia continues to attack on a daily basis.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy has not directly addressed Mykhailo Fedorov’s accusations of widespread corruption.Photograph: Oleksandr Magula/Suspilne Ukraine/JSC “UA:PBC”/Global Images Ukraine/Getty ImagesThe Nabu anti-corruption agency said it was conducting a special operation to expose what it said was a criminal conspiracy that involved “the participation of high-ranking officials from the office of the president” and several others.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt released a video saying those involved included a deputy head of the president’s office, a serving MP and a former MP, as well as the CEO and supervisory board head at a state-owned bank, though none were named.Nabu added that the group was accused of laundering 150m hryvinas (£2.5m) through the state-owned bank in order to post bail in June for the former energy minister Herman Haluschenko, himself facing anti-corruption charges.Haluschenko is a defendant inthe high-profile Midas corruption case, alongside the businessman Timur Mindich, who has fled the country. Mindich is a former associate of the president and former co-owner of the TV production company Kvartal 95, co-founded by Zelenskyy in the years before he went into politics.Mindich is accused of orchestrating a large-scale corruption schemethat was uncovered last Novemberin which kickbacks were demanded from companies seeking to supply the country’s state-owned nuclear power generator Energoatom.The scandal damaged Zelenskyy’s credibility. A fortnight later, his then chief aide,Andriy Yermak, resignedafter anti-corruption investigators searched his home. He was thenarrested in Mayon suspicion of money laundering. Yermak’s lawyer has dismissed the allegations as “baseless”. Mindich, who fled to Israel, also denies wrongdoing.Later on Wednesday, Zelenskyy presented 25 certificates giving housing to decorated veterans and their families. The president said Ukraine was a country that honoured its heroes and emphasised it was important to be thankful to its bravest troops.“Gratitude is what should accompany respect. It must be an integral part of a normal state, a normal society and normal people,” the president said. It was perhaps the closest he had come all day to making a comment of any kind on the crisis.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Couple who died with their daughter off Sussex coast named by police | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Officers still investigating deaths of Zeina Alayn, Hassan El-Khawas and daughter Sara El-Khawas at Shoreham-by-Sea
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Officers still investigating deaths of Zeina Alayn, Hassan El-Khawas and daughter Sara El-Khawas at Shoreham-by-Sea
Content: Hassan El-Khawas, his partner Zeina Alayn, and their 14-year-old daughter Sara El-Khawas.Photograph: Al-Arab in UKView image in fullscreenHassan El-Khawas, his partner Zeina Alayn, and their 14-year-old daughter Sara El-Khawas.Photograph: Al-Arab in UKWest SussexCouple who died with their daughter off Sussex coast named by policeOfficers still investigating deaths of Zeina Alayn, Hassan El-Khawas and daughter Sara El-Khawas at Shoreham-by-SeaMatthew WeaverWed 19 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 08.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA father, mother and their teenage daughter who died off the Sussex coast on Tuesday have been identified.Sussex police named the victims as Hassan El-Khawas, 55, his partner, Zeina Alayn, 37, and their 14-year-old daughter, Sara El-Khawas. A younger girl who was also part of the family is in hospital in a critical condition. She has not been named.The Palestinian embassy in London said El-Khawas was a British man of Palestinian descent.Police, paramedics, coastguard crews and a lifeboat attended the scene at Shoreham-by-Sea, where four people were pulled from the water.Sussex police said the cause of the tragedy was still being investigated. It could not confirm reports that the older girl got caught in a fishing net.The force said in a statement: “Following review of CCTV footage and initial witness accounts, the current hypothesis is that this was a tragic accident, with no third-party involvement.”Adnan Hmidan, the chair of the Palestinian Forum in Britain, said: “According to the information available to us, the family encountered strong currents while at sea. Their daughter, Sara, became caught in a fishing net and her father attempted to help free her.“As the waves and currents intensified, her mother, Zeina, also entered the water to try to save them, followed by their younger daughter.”View image in fullscreenA woman lays flowers in memory of the three family members on the beach at Shoreham-by-Sea.Photograph: Yui Mok/PATwo other children from the family were in the care of their paternal uncle, he said.“The Khawas family are British citizens of Palestinian origin, with roots in Rashidieh refugee camp in Lebanon,” he said. “Like many Palestinian families, members of their extended family have lived in Britain for many years and have built a strong and close-knit community here.“Our thoughts and prayers are with the entire family, particularly the children, who are facing an unimaginable loss. We ask everyone to respect their privacy and dignity at this painful time.”Andy Burnham said the incident was “a terrible family tragedy” and a reminder of the dangers of open water swimming.There was a huge emergency service response tothe incident on Tuesdayafternoon, when police were told four people had got into difficulty in the water.Sussex police said they believed all four entered the water to swim. Ch Supt James Collis confirmed that a man, woman and a teenage girl had died at the scene.View image in fullscreenTwo air ambulance helicopters and a critical care team were sent to the scene and Shoreham RNLI said its lifeboat had been called out at 3pm.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAAsked if the government needed to do more on water safety, Burnham said: “Always. It’s so sad to hear what happened yesterday, and obviously we think there’s a young girl still in the hospital fighting for her life, and we send our best wishes and love to wider friends and family. But a real tragedy, a real terrible family tragedy.”Speaking on a visit to north-east England, Burnham added: “Obviously, we will look in detail at what happened. The thing I can say today, and there is still, I think, a further heatwave to come in this summer period, it is just to remind people about the dangers of open-water swimming. The coldness, even when it feels hot outside, it can shock people, and that can cause the difficulties. So people just need to remember that at all times.”Two air ambulance helicopters and a critical care team were sent to the scene and Shoreham RNLI said its lifeboat had been called out at 3pm.Burnham paid tribute to those who tried to save the family. “I do need to praise the emergency services, who I know were on scene very quickly yesterday. They’ve had a busy summer, but they were there, and we thank them. As I say, just huge sympathy to the friends and the family,” he said.View image in fullscreenA note left among the floral tributes on Shoreham-by-Sea beach.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThere have been a series of water-related deaths across the country in a summer of record-breaking heat. On Saturday, a 12-year-old boy drowned in the River Lea, near Hackney Marshes in north-east London.In April, a woman and her young child died after getting into difficulty in the water in west London. Both died at the scene in Elthorne Park, Ealing, the Metropolitan police said. There have been at least 35 drowning deaths, including eight in July, according to astudy by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.Joss Loader, the chair of Shoreham Beach Residents’ Association, said: “There’s just a really strong sense of shock, obviously people are really concerned for the young girl. A small, tightly knit community with a very deep sense of shock and that sense of disbelief you get after a tragedy because it has come out of nowhere.”Shoreham beach is a spit of land with water on three sides from the River Adur, the estuary and the sea, and Loader said she understood the “tragic events” had happened in the estuary.“It’s school holidays and we have had a wonderful summer so the beaches have been packed with families,” she said. “People swim from those beaches even in the winter, generally it is considered as safe as the sea can be. You wouldn’t be swimming there and think you were taking a risk.”Anna Peacock, 81, who lives near Kingston beach across the water from Shoreham Fort, said emergency services were on the scene very quickly.“People come down to swim, particularly in the summertime and I don’t think they realise there’s a riptide along here,” she said. “It’s very inviting to come to the sea, but the tide could carry you out in seconds, and I don’t think people have realised that.”Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel admits its soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killed | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Military orders criminal investigation into deaths of five-year-old and six family members in Gaza in 2024
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Military orders criminal investigation into deaths of five-year-old and six family members in Gaza in 2024
Content: Hind Rajab died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent in which she pleaded for rescue.Photograph: Family Handout/APView image in fullscreenHind Rajab died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent in which she pleaded for rescue.Photograph: Family Handout/APGazaIsrael admits its soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killedMilitary orders criminal investigation into deaths of five-year-old and six family members in Gaza in 2024Jason BurkeWed 19 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Israeli military admitted on Wednesday its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing.The killing of Hind and her family was one of the most high profile of a series of incidents involving civilian casualties during the first months of theGazaconflict which prompted international outrage.Hind died aftera desperate three-hour phone callto the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as the family sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) repeatedly denied its troops had been present in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.View image in fullscreenA child looks at the car in which Hind Rajab died in January 2024.Photograph: ReutersPalestinian paramedics dispatched an ambulance to rescue Hind and stayed on the line until contact was lost, but the ambulance too came under fire, killing two medics. The bodies of the casualties were only retrieved 12 days later when Israeli troops withdrew. The IDF also admitted Wednesday that troops had fired on the ambulance.“Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of thePalestineRed Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by military police criminal investigation division,” the military said on Wednesday.Criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.The IDF published reviews on Wednesday into four other high-profile incidents in Gaza, saying it was launching a criminal investigation into the killing in near the southern city of Rafah of15 Palestinian medics and humanitarian personnelin March 2025.0:14Recording of Hind Rajab and phone operator – audioTroops lying in ambush for Hamas militants initially shot at an ambulance that was trying to retrieve casualties from an Israeli offensive, then fired on a series of emergency vehicles which approached their positions, according to phone footage and the sole survivor of the shootings.The soldiers then bulldozed over the bodies and vehicles, burying them in a mass grave. UN and rescue workers were only able to reach the site a week later.“They were killed in their uniforms. Driving their clearly marked vehicles. Wearing their gloves. On their way to save lives. This should never have happened,” said Jonathan Whittall, a UN official who helped recover the bodies.The Israeli military initially said it had opened fire because the vehicles were “advancing suspiciously” without headlights or emergency signals. But it backtracked from that account after footage emerged showing the Red Crescent and civil defence teams driving slowly with their emergency vehicle lights flashing and logos visible.View image in fullscreenRed Crescent paramedics arrive at the mass grave where their colleagues bodies were buried.Photograph: OCHA/Red CrescentMunther Abed, a Palestinian paramedic who was present at the incident in which 15 of his colleagues were killed, said he hoped “those who killed ⁠my colleagues, who were like family to me, face justice, real justice”. “I want to say to the whole world, ambulances 101 ​is not a target and they must be protected,” he said referring ​to the speed dial number for the Red Crescent service ​in Gaza.The IDF said it had decided not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of World Central Kitchen vehicles, killing seven humanitarian workers from the US-based aid group, which has distributed food in Gaza throughout the war.The aid group said at the time it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars. The vehicles, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air, were left incinerated and mangled, indicating a series of targeted strikes.View image in fullscreenOne of the World Central Kitchen vehicles hit by an Israeli airstrikePhotograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThe IDF said on Wednesday it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the convoy deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.One of those killed in the strike wasAustralian aid worker Zomi Frankcom. The Australian government has called the deaths a “tragedy and an outrage” and pressed for full accountability and “any appropriate criminal charges”. In February this year the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had made it clear to Israel and its president, Isaac Herzog, that there be transparency about Israel’s then-ongoing investigation into the incident.In April this year Australia’s foreign minister Penny Wongpaid tribute to Frankcomon the second anniversary of her death, saying “people like Zomi are rare and their selflessness should not only be celebrated but protected”.World Central Kitchen said it strongly disagreed with Israeli officials’ account of the airstrikes and their decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.“At the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody. It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”The military also decided not to take criminal action over the killing of four humanitarian workers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. Israel later effectively barred the medical charity from operating in Gaza.Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din, an Israeli rights organisation, said that over the last decade only a tiny proportion of investigations had led to indictments while growing political pressure “further deters Israeli ⁠law-enforcement authorities from holding those responsible accountable, even when clear evidence does exist”.A UN reportpublished in February described “a pervasive climate of impunity” by Israel in occupied Palestine “in relation to gross violations of international human rights law and serious violations of international humanitarian law … some constituting war crimes and possibly other international crimes”.Israeli forces say they never deliberately target civilians in Gaza and accuse Hamas of using civilians to shield its militants.The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law, it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”. “For more than a thousand days, the IDF has been conducting intensive combat across numerous fronts, carrying out a wide range of military missions in an exceptionally complex operational reality,” it said in a statement.The war began in October 2023 when Hamas launched a surprise attack into southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and abducting 250. Israel’s ensuing offensives in Gaza have killed more than 73,000, mostly women and children, including more than 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October.On Wednesday, ⁠Israeli airstrikes killed ⁠seven Palestinians. Israeli military officials told local media one strike that killed sixhad targeted a meeting of Hamas commandersin Gaza City.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsraelIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Taxpayers to fund clear-up of illegal dumps in West Yorkshire, Surrey and Kent  | Waste | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham promises drive to tackle toxic waste, raise fines and use AI-powered drones to detect illegal activity
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Andy Burnham promises drive to tackle toxic waste, raise fines and use AI-powered drones to detect illegal activity
Content: Hundreds of illegal waste sites have been reported across England, including 11 ‘supersites’ which contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHundreds of illegal waste sites have been reported across England, including 11 ‘supersites’ which contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianWasteTaxpayers to fund clear-up of illegal dumps in West Yorkshire, Surrey and KentAndy Burnham promises drive to tackle toxic waste, raise fines and use AI-powered drones to detect illegal activityKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 19 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIllegal dumps inWest Yorkshire, Surrey and Kent will be cleared up using taxpayer money, Andy Burnham has announced, as the prime minister promises a new drive to tackle toxic waste.Ministers have identified dumps in Bradford, Runnymede and the Isle of Sheppey, which collectively contain about 22,000 tonnes of illegal waste, to be cleared in the next phase of the government’s national clear-up effort.Meanwhile, fines will be raised for rogue dumpers, and AI-powered drones will be used to detect illegal activity while it happens, as the government looks to prioritise prevention alongside clean-up efforts.Burnham said in a statement: “These toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long. I said we would clean them up – and that’s exactly what we’re announcing today.”He added: “These mountains of rubbish have been a clear sign to communities that politics hasn’t been working for them or their area. This government is going to tackle the issues that have been ignored by Westminster for too long and bring back hope.”Hundreds of illegal waste sites have been reported across England, with a BBC investigationrecently uncovering11 “supersites” that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish.One of the country’s most notorious sites is in Burnham’s own constituency of Makerfield, where a rotting, rat-infested mountain of waste has remained for more than 20 months. The site was identified for clean-up in March alongside two others, but locals say they have seen little improvement in the site since then.During the byelection campaign, which Burnham won earlier this year, voters in the areatold the Guardianthey would vote for him specifically to get rid of that one site.The Environment Agency says it has made 42 site visits, suspended or revoked 17 permits and launched more than 30 criminal investigations as part of its initial crackdown.In February, Varun Datta, the ringleader of a waste crime gang,was orderedto pay £1.4m after being convicted for the organised illegal dumping of mostly municipal waste at a network of 16 sites across the country, including at a historic manor house and a nature reserve in Lancashire.Downing Street said the three new sites identified on Wednesday had been chosen because of their scale, the risk to nearby communities, their environmental damage, and links to organised crime.Officials said the new push to prevent illegal dumping would work better than previous approaches, in part because of new AI-powered drones which are designed to detect dumping while it happens.The 33 drones will be fitted with light detection and ranging technology, which can create highly detailed maps of illegal waste sites.Burnham also said he wanted police and the NationalCrimeAgency to be given a bigger role, as he announced fines for people who dump waste illegally or fail to treat it correctly would rise from £300 to £5,000.Tougher sanctions, including imprisonment, are already available for more serious offences.Meanwhile, in West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester mayors and council leaders will be asked to coordinate councils, police, regulators and other enforcement agencies to ramp up crime prevention efforts.Explore more on these topicsWasteEnglandKentSurreyWest YorkshireAndy BurnhamPollutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zuckerberg lied about concern for child safety, Meta whistleblower testifies at landmark trial | Meta | The Guardian
description: Arturo Béjar, former Meta safety engineer, tells jury tech company was aware of products’ potential harm to children
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Arturo Béjar, former Meta safety engineer, tells jury tech company was aware of products’ potential harm to children
Content: Arturo Béjar, a former Facebook safety engineer and Instagram consultant, arrives at court in Oakland, California, on Wednesday.Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/ReutersView image in fullscreenArturo Béjar, a former Facebook safety engineer and Instagram consultant, arrives at court in Oakland, California, on Wednesday.Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/ReutersMetaZuckerberg lied about concern for child safety, Meta whistleblower testifies at landmark trialArturo Béjar, former Meta safety engineer, tells jury tech company was aware of products’ potential harm to childrenDara KerrWed 19 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMetahas taken a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its social media platforms, according to awhistleblowerwho testified during alandmark trialagainst the company on Tuesday and Wednesday.Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer, told the jury that the company was aware of the harm its products caused children, which included its recommendations pushing content from sexual predators and violent and graphic images. He said he repeatedly raised the issue to various Facebook and Instagram executives but that they did little to resolve it.In his testimony, Béjar said his job often included him briefing Meta’s CEO,Mark Zuckerberg, on product issues. He estimated that he spoke to the CEO at least 100 times. One email Béjar sent to Zuckerberg in 2021 showed the engineer warning of constant reports of harmful content and damage to teenage wellbeing on Facebook and Instagram. Béjar said he emailed Zuckerberg after the CEO publicly said the company doesn’t prioritize profit over safety.“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar testified.US states accuse Meta of covering up research on teen social media addiction in pivotal trialRead moreBéjar added that he sent those reports directly to Zuckerberg because, “in my experience, when Mark makes something a priority, mountains move”.“Did he ever respond to you?” the attorney representing the government asked.“No,” Béjar replied. “I didn’t hear back from him.”Béjar was the first witness called to the stand in the federal trial that started with opening statements on Tuesday.The casewas brought against Meta by 29 US state attorneys general, who allege the social media company deliberately designed addictive products that lured in young people and led to them being harmed. The legal officials also claim the trillion-dollar company regularly collects data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws.“I heard from many of you at jury selection that the health and wellbeing of kids is a shared responsibility,” said Megan O’Neill, deputy attorney general forCalifornia, in her opening statements. “Meta didn’t do its share.”Other witnesses to be called include Zuckerberg and Instagram’s CEO, Adam Mosseri, along with other executives and experts on children’s mental health and addiction. Reams of Meta’s internal documents and emails have also been released as evidence.The trial, which is taking place in Oakland,California, is expected to last at least six weeks.Meta denies all allegations in the case. Paul Schmidt, an attorney forMeta, said in his opening statements that there was “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but that Meta had “come up with tools to try and address that”. He added the company did not allow children under the age of 13 to register for accounts on its social networks and that it had disabled more than 1m accounts of those young users.The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for Meta. If the company is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The lawmakers are also asking that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which could have lasting effects on the company’s business model.Whistleblower testimonyDuring his two days on the stand, Béjar spoke about his research on harm to children as well as Meta’s reliance on advertising to make money. He said features like infinite scroll, which have been described as keeping users glued to social networks, had been a boon for Meta.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“On scroll, the more views you have, the more ads you sell, the more revenue you make,” Béjar testified.The safety engineer worked in senior positions for Meta for about eight years, in two separate stints, and has been an outspoken critic of the company’s child wellbeing practices since leaving in 2021. He has testified before a US Senate committee and has served as a witness in other social media cases that involve harm to children.One of his motivations for first tackling the issue inside the company was seeing how his own teenage daughter was treated on Instagram. He said she received unwanted sexual advances and photos of male genitals as well as misogynistic insults. Later, she told her father that reporting these abuses through Instagram’s established processes was either ineffective or not possible.Béjar said that he started conducting surveys of teen’s experiences on Instagram. He found that 51% of users said “yes” to having had bad or harmful experiences within the previous seven days. Of those users, the content was taken down only 0.02% of the time, according to his testimony.Béjar said he sent those findings to Meta’s top executives, including Zuckerberg and Mosseri.In a quick back-and-forth, the lawyer for Meta tried to downplay Béjar’s testimony. He highlighted the engineer’s good working relationship with both the company and its leadership, asking questions like: “You had the support of Mr Zuckerberg?”, “You did not leave on bad terms?” and “You’re still proud of the work you did at Meta?”To all, Béjar answered: “Yes.”Explore more on these topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergInternet safetyChildrenMental healthSocial mediaDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Young vapers ‘at risk of breathing problems and becoming smokers’ | Vaping | The Guardian
description: Review by paediatricians links child vaping with poor respiratory health such as coughing, wheezing and asthma
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Review by paediatricians links child vaping with poor respiratory health such as coughing, wheezing and asthma
Content: Health experts are ‘extremely concerned’ about  the harmful effects of e-cigarettes on millions of teenagers and young people around the world.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenHealth experts are ‘extremely concerned’ about  the harmful effects of e-cigarettes on millions of teenagers and young people around the world.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAVapingYoung vapers ‘at risk of breathing problems and becoming smokers’Review by paediatricians links child vaping with poor respiratory health such as coughing, wheezing and asthmaRachel HallWed 19 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung people who start vaping risk developing breathing problems and going on to smoke cigarettes, children’s doctors have warned.Child vaping is consistently linked with poor respiratory health, such as coughing, wheezing, bronchitis symptoms and asthma exacerbations, while vapes have been shown to act as a gateway to smoking cigarettes, according to one of the most comprehensive reviews of the available evidence so far undertaken by the Royal College of Child and Paediatrics Health.The review’s co-author, Prof Will Carroll, said: “Vaping should not be seen as a harmless part of growing up. The evidence shows clear links with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking, while concerns about wider impacts on young people’s health continue to grow.”He urged the government to quickly implement thenew measures announced in Julyunder theTobacco and Vapes Act, which include plain packaging, moving vapes out of sight in shops, and restrictions on vape flavour names to move away from names inspired by sweets, desserts and alcohol in favour of simpler names such as “apple”.Carroll also called on the government to go further, including by limiting the number of flavours available.View image in fullscreenThe government is urged to implement measures such as plain packaging and moving vapes out of sight in shops.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianVaping has surged in popularity over the past decade, with rates of experimentation and regular use among young people increasing about tenfold, and use often beginning in adolescence.
