An estimatedone in fiveof 11-17-year-olds in Britain have tried vaping.Cardiologists, researchers and health experts have said they are“extremely concerned” about the harmful effectsof e-cigarettes on millions of teenagers and young people around the world, including exposure to toxins and carcinogens.The review, which is published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood and looked at 14,000 published articles and 81 studies, also identified evidence linking vaping to poor oral and dental health, including inflammation, ulcers and dry mouths; and negative mental health outcomes, such as anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation.Emerging evidence indicated potential impacts on sleep, eye health and allergies, and adverse outcomes associated with infants and babies exposed to nicotine during pregnancy.The RCPCH vice-president for policy, Dr Mike McKean, said that as vaping was a relatively new product, “there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people”.He added: “But a clear and concerning picture is emerging. Continued research and monitoring essential if we are to properly understand the risks and respond to emerging evidence.“The Tobacco and Vapes Act is an important step towards protecting children from nicotine addiction, but it must not be seen as a one-and-done solution. We need to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market and continue to take action to protect children from nicotine products that are deliberately made and marketed to appeal to them.”View image in fullscreenRegular vaping has increased about tenfold among young people in the last decade.Photograph: Justin Case/Getty ImagesAndrew McCracken, the director of external affairs at Asthma + Lung UK, called for more research on the impact of vaping, and a quicker response from policymakers to protect children’s lungs, which he said were “paying the price” for vape manufacturers’ targeting through products designed to look and taste like sweets.“Urgent action is needed to stop the brazen marketing of vapes to children. Vapes can play an important role for current smokers looking to quit, but anyone who doesn’t smoke shouldn’t vape, and that is especially true for children,” he said.“More research on the impact of vaping is needed, and as our understanding develops, policymakers need to be ready to adapt and put in place measures to protect people’s lungs.”Hazel Cheeseman, the chief executive of Action onSmokingand Health, said that regulations to restrict the promotion of vapes to children should not make it difficult for adult smokers to access vapes to help them quit. “As it was with tobacco, strong controls on marketing and promotion will be key to reducing youth vaping,” she said.A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Children should never vape and this evidence shows just some of the risks associated.“We have already banned single-use vapes and have legislated to ban advertising and sponsorship from next year too. We’re also consulting on proposals to crack down on packaging that appeals to children.“Through the Tobacco and Vapes Act, this government will protect children and young people from the potential harms of vaping, smoking and risks of nicotine addiction and create the UK’s first ever smoke-free generation.”Explore more on these topicsVapingChildrenSmokingYoung peopleTobacco industryHealth policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tice should apologise to firefighters for ‘enjoy it’ remark on extreme heat, says Labour | Richard Tice | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Bridget Phillipson’s comments show her party feels voters have been alienated by Reform net zero attacks
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Bridget Phillipson’s comments show her party feels voters have been alienated by Reform net zero attacks
Content: Tice said this week: ‘When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTice said this week: ‘When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRichard TiceTice should apologise to firefighters for ‘enjoy it’ remark on extreme heat, says LabourExclusive: Bridget Phillipson’s comments show her party feels voters have been alienated by Reform net zero attacksKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 19 Aug 2026 12.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard Tice should apologise to firefighters for his comments this week urging British people to “enjoy” this summer’s extreme heat, according to the Labour party chair.Bridget Phillipson has called on Reform’s deputy leader to say sorry to those who, over the last few weeks, have battled wildfires across the country that have forced evacuations and destroyed homes.Her comments underline Labour’s confidence that voters have been alienated by Reform’s increasingly strident attacks on net zero policy, even as the prime ministercomes under pressurefor saying relatively little on the issue.Tice told a press conference this week: “When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic.“Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.”Reform’s Tice accused of misinformation after urging people to enjoy heatwavesRead morePhillipson told the Guardian on Wednesday: “I think he owes an apology to the firefighters who were battling in extreme conditions, putting themselves and their lives at risk in order to protect people’s homes and deal with these extraordinary fires that we’ve seen. He should apologise to them.“It’s not funny to crack jokes about sparkling wine at a point at which our brave firefighters are out there kind of battling the real-world impact of what we’re seeing from climate change.”Reform did not respond to a request to comment.Labour has sought to highlight Tice’s comments in recent days, including by releasinga videoputting his words next to footage of homes destroyed in theStourbridge wildfire.He made the remarks as part of a broader attack on net zero policies, which have also been a target of the Conservative party in recent days, despite the increasing frequency of extreme heat events.Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy secretary, gave a speech on Wednesday criticising the government’s push to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2050. She said the UK “should focus all our attention on making electricity cheap, and then let consumer choice be king”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAndy Burnham has been criticised by climate campaigners for saying little about the climate crisis. The prime ministerheld a Cobra meeting last weekto discuss the impact of the heatwave and drought, but failed to mention climate breakdown, focusing instead ondisposable barbecues.Later, on a visit to Stourbridge, he said: “We have to face up to the changing climate … there’s no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy.”Ministers are expected to announce in the coming weekswhether they will approvetwo new giant oil and gas fields in the North Sea.Phillipson defended Burnham’s record on the climate crisis. “I don’t think it’s fair to say he hasn’t spoken about it,” she said. “And he’s seen it first-hand on his visit to the West Midlands – the real impact of what this means in terms of people’s lives, their communities, their homes, the devastation that’s been caused.”Explore more on these topicsRichard TiceReform UKBridget PhillipsonLabourClimate crisisExtreme heatEnvironment policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth? | Economic growth (GDP) | The Guardian
description: PM wants to reduce department’s stranglehold on public purse and bring long-term thinking to economic policy
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: PM wants to reduce department’s stranglehold on public purse and bring long-term thinking to economic policy
Content: Andy Burnham said the ‘new No 10 North innovation is more significant than people realise.’Photograph: Jeff Overs/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said the ‘new No 10 North innovation is more significant than people realise.’Photograph: Jeff Overs/ReutersEconomic growth (GDP)AnalysisCan Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?Heather StewartPM wants to reduce department’s stranglehold on public purse and bring long-term thinking to economic policyWed 19 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShareAndy Burnham is far from the first prime minister to dream of taming the power of the mighty Treasury.Boris Johnsonall but forced the resignation of Sajid Javidby handpicking his team; Margaret Thatcher favoured her economic adviser Alan Walters over Nigel Lawson, prompting the latter’s furious resignation; and Tony Blair and Gordon Brown’s power struggle was the stuff of Whitehall legend.Burnham’s approach harks further back still to Labour prime minister Harold Wilson’s Department for Economic Affairs (DEA), a short-lived attempt to bring long-term thinking to British economic policymaking.Rising inflation underlines scale of Andy Burnham’s cost of living challengeRead moreThe PM made the historical analogy as he gave fresh details this week ofhis plan to take control of growth policy from the Treasury and hand it to a new No 10 department in Manchester.The DEA was responsible for drawing up a national plan for the economy,which beganwith the timeless exhortation: “We must pay our way in the world and produce more wealth inside this country.”The baleful influence of the Treasury, with its stranglehold over the public finances, has long been lamented by leftwingers, who accuse it of short-term thinking and ingrained, institutional caution.“The dual job of growth and control of the public finances sometimes clouds the growth mission,” Burnham told the Times. “Having No 10 leading on that growth mission means you’ve got maximum power to unlock the blockages where they exist in the Whitehall system.”Some of the most criticised decisions of Keir Starmer’s tenure were seen by many Labour MPs as resulting from this “Treasury brain” – from slashing winter fuel allowance to caving in to City lobbying on a bank windfall tax.Burnham hopes the new prime minister’s department, overseen by his powerful cabinet allyLouise Haigh, will open the space for some fresh thinking. “The new No 10 North innovation is more significant than people realise,” he said.View image in fullscreenBurnham ally Louise Haigh oversees No 10 North.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesBurnham’s route to growth runs through devolutionOne of the few detailed policy publications the new cabinet has so far produced was on radical plans for devolution. The PM hopes handing additional powers to metro mayors will help bring together growth policies now scattered across Whitehall.Ruth Curtice, director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank and a former longtime Treasury official, says coordinating across these different policy areas – housing, education, planning and so on – could be the most effective use of the new Manchester-based unit.“No one department has all of the levers – the Treasury don’t own all of the levers,” she says. “I would see it as a positive thing that this No 10 says, ‘Given what a priority this is, we’re going to put more force behind it.’”Former Brown adviser Michael Jacobs, emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, draws a comparison with the Office for Climate Change, which helped to coordinate policy across government.Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by ChristmasRead more“The really interesting version of this to me would be a new growth unit, drawing on and made up of officials from all the relevant departments.”Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, points out that Burnham’s pick for chancellor, John Healey, was instrumental in the creation of regional development agencies, way back in the Blair-Brown era.These were meant to bring a regional dimension to growth and industrial policy – but were scrapped by the 2010 Conservative-Lib Dem coalition. George Osborne went on to create and empower city region mayors as the focus for devolution.Given the pair’s joint interest in devolution, Raja argues that far from clipping Healey’s wings, “this is one of the more merged tag teams in No 10 and No 11 that we have seen”.Treasury power is inescapableYet not everyone is convinced that it makes sense to create a policy counterweight to the Treasury. Former Conservative chief secretary to the Treasury David Gauke says the Treasury’s control over tax and spend, which it will maintain under the shake-up, means it is inevitably powerful. “The Treasury is always going to be the most important department.”Indeed, he suspects stripping growth out of the Treasury’s remit would just exaggerate its tendency to fixate on penny-pinching.He also questions whether No 10 North can work: “You’re going to have this office, which will get at best a day a week of face-time with the PM, and little access to other ministers – and it will be trying to push the government in a more pro-growth direction.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Treasury source stresses that, as the initial government announcement said, No 10 North will focus on “local growth”, and in particular devolution – rather than taking over economic strategy from No 11.The Treasury has “lent” a small number of staff to the new unit, while its second permanent secretary, Beth Russell, who was instrumental in the creation of the Treasury’s own northern outpost, the Darlington Economic Campus, has been working closely with the Manchester team.View image in fullscreenThe Darlington Economic Campus, the Treasury’s own Northern outpost, has been working closely with No 10 North.Photograph: David Dixon/AlamyMore civil servants are being transferred from other departments, including housing and local government, and former Times journalist Sam Lister has been appointed as No 10 North’s director. However, Whitehall veterans point to the new department’s relatively modest resources thus far.Jonathan Portes, a former senior government economist and now professor at King’s College London, says the most important question, as Burnham’s new arrangements bed in, will be how the inevitable policy clashes will be resolved.“What happens when No 10 wants to do something, and Treasury says no – or says, ‘yes, we’ll pay lip service to this but don’t expect any spending to go along with it’?” he says. “That has been the historic response of the Treasury when No 10 has got more powerful.”Hannah Peaker, deputy chief executive of the NewEconomicsFoundation thinktank, says the priority should be ensuring economic decision-makers – including the Treasury and No 10, but also the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility – work better together. “While a more devolved approach could help accelerate regional growth, the most important remedy is better coordination between economic institutions so that they are all pulling in the same direction.”Will No 10 North open the space for more radicalism?Inan article for the progressive Renewal journalearlier this year, Haigh complained of the Treasury that, “faced with the dual mandate of maintaining fiscal control and supporting economic growth, the institution defaults toward caution, prioritising near-term debt dynamics over longer-term economic outcomes”.View image in fullscreenHarold Wilson pictured in 1964. Burnham’s approach harks back to then Labour prime minister’s Department for Economic Affairs (DEA), a shortlived attempt to bring long-term thinking to British economic policymaking.Photograph: Keystone/Getty ImagesIn the run-up to Burnham’s bid for power, he appeared to suggest large-scale renationalisation of public utilities and radical tax reform would be on his agenda – alongside the long-promised shake-up of social care.But some of these ambitious and potentially costly plans are likely to come into sharp conflict with the institutional caution Haigh identified.With a critical budget fast approaching, the new cabinet – north and south – faces a string of decisions on tax and spend; and other key choices loom, including on how to shape the future of the beleaguered privatised water industry.In the run-up to the last two Labour budgets, debate was dominated by the immediate challenges for fiscal policy, often played out noisily in public against a backdrop of febrile government bond markets.Burnham clearly hopes to shape a different debate, both inside and outside government, but the historic precedent he highlighted, in the Wilson era, underlines the difficulties of reining in the Treasury.Wilson’s temperamental secretary of state for economic affairs, George Brown, moved on after two years, by which time the national plan had been blown way off course.His role was then downgraded so it was no longer a cabinet position and, by 1969, the experiment with a separate Department for Economic Affairs was over – and its powers had been sucked back into the Treasury.Explore more on these topicsEconomic growth (GDP)Economic policyAndy BurnhamEconomicsLouise HaighPublic financeGovernment borrowinganalysisShareReuse this content

title: Did someone wearing Meta Glasses film you today? Are you sure? | Meta | The Guardian
description: People say they’ve been secretly filmed in their own homes, at concerts and at work. Are the wildly popular smartglasses the final nail in the coffin of personal privacy?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: People say they’ve been secretly filmed in their own homes, at concerts and at work. Are the wildly popular smartglasses the final nail in the coffin of personal privacy?
Content: ‘Here we have a leap in the erosion of our privacy rights through this slick technology that big tech promises will enrich our lives,’ says Ryan Clarkson, one of the lawyers bringing a class-action suit against Meta over its privacy assurances.Illustration: Saratta Chuengsatiansup/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Here we have a leap in the erosion of our privacy rights through this slick technology that big tech promises will enrich our lives,’ says Ryan Clarkson, one of the lawyers bringing a class-action suit against Meta over its privacy assurances.Illustration: Saratta Chuengsatiansup/The GuardianMetaDid someone wearing Meta Glasses film you today? Are you sure?People say they’ve been secretly filmed in their own homes, at concerts and at work. Are the wildly popular smartglasses the final nail in the coffin of personal privacy?Maggie Harrison DupréWed 19 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 16.03 EDTShare“I’ve had one person who told me that their intentions were creepy,” a man tells me over a video call, on condition of anonymity. He’s based in Los Angeles, and while we speak, he eats what appears to be tuna directly out of the can. “He said: ‘I go to strip clubs, and I want to record the strippers … Normally I put my phone in my chest pocket, but the glasses are more convenient.’”The man I’m talking to runs a business calledGhost Metas. He’s one of hundreds of vendors, easily discoverable online, who specialise in disabling the flashing LED light embedded in Meta’s smartglasses that blinks when wearers capture photos, videos and audio. After Ghost Metas disables the LED, it’s impossible for someone to know they’re being filmed.He flips his camera over to show me hiswork bench, revealing painter’s tape, a drill, a hole puncher, a dental pick and a tube of resin. He says he’s worked on about 100 pairs of glasses, and that one pair only takes him about 15 to 20 minutes.“In public, I don’t think we have privacy any more, period,” he says, when I ask whether what he’s doing feels wrong. “My argument is if you’re really worried about your privacy, don’t go outside.”‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinionRead moreThe success of Ghost Metas is parallel to the runaway success of Meta Glasses, designed in partnership with established glasses brands Ray-Ban and Oakley. Meta said that it soldroughly 7 million pairsin 2025 alone, practicallytriplingcombined sales numbers from 2023 and 2024.Influencers,athletesand global celebrities such asChris HemsworthandTeyana Taylorhave embraced the tech in sponsored posts and buzzy ads. The glasses mark a turnaround for a company that made big missteps by overinvesting in virtual reality “metaverses” and trailing behind in the AI race.The most notable endorser has been Kylie Jenner who, in June, collaborated with Meta on her own line of AI glasses. “Hey Meta – take a picture,” Jenner commands her $399 Starfire glasses in anadvertisementfor the collab. Meta promises that users can ask Kylie’s glasses any question, and the AI will issue “every response in Kylie’s voice”.The reality of how people are using the glasses has been less benign. They have been widely used for exploitation and privacy violations, much of which has been bragged about on social media by bad actors themselves. Online creators – primarily men – have used the glasses totroll boardwalks, college campuses and streetsoutside bars in search of women to hit on, and then post the interactions. Some men have recorded overtly racist videos in which they enter massage parlors staffed by Asian women and ask for “happy ending” massages. Others have used the glasses to record bathing suit-clad women at the beach.I’ve spoken with people who sayMetaGlasses have been used to secretly record their private interactions, with one source describing an incident inside her house that she felt endangered her children.Many of these videos are captured and posted online without the consent of their subjects, often by influencers who want to humiliate the subjects they’ve filmed.To protect against this, on every pair of glasses there’s an LED light that’s supposed to let people know the glasses are recording. Meta makes assurances that the glasses won’t record when the LED light is blocked or obscured. But the man behind Ghost Metas says it’s easy to modify the glasses to block the light without triggering the refusal failsafe.He acknowledges that the overwhelming majority of his clients have been men but he doesn’t agree that the glasses are only being used for spying. Many of his customers are parents, who he says tell him: “‘I want to record my kid, but every time the light’s on, the kid just keeps looking at the light.’” He also said he’s done several pairs for food delivery drivers and others with similar jobs, who have told him that they want to protect themselves from false claims of undelivered orders or unwanted harassment.What Ghost Metas is doing clearly breaks the terms of service of Meta Glasses. But could Meta argue it’s an inversion of their appeal? Meta’s CEO,Mark Zuckerberg, who has positioned the glasses as a smartphone killer, said in September 2025 that “the promise of glasses is to preserve this sense of presence that you have with other people”. Smartglasses bring the functionality of smartphones, cameras included, into every moment. Several people I spoke to said that even when the LED is functioning as intended it can be subtle and difficult to spot from far away, especially if you aren’t aware of how smartglasses work. Others shared that they sought out the glasses to capture more “natural” footage of those around them, explicitly because people act differently when they know they’re being recorded. As Meta themselves put in their advertising materials: “Record life as you live it – every detail, every angle.”View image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg records video using the Orion augmented reality (AR) glasses, triggering a small light on the frames, during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, in September 2024.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOther tech giants have tried – and failed – to successfully market smartglasses. In 2013, Google released Google Glass, but discontinued them in 2015 amid backlash that resulted in a journalistgetting assaultedin the street for wearing a pair. Snapchat tried for years to push Spectacles, first released in 2016, to no avail. (It’s now slated to release augmented-reality glasses called Specs later this year, though between theirawkwardly bulbousappearance and$2,195 price tag, they may be dead on arrival). Apple’s Vision Pro, meanwhile, has seendisappointing salessince its release in early 2024. Beyond headwear, there have been products like an always-listening version of Amazon’s Halo Band bracelet, which the Washington Post oncecalled“the most invasive tech we’ve ever tested”. Amazonscrappedthe always-on microphone in 2021, again in response to people finding the update wildly creepy, and the Halo line wasdiscontinuedentirely by 2023.So why did Meta Glasses succeed when so many of their competitors were deemed creepy and ugly? One big answer seems to be fashion.Unlike their predecessors, Meta Glasses have familiar designer names behind them. EssilorLuxottica, the Italian corporation that owns Ray-Ban and Oakley, is an eyewear titan thatraked inabout $33.8bn in 2025, with about 12% of its overall sales attributed to Ray-Ban.“Ray-Ban is fashionable in a perennial sort of way, not a fleeting sort of way,” said Amy Odell, fashion journalist and author of theBack Rownewsletter. Zuckerberg, she added, “is right that in order to get these things to sell, they do have to be great glasses first. And you really can’t go wrong by going to the most iconic sunglasses brand.”double quotation mark[These products are] designed to maximise profits, and to turn every person who buys one into a Trojan horse of surveillanceRyan Clarkson, Clarkson Law FirmMeta also makes a number of privacy assurances about the glasses, promising users they are “designed for privacy” and that Meta doesn’t have access to recordings made by using the glasses. However, ajoint investigation by the Swedish newspapers Svenska Dagbladetand Göteborgs-Postenrevealed that Meta was, in fact, storing recordings made by glasses wearers. The papers interviewed Kenyan whistleblowers working for the controversialcontent moderation sweatshop Sama, which is subcontracted by Meta to sort through and annotate content that may be fed into Meta’s AI models.“In some videos you can see someone going to the toilet, or getting undressed,” one contractor told the Swedish newspapers. “I don’t think they know, because if they knew they wouldn’t be recording.” Other Sama employees shared stories of reviewing content collected while glasses wearers were having sex, looking at their or their partner’s naked body, or viewing sensitive documents that revealed personal identifying information. The reporting quickly prompted a class-action lawsuit in San Francisco federal court, which alleges that Meta engaged in false advertising in relation to its privacy assurances.In a statement, Meta said that “unless users choose to share media they’ve captured with Meta or others, that media stays on the user’s device. When people share content with Meta AI, we sometimes use contractors to review this data for the purpose of improving people’s experience … we take steps to filter this data to protect people’s privacy.”The lawyers bringing the class action disagree. “These products aren’t designed for user control and privacy,” said Ryan Clarkson, managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, which filed the suit. “In my opinion, they’re designed to maximise profits, and to turn every person who buys one into a Trojan horse of surveillance.”‘I felt extremely violated’Nonconsensual recordings can happen to anyone, anywhere. People have been secretly recorded in their workplace; one lawyer said that he was covertly filmed by potential clients during a free consultation. Some Meta Glasses wearers have recorded videos of trips to hospitals and children’s dentist’s offices and shared them online.You could even be covertly recorded in your own home – as was the case for Brek Mettra, a mother of two in Utah who was secretly filmed in her house during a transaction with a local vintage clothing seller. After the pair connected on Facebook Marketplace (also run by Meta), the seller met Mettra at her home to buy a T-shirt. Unbeknownst to her, he had used Meta Glasses to record their exchange, which he then uploaded to social media as content to promote his business.double quotation markIf he would’ve pulled out a camera, I could have said noBrek MettraMettra said it wasn’t until a “random guy” in Philadelphia contacted her to inquire about a T-shirt he had seen in the clip that she knew the video even existed.In the video, a copy of which was reviewed by the Guardian, Mettra’s face is visible, as are the faces of her two very young children. Though Mettra wasn’t tagged, the video revealed her identifying information: the vintage seller had paid Mettra using Venmo, and her full name was visible on her Venmo profile, which was how the stranger in Philly found her. “I honestly felt extremely violated,” said Mettra, who added that she does not remember seeing an LED light on the glasses.After making multiple requests for him to take the video down, the seller deleted the post once Mettra warned him that she had contacted Instagram. “Please, for my children and myself I really hope you delete it,” Mettra pleaded in one message to the seller, which was reviewed by the Guardian. The seller didn’t respond to a request for comment but he has posted several similar recordings across multiple Instagram and TikTok accounts, with a tag included in his Instagram captions noting that the videos have been recorded with “Ray-Ban Meta glasses”.‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ contentRead moreOthers say they’ve been harassed by Meta Glasses wearers in spaces they had previously felt safe in. Karina and Kyle, a young couple who asked to be identified by their first names to protect their privacy, are avid ravers who, earlier this year, had a disturbing encounter with a man who was using Meta Glasses to record young women’s bodies at a large EDM festival in Las Vegas.The couple initially bumped into the man on the dancefloor, where they caught him leering at Karina’s breasts through a pair of Ray-Bans. They were close enough to notice that an LED on the glasses was flashing, signaling that the man was filming. Asked to stop recording, the man stormed away. A little while later, though, they saw the man again. This time, he was sitting on the ground beneath two bikini-clad young women, who were perched on tall barstools as they watched the show. Glasses on, the man stared at their bodies from below. It wasn’t until he took out his phone and attempted to take additional recordings, the couple said, that people around him realised he was recording and notified the women.Karina is still unsettled by the knowledge that nonconsensual recordings of her may be out there. “It’s really disgusting … there are so many possibilities of what people could do,” she said.Meta refuted to the Guardian that the main purpose of the glasses is to make unnoticeable recordings. But each victim of nonconsensual recordings called attention to the innocuity of the glasses, and how much more difficult – if not impossible – the glasses were to spot compared with handheld cameras or smartphones. And Mettra, for her part, said she doesn’t remember seeing a recording light. “If he would’ve pulled out a camera, I could have said no, or leave if you’re going to do that,” said Mettra. “It opened my eyes to be a little bit less trusting in people.”“I feel like that’s the whole point of these glasses,” added Karina, “that they’re inconspicuous.”‘A red line society must not cross’Being secretly recorded is currently the primary fear associated with Meta Glasses. But covert recordings may just be the first step in a more sophisticated surveillance apparatus integrated with another deeply controversial technology: facial recognition.In February, theNew York Times reported onan internal Meta Reality Labs document in which the company discussed its plans to integrate a facial recognition feature called “NameTag” into its smartglasses.In the document, dated to May 2025, Meta said that it planned to launch NameTag “during a dynamic political environment where many civil society groups that we would expect to attack us would have their resources focused on other concerns”.In response to the Times’ reporting, Meta said that NameTag was something it was “still thinking through” and promised to “take a thoughtful approach if and before we roll anything out”.A few months later, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)issued an open letter to Metasigned by 75 organizations condemning the integration of a feature like NameTag into smartglasses as “a red line society must not cross”.By then, though, NameTag was already further along than was publicly known. A JuneWired investigation revealed thatlatent code for NameTag was secretly rolled to Meta smartglasses as early as January 2026. While technically unreleased and inaccessible to consumers, the code contained the architecture for a system that would save faces viewed through Meta smartglasses as biometric “faceprints” and store them on users’ devices.“You don’t put code like this in your app unless you’re planning to release that feature very soon,” said Cooper Quintin, a security researcher and senior public interest technologist with the Electronic Frontier Foundation Threat Lab, who independently reviewed the NameTag code discovered by Wired.A few days after it was discovered, Meta quietly deleted the inactive code.View image in fullscreenThe privacy light embedded within Meta’s smartglasses.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersTechnically, building facial recognition into smartglasses isn’t difficult. In late 2024, two Harvard dropouts wereable to embedthe facial recognition library PimEyes into a pair of Meta Ray-Bans; coupled with help from a large language model, the glasses were successfully able to connect strangers’ faces to their name, job, social media, address, contact information, information about family members and other personal data. (Meta told the Guardian that “these students simply used publicly available facial recognition software, PimEyes, on a computer that would work with photos taken on any camera, phone or recording device … Meta’s AI glasses do not have facial recognition technology”).But just last week,404 Media reportedthat Meta filed a patent for a facial recognition feature for its AI glasses that would identify people in the frame and use that information to create highlight reels of that person or people. The example given in Meta’s patent was identifying and creating videos of guests at a dinner party.According to Kade Crockford, the director for technology and justice programs at the American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts, the uncovered NameTag code signals a step toward a radical transformation of our existing privacy landscape – and they’ve “been dreading this moment for 20 years”.Meta is keen to emphasise that their glasses are uniquely beneficial for blind and low-vision people, many of whom say the tech has been transformational for theirdaily independenceandsafety. While discussing NameTag in arecent podcast interview, Meta’s CTO, Andrew “Boz” Bosworth, emphasised that putting facial recognition into smartglasses could offer additional support to people living with vision or memory disabilities.But the reasons to not introduce unchecked facial recognition into smartglasses are vast, privacy advocateshave warned. Citizens attending protests could wind up with their names and faces being sucked into a database. To that end, ICE officers have already been caught using Meta Glasses to surveil demonstrators, and earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Securityrequested millions of dollarsin order to build facial recognition into smartglasses. A woman could brush off an advance by a stranger in a bar, or on a bus or at a workplace, only for that stranger to already know her name, which they may use to find her address and other information. Other vulnerable demographics – LGBTQ+ people, immigrants, people of color – may also be stalked, harassed and targeted by abusers receiving assistance from facial recognition.Asked about Meta’s facial recognition plans, a spokesperson for Meta said that “we’re exploring these types of features as people regularly express interest in seeing them. Nothing has shipped to consumers and no final decision has been made on what to do here, if anything. If we do decide to roll something out, we will take a thoughtful approach and do so with full transparency. One decision we can be clear about – we are not building a central face database.”A brewing backlashAs Meta promotes the glasses with paid influencer content and high-profile partnerships, resistance against the tech is intensifying. Activists recently plastered London bus stops withanti-glasses guerilla ads, one of which depicted the infamous pedophile Jeffrey Epstein in the Ray-Bans with the tagline “glasses for people who don’t do consent”. Someglasses ownerssay they’ve started leaving the spectacles at home because they don’t want to be associated with creeps. A professor in Germanybuilt an appcalled Nearby Glasses, a free, open-source service that detects when smartglasses are close by and issues an alert. And during a July performance at a music festival in Madrid sponsored by Ray-Ban, the singer Lordetold the crowdthat “you don’t know if someone’s wearing sunglasses, or if they’re wearing those fucked-up fucking … can I just say, for the record, fuck the glasses! Don’t get the glasses. Not sexy.”double quotation markThe argument for federal privacy legislation is stronger every dayCooper QuintinIn early July, Metaannouncedthat it would push an update to detect when an LED light has been “physically tampered with or destroyed” and stop people filming using those glasses. Two months after we spoke, Ghost Metas decided to pause his business as a result of the update. “Too much risk,” said the now former LED disabler. One client, he added, had gotten in touch to say that his glasses were no longer working.“People use our glasses because they’re genuinely helpful … for those wearing them and the people around them. Trust matters,” a spokesperson for Meta said when asked about disabling the LED. “That’s why we built privacy into our AI glasses from the ground up. Every pair has a capture LED that blinks when you take a photo or video that you can save or share, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or damages the LED, the camera is disabled.”But many other LED disablers said they’re still working, even after Meta’s update.“The new update hasn’t been impacting the glasses at all,” said one disabler in early August, after Facebook had announced the update. Since the update, he said he’s tampered with the lights on the Gen 2 and Kylie Jenner models, and that “they work fine”.“I’ve done hundreds and [only] one person is having problems out of hundreds, so I chalk that up to him being a dumbass,” said another. “Mine are working perfect still.”View image in fullscreenA billboard advertising Kylie Jenner’s Meta Glasses collaboration in Los Angeles, California, on 27 June.Photograph: Barry King/AlamyOthers are still able to get by with lower-risk alternatives to physically drilling out the LED – includingan Engadgetjournalist, who found they were able to successfully block out the recording light with a $2 sticker.Things have gotten so bad that Instagram, which is also owned by Meta, is publicly warning that the glasses are being used to harass people and warns about posting content from Meta Glasses. “If you’re posting content that is taking advantage of people and harassing them, like a lot of these pickup-line kind of videos that we’ve heard of and seen, then we’re going to take the content down,” the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said in a video announcing a crackdown on harassing content. “We’re trying to fight that every way we can.”As part of this purported crackdown, Instagram deactivated the accounts of several pickup artists with large followings. As of publishing this story, however, dozens of pickup artist videos filmed with Meta Glasses are still easily discoverable on Instagram, clearly marked by captions such as “POV MILF RIZZ”, “POV LATINA RUNDOWN” and “POV COLLEGE RIZZ”. After we notified Meta to multiple active accounts dedicated to pickup artist content, the accounts were deactivated.Though taking pictures and videos in public spaces is generally legal in the US, existing laws regarding two-party consent and wiretapping, particularly on the state level, may have rendered some nonconsensual recordings captured by Meta Glasses illegal. (Of course, victims would generally have to know that recordings exist in order to take action against them.) Even so, the passage of meaningful federal privacy regulation in the US would take policy out of the hands of corporations, replacing patchworked state laws and setting standards that would shift the regulatory burden to companies instead of individuals.“The argument for federal privacy legislation is stronger every day, and Congress’s seeming commitment to do nothing is also stronger,” said Quintin. “I think privacy is a human right, and we should expect it. We used to expect it, and I don’t know why we as a society have largely just given up on that. I think we should demand it, and demand that Congress take action and regulate privacy.”‘The bot asked me four times a day how I was feeling’: is tracking everything actually good for us?Read moreBut Meta has proven a market, and other tech companies are chasing. Google has apartnershipwith Samsung and the designer eyewear company Gentle Monster, and is also working on a collaboration with the affordable glasses-maker Warby Parker. And Apple is not only working on its own glasses, but is also rumoured to be infusing cameras into its popular AirPods designed to feed an AI system information about the wearer’s surroundings,according to Bloomberg. Across Silicon Valley, AI hardware startups – including many designing AI wearables beyond glasses – abound.Meta itself ismining deeperinto higher echelons of luxury fashion. In 2025, it released alimited-editionpair of smart Ray-Bans with the French clothing brand Coperni, and it’s due to release a pair of smartglasses designed in collaborationwith Prada. (In February, Zuckerberg evensat front rowat a Prada fashion show.) The fashion industry seems excited to make this new era of surveillance as chic as possible.“We’re frogs in a boiling pot, and the temperature is getting hotter and hotter,” said Clarkson, the lawyer. “So here we have a leap in the erosion of our privacy rights through this slick technology that big tech promises will enrich our lives, make us more connected, smarter, more efficient – when instead it’s going to move us, by an order of magnitude, toward a far more surveilled state of existence.”In the modern world, anonymity is a precious resource. If smartphones have made constant filming more acceptable, smartglasses are among a class of technologies that make it quieter – omnipresent, but less and less visible.A pair of glasses suddenly come with endless question marks, and a humming fear that our presence in public spaces involves a Foucauldian forfeiture of privacy. When you feel like anyone could be filming you, you act like you’re always being filmed.

title: Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerve | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Senator Jon Ossoff, who is up for re-election, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections so far
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: Senator Jon Ossoff, who is up for re-election, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections so far
Content: Senator Jon Ossoff speaks to a capacity crowd at a rally in Atlanta on Sunday in Atlanta, Georgia.Photograph: Robin Rayne/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSenator Jon Ossoff speaks to a capacity crowd at a rally in Atlanta on Sunday in Atlanta, Georgia.Photograph: Robin Rayne/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThis Week in TrumplandDonald TrumpAnalysisUnhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerveAdam GabbattSenator Jon Ossoff, who is up for re-election, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections so farWed 19 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTShareJon Ossoffreally struck a nerve. That much is clear.The US senator for Georgia, running for re-election in November, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections campaign so far when discussingDonald Trumpat a rally on Sunday.“While the sailors on the[USS Abraham] Lincolnfight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks,” said Ossoff. “See, he doesn’t want to do the job.“He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”Not only did the remark enter into national consciousness the existence of “Natalie” –Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old aide to Trump who rarely leaves the president’s side– Ossoff’s riff also succeeded in upsetting Steven Cheung, Trump’s director of communications.Who is Natalie Harp? Trump’s closest and most devoted aide is in the spotlightRead more“Jon Jackoff,” Cheungwrote on Xon Monday, misspelling, perhaps deliberately, the name “Ossoff”, “has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he’s a miserable person who hates this country. It’s because he’s a radical, extremist Dumocrat.”Even for someone in Trump’s orbit, where outbursts against political opponents are commonplace, this plumbed new lows. What could possibly have triggered Trump’s stoutly built, middle-aged communications guru into attacking Ossoff, the handsome, athletic, 39-year-old senator?It’s hard to be sure. But, apropos of nothing,this essayby Dana Schwartz, from 2016, examined why rightwing men are obsessed with calling people “cucks”:“‘Cuck’ is a concept borne [sic] out of insecurity: a fear that one is inadequate, sexually or otherwise, and that inadequacy will lead to the loss of the things that are important to him,” Schwartz wrote.In any case, Trump wasn’t far behind Cheung, calling Ossoff a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike” – a reference to a TV and film character whose popularity peaked 40 years ago. (Trump has also called Ossoff “Pinky Herman”, which is neither a character nor a thing.)The anonymous White House Rapid Response X account joined in too, branding a CNN reporter who had asked Trump about Ossoff a “disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession”, and laterposting:“Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.”It’s hard to really be shocked by any of this any more, with daily attacks on the media from the president and his most senior aides, but an official White House account, with 2.2 million followers, invoking a reporter’s children prompted widespread criticism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis Week in TrumplandA deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administrationEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn truth the rhetoric from Trump and his acolytes, always bellicose, has been getting worse for a while – and people who dare to publicly question Trump’s narrative that he is a successful, popular president, seem to particularly trigger those on the right.Take James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Texas, who is running neck and neck against Ken Paxton, whom Trump picked for the Republican side.Talarico’s popularity in a traditionally red state has seen Republicans come out swinging. Trump dubbed the Democrat“Talafreako”in July; earlier US senator Bernie Moreno hadcalledTalarico, “a far left freak”, while a Texas congressman falsely claiming Talarico “daydreams about trans kids”. (There was also Trumpbranding a reporter “piggy”after she asked him a question onboard Air Force One.)Perhaps the fury is prompted whenever something, or someone, succeeds in puncturing the alternate reality that Republicans have created for themselves: a reality where the GOP is not predicted to suffer heavy losses in November’s midterms, and one where Trump is a spry, capable president.When someone points out that Trump is an 80-year-old, easily distracted man who is overseeing an ill-defined, meandering war in Iran, while doing little as prices soar at home, it appears to bring out the particularly vulgar insults. Ossoffdid all this on Sunday– and sparked fresh speculation about the president’s relationship with a close aide.With Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, stepping down, there is some jostling taking place in Trump’s circle to replace her, perhaps explaining the amped up language as each potential successor seeks to be more pugnacious than the last.And given Democrats in Congress will be running on Trump’s unpopularity this November, there’ll be plenty of opportunity for bellicose responses from the White House. We should brace ourselves for plenty more of this sort of thing.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThis Week in TrumplandUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026newslettersShareReuse this content

title: John Hall obituary | Aeronautics | The Guardian
description: Other lives: Pilot who flew Spitfires and tested the UK’s cold war Lightning fighter jet before moving on to a commercial airline
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Other lives: Pilot who flew Spitfires and tested the UK’s cold war Lightning fighter jet before moving on to a commercial airline
Content: John Hall with a Lightning prototype in the 1950sView image in fullscreenJohn Hall with a Lightning prototype in the 1950sOther livesAeronauticsObituaryJohn Hall obituaryColin SmithWed 19 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the late 1950s my friend and Guernsey neighbour John Hall, who has died aged 98, was part of an intrepid team of British test pilots. During the cold war they helped with the birth of the English Electric Lightning, the first – and last – entirely British-built supersonic jet fighter.John HallPhotograph: Maxwell HallFor years the Lightning was the RAF’s main interceptor, with a phenomenal rate of climb. American fighter pilots envied its performance; they called it “the pocket rocket”. To achieve such power, the prototypes required rigorous testing from John and his pals, who pushed them to their limits.Once he took a Lightning up to 36,000ft for something called a “cold soak” – an endurance test in which he ended up flying for 90 minutes with the plane in a completely frozen state. His hands became almost useless in cold agony, while the controls began to stiffen and he could only work them with jerky movements. Unable to lower the undercarriage normally, he just about managed a landing, after which the ground crew prised his 6ft 2in frame out of the aircraft and, hardly able to walk, he was led to safety.He was fortunate to survive that escapade, and just as lucky to come back from a “structural integrity test” during which he took a Lightning out to one of the RAF’s North Sea firing ranges, trying to discover if it was possible to simultaneously empty the magazines that fed its three 30mm Aden cannon before the recoil from such heavy calibre ammunition shook the aircraft apart. He expected the entire body to crack apart, but fortunately, after “a bloody great bang” and the flashing of all sorts of warning lights, it held together.John was born in East Bridgford, Nottinghamshire, close to the market town of Southwell, where he attended Southwell Minster grammar school. He was 10 when the second world war broke out, and like many of his contemporaries longed to fly Spitfires. At 18, after the war was over, he trained at RAF Cranwell and his dream was fulfilled when he joined a Spitfire squadron that saw active service in the Suez canal zone.In 1952 he returned to the UK as an instructor on Meteor jet bombers, and by the late 50s he was part of the English Electric Lightning test pilot team. He then left the RAF to work directly for English Electric (later BAE), but continued to test jets for the RAF on a part-time basis until a final move to British Caledonian airlines, with whom he flew commercial transatlantic flights in Boeing 707s for 25 years until retirement.John’s first marriage, to Shelagh Stone, ended in divorce, and afterwards he moved with his second wife, Tessa (nee Maxwell), to Guernsey, where he especially enjoyed the local swimming.He is survived by Tessa, three sons, James, Patrick and Richard, from his first marriage, and another son, Maxwell, from his second.Explore more on these topicsAeronauticsOther livesRoyal Air ForceMilitaryAerospace industryAir transportobituariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I love provocative stories’: producer Christine Vachon on fighting for her ‘offensive’ movies | Movies | The Guardian
description: The maker of indie classics Kids, Swoon and Poison on daring to have a temper in the 90s, what some producer credits mean – and what happened between her and Joaquin Phoenix
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: The maker of indie classics Kids, Swoon and Poison on daring to have a temper in the 90s, what some producer credits mean – and what happened between her and Joaquin Phoenix
Content: ‘A real point of view’ … Pretty Babies, written and directed by Tyler-Marie Evans and produced by VachonPhotograph: Courtesy EIFFView image in fullscreen‘A real point of view’ … Pretty Babies, written and directed by Tyler-Marie Evans and produced by VachonPhotograph: Courtesy EIFFMoviesInterview‘I love provocative stories’: producer Christine Vachon on fighting for her ‘offensive’ moviesRyan GilbeyThe maker of indie classics Kids, Swoon and Poison on daring to have a temper in the 90s, what some producer credits mean – and what happened between her and Joaquin PhoenixWed 19 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrailblazing producer Christine Vachon bestrides the world of US independent film-making like a colossus. She has championed idiosyncratic American cinema for more than 35 years, scoring hits such as the romcom Materialists, which starred three superhero actors (Dakota Johnson, Pedro Pascal, Chris Evans) and grossed $108m, alongside curiosities such as Zola, a strippers’ road-trip comedy based on a string of viral tweets.Vachon got her start in the early 1990s. Her often scandalous movies – from Poison (gay prison sex) and Swoon (gay child killers) to Happiness (paedophile dad) and Kids (delinquent teens) – dominated the cultural conversation decades before boutique studio A24 had sold its first tote bag. Her production outfit Killer Films, which she founded in 1995 with Pamela Koffler, has as its logo a cartoon bunny with a target for a body, mischievously evoking the company’s blend of irreverence and danger. “I don’t think we’ve ever made a movie that somebody hasn’t been offended by,” Vachon said in 2000.Times change. Back then, Killer was on the brink of respectability thanks to Boys Don’t Cry, for which Hilary Swank won an Oscar for playing the murdered transgender man Brandon Teena. In 2024, Materialists director Celine Song’s gorgeous but conspicuously uncontroversial debut Past Lives became the first Killer film to receive a best picture Oscar nomination.View image in fullscreenDelinquent … Rosario Dawson and Chloë Sevigny in Kids.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyIt has been a while, then, since Killer was the industry’s scrappy outsider. “I sometimes say we’re the adults in the room,” Vachon tells me. Now 63, the tousle-haired, New York-based producer is speaking from a terrace overlooking the sea in Trouville-sur-Mer. She is visiting family here before heading to theEdinburgh film festivalfor the world premiere of Killer’s latest production, Pretty Babies. Written and directed by newcomer Tyler-Marie Evans, it follows two aspiring teenage actors who run off to Los Angeles, seduced by the glamour of old Hollywood, only to slide into sex work. It is rather as if Thelma and Louise’s road trip had taken them to David Lynch’s Mulholland Drive.double quotation markI’m not sure Joaquin would want to work with me againWhat makes Pretty Babies a Killer film? “We love to encourage stories that feel personal and provocative and have something to say,” says Vachon. “It was not as if Tyler’s script was utterly original in terms of the issues she was dealing with. But she approached them in an original way. She has a real point of view and she can speak about her work very well.” She can indeed: at a recent screening, Evans explained that she intends the movie “to show that sexually objectified young women ask themselves the same questions as Dostoevsky”.It is a confident, eye-catching debut but the likelihood of a controversy equal to Kids, which had viewers clutching their pearls at the sight of skateboarders having unprotected sex, appears slim. Would a new Kids have that effect now? “If you made the 2026 version, it probably would be shocking,” Vachon says. “Or you might say: All you’ve got to do is go on TikTok.”View image in fullscreenChristine Vachon at the Tribeca film festival in 2025Photograph: Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Tribeca FestivalPretty Babies fits the template by heralding an emerging talent. “One of the things we can do with a first-time film-maker is put our weight behind a project to give assurances to the financiers,” says Vachon, who produced the feature debuts of, among others, John Cameron Mitchell (Hedwig and the Angry Inch), American Psycho director Mary Harron (I Shot Andy Warhol) andTodd Haynes(Poison), whom Vachon met at Brown University in the late 1980s.Haynes’s debut, which interweaves three tales of transgression including a prison love story complete with graphic expectorating scene, won the grand jury prize at Sundance in 1991. That put Poison on the radar of rightwing US politicians with an axe to grind.“The film had received a National Endowment for the Arts grant,” says Vachon. “That triggered an eruption in Congress: ‘Your tax dollars are being used to fund a movie about homosexuals spitting in each other’s mouths and touching each other’s dicks!’ Suddenly there were lines around the block to see the film. Yes, the controversy helped. But what really helped was an under-represented audience getting to see itself on screen. It taught me that if you make a movie for the right amount of money for a specific audience, and only they show up to see it, you can still make your money back.”She has produced all Haynes’s work since then including the melodrama Far from Heaven and the forthcoming De Noche, which recently finished shooting. This drama about a volatile cop (Pascal) and a schoolteacher (Danny Ramirez) who flee 1930s LA together for Mexico has a stormy history. The project was the brainchild of its original star, Joaquin Phoenix, who brought to Haynes the idea of a gay, sexually-explicit period love story; the director then co-wrote the screenplay with Jon Raymond. Sets were built in Guadalajara, the crew assembled. Five days before shooting was due to begin in August 2024, Phoenix pulled out. Variety magazine estimated at the time that losses “could exceed seven figures”.View image in fullscreenCate Blanchett in Todd Haynes’s lesbian romance Carol.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyDid Vachon have any inkling of trouble ahead? “You know, I really didn’t,” she sighs. The reasons for Phoenix’s departure have not been made public, though an unnamed source told Variety that the actor got “cold feet”. Vachon took to social media to quell tittle-tattle: “If you are tempted to finger wag or admonish us that ‘that’s what you get for casting a straight actor’ – DON’T. This was HIS project that he brought to US.’”She is reluctant to discuss the details today, and won’t speak on the record about whether Phoenix will receive a credit on the movie he co-created and then sabotaged. “Look, I don’t know what happened. He decided he didn’t want to do it. And, you know, I went to Guadalajara with a mop.” For a while, the film was dead in the water. “It was the passion of Todd and Pedro that allowed us to move forward.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBusiness often overrules personal enmity in Hollywood. Even after Harvey Weinstein reportedly viciously insulted Haynes for refusing to partner with his company Miramax on Far from Heaven, Haynes and Vachon still teamed up with him on the kaleidoscopic Bob Dylan biopic I’m Not There and the lesbian romance Carol. So would Vachon work with Phoenix in the future? “I don’t know. That’s a difficult question to answer. I’m not sure Joaquin would want to work withmeagain.” She makes it sound as if she gave him hell – or will do when she sees him.The film historian Peter Biskind has written of Vachon’s “formidable temper” and claims she “was reputed to have terrorised the British crew” of Haynes’s 1998 glam-rock odyssey Velvet Goldmine. “That is so not true!” she protests. “Iwas terrorised bythem. A lot of the crew were old-school. We had a female director of photography, Maryse Alberti, and only now do I realise what she went through. Essentially it was: ‘We don’t want to work for this woman.’ Every day, I had to gird my loins.”View image in fullscreenTeo Yoo and Greta Lee in Past Lives.Photograph: Album/AlamyShe admits she had “a bigger temper” in the 1990s. “But I didn’t mind if people thought that, because it was so hard to be a female producer. You were damned either way: if you had a temper, you were a bitch, and if you didn’t, it meant people could walk all over you. Whereas if you were a man and you showed any sign of anger, you were commended for being tough.”Producers rarely become household names unless, like Weinstein, they are also criminals. The job can even be a source of derision, as anyone who has sat with an impatient cinema audience through interminable company logos and producer credits can attest. Pretty Babies lists three producers: Vachon, Jordan Wagner and one of its stars, Ashley Benson. No fewer than 36 other names – executive producers, associate producers and so on – clutter up the end titles.The question of who is entitled to a credit is, says Vachon, “a source of distress and consternation and real knock-down, drag-out fights. A movie like Pretty Babies has an unproven director and a provocative subject matter. If somebody’s willing to put their money at risk, a credit tends to be what they want in exchange.”I remind her of a line from David Mamet’s movie-business comedy State and Main: “An associate producer credit is what you give your secretary instead of a raise.” In return, Vachon signs off with another gag about the slippery, deal-making, belt-tightening line of work to which she has devoted her life. “How many producers does it take to change a lightbulb?” she asks. The answer: “Does it have to be a lightbulb?”Pretty Babies screened at Edinburgh international film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmEdinburgh film festivalFestivalsTodd HaynesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reunite | Music | The Guardian
description: Alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer created a feminist punk vernacular that’s still inspiring the likes of Olivia Rodrigo. They recall the clarity and conviction of their historic teenage exploits
Author: Jenn Pelly
Headline: Alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer created a feminist punk vernacular that’s still inspiring the likes of Olivia Rodrigo. They recall the clarity and conviction of their historic teenage exploits
Content: ‘I wanted people to feel what I was feeling’ … (L-R) Tracy Sawyer and Corin Tucker of Heavens to Betsy.Photograph: Chloe AftelView image in fullscreen‘I wanted people to feel what I was feeling’ … (L-R) Tracy Sawyer and Corin Tucker of Heavens to Betsy.Photograph: Chloe AftelMusicInterview‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reuniteJenn PellyAlongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer created a feminist punk vernacular that’s still inspiring the likes of Olivia Rodrigo. They recall the clarity and conviction of their historic teenage exploitsWed 19 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in June, a cut-and-paste photocopied flyer began appearing on telegraph poles around Portland, Oregon, promoting a DIY show by an apparently defunct band at an intimate community space. The band hadn’t mentioned it online, but hopeful fans bought every ticket anyway. Their bet paid off: the gig really was the first in 32 years for Heavens to Betsy, the pioneering feminist punk duo of drummer Tracy Sawyer and singer-guitarist Corin Tucker – the latter’s band beforeSleater-Kinneyunleashed her visceral vibrato unto the world. Tucker proudly made the flyer herself.Heavens to Betsy were barely out of high school when they played their very first show, 35 years ago this week, in Olympia, Washington, a two-song set as part of a now-mythical indie fest dubbed the International Pop Underground Convention. The festival also featured the likes of Fugazi, Bikini Kill and Melvins; meanwhile Heavens to Betsy had practised only a couple times. Before an audience of about 100, Sawyer was so terrified that all she could think was, “This has to be over soon.”This summer’s gig was less frightening, looking out on kids the same age that Tucker and Sawyer were when they started the band. “They were singing along to a lot of the songs,” Tucker, now 53, says on a video call from her home in Portland. “They knew all the words and were screaming them at the top of their lungs.” After the gig, Sawyer, 52, recalls from her yard in Oakland, California, “20-year-old kids came up to me and said, ‘I’m learning to play drums by listening to Heavens to Betsy records.’”View image in fullscreen‘I will decide my life’ … Sawyer (left) and Tucker.Photograph: Hannah SternsheinThose early-90s feminist-revenge songs – about body image, sexual abuse, abortion, periods, worker exploitation, defying a world that conditions women to be small – will underpin the band’s upcoming tour of the US, as well as Baby’s Gone, a new LP collecting a 1992 rare demo tape and two 7in EPs. That inventive eight-song demo was recorded by Molly Neuman of Bratmobile with a four-track she checked out of the media library from Evergreen State College in Olympia, and only circulated on around 100 cassettes dubbed by the band.Active from 1991 to 1994, Heavens to Betsy released one album, Calculated, and rounded out riot grrrl’s OG trifecta alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile (who have both reunited in recent years to rapturous crowds). Turning their spare setup into an extreme sound, Heavens to Betsy made songs that were emotional, fearsome and dead serious. “I will decide my life / No man is gonna rule my life,” they declared on Decide.Riot grrrl records and zines – which, in Tucker’s words, put academic feminist ideas into a teen-girl vernacular – have struck a chord with every subsequent generation, echoing through the DIY underground on to the 2010s defined by Tavi Gevinson’s Rookie magazine. Olivia Rodrigo claims it as an influence; Bikini Kill will play her women-led Daisy Chain Fields festival in California this month. But the enduring power of this incendiary music has always been how its rawness leaves the door open, telling fans that they could do this, too.Heavens to Betsy: Terrorist (live at Turn! Turn! Turn! in Portland) – videoHeavens to Betsy were originally signed to Kill Rock Stars. Last autumn, the label approached Tucker and Sawyer about a long-overdue wide release for the demo. “The whole thing felt like an impossible dream,” Tucker says. “I thought I had lost the physical master a long time ago.” But the label was able to make a new master from the cassette, and as they emailed back and forth, they slyly floated another idea: “And you guys could do a show, maybe?”“I think both of us were like, I don’t know!” Tucker laughs nervously.The duo had only kept in touch “a little bit”, Sawyer says, in the decades since their breakup; both are mothers of two. “I was apprehensive about the thought of playing these songs from when we were so young,” Sawyer admits. “Playing them now in our 50s felt daunting, like, does that even make sense? A whole lifetime has passed. But the more we talked, and the more I started listening to the songs again, it absolutely made sense.”Tucker hadn’t listened to some of those spartan demo recordings since the tape came out. “There’s a really particular voice with Heavens to Betsy, a way of writing a song that speaks to the clarity you have as a young person:This is wrong. This is not OK.I felt really energised and empowered by that voice coming back into my life,” she says. That invigorating clarity pierces Heavens to Betsy songs in bloodcurdling, teen-girl screams – which, Tucker concedes, she could not realistically pull off in 2026 and make it through a whole show. But she hopes her conviction will communicate that anger. “It’s really important to me that that comes across in a way that’s absolutely not softened for people,” Tucker says. “The voice of Heavens to Betsy was uncompromising, unfiltered and it never apologised for its rage and revenge-seeking.”Tucker and Sawyer first met as middle schoolers in Eugene, Oregon, bonding over REM, the Cure, and Depeche Mode at sleepovers. They saw shows constantly – the Replacements, Firehose – and watched the music documentary Athens, GA: Inside/Out relentlessly. Their fixation on the Athens scene – including REM and the likes of B-52’s and Pylon – incited what Tucker calls a “pretty bonkers” and penniless cross-country train trip in summer 1990. The pair rented an apartment for a month to “study the scene”, bought a drum kit, watched Pylon through the window of the 40 Watt Club (they were too young to enter), and dubbed themselves Heavens to Betsy.By the time Tucker arrived at Evergreen State College in Olympia that autumn, she had already crossed paths with Bratmobile singer and Girl Germs zinemaker Allison Wolfe, who hipped Tucker to the fiercely independent Oly scene. That year, Tucker made a film about local music and closely studied the bands she saw live: Beat Happening, Mecca Normal, Calamity Jane. Heavens to Betsy was still just an idea, but Tucker wrote lyrics to a song about menstruation and societal shame she called My Red Self. “I started telling people about our band when we hadn’t played a single show,” Tucker says. “Or had a practice. No songs either,” she laughs. “We had a concept.”View image in fullscreenHeavens to Betsy performing in Kentucky in 1992.Photograph: Courtesy of the bandThat’s an instructive blueprint. “You manifest it,” Sawyer offers.“And believe in it,” Tucker adds. “You have to create the world before anything else, and cling to it. That’s true about every creative idea: you need to commit to that world. And onceyoudo, then you can make it real for everyone else.”When they were asked to play “Girl Night” at the International Pop Underground Convention, they anxiously accepted and Tucker sprang into action: many of the songs on their demo were written in her childhood bedroom. Fugazi’s Ian MacKaye was so impressed by Heavens to Betsy’s live debut that he sought them out to shake their hands.“There was an openness to my voice that I think grabbed people right away,” Tucker says. “There wasn’t much filter between my emotions and my voice, so when I sang, it was really sad and angry at the same time. We kept our music really simple and focused. I wanted people to feel what I was feeling. People cried at that show. There was this movement of girls that were like,I need to talk about these things that we’re not supposed to talk about.I think my voice was just waiting for that door to open.”At the centre of Baby’s Gone is a taut, unflinching song called My Secret in which Tucker lucidly blasts an abuser. She had been influenced by the directness of Bikini Kill frontperson Kathleen Hanna’s writing. “I felt brave because of what was happening around us,” she says. “It made me realise that I needed to let out my own feelings about things that had happened to me. It put me in the position of power.” Sawyer’s minimal, pounding beat “created this shield and weapon”, Tucker adds. “I was able to harness that into a song about being sexually abused. It turned the tables on everything, and it let go of everything, and it also freaked everyone out. It was incredible. It changed my life in a way. I was able to open a door to how maybe the rest of my life was gonna go. I didn’t need to hold on to those feelings any more.”Heavens to Betsy’s songs were sometimes written in character, but informed by reality. The title track of Baby’s Gone narrates a young woman’s decision to have an abortion under conditions that leave her dead. “Back then, you couldn’t even say the word ‘abortion’, so there was a lot of euphemism around it,” Tucker says. “Young women had to deal with all of the consequences of heterosexual sex, which took all of the pressure off men in our society. I find that to be incredibly unfair.” Tucker wrote the song to ask, “What if the young woman who died having an abortion came back and wrote about her experience? What if a ghost came back and wrote the song? How would that make you feel?” She lets out a self-aware laugh.“Connecting with your rage and your anger, in a way that lets it out – it feels important,” she adds, especially in light of the current political nightmares. “The past few years have been awful, and we really don’t have a way to process it. Liking things on my phone doesn’t cut it for me.”The Baby’s Gone songs excavate trauma – “I want you to stay dead!” Tucker fumes at a memory – allowing the band’s one album, 1994’s grungier Calculated, to more explicitly claim power. “The first songs we wrote were really personal, and they were out of sheer necessity,” Tucker says. A few seem to describe vexed mother-daughter dynamics. “That relationship is always ripe for conflict,” she says. “Part of becoming a person in the world is differentiating yourself and saying, ‘No, I’m going to do things my way.’ Being a mom myself now, I’ve been on both sides of that, and it’s complicated.”View image in fullscreenTucker and Sawyer today.Photograph: Chloe AftelWe’ve spoken for an hour and a half when Sawyer has to leave for a work meeting (she has a job at a pet supply company). Tucker and I keep chatting. The Heavens to Betsy reunion has offered an opportunity to revisit the music as well as to rekindle their friendship. “Getting a second chance feels like a real gift,” she says. “I’ve really enjoyed getting to know what Tracy’s life has been like and what we have in common.” When they drifted apart after Calculated came out, something they blame on having poor communication skills at that age, Tucker had already formed Sleater-Kinney alongside Carrie Brownstein, then guitarist in queercore band Excuse 17, who Heavens to Betsy had toured with.Riot grrrl pioneer Kathleen Hanna: ‘A lot of men really get off on watching a woman get angry’Read moreTucker sounds not especially fazed by where Heavens to Betsy might fit into modern music. But I mention Wednesday’s Karly Hartzman, and she joyfully recalls a Portugal festival where she heard her scream from stage. She also brings up Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain fest: “It’s both cool and terribly sad that we’re still holding a rock show to try and talk about our needs instead of having the kind of cultural, political, and economic power that would give us full equality.”I ask about the lessons Tucker has gleaned from returning to this formative period of her life. “That courage you have as a young person to speak the truth and to find out what that means for you, that’s a really special thing to learn how to do, and it’s not always easy to maintain that when you’re becoming a mom and taking care of other people,” she says. “I do think there’s something really special about returning to Heavens to Betsy as my youngest goes off to college. I suddenly am rediscovering, what do I want, and who am I? There’s something very full circle about reconnecting with this voice that was like, ‘These are my feelings. This is my truth.’”Baby’s Gone is released via Kill Rock Stars on 16 October. Heavens to Betsy tour the US from 17 October.Explore more on these topicsMusicPunkIndieSleater-KinneyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Can anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was me | Katriona O'Sullivan | The Guardian
description: LBC’s Nick Ferrari can’t see what is stopping people buying a cheap toothbrush, but the grinding reality of living in poverty creates its own priorities, says psychologist, author and professor Dr Katriona O’Sullivan
Author: Katriona O'Sullivan
Headline: LBC’s Nick Ferrari can’t see what is stopping people buying a cheap toothbrush, but the grinding reality of living in poverty creates its own priorities, says psychologist, author and professor Dr Katriona O’Sullivan
Content: Illustration: Jess Clark/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jess Clark/The Guardian/Getty ImagesOpinionPovertyCan anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was meKatriona O'SullivanLBC’s Nick Ferrari can’t see what is stopping people buying a cheap toothbrush, but the grinding reality of living in poverty creates its own prioritiesWed 19 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTShareIdon’t listen to Nick Ferrari on LBC very often. His antagonistic way of dealing with complex problems gets me screaming at the radio far too easily. Last month was a perfect example. Someone from the Joseph Rowntree Foundation was on discussing research showing that about 7 million people arestruggling to afford basic essentials, including toothpaste and toothbrushes, because of the cost of living crisis.This did not strike me as a controversial finding.
