The cost of fuel, heating, food, school, clothes – everything – has gone up, while wages and benefits have not risen enough to keep pace. Ferrari, however, latched on to the toothbrushes. I found myself listening to him talk about the price of cheap toothbrushes in pound shops and at Asda. At times, it sounded like a price-comparison advert. At other times, it sounded like lazy journalism: take a complicated issue, strip it of all context and turn it into something that will generate outrage, clicks and applause.Had I been on the show, I would have brought both my lived experience and my academic knowledge to the argument. I would have explained why a person living in poverty might buy cheap wine instead of a cheap toothbrush.The first thing I would have talked to Ferrari about is decision-making. How we decide what to buy, what not to buy and where to spend our money is shaped by far more than price. One of the first questions we ask, often without realising it, is whether the thing we are buying will help us now or later.You know those people who buy 48 toilet rolls because they are on special offer? They can look ahead and think: spending more now will save me money later. Psychologists might describe this as delayed gratification. It requires the ability to resist an immediate need or reward in order to benefit in the future.Stress makes that much harder. When people are under constant pressure, they tend to focus on the here and now. What can I fix today? What problem is shouting loudest? What can make things feel slightly better for the next few hours? A toothbrush is an investment in the future. So is going for a run. So is buying healthier food that costs more and takes longer to prepare. The benefit is delayed.Poverty, on the other hand, creates urgent problems. The debt collector is knocking at your door for his money. The electricity is about to run out. The school is asking for payment for a trip. Your son is being bullied because he is wearing cheap trainers instead of Nikes. These things feel immediate. The possible dental problems caused by not replacing a toothbrush feel far away. That does not make the decision sensible. It makes it human.Long-term planning becomes more difficult during periods of stress. It is also shaped by how and where you grow up. If you are raised in an environment where life feels unstable and the future feels uncertain, it can bemuch harder to believethat sacrificing today will bring a reward tomorrow. According to some studies, growing up poor can even affect thedevelopment of your brain– the areas associated with reward are more active than those responsible for reasonable decision-making.That is part of the reason poverty is associated with higher levels of addiction and criminality. Not because poor people are naturally reckless or immoral, but because deprivation, stress and hopelessness shape our brains and our behaviour.Had I been sitting opposite Ferrari, I might have asked him whether he had ever been told to change his habits. Most of us have struggled to change something about ourselves, even when we knew exactly what we were supposed to do. If making the right choice were simply a matter of knowing what was best, we would all eat the salad, go for the run, stop smoking, drink less and buy the toothbrush.But human beings do not make decisions like machines. Our choices are influenced by stress, habit, upbringing, perceptions of self-worth, addiction, fear, exhaustion and whether we believe there is any point in planning for the future. I know this because I have made the choice not to buy toothpaste many times.I did not do that because I was stupid or a bad person. I did it because ofhow I lived, how I grew up and how I felt about myselfshaped what I believed was worth spending money on. My parents did not brush their teeth or ours. Looking after your teeth was not something I had been taught to value. I had such low self-worth that my own health was often the last thing on my mind.The same was true of sanitary products. When I was living on around £35 a week benefits in the 1990s, I sometimes bought three bottles of Diamond White rather than spending 50p on tampons. You might judge me for that. But when you live in shit, when nobody seems to care about you and you have stopped caring about yourself, a few bottles can feel like an escape. It felt easier to stuff my knickers with toilet roll from the cash-in-hand job I worked and have one night away from the misery than to sit sober with the constant belief that I was failing myself and my son. At times, it felt like the choice was three bottles or dying.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat may seem hard to understand when your life has always contained safety, options and hope. But all you have to do is ask yourself one important question – would anyone choose that type of life if they could choose another? The answer to that is simple.I am glad I stayed alive long enough to learn that poverty is not created by the bad choices of poor people. It is created and maintained by systems that leave people without security, support or genuine options – and by powerful people who reduce those lives to lazy tropes that reinforce stereotypes about irresponsibility. You cannot call something a choice when the alternatives are not equally available.Putting a 49p toothbrush on a supermarket shelf does not mean everyone has the money, the stability, the knowledge or the headspace to buy it. Availability is not the same as access, and access is not the same as capacity.Of course, people should buy toothbrushes. But repeating the price of one as though it disproves poverty is not analysis. It is ignorance dressed up as common sense. Choice is far more complicated than that. I think choice is a myth for many people; it is an idea that is inflicted on poor people by people in positions of power so they don’t have to do anything to help.Dr Katriona O’Sullivan is a psychologist, author and professor at Maynooth University. She is the author of the bestselling memoirsPoorandHungry, and is a weekly columnist for the Irish IndependentDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Reform says we need to choose between climate and economy. It’s wrong | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: The party’s deputy leader Richard Tice says we should stop worrying about extreme heat and enjoy it. This dangerous nonsense will wreck our finances and the planet, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: The party’s deputy leader Richard Tice says we should stop worrying about extreme heat and enjoy it. This dangerous nonsense will wreck our finances and the planet, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: Wheat in a field in Cheshire. Most of England and Wales is in drought, affecting harvests.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWheat in a field in Cheshire. Most of England and Wales is in drought, affecting harvests.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisReform says we need to choose between climate and economy. It’s wrongLarry ElliottThe party’s deputy leader Richard Tice says we should stop worrying about extreme heat and enjoy it. This dangerous nonsense will wreck our finances and the planetWed 19 Aug 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.23 EDTShareSo now we know: the smart response to the UK’s summer of record temperatures is to do precisely nothing.According to Richard Tice, Reform UK’s deputy leader, the climate crisis is just one of those things. Nothing can be done about it, so we should simply bask in the sunshine.It is reasonable to assume Tice would not have said anything quite as crass had he been addressing people in Stourbridge who haveseen their homes burn to the ground. Or the farmers whose crops shrivelin parched fields. Or thefirefighters exhausted from battling wildfires across Britain.Yet Tice clearly thinks he is on to something. The cost of living crisis has put the government’s commitmentto achieving net zero by 2050under the spotlight. The assumption underlying Tice’s comments is that there is a trade-off between tackling the climate emergency and raising, or even maintaining, living standards – and that for the time being, the latter should take priority.The government has certainly been acting as if it believes this is the case. While the droughtaffecting most of England and Walesmakes the strongest possible case for hastening the green transition, Andy Burnham’s focus has been on reducing prices for consumers, including bycutting VAT on electricity bills.It took the prime minister an awfully long time to use the words “climate change” to explain this summer’s heatwaves. He did so only after the devastating fires in Stourbridge and whenprodded by a letter from green groupscalling on him to end his silence.Burnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big risk | Gaby HinsliffRead moreAt one level, the emphasis on putting cash in people’s pockets makes sense. Traditionally, interest in the environment waxes during periods of strong economic growth and wanes when times are tough. Climate breakdown slips down the list of priorities for voters when they are worried about losing their jobs or struggling to pay their bills. Peaks in concern have tended to come at the end of long booms, such as the early 1970s or the late 1980s.But opinions are changing across the political spectrum. As the Conservative peer David Willettshas pointed out, 86% of Britons see climate breakdownas at least partly responsiblefor the recent heatwaves, and even 63% of net zero opponents make that connection. More than a third of Reform UK voters said tackling climate breakdownshould be more of a priorityin a recent poll.There are good reasons for the high level of public concern. The rate of food price inflation has also been coming down in recent months, but a poor harvest means that trend could well go into reverse soon.Meanwhile,a reportby the German insurance company Allianz has exploded the myth that governments have a choice between growth and the environment. The study shows that extreme heat poses structural challenges to many rich countries because, as temperatures rise above 30C, workers struggle to do their jobs and their productivity suffers. The higher the thermometer rises, the greater the losses.For the most exposed countries – especially those in continental Europe – the hit to economic activity will be considerable: over a five-year period the impact of extreme heat could knock a cumulative 5-7% off GDP.According to Allianz, the UK has hitherto been below the 30C threshold and has not been one of the countries at risk from extreme heat. But on the basis of this summer, Britain may soon become a higher-risk country alongside France and Spain.To be sure, Britain is responsible for only a small fraction of the world’s CO2 emissions, and there is a legitimate debate about how to achieve net zero. But the warning signs are flashing red. Now is not the time to go slow on tackling climate breakdown. The longer that action – global as well as domestic – is delayed, the greater the risk that the climate crisis will eventually wreck the economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA failure to invest in basic infrastructure needs to be remedied fast. People faced with hosepipe bans have the right to ask whyBritain has not built a reservoir in 30 years. The electricity grid was designed and built for fossil fuels rather than renewables, andmany green projects are held upby a lack of capacity.The UK’s housing stock is woefully inefficient. Household bills would be lower if existing homes were retrofitted with insulation. New homes should be subject to tougher building regulations to make mechanical ventilation – which keeps temperatures stable year-round – mandatory.None of this comes cheap. The state will have to invest in new infrastructure as well as making changes to the planning laws. Subsidies will be required to provide incentives for consumers to go green. No question, there are costs involved in the net zero transition, but they are outweighed by the benefits. These include cheaper running costs for electric vehicles and lower energy bills for homes where gas boilers are replaced by heat pumps.Governments can always find the money when the occasion dictates. When the security of the nation is at risk, ways to finance extra spending are found. To take one example, ministers havecommitted to raising defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035because of the perceived threat from Russia.But which is the greater threat? Is it Russia, bogged down in Ukraine after more than four years of attritional fighting, or is it the climate crisis? The answer should be obvious.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionRichard TiceReform UKEnvironment policyWildfiresGreenhouse gas emissionscommentShareReuse this content

title: Reform politicians are such a joke, they deserve a slot on the Edinburgh fringe | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Nige’s gift, Dicky’s love of global heating and so much more – what fun it is watching the party implode
Author: John Crace
Headline: Nige’s gift, Dicky’s love of global heating and so much more – what fun it is watching the party implode
Content: Nigel Farage’s one-man band has come to resemble an an anarchic end–of-the pier clown show.Photograph: Dinendra Haria/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNigel Farage’s one-man band has come to resemble an an anarchic end–of-the pier clown show.Photograph: Dinendra Haria/SOPA Images/ShutterstockThe politics sketchReform UKReform politicians are such a joke, they deserve a slot on the Edinburgh fringeJohn CraceNige’s gift, Dicky’s love of global heating and so much more – what fun it is watching the party implodeWed 19 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTShareYou would need to have a heart of stone not to fall about laughing. There was a time not so long ago when Reform could give a passable impression of a vaguely functional political party. One that knew its audience and had learned how to get its message across through the media. Admittedly this was largely because the party was a one-man band with all its MPs accepting that they owed their entire existence to Nige. They were satellites to his sun.Nigel Faragewas Reform, and Reform was Nige.In recent months, though, things have been falling apart and Reform now resembles an anarchic end-of-the-pier clown show. And chaos has seldom been this entertaining. The fun started when Nige had an uncharacteristic fit of humility and tried to pretend he was only a first among equals with the grandiose announcement of a “shadow cabinet” of four people. Largely because that’s about as many serious politicians as he had at his disposal.The trouble with this was the country took one look at Robert Jenrick, Suella Braverman,Richard Ticeand Zia Yusuf and thought it must be a joke. Was that really it? The idea of any of them in charge of a government department was genuinely terrifying. And Zia can’t even get elected as an MP. It’s doubtful any Reform constituency association wants anything to do with him. He’s a man whom people dislike on sight – it saves time that way – and who appeared to have been admitted to the Reform elite only because he had a lot of money that he was prepared to give to the party.That was just the start, though. Then came the money troubles. The£5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harbornethat Nige has never satisfactorily managed to explain. Other than as the going rate for a lifestyle most of his Clacton constituents could only dream of. There were also the financial transactions that originated from Posh George and his mum that were deemed worthy of investigation for money laundering. Hardly the stuff of the man of the people. As for Nige’s decision to call a diversionary byelection, that too has backfired spectacularly. Beating a man with a bin on his head was hardly sticking it to the establishment.With Nige having taken to lying low, Reform appears to be in freefall. Its latest circus act has been to suspend one of its most prominent members,Tim Montgomerie, and for the row to become public. Montgomerie was about as loyal to Reform as someone who defected from the Tories a while ago could be. Which is to say, he was as close to being a loyalist as you can get. He actually believes in what the party is doing, rather than using it for career advancement.Though, for a bright man, Tim has been extraordinarily dim. He thought that when Nige had told him he wanted intelligent voices to challenge his ideas, he had actually meant it. Forgetting that Nige is a narcissist through and through who can’t tolerate a word of criticism. When Nige says he wants to test his ideas, what he actually has in mind is a few emails from Tim telling him how marvellous he is. As Dicky Tice will tell you, the only safe place with Nige is when your head is firmly implanted in his bum.Even so, Tim might have survived if he had contented himself with just sending a few unwanted messages to Nige. But Tim is a believer who can’t keep quiet. He’s a top rent-a-gob on the rent-a-gob media merry-go-round. Seldom off the radio or TV. So Tim made no effort to hide his dissatisfaction with Zia. In particular, he didn’t like the way Zia appeared to be enjoying himself when he was announcing ever more extreme ways to control immigration. It wasn’t that Tim didn’t believe in the policies. He just thought Reform should appear to adopt them with a heavy heart.Things get even more tricky for Dicky Tice, the Reform deputy with lots of cash but zero self-awarenessRead moreThis was a bad category error. Tim should have realised that taking pleasure in being unpleasant to foreigners is central to Reform’s appeal. When Zia suggests he wouldn’t mind firing shots into the small boats or starting a war with France, he is only saying what other members of Reform are thinking. The word made flesh. Reform isn’t about Making Britain Great Again. It’s about bringing the fun back into politics. Making the profane sacred.But this wasn’t even Tim’s biggest mistake. That was to imagine he was allowed to utter a word of criticism, no matter how helpfully intended. The rules on this are strict. Only Nige is allowed to fall out with other members of the Reform inner circle. He makes the rules as he goes along. What’s acceptable one day may not be so the next. So it’s quite possible that Nige is equally fed up with Zia but isn’t ready to do anything about it. Tim should have learned to keep his mouth shut. And he has found himself learning the hard way.In the meantime, Zia has been rushing on his run. Perhaps realising that his time in Reform may be limited and determined to take the party down with him. Not caring whom he offends in his efforts to settle a few scores. Just the other day he posted on X that those MPs with the title “right honourable” were generally the most dishonourable people he knew. Now, you might think that was a dig at some Labour and Tory privy councillors, but it can’t have escaped his attention that two of them are Honest Bob and Suella. He is starting his own civil war.And it’s catching on. Albeit in Dicky’s case almost certainly by accident. Because Nige’s silence has allowed Dicky to imagine he has a mind of his own. Which, of course, he doesn’t. So that’s why he has been holding press conferences in which he has been happy to embarrass himself and make Reform look stupid. For instance, byappearing to welcome the climate crisis, with the suggestion we should all be taking advantage of the drought by embracing food insecurity and increased deaths among the over-60s.But in an otherwise quiet August, they are doing us a favour with some of the best entertainment on offer. Next year they should try the Edinburgh fringe.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchNigel FarageTim MontgomerieRichard TicecommentShareReuse this content

title: All power to the UK competition watchdog’s war on ‘drip pricing’ | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Competition and Markets Authority on message with PM’s planned purge of hidden fees and add-on charges
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Competition and Markets Authority on message with PM’s planned purge of hidden fees and add-on charges
Content: Shares in Trainline, the only listed company on the Competition and Markets Authority’s investigation list, plunged by 14% on Wednesday.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenShares in Trainline, the only listed company on the Competition and Markets Authority’s investigation list, plunged by 14% on Wednesday.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersNils Pratley on financeCompetition and Markets AuthorityAll power to the UK competition watchdog’s war on ‘drip pricing’Nils PratleyCompetition and Markets Authority on message with PM’s planned purge of hidden fees and add-on chargesTrainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School face investigationWed 19 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is on-message with Andy Burnham’sdeclaration of waron the small – and sometimes not-so-small – hassles and expenses of everyday consumer life created by companies’ underhand and misleading pricing tactics. Trainline,Virgin Atlanticand Red Driving Schoolfound themselves under investigationon Wednesday for various forms of alleged“drip pricing”– not being upfront about mandatory add-on charges, in other words.The prime minister had nothing to do with the CMA’s pursuit, it should be said. The watchdog’s“consumer protection drive”pre-dates his arrival and was encouraged by legislation under the last Tory government – the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act of 2024, which gave the regulator “direct enforcement” powers, meaning it no longer had to go to court under consumer protection laws. And it is using those powers: eight cases were opened last November and driving schools AA and BSM plus theticketing site StubHub UK have already been fined.This is very welcome. Putting a few household names in the spotlight sends a usefully strong message. By way of boosting that signal, shares in Trainline, the only quoted company on Wednesday’s list, plunged by 14%.View image in fullscreenVirgin Atlantic has been placed under investigation by the UK’s consumer watchdog.Photograph: Trevisan Aviation Images/AlamyIt’s merely an investigation at this stage, so one can’t draw conclusions, but there was a curious line in Trainline’s statement. “Trainline has proactively engaged with the CMA over several months and is taking steps to enhance the presentation of certain fees,” it said.The obvious question is why, if the regulator has been on the warpath for months, Trainline didn’t just give it everything it wanted on day one. Regular users of the slick app know there can be a fee at the end of the booking process (for about 30% of journeys), so they are unlikely to be deterred by a message to that effect displayed prominently at the outset.There may be complicating details. Trainline adds its value for consumers by navigating the hellishly complicated fare structures on Britain’s railways by, for example, identifying so-called “split tickets” (multiple tickets covering legs of a single journey) or cases where an obscure railcard will almost pay for itself. If Trainline’s fee depends on the type of ticket, perhaps it’s not possible to state the fee precisely until the punter has chosen.But such dry technicalities were, presumably, mentioned in the months of engagement with the CMA. So it would be fair for Trainline shareholders to ask how this affair has even reached the stage of a formal investigation by a regulator with the power to order refunds and fine 10% of turnover. It’s not as if large sums are involved – the CMA said it observed transactions with additional fees ranging from 50p to £2.79.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo repeat, no wrongdoing has been found. But the investigation comes at a bad moment as Trainline waits to see if the state, in the form of the newGreat British Railways, gets round to launching a rival fee-free ticketing app. A regulatory quarrel over transparency is the last thing it needs.Explore more on these topicsCompetition and Markets AuthorityNils Pratley on financeConsumer affairsConsumer rightsAndy BurnhamRegulatorsRail farescommentShareReuse this content

title: At 43, I was fit and happy. Then I developed a nasty – and very expensive – case of shingles | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Healthy women under 50 are now more at risk of the condition. What I didn’t know is that intense exercise could be to blame and the condition could cost me hundreds of dollars, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Healthy women under 50 are now more at risk of the condition. What I didn’t know is that intense exercise could be to blame and the condition could cost me hundreds of dollars, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘I was getting pretty jacked.’Photograph: Posed by model; FG Trade/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I was getting pretty jacked.’Photograph: Posed by model; FG Trade/Getty ImagesOpinionHealthAt 43, I was fit and happy. Then I developed a nasty – and very expensive – case of shinglesArwa MahdawiHealthy women under 50 are now more at risk of the condition. What I didn’t know is that intense exercise could be to blame and the condition could cost me hundreds of dollarsWed 19 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTShareIf you’re in your 40s, I have a great trick for getting people to spontaneously tell you how young you are: develop shingles. Friends, acquaintances and medical professionals will rapidly inform you that the painful rash is an older person’s disease and, “You’re a bit young to get that, aren’t you?”I say this because at the tender age of 43, I have come down with a horrible case of ocular shingles. When I first went to urgent care about a weird red spot on my nose, a swollen eye and a terrible headache, the nurse looked dubious when he told me it might be shingles. “You’re a bit young,”he said. When I then went to the ER as instructed – shingles near the eye is a medical emergency that can blind you – the ophthalmologist said the same thing. According to conventional medical wisdom, shingles is a disease you get if you’re elderly or immunocompromised.But that wisdom is outdated. Shingles is becoming significantly more prevalent among immunocompetent people under 50 globally, particularly women. Funnily enough, just a few days before I got sick, I’d read apiece in the Guardianabout the worrying rise of shingles among millennial women. Nobody knows exactly why this is happening, but one of many theories is that we’re all chronically stressed. It seems my shingles case means I am very much on trend. So is my wife: she got shingles two years ago, age 41, on her back. Which is bad but, as I keep informing her, not as bad as getting it ON YOUR EYELID. Not that it’s a competition.I don’t want to stress you out, but there’s a good chance that shingles could happen to you, if it hasn’t already. If you’ve had chickenpox or even the chickenpox vaccine, you can get it. The varicella-zoster virus which causes chickenpox lurks in your body until your immune system lets its guard down; then it unleashes itself upon your nervous system, causing a painful and itchy rash that blisters and, if you’re unlucky, long-lasting nerve pain. The Danish word for the condition ishelvedesild, (“hell fire”) and pretty much sums it up: I have never experienced pain like shingles. One minute I felt like someone was striking my head with an ice pick, the next my face was on fire. If you’re eligible for the vaccine, you should get one immediately.The funny thing about my hot shingles summer is that, just before the pox, I thought I’d never been healthier. My diet was decent, I’d cut down on alcohol, and I was at the gym all the time. Not to boast (OK, just a little boast), but I was getting pretty jacked. It’s possible, however, that going hard in the gym might have played a part in the shingles: some have reported that intense exercise was a trigger for them. It may also have been Karma. Literally. My neighbour’s cat Karma (a cutetroublemaker), had been stressing me out by bleeding all over my patio thanks to a wound that kept opening. I was worried about Karma, but also about my furniture.Thankfully, I started antivirals early enough to avoid vision issues and, two weeks after the rash started, I’m almost feeling normal again. But, while all ended well, the experience left me depressed about US healthcare. The reason I went to a walk-in urgent care clinic first is because it’s hard to get a same-day doctor appointment. Then, after leaving that clinic, I waited in the ER for five hours. (In Philadelphia, no less – home to some of the best medical institutions in the country.) One of my compatriots in the waiting room told me she’d been there for 10 hours on her last visit. A key talking point against socialised medicine in the US is that it would result in long waits. But I’m sure I would have seen a doctor sooner if this had happened in the UK.More importantly, I wouldn’t be stressing about medical bills like I am now. My bill was $2,496, just for an ER visit, where I was seen in a hallway because it was so crowded. Insurance paid $838 and now I’m on the hook for $1,658. That’son topof the $783 a month for health insurance my wife pays for our family of three. That’s just her contribution: her employer pays the rest. And who knows what my follow-up ophthalmologist visits are going to cost. So while my eye is fine, I’ve got a feeling this painful ordeal is going to cost me an arm and a leg.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionHealth insuranceImmunologyMedical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicated | Bernie Sanders | The Guardian
description: Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged
Author: Bernie Sanders
Headline: Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged
Content: ‘The very rich get richer, while working families struggle.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The very rich get richer, while working families struggle.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersOpinionUS politicsWhy are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicatedBernie SandersPoll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is riggedWed 19 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTShareThe media pundits have written article after article desperately trying to understand why progressive candidates, despite being heavily outspent, keep defeating establishmentDemocratsin primaries around the country. Well, the answer is not complicated.Whether it is a corrupt campaign finance system, unprecedented income and wealth inequality, a broken and wildly expensive healthcare system, the enormous threats posed by AI or an immoral and destructive foreign policy, progressives are talking about the real issues facing working families. And they are providing real solutions. Establishment Democrats are not.Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged. The very rich get richer, while working families struggle. Today, while 60% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good.Trump has made our K-shaped economy even worse | Steven GreenhouseRead moreWe now have more income and wealth inequality than at any time in American history. The top 1% now own more wealth than the bottom 93% and one man, Elon Musk, owns more wealth than the bottom 50% of US households.Not surprisingly, working families are tired of status quo politics and the same old, same old establishment policies that have failed them for years. They want change, real change – and are supporting progressive candidates who are fighting for that change.In the richest country in the history of the world, Americans do not want to have to struggle every single day just to pay the bills. Working-class people do not want to die years younger than they should because of illnesses caused by the never-ending stress they experience just to survive. And, like past generations, they do not want their kids to have a lower standard of living than they do.Establishment politicians and the establishment media have described the agenda that progressive candidates are winning elections on as “radical”, “far left”, “extremist” or, in the words of Donald Trump, “communist” . All that is nonsense. On major issue after major issue, the progressive agenda is reflecting exactly what a strong majority of the American people need and want.Let me take this opportunity to share with you some of the major proposals that most progressives support. And you tell me how “extreme” they are.Campaign finance reformProgressives believe that our current campaign finance system is corrupt and is undermining democracy. It is absurd that one man, Mr Musk, can spend $290m to help elect Donald Trump as president and that billionaires in both parties can spend unlimited amounts of money in campaigns through theirSuper Pacs.We believe that we must end the disastrous US supreme court decision on Citizens United, ban Super Pacs and move to the public funding of elections. We believe that democracy means one person one vote, not billionaires buying elections.The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | EditorialRead moreHealthcareProgressives believe that our current healthcare system is broken, dysfunctional and wildly expensive. We believe that it is immoral and fiscally irresponsible for us to spend roughly twice as much per capita on healthcare as do the people of other major countries, while 85 million Americans remain uninsured or underinsured.At the same time, we pay, by far, the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs. Progressives believe that healthcare is a human right and that we should do what all other major countries on Earth do, guarantee healthcare to all people. We agree with the 64% of Americans who want a Medicare for all single payer system.Protecting American workersProgressives believe that all Americans are entitled to a decent standard of living. We regard it as outrageous that in the year 2026 millions of workers continue to earn starvation wages and that the federal minimum wage remains at a disgraceful $7.25 an hour. We believe that the federal minimum wage should be raised to a living wage of at least $20 per hour.We also believe that employers should no longer be able to deny workers their constitutional right to join unions through illegal actions. Progressives support the passage of the Pro Act which will make it easier for workers to join unions and negotiate contracts that will provide them with better wages, benefits and working conditions.Tax the richProgressives believe that, at a time of unprecedented income and wealth inequality, the wealthiest people in this country must start paying their fair share of taxes. At a time when we have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any major country on Earth and when one-third of our senior citizens are struggling economically, it is absurd that billionaires have an effective tax rate lower than truck drivers or nurses.The wealthiest people in this country and large profitable corporations must start paying their fair share of taxes so that we can adequately fund the needs of working families, the children and the elderly.Regulation of AIProgressives believe that AI and robotics, developed and pushed by the wealthiest people on Earth, are the most transformational technologies in the history of humanity and that they will impact every man, woman and child in our country.At a time when AI is threatening to displace millions of workers, eviscerate our privacy, harm our environment, undermine our democracy and negatively impact the mental health of our children, we believe that the government must play a decisive role in making sure that these revolutionary technologies are used to benefit all Americans, and not just make the big tech oligarchs even richer.Climate changeProgressives believe that Trump’s assertion that climate change is a “hoax” is not only extraordinarily ignorant, but is a real danger to the planet. The last 11 years have been the hottest 11 years on record and the last three years have been the hottest three years on record.This past year the United States and countries throughout the world have seen major heatwaves, flash floods, increased drought and horrific forest fires – and scientists tell us the worst is yet to come.The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone | EditorialRead moreProgressives believe that we must forcefully take on the greed of the fossil fuel industry. The truth is that we can create millions of good-paying union jobs by transforming our energy systems away from fossil fuels and into energy efficiency and sustainable energy. For the sake of our kids, future generations and the habitability of the planet that is what we must do.Foreign policyProgressives believe that we need to fundamentally reform our foreign and military policies. The war in Vietnam was based on a lie. The war in Iraq was based on a lie. The current war in Iran is based on a lie. We do not need to spend $1.5tn a year on the Pentagon fighting endless wars and propping up dictatorships around the world.We certainly do not have to invest tens of billions supporting the extremist Netanyahu government in Israel, which has killed 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 173,000 more – the vast majority of them women, children and the elderly.Despite what the media will have you believe, progressives are winning across this country for a simple reason: the ideas they are running on are extremely popular. It’s time for the political establishment to stop telling the American people what they should believe and start listening to what they actually want.Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of CongressExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionBernie SandersDemocratsUS economyAI (artificial intelligence)Climate crisisUS foreign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: A rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalism  | Hugh Muir | The Guardian
description: Amid the grief and rage at a tragic loss, it’s right to differentiate between those who fought a culture war and others who just sought the truth, says Hugh Muir, executive editor, Opinion
Author: Hugh Muir
Headline: Amid the grief and rage at a tragic loss, it’s right to differentiate between those who fought a culture war and others who just sought the truth, says Hugh Muir, executive editor, Opinion
Content: A vigil for Jason Arday in Trafalgar Square, London, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA vigil for Jason Arday in Trafalgar Square, London, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionJason ArdayA rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalismHugh MuirAmid the grief and rage at a tragic loss, it’s right to differentiate between those who fought a culture war and others who just sought the truthWed 19 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 03.06 EDTShareEven now it is very difficult to process the scale of tragedy that engulfedJason Ardayand those who loved him. The unbearable sadness at his death; the wretched knowledge that the very public onslaught against him began with the malign machinations of a self-defined “race realist” – who believes that, in an ideal world, black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. The horror that a rightwing and far-right campaign seeking a victim to fuel its nativist prejudices can now crow that it found one.There is wide and profound grief and of course there is rage, focused and unfocused. Both were on display as thousandsjoined a protest vigil in Trafalgar Squareon Monday evening.His family – in a moving statement remembering an “amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son” – has said he was “subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor atCambridge Universityby those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him”. This we know. The right and far-right desire to identify and then defenestrate anyone or anything that could be seen as symbolic of progress is virtually pathological. The rightwing media, in a quiet summer – a quarry identified – led a charge that meant Prof Arday’s face was disobligingly displayed on almost every front page, every TV screen, for weeks. His family, who knew him best, are clear about what that ultimately meant for a man who was neurodivergent and by the end – according to reports – desolate. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”This stokes high emotions. A high-profile, successful black figure is something highly prized. Many attest to the professor’s kindness and the care he lavished on those he was responsible for and, through access programmes, on others he never really knew. Many others feel the very human protective emotion of anger, having witnessed a successful but vulnerable man manoeuvred into the crosshairs. They voiced their rage in Trafalgar Square. It bristles, too, on social media.The culture-war right did what it does, but what of others in politics and other media? The right in its hostile, partisan pursuit nevertheless uncovered doubts about the professor’s academic work – accusations of plagiarism – that could not be satisfactorily dismissed. The professor himself made public claims about his life and achievements that could not be verified. Of course that was a good thing for those who, for racist and political reasons, sought to denigrate him, but wasn’t that also a legitimate concern for those who bore him no ill will – indeed cheered his ascent – but see the importance of integrity in academia and public life?Amid the pain and understandable rage in recent days, there has been invective levelled at the right, but also a deal of social-media abuse levelled at progressive journalists – notably black journalists, and especially Guardian journalists who interrogated and reported on the claims made about and by the professor. There have been attempts to load them with at least partial responsibility for his death. Suggestions that, with their actions, they have betrayed their heritage: that they personally should be for ever haunted by his fate. One can try to be understanding and frame this as part of the outpouring of grief, but that makes those attacks no less corrosive, no less hurtful to the journalists themselves.There is a particular tension to being a black or minority journalist in a white-majority culture, whether here or in the US, Europe or Australia. As a minority citizen, one shares the joys and pains and achievements of others. Very many in their work focus on the particular concerns of minorities coping and maybe thriving on challenging terrain. They are not fated to do so, but these matters interest them and many see who they are and what they know, juxtaposed with the skills they have as journalists, as an ideal way to make a contribution to society.In my reporting career, I have covered domestic politics, international politics, international conflict – the whole gamut of journalistic subjects – but I drew great pride from being the recipient of the first Commission for Racial EqualityRacein the Media award in the national newspaper category. I worked as a community affairs correspondent for the BBC for the duration of Sir William Macpherson’s landmark inquiry into the murder of Stephen Lawrence, explaining the intricacies of that historic event to millions on radio and TV. It is not a motivation exclusive to black journalists, but the vast majority I have known and worked with tend to hope that their professionalism will somehow make a positive difference to and for their communities, and to wider society’s understanding of their communities.But here’s the thing: we are journalists. We are not activists. Often we work with activists and I am very proud to have done so. Often our hopes and agendas coincide, and when they do, injustices are exposed, wrongs are righted, sometimes laws and attitudes are changed, but we are adjacent, we are not the same. Activists vary, but almost by definition they seek a means to an end. A good journalist lays out facts. Sometimes those facts push that end further away; sometimes they are unpalatable.And so, if it appears that a prominent figure – be they black or white – is being less than honest in ways that meet the test of public interest, those black journalists have a right, indeed a duty, to interrogate that. I know well some of those who did so in the case of Prof Arday, carefully and professionally, and are now, amid the anger, confusion and rage, being abused and castigated for it. They were not responsible for what Lord Chris Smith, the Cambridge University chancellor, called the “racist feeding frenzy”. They, in interrogating all the claims in a way we would expect professional, responsible, empathetic journalists to do, just did their jobs. As journalists. Even the bits that made them sad, that were unpalatable. And what if they hadn’t? Was all of the reporting and inquiry to be done by the right, by those who coveted a scalp, by culture warriors?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere will be questions to ask in the weeks to come, about the institutions involved in Prof Arday’s career, about the claims that were made for and against him, about the media coverage – all of it – in its tone and scale, about whether there could and should have been more recognition of the professor’s vulnerability under the barrage of headlines and attention. There arecalls for a public inquiry. We will all be soul-searching.Those questions should be posed – a man has died – but we cannot yet know the answers. Those who seek them are right to. Those who mourn him should have space to respectfully do so. As for those who mark his passing by arbitrarily pointing the finger at others who also grieve his loss – don’t.Hugh Muir is executive editor, OpinionIn the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayOpinionRaceUniversity of CambridgeHigher educationNewspapersNewspapers & magazinescommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Grenfell Tower fire: Britain is letting companies pass the buck | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Victims received less compensation than shareholders in the company behind its flammable cladding. Parliament must make corporations pay for harm caused
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Victims received less compensation than shareholders in the company behind its flammable cladding. Parliament must make corporations pay for harm caused
Content: Tributes are seen on the fence surrounding the remains of Grenfell Tower ahead of the ninth anniversary of the fire that killed 72 people in June 2017.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTributes are seen on the fence surrounding the remains of Grenfell Tower ahead of the ninth anniversary of the fire that killed 72 people in June 2017.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionGrenfell Tower fireThe Guardian view on the Grenfell Tower fire: Britain is letting companies pass the buckEditorialVictims received less compensation than shareholders in the company behind its flammable cladding. Parliament must make corporations pay for harm causedWed 19 Aug 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThere is something profoundly wrong when the company behind Grenfell Tower’s flammable cladding paid more compensation to its shareholders than to victims of the disaster. Of Arconic’s £86m in Grenfell-related settlements, all but £1.5m was covered by insurers. Hardly enough to make a multinational think again. The company whose product the inquiry found was the “primary cause” of the fire’s rapid spread has ended up paying only a fraction of the wider social cost, while themultibillion-poundbill for making hundreds of buildings safe falls largely on the state. In June 2017, 72 people – including 18 children – died in London’s Grenfell Tower fire. Almost a decade later, nobody has been criminally charged over its causes. It’s hard to conclude anything but that Britain’s system of corporate accountability is rotten.A newreportby the thinktank Common Wealth and the financial investigations group FIND suggests putting right this state of affairs in England and Wales by adopting two changes that parliament could enact quickly. The first is a “failure to prevent” law that would make companies responsible for having adequate systems to prevent foreseeable serious harm. The second is to adopt a “punitive damages” approach. Rather than compensating victims for their loss, punitive damages ask what a company should pay for its conduct. Such an award against Arconic could have been used to meet the costs of remediation, the report says, “at no public cost”.This is possible in America. Some Grenfell families tried to bring a case underUS law, where damages can punish and deter corporate wrongdoing, not just compensate victims. Currently, Meta is accused in a California court of intentionally addicting children to Facebook and Instagram in pursuit of profit. It denies wrongdoing, but says litigation potentially exposes it to$1.4tnin penalties and changes to its products. Whatever the eventual outcome, the case shows how alleged social harm can be a company-sized risk.Arconic successfully argued that the Grenfell families’ case be heard in British courts, where civil compensation and criminal punishment are kept separate. The Metropolitan police areinvestigating57 individuals and 20 organisations as criminal suspects, but no charges are expected before Grenfell’s tenth anniversary. Compare that with Hong Kong’sWang Fuk Court fire, which killed 168 people in November 2025. Authorities immediately treated it as a potential crime involving corporate actors. Within seven months, seven people and two firms facedmanslaughtercharges. No one is suggesting authoritarian Hong Kong as a model. But nearly a decade without charges in Britain, against seven months in the far east, is an uncomfortable contrast.There are reasons why justice has taken so long: the Covid pandemicdisruptedthe Grenfell public inquiry involvinghundreds of core participants, and responsibility stretches across manufacturers, certifiers, architects, contractors and regulators. This exposes a deeper problem: the moreentitiesinvolved, the easier it becomes for blame for a disaster to disappear between them.Lawmakers know how to stop companies passing the buck. The polluter pays in environmental law. There are recallobligationsin product safety andcollective redress in competition law. Why aren’t legal principles that are already used to force companies to account for economic and consumer harms being extended to catastrophic social harms? Until they are, the law will remain better at protecting investors rather than the public from corporate wrongdoing.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid matters | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries
Content: Members of a Red Cross team carry the coffin of a suspected Ebola victim in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of a Red Cross team carry the coffin of a suspected Ebola victim in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionEbolaThe Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid mattersEditorialThe Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countriesWed 19 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareFor months health experts have warned that the scale of the Ebolaoutbreakin the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could surpass the one that swept west Africa in 2014-16. This week, the authorities in the DRCannouncedthat a grim milestone has already been passed: at least 2,325 people have died from the virus, making it the deadliest of the country’s 17 outbreaks and the fastest-growing in history.There is no effective vaccine against Bundibugyo – a rare strain of the virus that spread fatally undetected during the spring, often being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. In contrast to neighbouring Uganda, which succeeded in eliminating an outbreak, multiple factors are combining to let the disease rip through the DRC. The worst-affected region is contested by armed groups, and a context of population displacement and chronic insecurity has made monitoring and surveillance more difficult. Ebola treatment centres have beenattackedas a result of misinformation and community distrust.The impact of this dire set of circumstances has been disastrously compounded by choices made in the west and, above all, in the United States. International aid cuts have deprived the DRC of vital human and material resources with which to fight back. In 2014, as the scale of the Ebola crisis in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea became clear, Barack Obamaaddressedthe United Nations general assembly and mobilised a global response that was crucial in containing the outbreak. The US Agency for International Development (USAID)ledefforts to train local health workers, pursue contact tracing and implement an eventual vaccination programme.The contrast with the Trump administration is stark and shaming. Last year, as the de facto head of the now defunct “department of government efficiency”, Elon Musk was given licence to implement swingeing cuts that led to the eventualdismantlingof USAID. In the DRC, the direct consequence was the weakening of local health infrastructure and surveillance capacities, leaving one of the poorest countries in the world still more vulnerable. Also lost was a wealth of institutional experience and expertise gained in combating emergencies such as the one now unfolding.The US has further undermined the capacity for coordinated international action bywithdrawingfrom the World Health Organization, to which it had been one of the biggest donors. European countries, notably Britain, Germany and France, have also been viewing international aid as luxury expenditure and cutting back. Last year, Sir Keir Starmerannouncedthat from 2027 UK aid would be reduced from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3%.Against such a backdrop, the lack of diplomatic urgency over the current crisis, compared with 2014, should not perhaps come as a surprise. But that does not make it any less disappointing. The Ebola outbreak in westAfricalaid bare the risk of regional and global disruption as a result of inadequate health infrastructure. A thousand pieties were then uttered in the wake of the Covid pandemic regarding the need to invest in global health security and future preparedness.Subsequent actions by governments have belied those words, leaving the DRC exposed to an epidemic that is threatening to spiral out of control. Belatedly, the global community needs to mobilise to address the threat. More fundamentally, it needs to draw the right lessons from a case study in why international aid matters.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Food security is an issue we can no longer ignore | Food | The Guardian
description: Letters: Local community food-growing could be best line of defence, writes Dan Farag, while David E Alexander says the government must be more open about its emergency planning, and Antony So says we need to look beyond stockpiling food
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Local community food-growing could be best line of defence, writes Dan Farag, while David E Alexander says the government must be more open about its emergency planning, and Antony So says we need to look beyond stockpiling food
Content: ‘Strategic food reserves are only part of the answer. The other underused resource is our communities themselves.’Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Strategic food reserves are only part of the answer. The other underused resource is our communities themselves.’Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesFoodLettersFood security is an issue we can no longer ignoreLocal community food-growing could be best line of defence, writesDan Farag, whileDavid E Alexandersays the government must be more open about its emergency planning, andAntony Sosays we need to look beyond stockpiling foodWed 19 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTShareGeorge Monbiot is right that Britain has become dangerously complacent about food security (Britain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would help, 13 August). A country facing climate shocks, disrupted trade routes and increasingly volatile harvests – all of which contribute to not only the availability of food but its increased cost – cannot rely indefinitely on just-in-time supply chains and supermarket logistics.But strategic food reserves are only part of the answer. The other underused resource is our communities themselves. Researchhas shownthat during floods, infrastructure failures and other emergencies, local groups, charities and neighbours are often the real first responders, stepping in long before formal systems can fully mobilise. Resilience is not just about what sits in a warehouse; it is about the strength of local networks, trusted relationships and the capacity of people to act together.That is why food security should also be seen as a question of land use and reciprocal trust. Councils, NHS bodies, universities and other public institutions hold significant areas of underused land that could support community food-growing, local skills and stronger neighbourhood connections. Brilliant organisations such asIncredible Ediblehave proved this model can – and does – work. This landcan and should become civic infrastructure for food, nature and belonging.The lesson of recent crises is not limited to questions about government stockpiling of food; it should also be about investing in building the long-term sustainable community capacity that helps people withstand shocks together.Dan FaragDirector of innovation and practice, The Young FoundationGeorge Monbiot accuses the British government of complacency over national food security. By coincidence, on the day his article appeared, the UN publicised the recently released 86-pagereportRoadmap for Resilience: A UK Food Plan for 2050 by UK Research and Innovation.This detailed document provides foresight-based assessments of the national food situation and offers a palette of solutions to the problem of food security, supported by a significant amount of research. Interestingly, it does not mention stockpiling, Monbiot’s suggested solution. Hence there seems to be a divergence of opinions on strategy.Government bodies in the UK have been working on food security issues for decades. The silence of elected representatives is enigmatic because we don’t know whether they have shelved the problem or simply left it to civil servants and researchers to deal with. A more open debate, led by politicians, would help us assess whether theFoodPlan for 2050 is wishful thinking or the answer to the problem, and whether stockpiling of food is likely to be any use.David E AlexanderEmeritus professor of emergency planning and management, UCLGeorge Monbiot is right that Britain needs to take food security much more seriously, but stockpiling should be understood as part of a wider resilience strategy.Switzerland offers a useful example. Itsnational economic supply systemrequires the private sector to maintain stocks of essential foodstuffs, amounting to several months’ supply. Crucially, it also provides for stocks of agricultural inputs, including fertilisers. This recognises that if a crisis extends from weeks into whole growing seasons, national food security depends on being able to produce the next harvest.However, stockpiles can only go so far. A government can pre-emptively fill silos with grain and still watch its population go hungry if electricity grids collapse or fuel supplies are severed.Food securityultimately depends on the complex web of energy, transport, water, communications and other infrastructure.Britain should therefore ask not simply how much food we should stockpile, but what capabilities we need to preserve to keep people fed when the next crisis lasts longer than expected.Antony SoContributor, Just in Case: Narrowing the Civil Food Resilience Gap, National Preparedness CommissionHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Screens can play a key role in the classroom | Education | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dismissing screen use entirely fails to recognise the crucial role modern technology plays in equity, accessibility and basic school operations, says Charlotte Bleakley
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dismissing screen use entirely fails to recognise the crucial role modern technology plays in equity, accessibility and basic school operations, says Charlotte Bleakley
Content: ‘Technology in moderation is an invaluable tool, but it shouldn’t replace meaningful human interaction in the classroom.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Technology in moderation is an invaluable tool, but it shouldn’t replace meaningful human interaction in the classroom.’Photograph: AlamyEducationLettersScreens can play a key role in the classroomDismissing screen use entirely fails to recognise the crucial role modern technology plays in equity, accessibility and basic school operations, saysCharlotte BleakleyWed 19 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTShareYour article buries the real story beneath the headline (‘Our children are less cognitively capable,’ says neuroscientist who wants to cut screen use in schools, 16 August). Even Jared Cooney Horvath’s own data, cited mid-article, shows that moderate school device use is associated with better outcomes than no device use at all – it is only the heaviest use daily that drags results down. That is a case for sensible integration, not blanket alarm.The article’s most significant omission is what technology means for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and for those learning English as an additional language.With continual cuts to Send funding and learning-support staff, a single teacher cannot differentiate instruction for 30 children unaided. Assistive technology – text to speech, translation tools, audio versions of lesson content – is often the only thing that allows these students genuine access to the national curriculum.Technology in moderation is an invaluable tool, but it shouldn’t replace meaningful human interaction in the classroom. However, dismissing screen use entirely fails to recognise the crucial role that modern technology plays in equity, accessibility and basic school operations.When used thoughtfully and purposefully, moderate educational technology does not diminish learning, it democratises it.Charlotte BleakleyTeacher,Roding Valley high school, and digital lead at Chelmsford Learning PartnershipExplore more on these topicsEducationSchoolsPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolsTeachingSpecial educational needslettersShareReuse this content

title: Stop putting women through brutal hysteroscopies without pain relief | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Letter: The medical system is biased against women, says Carole Kendall, pointing to the very different way men who have colonoscopies are treated
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The medical system is biased against women, says Carole Kendall, pointing to the very different way men who have colonoscopies are treated
Content: ‘In the 21st century, theNHSshould be offering women a bit more than a paracetamol and the equivalent of a bit of ice.’Photograph: Posed by model; globalmoments/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In the 21st century, theNHSshould be offering women a bit more than a paracetamol and the equivalent of a bit of ice.’Photograph: Posed by model; globalmoments/Getty ImagesWomen's healthLettersStop putting women through brutal hysteroscopies without pain reliefThe medical system is biased against women, saysCarole Kendall,pointing to the very different way men who have colonoscopies are treatedWed 19 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTShareI fully endorse everything Anna Moore writes in her excellent article on the lack of pain relief for hysteroscopies (‘It was barbaric. I was crying my eyes out’: why are so many women left in agony by routine womb examinations?, 16 August).I have had three of these barbaric procedures, two of them being associated with being on hormone replacement therapy (HRT). All three were administered with very basic pain relief, ie a small amount of local anaesthetic, which I would compare to numbing a gum with a piece of ice and then proceeding with root canal treatment. I was offered a general anaesthetic on the third occasion, but this is way too much. At no point was anything else offered, like it is for colonoscopies.I feel the system is biased against women. The hysteroscopies were much worse than childbirth for me – it was zero dilation to full dilation in no time at all. As a result of my three awful experiences, I came off HRT, because I have no wish to experience this ever again.In the 21st century, theNHSshould be offering women a bit more than a paracetamol and the equivalent of a bit of ice. A bit of dignity would also help – a recovery space perhaps? Or even treat us like men who have colonoscopies.Carole KendallLetchworth, HertfordshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? description: Brief letters: Online ratings | School holiday scam | Back-row kisses | Barking | Champagne populism
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Online ratings | School holiday scam | Back-row kisses | Barking | Champagne populism
Content: ‘You’re left wanting to throw your purchase and/or your laptop across the room.’Photograph: Rawf8/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘You’re left wanting to throw your purchase and/or your laptop across the room.’Photograph: Rawf8/AlamyBrief lettersInternetLettersZero stars for this endless rating gameOnline ratings | School holiday scam | Back-row kisses | Barking | Champagne populismWed 19 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTShareTo Stuart Heritage’s excellent list of words to describe our tech dystopia (18 August), can I add “iRate”? This is when you make an online purchase and, even before you’ve had time to remove the packaging, receive an email asking “How was it for you?”, followed by another a few days later if you fail to review every detail of the transaction, and then another, and another, until you’re left wanting to throw your purchase and/or your laptop across the room.Elli WoollardLondonRather than criminalising parents who take their children on holiday during term time because it’s much cheaper (‘Cheap travel is not a defence’: the parents facing court for school absences in England, 15 August), why not address the blatant profiteering by travel firms charging inflated prices during school holidays?Max FishelBromley, LondonRe kissing in the back row in the cinema (Letters, 16 August), my local cinema in the 60s, the Elysian in Cheadle Hulme, had double seats at the end of every row – and usherettes with very bright torches!Trish CockayneLymm, CheshireA friend who used to live in Barking (Barking mad? How people in England’s ‘least friendly’ borough feel about the ranking, 19 August) once referred to a mutual acquaintance as “a bit East Ham”. I had to ask him what he meant. “One stop short of Barking,” he replied.Dr Glyn ThompsonLeedsRichard Tice’s answer to climate change is “Let them drink English sparkling wine” (Letters, 18 August).
