Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lorena Wiebes won the first stage of this year’s Tour of Britain, which started and finished in Cockermouth, Cumbria, on a circuit spanning 158.9km
Content: Lorena Wiebes crosses the line to win stage one.Photograph: Simon Wilkinson/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLorena Wiebes crosses the line to win stage one.Photograph: Simon Wilkinson/SWpix.com/ShutterstockTour of Britain WomenTour of Britain Women: Lorena Wiebes sprints to victory on opening stage27-year-old Dutch rider takes win in CumbriaGB’s Josie Nelson in third, Italy’s Chiara Consonni secondPA MediaWed 19 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLorena Wiebes took the victory in the first stage of this year’sTour of Britain. The opening stage started and finished in Cockermouth on a circuit spanning 158.9km in Cumbria.The Dutchwoman powered to victory in a thrilling sprint finish, where the Team SD Worx-Protime rider narrowly pipped her rivals over the line. Italy’s Chiara Consonni finished in second, while Great Britain’s Josie Nelson claimed third.Arabella Blackburn sparked a breakaway with around 90km remaining, and along with Audrey De Keersmaeker created a gap of nearly three minutes. The 18-year-old Scot Blackburn, the youngest rider in the race, suffered a slice of bad luck, however, and was stung by a bee, her challenge fading.Belgium’s De Keersmaeker was caught well before the finish and Wiebes, winner of the first two stages of the recent Tour de France Femmes, powered over the line ahead of the bunch.The race resumes on Thursday with the second stage taking place between Clitheroe and Blackpool.Explore more on these topicsTour of Britain WomenTour of BritainCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: US justice department defends prosecution of James Comey over ‘8647’ seashell post | James Comey | The Guardian
description: Justice department claims there’s ‘no dispute’ over whether ex-FBI head’s post could be read as a threat against Trump
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Justice department claims there’s ‘no dispute’ over whether ex-FBI head’s post could be read as a threat against Trump
Content: James Comey is interviewed onstage at 92NY on 30 May 2023 in New York City.Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJames Comey is interviewed onstage at 92NY on 30 May 2023 in New York City.Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty ImagesJames ComeyUS justice department defends prosecution of James Comey over ‘8647’ seashell postJustice department claims there’s ‘no dispute’ over whether ex-FBI head’s post could be read as a threat against TrumpAnna BettsWed 19 Aug 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Department of Justice has defended its prosecution of former FBI directorJames Comey, claiming in new court documents there is “no serious dispute” that his social media post last year featuring a photo of seashells arranged to read “8647” could be interpreted as a threat against Donald Trump.“There is no serious dispute that an objective viewer of Comey’s post could read it to mean ‘Kill President Trump’,” prosecutorswrote in a documentfiled on Tuesday in response to efforts by Comey’seffortsto have the case dismissed.Comey was indicted in April after a grand jury in North Carolinachargedhim withmaking a threat against the US presidentandtransmitting that threat, via social media, across state lines, over an image he posted on Instagramwhile vacationing in North Carolinalast May.In the photo, the seashells were arranged to read “8647”, which the president’s allies and supporters quickly denounced as a threat against Trump. The number “86” is often used as shorthand to mean to get rid of or remove something, while Trump is the 47th US president.Comey deleted the photo after the uproar, saying he didn’t know that it could be interpreted as a violent threat. “It never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down,” hesaid.In the court documents filed earlier this week, prosecutors with the eastern district of North Carolina continued to argue the post was a “coded message to his followers meaning ‘kill’ or ‘get rid of’ President Trump”.Comey has denied the charges against him and his lawyers have asked the judge to dismiss the case,arguingthat the post was protected speech and didnot amount to a “true threat”against the president.“The indictment alleges that Mr Comey’s ‘86 47’ post constitutes a ‘true threat; on the President’s life,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in a filing last month. “That claim is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense. ‘86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.”Comey’s lawyers have argued that “in this context, no reasonable observer would understand the phrase ‘86 47’ to connote violence at all – let alone to threaten that Mr Comey personally would commit violence against the President”.Comey’s lawyers have also said the caseshould be dismissedfor “vindictive and selective prosecution” and have said the indictment is “not based on a goodfaith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the President’s deep-seated animosity”.Trump has long feuded with Comey since his handling of the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election while he wasFBIdirector.Last year, the justice department alsoindictedComey in a separate case, alleging that he had lied to Congress. But those chargeswere later thrown outafter a judge ruled the prosecutor handling the case was unlawfully appointed.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsJames ComeyTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Compulsory GCSE resits in England harm teenagers’ mental wellbeing, study finds | GCSEs | The Guardian
description: UCL researchers warn repeated exam attempts may dent students’ confidence and raise risk of dropping out
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: UCL researchers warn repeated exam attempts may dent students’ confidence and raise risk of dropping out
Content: A study by academics at UCL compared the mental wellbeing of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.Photograph: Rui Vieira/PAView image in fullscreenA study by academics at UCL compared the mental wellbeing of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.Photograph: Rui Vieira/PAGCSEsCompulsory GCSE resits in England harm teenagers’ mental wellbeing, study findsUCL researchers warn repeated exam attempts may dent students’ confidence and raise risk of dropping outRichard AdamsEducation editorWed 19 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForcing teenagers who failGCSEsinto multiple resits has a negative impact on their mental health, according to research to be published as pupils receive their grades on Thursday.The study by academics at University College London (UCL) compared the mental wellbeing of students in England, Wales andNorthern Irelandwho failed to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in maths or English GCSEs – and found that only those in England, where resits are mandatory, showed significantly lower wellbeing.Compulsory maths and English GCSE resits too inflexible, says curriculum chiefRead moreRobbie Maris, a research fellow at UCL and one of the authors, said the dent to teenagers’ self-confidence when faced with resits could be a contributing factor to the rise in young people not in education, employment or training, known as Neets.Maris said: “Some [resitting] students will not turn up for their exams, they won’t enter them or they will drop out of education – these are the kids at highest risk of dropping out of education and becoming Neets.“It could be leading to further disengagement, which is a worrying thing. People need to pay more attention to this, because if you demotivate or demoralise young people it puts them at risk of dropping out of the education system entirely.”The resits policy inEnglandwas introduced in 2014 and requires students who have not achieved a grade 4 pass in English or maths GCSE at age 16 to continue to study those qualifications as a condition of their further education or college places being funded.This year, about 180,000 students who sat GCSEs last year will retake GCSE English and about 175,000 are expected to retake maths, after record numbers of 16-year-olds last year received grades below 4.View image in fullscreenThis year, about 180,000 students will retake GCSE English and 175,000 GCSE maths.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersMaris said the comparison between students with similar academic records inWalesand Northern Ireland and those in England, after adjusting for other factors, left the resits policy as a major difference between the two groups.“We see no impact really at all for failing English and maths in Wales or Northern Ireland but in England there’s a relatively large negative impact. This is strong evidence that it’s something to do with England’s policy setting that is generating these impacts,” Maris said.The study, to be published as a working paper by UCL’scentre for education policy and equalising opportunities, also found considerable differences between girls and boys. The biggest impact on girls was on those who narrowly missed out on a grade 4 in maths, while for boys the biggest impact was among those who were “substantially below” the threshold for a passing grade in English.In contrast, boys who failed to get a 4 in maths, and girls who failed in English, showed little or no downturn in wellbeing.“Girls already have low self-efficacy and anxiety in maths, on average, and we’ve got similar issues with boys doing English, anecdotally a lot of boys don’t like doing English. Being forced to resit these subjects where there are these particularly strong gender norms have large effects on boys and girls, it’s a very interesting pattern that emerges,” said Maris, adding that further research would be needed to explain why it occurred.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe mandatory resits policy for those remaining in education has been controversial since its introduction, with the success rate among 17- to 19-year-olds falling in recent years. Last year, fewer than 20% in the resitting age group received a grade 4 or above in English, while in maths about 15% got a 4 or better, and fewer than one in 100 got a grade 9.Angela Rayner, the then shadow education secretary, said in 2018 that a Labour government would scrap compulsory resits. But the skills white paper published last year left resits in place while proposing a new “stepping stone” qualification for resitting students with grade 2 or below.Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needsRead moreTheDepartment for Educationsaid: “We know that resitting exams repeatedly without improving grades can be demoralising, which is why we’re taking action to break the endless cycle of resits.“Our new 16-19 English and maths qualifications will properly prepare students before they resit their GCSE – with changes to the accountability framework to support this and ensure students only sit an exam when they are ready to progress.“We have also ensured that students will get at least 100 hours of teaching per subject, backed by extra funding and free teacher training, so they progress with a genuine chance of success.”This year’s resits may see some improvement in results after the government’s toughened requirement for providers to offer a minimum of 100 teaching hours for each subject, alongside increased funding.Explore more on these topicsGCSEsExamsYoung peopleSecondary schoolsDepartment for EducationEducation policySchoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifth Fifa vice-president turns against Infantino, saying he has ‘lost confidence’ in him | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino has lost the support of another one of Fifa’s vice-presidents, with the Hungarian football federation chief, Sandor Csanyi, the latest
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Gianni Infantino has lost the support of another one of Fifa’s vice-presidents, with the Hungarian football federation chief, Sandor Csanyi, the latest
Content: Sandor Csanyi, the president of the Hungarian football federation, has spoken out against Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAView image in fullscreenSandor Csanyi, the president of the Hungarian football federation, has spoken out against Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAGianni InfantinoFifth Fifa vice-president turns against Infantino, saying he has ‘lost confidence’ in himHungary’s Sandor Csanyi highly critical of Fifa presidentHe cites dismissal of COO Kevin Lamour as ‘final straw’Matt HughesWed 19 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino has lost the support of another one of Fifa’s vice-presidents, with the Hungarian football federation chief, Sandor Csanyi, criticising the president’s “professional judgment, ethical standards and leadership”.In an explosive letter sent to Infantino on Tuesday, which was first obtained by the news agency Agence France-Presse, Csanyi states that he has “lost the confidence I previously placed in you” and describes the “unexpected dismissal” of Fifa’s chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, as the “final straw”.Referees’ chief Howard Webb ‘really troubled’ by Folarin Balogun escaping World Cup banRead moreLamourwas sacked by Fifa on Mondayafter breaking ranks last month by criticising Infantino over his aborted plan to sell off shares in the World Cup to private investors.Csanyi’s letter continues the trend of senior global football figures deserting Infantino, with the Hungarian banker the fifth of Fifa’s eight vice-presidents to call for him to stand down.The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, Victor Montagliani of Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean Confederation – and Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al Khalifa of the Asian Football Confederation have all made their positions clear, as has the Football Association chair, Debbie Hewitt.Of the Fifa vice-presidents, only Alejandro Domínguez of South America’s Conmebol, Patrick Motsepe of the Confederation of African Football and Oceania’s Lambert Maltock are supporting Infantino.Csanyi is also a member of the 37-strong Fifa council, which is theoretically its main decision-making body, but has been repeatedly overlooked by Infantino.“My conviction that you are capable of continuing to lead Fifa successfully and effectively in accordance with the shared values that previously formed the basis of our cooperation has been undermined,” Csanyi wrote. “The final straw was the unexpected dismissal of Kevin Lamour.”The letter also cited “a number of controversial decisions” at this year’s World Cup, including Infantino’s involvement in “plans to outsource Fifa competitions and place them in the hands of external parties”.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Success story’ hailed as bluefin tunas caught off Yorkshire for first time since 1960s  | Fish | The Guardian
description: Researchers laud return of giant tuna to North Sea after being fished almost to point of extinction
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Researchers laud return of giant tuna to North Sea after being fished almost to point of extinction
Content: A bluefin tuna was caught off the Yorkshire coast for the first time since the 1960s after overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals had rendered the giant fish almost extinct in the North Sea.Photograph: 54 North Maritime trainingView image in fullscreenA bluefin tuna was caught off the Yorkshire coast for the first time since the 1960s after overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals had rendered the giant fish almost extinct in the North Sea.Photograph: 54 North Maritime trainingFish‘Success story’ hailed as bluefin tunas caught off Yorkshire for first time since 1960sResearchers laud return of giant tuna to North Sea after being fished almost to point of extinctionRaphael BoydWed 19 Aug 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleResearchers have lauded two giant bluefin tunas being caught off the coast ofYorkshirefor the first time in more than six decades as a “success story” for marine conservation.The tunas, which were caught a day apart off the coast of Whitby earlier this week, have mostly been absent along the north-east coast of Britain since the 1960s.While small numbers of the species have been spotted in the waters around Yorkshire in the previous years, the pair were the first to be caught for market from the North Sea since licences to catch the fish were issued in July.Rodney Forster, a professor at the University of Hull and head of the Hull marine laboratory, called the tuna’s reappearance a “success story about the management of fisheries” in Britain.“They were fished almost to the point of extinction in their spawning grounds in the Mediterranean through the 70s and 80s,” said Forster.“But now careful protection of the stock means they’ve increased, even to the point that they’re now spreading back out to their old grounds around the UK and even into the Baltic Sea.”View image in fullscreenTrainee Ada Peake, 18, was part of the landing of the giant bluefin tuna.Photograph: 54 North Maritime trainingForster said the tuna were not the only marine life that had returned to the Yorkshire coast, pointing out that minke whales and bottlenose dolphins had seen a noticeable increase in numbers around the North Sea over the past decade.Bryce Stewart, a senior research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, a marine charity based in Plymouth, called the return of bluefin tuna to the UK “fantastic” and lauded the work done by the International Commission for theConservationof Atlantic Tunas (Iccat) to re-establish populations.“It seemed like an era that had gone for ever, you know, I mean normally if we lose a large species like this from an area of sea, they don’t come back,” said Stewart. “So, as I said, both from a personal scientific point of view, this is a really wonderful thing to see.”Despite joy at the tuna population increasing around Yorkshire and beyond, concerns have also been raised that their increased numbers farther north could in part be linked to the effects of climate change.Both Forster and Stewart mentioned rising temperatures in the North Sea as another factor in the tuna’s return, albeit a less influential one than the management of fisheries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStewart said the warmer temperatures had a “sort of knock-on effect” as the small fish that tuna eat, such as herring and sprat, do better in warmer temperatures. Both of the fish caught in Whitby were notably well fed, with each weighing about 320kg (700lb), roughly double the size of the average tuna found on the south coast.Climate change is one of many factors alongside pollution and illegal fishing that could prevent the tuna from properly re-establishing themselves along the Yorkshire coast, but there are hopes that if properly managed they can thrive there and even move into Scottish waters.Calum Duncan, the principal policy specialist at the Marine Conservation Society, lauded the regeneration of the tuna populations, but warned that their continued survival hinged on consistent care and for British fishing policies to place a greater onus on protecting marine ecology.“We’ve got a long, long way to go, but it’s really encouraging to have achieved this,” said Duncan.“Stories like the return of bluefin tuna send a clear signal that human beings can manage our way out of environmental decline by making good decisions and working together, making good plans and – most importantly – implementing them. But we just need to do a lot more of it and need to ramp it up.”Explore more on these topicsFishMarine lifeWildlifeFishing industryFishingYorkshireEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Swimmers warned of toxic algae at newly designated Thames bathing site | Pollution | The Guardian
description: People told to keep themselves and their pets out of river at Ham amid anger over Thames Water’s plans to pump treated sewage
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: People told to keep themselves and their pets out of river at Ham amid anger over Thames Water’s plans to pump treated sewage
Content: Swimmers enjoying a dip in the Thames at Ham in May.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSwimmers enjoying a dip in the Thames at Ham in May.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianPollutionSwimmers warned of toxic algae at newly designated Thames bathing sitePeople told they and their pets should keep out of river at Ham amid anger over Thames Water’s treated sewage planSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentWed 19 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwimmers are being warned not to enter the water at the first official bathing site on the River Thames, in south-westLondon, because of toxic blue-green algae in the water.The blue-green algal blooms are rare in moving water but are likely to be caused by the extreme heat, low river flow, and nutrient pollution from sewage waste.Thames Water’s Hogsmill sewage treatment plant, in Kingston upon Thames, is situated three miles upstream of the Ham bathing site.The algae discovery raises further questions about plans by ThamesWaterto pump 75m litres of treated sewage a day into the river near the bathing spot, in a water recycling scheme that is in the pre-application stage for a development consent order.View image in fullscreenThe sign at the official Thames bathing spot in Ham on Wednesday.Photograph: Sandra Laville/The GuardianMarlene Lawrence, of the swimming group Teddington Bluetits, which successfully applied for the bathing water designation at Ham, said: “This is so unusual to get blue-green algae in a moving body of water. It is the first time in nearly six years of swimming here that this has happened.“The river is very low-flowing at the moment because of the lack of rain and the high temperatures we are having. With climate change, this is likely to happen more.”Thames Water’s recycling scheme has been opposed by the localLiberal Democrat MP, Munira Wilson,the council, and river users. But it has been designated a strategic infrastructure project, which means it can be pushed through over the heads of the local authority.The £250m scheme involves abstracting 75m litres of water a day from the Thames at Teddington when the river is in low flow at times of drought, and replacing it with the same volume of treated sewage from the nearby Mogden sewage treatment works via a new tunnel.The Environment Agency rejected a previous attempt to develop the scheme because the treated sewage would raise the temperature of the water during low flow, change the salinity of the river and adversely affect fish and biodiversity.Campaigners argue that the recycling project will provide only 75m litres of water a day while putting the river under huge environmental pressure. This is a fraction of the 570m litres of water the company leaks every day.View image in fullscreenBlue-green algae in the Thames on Wednesday.Photograph: Chloe WaltonThames Water has been in breach of its permit conditions at its Hogsmill works, which means it has discharged raw sewage in breach of the law.The company, which is £20bn in debt, had promised to upgrade the Hogsmill works last year as part of key environmental improvements, but it was one ofmore than 100 projectsthe struggling water company has postponed, and is now unlikely until 2028. The failure to upgrade the infrastructure is being investigated by the regulator, Ofwat.Lawrence said: “What Thames Water are planning to do – abstract river water when the river is at very low flow in drought and replace it with treated effluent – will make the river temperature at least 1C higher than before and put it under extreme environmental pressure.“The presence of this blue-green algae already shows that the river is under stress from the drought and high temperatures.”The Environment Agency, which tests bathing water areas inEngland, has put up a sign at the swimming spot to warn swimmers. It reads: “Do not enter the water. Do not let pets enter the water.”View image in fullscreenSwimmers enjoying London’s first official river bathing site on the Thames in July.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAThe bathing spot, designated in May under the EU water framework directive, wasthe first on the Thames in London.Swimmers across the country are applying for bathing water status in riversin an attempt to encourage a cleanupand highlight the scale of sewage pollution by water companies discharging raw and treated waste. Rivers are suffering from a toxic cocktail of sewage discharge, forever chemicals and road and agricultural runoff.Bathing water status requires more rigorous testing by the Environment Agency, which is required to monitor the water for faecal indicator organisms.Watercompanies have come under pressure to cut sewage pollution in areas designated for bathing.A Thames Water spokesperson said: “We would like to reassure river users that our proposed Teddington direct river abstraction project would not deteriorate water quality and would be required to meet strict environmental and water quality standards set by the Environment Agency.“The new treated water outfall would also be located downstream of the proposed bathing water site, meaning recycled water would flow downstream over Teddington Weir into the tidal Thames.”Explore more on these topicsPollutionWaterWater industryThames WaterSwimmingLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Otter spotted for first time in 100 years in New York City’s Bronx River | New York | The Guardian
description: Image captured in early June shows animal foraging in the waterway in first since early 1900s, signaling its recovery
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Image captured in early June shows animal foraging in the waterway in first since early 1900s, signaling its recovery
Content: A river otter in the Bronx River.Photograph: RJ Hawkins/Wildlife Conservation Society Education DeptView image in fullscreenA river otter in the Bronx River.Photograph: RJ Hawkins/Wildlife Conservation Society Education DeptNew YorkOtter spotted for first time in 100 years in New York City’s Bronx RiverImage captured in early June shows animal foraging in the waterway in first since early 1900s, signaling its recoveryOliver MilmanWed 19 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn otter has been spotted in the Bronx River for the first time in more than 100 years, in a further sign that New York’s previously befouled waterways are recovering some of their ecological health.The North American river otter was photographed by a motion-activated camera foraging near some vegetation in the Bronx River, a waterway that flows through New York’s Bronx and empties into the East River.The image, captured in June by the camera of RJ Hawkins, a scientist affiliated with theWildlifeConservation Society’s Bronx zoo, is the first documented sighting of a river otter in the river since the early 1900s, according to the society.Netanyahu party campaign billboard likens Mamdani to leaders of Iran and HezbollahRead more“When I first reviewed the images, I could hardly believe what I was seeing,” said Hawkins. “Knowing this may be the first documented river otter in the Bronx in generations was an incredible moment. It shows why long-term wildlife monitoring and environmental restoration efforts matter.”River otters are found across North America and were once plentiful in New York’s rivers but vanished due to rampant water pollution, habitat loss and trapping for their fur.The Bronx River, in particular, was treated as an open sewer and a dumping ground for New York’s rapidly expanding industrial base as the city grew into an economic powerhouse in the 19th and 20th centuries.Factories and slaughterhouses dumped chemicals, oil and animal blood directly into the water, with untreated sewage also seeping into the waterway. The river faced the further indignity of becoming a sort of garbage tip, as people threw old tires, appliances and other unwanted materials into it.This decimated local wildlife, but concerted conservation efforts and laws such as the Clean Water Act have in recent years helped restore the Bronx River’s fortunes, to the point that species such as oysters have returned.In 2007, beavers returned to the river for the first time in more than 200 years, the zoo said, and the appearance of a river otter suggests the waterway, which is New York City’s only freshwater river, is continuing to recover from decades of pollution.While the sighting of a single otter doesn’t confirm a larger resident population, it is encouraging as river otters require clean water and abundant fish.Measuring up to 5ft in length and sporting a muscular tail that comprises 40%of their body, river otters are considered playful creatures and adept hunters. When frightened, they can emit a scream that can be heard 1.5 miles away.“There are moments in conservation that remind us why this work matters, and this is one of them,” said Craig Piper, director of Bronx zoo.“Thanks to a broad coalition of public and private partners, we can celebrate the return of an otter as a result of decades of restoration work to provide cleaner water and healthier habitat. It’s a win for both wildlife and people.”Explore more on these topicsNew YorkWildlifeAnimalsRiversnewsShareReuse this content

title: Human remains again found at Lake Mead as water levels drop amid drought | Nevada | The Guardian
description: Discovery marks latest grim finding in lake as water levels in crucial reservoir outside Las Vegas continue to decline
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Discovery marks latest grim finding in lake as water levels in crucial reservoir outside Las Vegas continue to decline
Content: A mineral-stained ‘bathtub ring’ marking previous water levels is visible along the shoreline of Lake Mead, near Boulder City, Nevada, on 12 August 2026.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreenA mineral-stained ‘bathtub ring’ marking previous water levels is visible along the shoreline of Lake Mead, near Boulder City, Nevada, on 12 August 2026.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersNevadaHuman remains again found at Lake Mead as water levels drop amid droughtDiscovery marks latest grim finding in lake as water levels in crucial reservoir outside Las Vegas continue to declineVictoria BekiempisWed 19 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHuman remains have once again been discovered at Lake Mead outsideLas Vegas, Nevada, marking the latest in a line of gruesome discoveries as water levels in the crucial reservoir continue to drop, authorities said.These remains were discovered on 16 August, USA Todayreported. The National Park Service (NPS) told the outlet there did not appear to be anything suspicious about the body.Las Vegas police reportedly said “a non-criminal, dead body report was taken for the remains”. The local coroner said authorities were trying to identify the deceased person, as well as determine the manner and cause of death, USA Todaysaid.As water levels have declined in recent years, authorities have found multiple bodies. In 2022, authorities recovered a body in a barrel,USA Today noted.Authorities reportedly said the man seemed to have been shot, potentially during the late 1970s or early 1980s. Some experts believe Lake Mead’s location near Las Vegas – an organized crime hotspot – means it’s probable still more remains will be discovered.This week’s grim finding underscores Lake Mead’s perilously low water levels amid a historic drought and broader water crisis in the US west. Weeks ago, Lake Mead’s water leveldippedto 1,040.4ft above sea level, nearing the 28 July 2022 record low.Lake Mead is integral for water storage on the Colorado River, which provides water to about 40 million people across seven states, as well as tribal nations and Mexico. The river basin is reeling from a mix of extended drought, extreme heat, waning snowmelt and over-consumption.The second major reservoir on the river, Lake Powell, is also seeinghistoric low levelsas the global climate continues to warm.“In the 21st century, the ultimate cause of the problem is declining runoff,” Jack Schmidt, director ofUtahState University’s Center for Colorado River Studies, previously said of the water crisis. “There’s less water in the system. It’s caused by a warming climate, period.”Explore more on these topicsNevadaWaterClimate crisisLas VegasDroughtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by Christmas | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: PM says public money alone won’t solve problem but ‘we did it in the pandemic, we can do it again’
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: PM says public money alone won’t solve problem but ‘we did it in the pandemic, we can do it again’
Content: Tents line Euston Road in London.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTents line Euston Road in London.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockHomelessnessAndy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by ChristmasPM says public money alone won’t solve problem but ‘we did it in the pandemic, we can do it again’‘Burnham’s writing cheques, this one might bounce’: homeless people doubt PM’s planRowena MasonandJessica MurrayWed 19 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 10.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said government money alone may not be enough to get rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas, as experts called for more of a plan to deal with the problems that cause homelessness.I won’t abandon anyone to sleep rough on our streets. That’s my £442m promise | Andy BurnhamRead moreSpeaking on a visit to the north-east of England, the prime minister said he felt “very passionately” about tackling rough sleeping and wanted the wider society to play a part in wiping it out.He acknowledged that not every rough sleeper may take the offer “for their own reasons”. But he said a nationwide effort to stop as much rough sleeping as possible by Christmas was the aim – replicating what happened in the Covid pandemic.Burnham told reporters: “The government money may not fully get us there, and I’m saying to wider society, faith organisations, let’s see if we can do this together.“Let’s see if Britain can do this. Give everybody an offer to come inside before Christmas. You know, that is just something we can do.“We did it in the pandemic. We can do it again, and it’s a rallying call, really, that I’m putting out there today, with a lot of government money behind it.”Burnhamwrote in the Guardian on Tuesdaythat rough sleeping has become so common it now “feels like part of the scenery”, as he pledged another £100m to tackle the problem this winter.The announcement puts tackling homelessness as a central policy for Burnham’s government, and gives voters a measure by which to judge his success.View image in fullscreenA row of tents outside the Midland hotel in Manchester last year.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAs mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again.He said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support, and understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.He added: “So my point is, we can do this, but only if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve – to make this a nationwide initiative as we go into the Christmas period, getting everybody behind it.”He said people being left to sleep on the streets “can often cost more to the state because people can be in and out of A&E, and in and out of hospital beds, and sometimes in contact with the police”.As part of the national effort, Burnham said he would host a summit this autumn to “bring together leaders from across society – from business, finance, charities, health, faith communities and more – to ask what role each of them can play in ending rough sleeping”.11:13Will Andy Burnham get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas? – The LatestCouncil leaders and experts have applauded Burnham’s aims but also called for more work on how to deal with issues underlying rough sleeping, from mental health problems to addiction.Liam Robinson, leader of Liverpool city council and chair of the Local Government Association’s inclusive growth committee, said there may need to be “future conversations” about more funding to tackle homelessness, including the thousands of people living in temporary accommodation.“It does need to be resourced more,” he said. “We know councils are spending £950m more than they were five years ago on this issue, so we’re really just talking about the tip of the iceberg with rough sleeping. There may be a requirement for more funding.”He added that extra money may need to be for “more than just housing-related funding”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It probably requires more NHS investment for better mental health and addiction support,” he said. “It’s more than just paying the bills of hotels and landlords.”Ish Camp, regional head in east London for the homelessness charity St Mungo’s, added: “Yes it’s good to give everyone a bed for the night but what else are we doing to support them to stay in it?“Entrenched rough sleepers have usually been round and round all of the systems that are available multiple times before, and it hasn’t worked. So we need to look at why it hasn’t worked and what we can do differently this time around.”She added that the UK needed to learn from the “temporary accommodation nightmare” to ensure the new funding was not funnelled straight into the pockets of private companies.“If we publicly say all this money is to give people somewhere to stay for the night and we know there’s no social housing to put anyone in, what will hotel owners do? Put their rates up and charge us £250 a night. That money then gets eaten up very, very quickly,” she said.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with officials from the homelessness charity Changing Lives in Newcastle on Wednesday.Photograph: Scott Heppell/Getty ImagesBurnham also said on Wednesday that he would be donating 15% of the additional salary he gets as prime minister to homelessness causes.Speaking to the Big Issue, he said he wanted to continue what he had been doing as mayor of Greater Manchester. He has already said he would donate 15% of the salary he gets for being an MP to local causes in his constituency of Makerfield.He told the magazine: “For the best part of nine, almost 10 years, I donated 15% of my salary as mayor of Greater Manchester to tackling homelessness in Greater Manchester.“I am making a commitment to donate the same of my prime minister’s salary. I’m donating part of my constituency MP salary to local organisations, but the extra bit that comes with being prime minister, I’m making the same commitment.“I wouldn’t want to ask anybody to do anything that I’m not prepared to do. I want to lead from the front. This issue matters massively to me.”The latest annual national statistics, published in February, estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025 in England. This was a new record and the fourth annual increase in a row, with 43% of those people sleeping rough in London and the south-east.Explore more on these topicsHomelessnessHousingPovertySocial exclusionAndy BurnhamCommunitiesLocal governmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lewes derailment: images show track defect before incident on hottest day | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: Network Rail and Southern owner GTR apologise after investigators reveal picture of possible heat-buckled track
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Network Rail and Southern owner GTR apologise after investigators reveal picture of possible heat-buckled track
Content: The RAIB investigation published an image that appeared to show that the track near Lewes, East Sussex, had buckled – something that can happen in high temperatures.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenThe RAIB investigation published an image that appeared to show that the track near Lewes, East Sussex, had buckled – something that can happen in high temperatures.Photograph: James Manning/PARail transportLewes derailment: images show track defect before incident on hottest dayNetwork Rail and Southern owner GTR apologise after investigators reveal picture of possible heat-buckled trackAlex DanielWed 19 Aug 2026 10.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRail operators have apologised after a report into last Thursday’sderailment in East Sussexfound a track defect on the approach to where the train derailed on the hottest day of the year so far.Aninterim reportby the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) said CCTV images showed the “track geometry irregularity” existed before the incident near Lewes injured 30 people.The watchdog published an image that appeared to show the track had buckled – something that can happen in high temperatures – before the Southern train derailed.View image in fullscreenRear-facing CCTV image from a train that passed the derailment location on 13 August shows the track irregularity visible by the white ballast bags.Photograph: Courtesy of Greater Thameslink RailwayIt said its investigation was taking weather conditions into account, as well as the status of the track, embankment, condition of the train and the effectiveness of any measures taken to mitigate the hot temperatures.The report said there had been “a sustained period of hot and dry weather” and that the ambient air temperature at the time was about 27C, according to the nearest weather station to the site.In a joint statement, Network Rail and Greater Thameslink Railway (GTR), which runs Southern, said they were “very sorry that this happened on our railway”.“We also recognise the ongoing impact the incident has had on customers, local communities and railway colleagues,” said Lucy McAuliffe, Sussex route director at Network Rail, and John Whitehurst, chief executive at GTR.“Safety is and will always remain our highest priority. While Britain’s railway is one of the safest in the world, when incidents like this occur it is essential that we understand exactly what happened and identify any lessons that can be learned.”The stretch of railway between Lewes and Haywards Heath is scheduled to remain closed until at least the end of service on 26 August. That will give time for the train to be recovered – a complex job involving the derailed carriages being lifted by crane – and for recovery teams to make sure evidence is preserved.View image in fullscreenRail workers at the scene of the Greater Anglia train derailment south of Wickford railway station in Essex, which occurred a day after the Lewes derailment.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAThe incident happened on 13 August amid the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer, during whichtwo trains derailed in less than 24 hours. The second derailment occurred on Friday when the rear carriages of a Greater Anglia train came off the track “in an upright position” at Wickford railway station in Essex, with no reported injuries.The embankment on which the railway sits near the Lewes derailment site is made of clay, meaning it is “sensitive to variations in water content and may undergo movement as moisture levels change”, the RAIB said.It added that “although, at this stage, there is no evidence to indicate that a significant embankment slip occurred before the accident, there is evidence that some movement had previously taken place”.RAIB investigators said they had received “several reports of rough riding” from passengers on other trains in the same location.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is understood that investigation teams still consider the inquiry to be in its very early days and the final report may not be published for a year or longer.The Office of Rail and Road (ORR). said it was also “investigating the circumstances of the incident” but declined to comment further. Unlike the RAIB, the ORR’s remit is to look into potential “breaches of health and safety law” and it has the power to prosecute on those grounds.The train was travelling at about 65mph – within the 70mph speed limit – as it approached the site of the incident, with about 150 people onboard.Three carriages ended up on their side, trapping passengers and injuring 30 people, including 20 who required hospital treatment, the RAIB said. “Significant damage was caused to the train and to railway infrastructure,” the watchdog added.James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat MP for Lewes, said the early findings “raise serious concerns”, and the fault on the track was “deeply concerning”.“I travel this line very regularly and reported to the authorities just how bumpy this section of track had become. We cannot assume that this is related, but that makes the current findings even more troubling.”The Department forTransportsaid: “Safety remains the absolute priority across our rail network, and we will ensure the industry acts on any findings in the Rail Accident Investigation Branch’s full report when published.”Explore more on these topicsRail transportRail industryTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: British energy bills forecast to hit three-year high this winter | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Expected quarterly price cap rise of 4% likely to wipe out benefits of Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Expected quarterly price cap rise of 4% likely to wipe out benefits of Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills
Content: Energy market prices are soaring amid the Middle East war, compounded by the extra use of expensive gas in power plants during heatwaves across Europe.Photograph: Richard Newstead/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEnergy market prices are soaring amid the Middle East war, compounded by the extra use of expensive gas in power plants during heatwaves across Europe.Photograph: Richard Newstead/Getty ImagesEnergy billsBritish energy bills forecast to hit three-year high this winterExpected quarterly price cap rise of 4% likely to wipe out benefits of Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity billsJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentWed 19 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 08.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHousehold energy bills across Great Britain are expected to climb to a three-year high this winter as the impact of the Middle East war wipes out Andy Burnham’s tax cut on electricity bills.The government’s cap on energy prices is on track to rise by 4% from this October to the equivalent of £1,729 a year through the last three months of 2026, which could hit struggling households especially hard this winter, according to analysis by the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight.The forecast quarterly price cap would be the highest since July 2023, after soaring energy market prices from the Middle East were compounded by the increased use of expensive gas in power plants during heatwaves across Europe.The rising cost of gas will more than offset the new prime minister’s promise to cut VAT from household electricity bills from October, which aimed togive voters “some breathing space”on living costs by shrinking bills by an average of £45 a year.Craig Lowrey, the principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, said: “It is a stark reminder that our energy bills remain tied to events thousands of miles away. Moments like this are the strongest argument for reducing Britain’s reliance on volatile international gas.“While temporary relief like VAT cuts help soften the blow, they don’t touch the underlying fact that Britain is heavily dependent on imports of natural gas. As long as we’re exposed to global markets, the risk of these price shocks will remain.”Graph showing energy price caps implemented for typical levels of consumption, direct debt accountsOfgem is due to set the price cap next Wednesday. The regulator determines the maximum price of each unit of gas and electricity based on the cost of supplying energy to homes, including the average wholesale market costs in the months leading up to the start of each new cap.The analysts have estimated that electricity rates will rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.57p, and gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.90p for households that pay via direct debit.This is the equivalent of an annual dual fuel bill of £1,729 for the typical UK household, under the energy regulator’s new calculations, which assume that households use less energy than before. Under the previous methodology, the price cap would rise to £1,940.69 from October, according to Cornwall,from £1,862 in the three months from July.“Rising energy bills aren’t welcome at the best of times, but with winter approaching, this latest hike will hit struggling households especially hard,” Lowrey said.The consultancy expects bills to rise again in January based on current market prices, although this could change depending on developments in the Middle East.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Ralston, the head of energy at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said: “To many households this will feel like a horrible reminder of the first gas crisis after Russia invaded Ukraine. What’s even more worrying is that wholesale gas prices have reached a near four-year high, which is likely to cause more increases to future bills.”Ralston said the UK’s reliance on gas for home heating was “a particular concern as although electric heat pump sales are on the up, we still lag behind European neighbours going further and faster to reduce gas dependence”.A government spokesperson said: “We’re acting to give consumers breathing space with the cost of living – cutting VAT on energy bills, ensuring around 6m households get the £150 warm home discount this winter, and making millions of homes cheaper to run through our warm homes plan.”The spokesperson added: “Alongside our efforts to support rapid de-escalation in the Middle East, we will do everything we can to shield consumers from global energy shocks and bring down bills for good.”Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsEnergy industryHousehold billsConsumer affairsUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: London flat where boy fell to death could have had more safeguards, inquest told | Housing | The Guardian
description: Aalim Ahmed, five, fell from 15th-floor window at tower block family had asked to be moved out of, court hears
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Aalim Ahmed, five, fell from 15th-floor window at tower block family had asked to be moved out of, court hears
Content: Jacobs House in Plaistow, east London, where Aalim Ahmed died after falling from the 15th floor in May 2024.Photograph: PA/AlamyView image in fullscreenJacobs House in Plaistow, east London, where Aalim Ahmed died after falling from the 15th floor in May 2024.Photograph: PA/AlamyHousingLondon flat where boy fell to death could have had more safeguards, inquest toldAalim Ahmed, five, fell from 15th-floor window at tower block family had asked to be moved out of, court hearsNadeem BadshahWed 19 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn inquest into the death of a five-year-old boy who fell from a 15th-floor window has heard that more measures could have been taken to make it safer.Aalim Ahmed, who was autistic,died when he fellfrom a kitchen window at a residential block in Plaistow, east London. His father, Makail Ahmed, rushed from the top floor temporary social housing flat and discovered his body shortly before 6am on 16 May 2024.There was a long history of complaints about the council accommodation from the family, who had asked to be moved, the court heard.East London coroner’s court heard that the Newham council property manager Nnenna Muoma thought “more restricted features could have been installed” after visiting the Ahmed family on the afternoon he died.In a note to the council after seeing the family at Jacobs House, the property manager wrote: “Following the horrible incident and fatality, I visited the family yesterday. The kitchen window from where the child fell off is functional but can be operated by a child, hence the incident.“There is [a] restricted feature to allow a limited opening. More restricted features could have been installed to reduce this risk.”Muoma told the court: “That was my personal thought. I have seen other households with children with special needs with different gadgets which can be done to make it safer.”She said she was not an expert in the area and did not know the window restrictors in place could be locked.View image in fullscreenThe family had asked to be moved from Jacobs House in Plaistow, east London.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Makail Ahmed and Aalim’s mother, Sahra Osman, have described their son’s death as “preventable” and blamed Newham council, after claims safety concerns about the flat were reported on multiple occasions.A postmortem examination found Aalim died from “multiple injuries due to or as a consequence of trauma” from a “fall from height”.Osman has told the court she was “scared” and “horrified” when the council put them in the top-floor flat, which needed repairs, because her son had “no sense of danger”. She felt the property was not suitable for her young family, which also included a newborn girl, but felt obliged to take it or risk homelessness.On the day Aalim died, Osman was sitting on a bed with her arms wrapped around herself when Muoma saw her. One of the first things Osman told her was: “I asked to be moved and nobody listened to me.”Muoma told the court: “I said I do not have that information but I am sorry. We want to assist you and if [you] cannot stay overnight I can find you a place to stay.”Muoma said she tried the window twice and was able to open it on the second attempt, but could not remember exactly how she did it.The council property manager said she may have pressed a button to help open it but did not give details about the restrictor or the position of the handle. She also took a photograph of the open position to show her manager how far it could open, she told the court.Newham council said it would be unable to comment until after the inquest concluded.The hearing continues.Explore more on these topicsHousingLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kim Jong-un’s sister casts doubt on Trump’s claims of secret US-North Korea talks | North Korea | The Guardian
description: President says he plans to meet dictator this year but Kim Yo-jong says US remains enemy of Pyongyang
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: President says he plans to meet dictator this year but Kim Yo-jong says US remains enemy of Pyongyang
Content: Donald Trump (right) and Kim Jong-un in 2018. On Wednesday the US leader declined to say whether or not the two were in direct contact.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump (right) and Kim Jong-un in 2018. On Wednesday the US leader declined to say whether or not the two were in direct contact.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APNorth KoreaKim Jong-un’s sister casts doubt on Trump’s claims of secret US-North Korea talksPresident says he plans to meet dictator this year but Kim Yo-jong says Washington remains Pyongyang’s enemyAndrew Rothin WashingtonWed 19 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said he is planning to meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un later this year, though the reclusive leader’s younger sister cast doubt on their communications and dampened hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough between them.Trump, who also claimed North Korea had 57 nuclear weapons, had suggested he and Kim were holding secret negotiations on Tuesday after announcing the US woulddowngrade its participation in military exercisesheld by South Korea, a US ally. Asked whether Kim had responded to his request for a conversation, Trump said: “Yeah, he has.”The Wall Street Journalreportedon Tuesday that Trump was pushing aides to set up an in-person meeting with Kim, potentially during a trip to Asia in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.In cutting joint drills, Trump has given South Korea’s president what he wants. So why is Seoul so uneasy?Read moreBut on Wednesday Kim Yo-jong, thepowerful sister of North Korea’s supreme leader, said she knew “absolutely nothing” about the supposed communications, and that while Trump and Kim had an excellent relationship, the US remained an enemy of Pyongyang.“The United States’ hostile policy toward the DPRK has not changed, and the United States and its followers are vigorously carrying out hostile military activities against the DPRK even at this very moment,” she said in a statement carried by North Korean state media.Journalists questioned Trump further about his talks with Kim in front of Marine One on Wednesday. He declined to say whether or not he was in direct contact, but asked whether he was planning to meet Kim later this year, he said: “Yeah, I will be.”“I knowKim Jong-unvery well and he’s gonna be fine,” Trump said. “As long as we have a smart president, he’s gonna be fine. If we have a dumb president, then he’s probably not going to be so fine.”Trump also made the unusual disclosure that North Korea had 57 “very powerful nuclear weapons”, revealing exact intelligence that may not ordinarily be made public. He added that Iran should not be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon.In her statement, Kim’s sister lauded the relationship between him and Trump, saying he had “personally good memories and feelings” toward the US president.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe cast doubt on whether her brother had secretly been in communication with Trump. “Perhaps it is the only matter I do not know about in relation to our supreme leadership’s foreign policy,” she said.She denied claims by Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that North Korea planned to deploy tens of thousands of troops to fight for Russia.Explore more on these topicsNorth KoreaKim Jong-unSouth KoreaDonald TrumpUS foreign policyAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Edmonton Marathon admits 2026 route was more than half a kilometre too long | Marathon running | The Guardian
description: Canadian contest sparked outrage from scores of frustrated runners online and in Canadian media
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Canadian contest sparked outrage from scores of frustrated runners online and in Canadian media
Content: Runners reported their energy waning unexpectedly in the last kilometre of the race.Photograph: caronwatson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRunners reported their energy waning unexpectedly in the last kilometre of the race.Photograph: caronwatson/Getty ImagesMarathon runningEdmonton Marathon admits 2026 route was more than half a kilometre too longCanadian contest sparked outrage from scores of frustrated runners online and in Canadian mediaOlivia BowdenWed 19 Aug 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe organisers of the Edmonton Marathon have admitted the course was more than half a kilometre too long, after outrage from scores of runners who complained about the distance.The error resulted in the upending of runners’ personal bests and potentially prevented some from breaking records.Participants who were hoping to use Edmonton as a qualifier for the Boston Marathon may have also faced disappointment, as mere seconds can make the difference between being accepted or denied a spot in the prestigious race. Many runners are drawn to the Edmonton race for a chance to gain entry to Boston.After a cascade of frustrated runners voicing their concerns online and in Canadian media, race organisers had initially said the course was officially certified and undoubtedly the correct distance. But in statements on Tuesday, they admitted a mistake was made.“We do not take this lightly,” said race director, Tom Keogh. “We hosted the nation’s best athletes and their finishing times did not truly reflect their amazing performances,” he said.After a thorough examination, the event team for the race concluded it was an additional 674.4 metres (0.41 miles) longer than the standard of 42.195 kilometres (26.22 miles), said Keogh in a statement on Tuesday.The review found the added length to the course was caused by a detour implemented to avoid construction around the Wellington Bridge. The race, which took place on Sunday, will undergo a review of its certification process to ensure the error never occurs again, said Keogh.Runners reported their energy waning unexpectedly in the last kilometre of the race. On Monday, Olympian Natasha Wodak told theCanadian Broadcasting Corporationshe noticed her pace was slower than usual as she ran the final few hundred metres.When she saw her final time, she said she thought: “What in the world?” An accurate course length is crucial to all participants who spend money in order to achieve a personal best, she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It really is the most important thing of a race, besides safety,” she said.Explore more on these topicsMarathon runningCanadaAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Star’s extreme proximity to Sagittarius A* means it could open new window onto black hole’s fundamental properties
Author: Hannah Devlin
Headline: Star’s extreme proximity to Sagittarius A* means it could open new window onto black hole’s fundamental properties
Content: Several stars orbiting Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the centre of our galaxyPhotograph: ESO and Digitized Sky Survey 2/ReutersView image in fullscreenSeveral stars orbiting Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the centre of our galaxyPhotograph: ESO and Digitized Sky Survey 2/ReutersAstronomyAstronomers detect fastest known star in Milky WayStar’s extreme proximity to Sagittarius A* means it could open new window onto black hole’s fundamental propertiesHannah Devlinscience correspondentWed 19 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstronomers have detected the fastest known star in the Milky Way, hurtling around the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy.The star, called S301, travels at about 25,000km (15,500 miles) per second, 100,000 times faster than a commercial plane. It is also the closest known star to the Milky Way’s central black hole, Sagittarius A*, approaching it around the distance of Saturn to the Sun.“What is special about this star is that it’s orbiting Sagittarius A* on a very tight orbit, taking just 8.7 years to complete it, and is approaching the black hole at a mere 12 times the distance of Earth to the sun. That is unprecedented,” said Felix Mang, a PhD student at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE) in Garching, Germany, and an author of the study published on the findings.The star’s extreme proximity to Sagittarius A* means that it could open a new window on to the black hole’s fundamental properties and the extreme environment surrounding it.Like many objects in the night sky, black holes are predicted to spin. According to Einstein’s general theory of relativity, a spinning black hole drags spacetime along with it, warping the orbits of surrounding stars. This effect is only meaningful for objects orbiting fast-rotating black holes at close range.S301 appears to have the perfect combination of a highly eccentric (lopsided) and very tight orbit.“For the first time, we would actually be able to measure very directly the spin of a massive black hole, which would be a key test of Einstein’s theory,” said Dr Stefan Gillessen, a senior scientist at MPE and a co-author of the study, which ispublished in the journal Nature.View image in fullscreenA sequence of images from the ESO’s VLTI shows several stars orbiting Sagittarius A*. S301 passes closer to Sagittarius A* than the others; the solid curve shows the portion of its orbit already completed, while the dashed curve shows the path it will follow.Photograph: ESO/Gravity/ReutersPreviously it had been assumed it would require measuring the motion of multiple stars for several decades to estimate the spin of Sagittarius A*. The scientists were able to trace S301’s orbit back to 2017 and, by tracking it through its next closest passage in 2031, hope to have enough data.“With this star we hope to measure, within the next 10 years, the spin of the black hole,” said Mang.The observations were made using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope Interferometer (ESO’s VLTI) at the Paranal Observatory in Chile, which combines the light from four 8-metre telescopes.Although the star is unusually close to the central black hole, it is not expected to cross its event horizon, the point beyond which objects can never escape.“Black holes are perceived as these cosmic vacuum cleaners engulfing everything they can get a handle on,” said Mang. “But it’s just a massive object. It’s not really much different from something orbiting the sun and it’s going to remain on this orbit.”Dr Ziri Younsi, an astrophysicist at University College London, who was not involved in the observations, said: “This is incredibly important as a discovery. It’s very exciting because this thing comes insanely close to Sagittarius A* and it’s travelling, at its peak, at about 8% of the speed of light, which is crazy.”Younsi said that using the orbit to provide a measurement of the black hole’s spin would be a gamechanger for understanding the evolution of the Milky Way.Explore more on these topicsAstronomyBlack holesSpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn | Spain | The Guardian
description: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back
Content: Tents being set up in a public car park in Ceuta on Tuesday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenTents being set up in a public car park in Ceuta on Tuesday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersSpainSpain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turnMadrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent backEurope live – latest updatesStephen Burgenin BarcelonaWed 19 Aug 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland.The majority of the estimated70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta– a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.On 13 August, the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, had said: “Anyone who illegally enters Ceuta or Melilla [another Spanish enclave in north Africa] knows they will be sent back because Spain andMoroccowork together to this end. They will not reach the peninsula, nor the European continent and nor will they remain indefinitely in Ceuta or Melilla.”The transfer of the children to the Spanish mainland is a sensitive political topic as several regions governed jointly by the conservative People’s party and the far-right Vox are reluctant or opposed to receiving their quota.To minimise conflict, the youth ministry, in coordination with the Ceuta government, is devising an urgent plan under which NGOs and child protection agencies take charge of the most vulnerable children, girls in particular, without transferring their guardianship to Spain’s regional governments.Rubén Pérez Correa, the secretary of state for children, has been in Ceuta since Sunday in an effort to resolve a situation in which hundreds of children are living on the street and existing on handouts from Ceuta residents.News of the government’s plan came only hours after the European Commission said that under EU law all of the migrants should be returned to Morocco. Asked to clarify, the commission’s spokesperson on internal affairs, Markus Lammert, said that by law all irregular migrants remaining in Ceuta should be sent back, “including unaccompanied minors”.Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreThe People’s party has rejected the government plan, saying the best place for the children is with their families. “If Morocco has asked for the children to be returned and if Europe says the illegal immigrants should all be returned, whether children or not, what more does the government need?” the People’s party deputy finance spokesperson, Juan Bravo, said in a television interview.The mixed messages partly derive from the fact the latest European pact on immigration has not yet been incorporated into Spanish law and therefore Spain’s own legislation on the treatment of unaccompanied minors remains in force.According to Spain’s ministry of inclusion and migration, as of lastMarch21,104 people aged 16-23 were guardians of the state, of whom about 3,500 were under 17. Approximately 50% were from Morocco. Girls made up about 8% of the total.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeEuropean UnionMoroccoMigrationAfricaRefugeesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School investigated over hidden fees | Competition and Markets Authority | The Guardian
description: UK competition watchdog investigation is part of broader clampdown on illegal ‘drip pricing’
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: UK competition watchdog investigation is part of broader clampdown on illegal ‘drip pricing’
Content: Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School are under investigation for displaying misleadingly low prices.Composite: Alamy/Getty/PAView image in fullscreenTrainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School are under investigation for displaying misleadingly low prices.Composite: Alamy/Getty/PACompetition and Markets AuthorityTrainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School investigated over hidden feesUK competition watchdog investigation is part of broader clampdown on illegal ‘drip pricing’Nils Pratley: all power to UK watchdog’s war on ‘drip pricing’Lauren AlmeidaWed 19 Aug 2026 07.14 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 04.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s competition watchdog has launched investigations into Trainline,Virgin Atlanticand Red Driving School over concerns that all three companies displayed misleadingly low prices to their customers.The Competition and Markets Authority’s investigations are part of a broader clampdown on“drip pricing”, an illegal practice that makes a product appear cheaper by not including all mandatory fees.The regulator said it had opened investigations into the companies amid concerns that customers had not been shown the total price up front when buying train and coach tickets, holidays or driving lessons.“The first price customers see should be the price they pay,” said Emma Cochrane, the executive director for consumer protection at the CMA. “Clear pricing helps people compare offers confidently and choose the option that works best for them.“Unexpected mandatory charges make this much harder, which is why the CMA initially put these firms on notice over concerns about their pricing practices and is now opening formal investigations.”Trainline said in a statement to the stock exchange that it had “proactively engaged with the CMA over several months” and was “taking steps to enhance the presentation of certain fees”. Shares in the business, which is the only one of the three companies that is listed on the stock exchange, fell by as much as 14% in early trading on Wednesday.Virgin Atlantic said mandatory fees were “indicated at multiple stages” when customers were booking trips but it was reviewing the concerns and would cooperate with the regulator.Red Driving School said it valued transparency in its customer interactions and was engaging with the CMA.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK retailers too slow to pass on fuel price falls, watchdog saysRead moreThe CMA’s investigations have been launched using its new consumer protection powers, which weregranted last year.These powers allow the regulator to decide whether consumer laws have been broken, rather than having to go through the courts. If the CMA finds there has been an infringement of the law, it can order businesses to pay compensation to affected customers and can fine companies up to 10% of their global turnover.Earlier this year the CMA ordered the ticket sellerStubHub to pay out nearly £1.5min customer refunds and penalties for drip pricing. It also fined the AA £4.2m and ordered it to repay more than £760,000 to learner drivers over drip pricing.Andy Burnham has also promised to end “rip-off” business practices. Writing in the Guardian this month, the prime minister said his government wouldstep in wherever it could, as he seeks to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.Get in touchContact the Guardian Business teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
