Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging.When asked who you wish to contact please select the ‘Business (UK & Global)’ team.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsCompetition and Markets AuthorityConsumer affairsRegulatorsVirgin AtlanticAirline industryRail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Jaecoo owner Chery takes ‘next step’ in UK push with R&D centre | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Owner of firm behind ‘Temu Range Rover’ will open facility in Bedfordshire in autumn
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Owner of firm behind ‘Temu Range Rover’ will open facility in Bedfordshire in autumn
Content: Chery’s Jaecoo 7 became the top-selling model in the UK in March.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenChery’s Jaecoo 7 became the top-selling model in the UK in March.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersAutomotive industryJaecoo owner Chery takes ‘next step’ in UK push with R&D centreOwner of firm behind ‘Temu Range Rover’ will open facility in Bedfordshire in autumnAlex DanielWed 19 Aug 2026 11.12 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Chinese carmaker behind theirreverently nicknamed “Temu Range Rover”is plotting further UK expansion with a major research and development centre in England.Chery, which makes the Jaecoo and Omoda car brands, said the launch of a new R&D site was “the next step in our long-term plan” for Britain as it also moves towards manufacturing its cars in the UK.Chery’s sales are growing at breakneck pace in Britain. In July, the Chery, Omoda and Jaecoo brands accounted for nearly 8% of UK market share, up from 3% last year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.The China-built Jaecoo 7, known as the “Temu Range Rover” for its low price and techy add-ons, became thetop-selling model in the UK in March, but Chery currently has to bring it in from abroad.The company is part-owned by the Chinese state andhas already signed a deal with Nissanto build its cars at its Sunderland plant, in a move that would begin mass-market Chinese car production in Britain for the first time from 2027.View image in fullscreenChery’s new R&D facility at Millbrook, Bedfordshire, will give it access to test tracks to fine-tune its cars for UK roads.Photograph: Rick Noel/Sprite PhotographyThe new R&D facility would open in late autumn, Chery said on Wednesday. Gary Lan, the chief executive of its UK business, said: “We waited over 20 years for the right time to enter this market, and our ambition has always gone much further than simply bringing vehicles here.”An existing vehicle testing centre inBedfordshirethat is used by engineering and motorsport companies – as well as the Ministry of Defence – will be the site of Chery’s new R&D facility.The centre, called UTAC Millbrook, will give Chery access to more than 70km (43 miles) of purpose-built test tracks for it to fine-tune its cars for UK roads. Further down the line it will also use the site to work on self-driving cars and artificial intelligence.Chinese manufacturers’ arrival as a major force in the car industry hasput enormous pressure on traditional European rivals. Chinese companies have been able to undercut European companies in building electrified cars because of state subsidies, lower labour costs and the country’s dominance in the battery industry.Chery alsolaunched its Lepas brand– its fourth in the UK – last February, aimed at younger families in the European market.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLepas, Chery, Jaecoo and Omoda models on the Millbrook ‘bowl’ test track.Photograph: Rick Noel/Sprite PhotographyKirsty Andrew, the vice-president of UTAC UK, said the new R&D centre was “a significant commitment to engineering and vehicle development in the UK”.She added: “Creating a stand-alone engineering centre here means Chery Automobile can develop and validate vehicles against the particular demands of UK roads and UK drivers, with direct access to our engineering expertise and testing environments throughout that process.”Chery said it eventually planned to recruit local talent and create engineering jobs in the area – but did not say how much it would invest in the site or how many jobs would be created.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryChinaManufacturing sectorAsia PacificEuropeEnglandBedfordshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shares in humanoid robot firm Unitree surge 600% on Chinese stock market debut | Robots | The Guardian
description: Company’s robots have gained global fame via videos of them performing martial arts and as dancers for pop stars
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Company’s robots have gained global fame via videos of them performing martial arts and as dancers for pop stars
Content: A Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Analysts project sales of humanoid robots could rise from $2bn in 2025 to $300bn in 2035.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Analysts project sales of humanoid robots could rise from $2bn in 2025 to $300bn in 2035.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesRobotsShares in humanoid robot firm Unitree surge 600% on Chinese stock market debutCompany’s robots have gained global fame via videos of them performing martial arts and as dancers for pop starsLauren AlmeidaWed 19 Aug 2026 03.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnitree, the world’s biggest humanoid robot maker, has made a spectacular entry on to China’s stock market, with its shares surging by more than 600%.The Chinese company’s robots have gained global fame viaviral videos of them performing martial arts, running at Olympic speeds and serving as backup dancers for pop stars.View image in fullscreenTwo Unitree robots in a fighting demonstration at the World Robot Conference in Beijing on Wednesday.Photograph: Adek Berry/AFP/Getty ImagesShares in the business, officially known as Yushu Technology Co, rose to as high as 1,100 yuan (£120.39) on Wednesday, up from an IPO price of just 150.8 yuan. Its gains were later pared back to a rise of nearly 500%.Investors are searching for winners in robotics development, which has emerged as one of thekey battlegrounds in the AI race.Unitree, which was founded in 2016, shipped more than 5,500 humanoid robots last year.The market for human-like robots is expected to grow rapidly, with analysts projecting that sales could rise from around $2bn (£1.5bn) in 2025 to $300bn by 2035.There was exceptional demand from Chinese retail investors in Unitree’s IPO, with the tranche of shares dedicated to non-professional stockpickers oversubscribed by thousands.Unitree is one of the few listed humanoid robot makers in the world. Its biggest competitor, AgiBot, is private and its smaller rival UBTech is listed in Hong Kong.However, at least half a dozen other Chinese humanoid robotic businesses are preparing to go public, including Deep Robotics and Leju Robotics.Wang Xingxing, who founded Unitree in 2016 and remains its chief executive, owns about a fifth of the business. The spike in its share price means his personal wealth is now worth more than $12bn on paper, according to Reuters.Unitree’s market debut also coincided with the opening of the World Robot Conference in Bejiing on Wednesday, where hundreds of companies, mostly Chinese, will launch new products and demonstrate their technical developments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast month, the US Federal Communications Commissionbanned imports of future modelsof foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots based on national security concerns.3:48Why the US government is banning Chinese robots – video explainerThis summer the Pentagon also added Unitree to a list of Chinese military companies, describing it as a “contributor to the Chinese defence industrial base”. Unitree has previously said its robots are for civilian use.The business is backed by several big Chinese technology companies, including Tencent and Alibaba.Explore more on these topicsRobotsIPOsStock marketsTechnology sectorChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Will AI give you the job? Automated hiring tools spark discrimination and secrecy lawsuits | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: A rise in lawsuits over AI use in employment decisions is raising questions about how companies hire and fire
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: A rise in lawsuits over AI use in employment decisions is raising questions about how companies hire and fire
Content: ‘Companies in the US are increasingly turning to AI to make faster and more efficient workplace decisions, often under the guise of objectivity.’Composite: Alvaro Dominguez/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Companies in the US are increasingly turning to AI to make faster and more efficient workplace decisions, often under the guise of objectivity.’Composite: Alvaro Dominguez/The GuardianReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)Will AI give you the job? Automated hiring tools spark discrimination and secrecy lawsuitsA rise in lawsuits over AI use in employment decisions is raising questions about how companies hire and fireSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesWed 19 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the last four years, Erin Kistler has applied for thousands of jobs at companies likePaypal,MicrosoftandNetflix, only to find her résumé disappear into a black hole. A product manager with nearly 20 years of experience, Kistler believes she was qualified for every role, yet she never received a single interview.Now, Kistler is suing Eightfold AI, the Silicon Valley maker of hiring software used by hundreds of companies, including those where she applied, ina class-action lawsuit. The case, filed in January in California court, is one of the first to argue that automated screening functions as an undisclosed consumer report or applicant dossier, ranking job applicants on their likelihood of success without giving them the chance to see or challenge the results, according to Kistler’s legal team.The lawsuit is one of several new legal battles over companies’ use of AI in employment decisions. Workers are also suing Meta over an internal AI system that allegedlytargeted them for layoffs because they took parental or medical leave. And a recent lawsuit against IBM alleges that AI tools discriminated against older workers.Companies in the US are increasingly turning to AI to make faster and more efficient workplace decisions, often under the guise of objectivity. But experts who study this type of software say it can also introduce or exacerbate bias that could follow candidates across companies. Lawmakers are taking notice. The outcomes of the legal battles could shape future employment practices, transparency around them and the power candidates have in the process.“There’s actually no law requiring a notice or disclosure of the use of these AI hiring systems,” said Ifeoma Ajunwa, a professor at Emory University School of Law and founding director of the AI and future of work program. “So companies are not necessarily telling workers when they’re being evaluated with AI.”AI use in hiring is growingLast year, 90% of employers used some form of automation in the hiring process, according to areportfrom the World Economic Forum. These tools range from basic filtering – like excluding candidates who don’t have a four-year degree or another prerequisite – to using AI to conduct assessments of a job applicant’s skills or even to perform the initial phone interview.In the case of Eightfold, the company bills itself as “the world’s largest, self-refreshing source of talent data”. It constantly updates an internal database with information from the résumés, LinkedIn profiles, and social media profiles of over a billion workers who have applied for jobs through its platform. Using this data, it uses AI to score applicants on a scale of 0 to 5, predicting how well they would perform in a given job. Ultimately, the score could prioritize some candidates over others for interviews.“A large part of the problem is that job applicants don’t know … what the reports say,” said Rachel Dempsey, an attorney representing Kistler.Dempsey argues that job applicants deserve the same transparency into what goes into the hiring process that Americans already get in their credit reports. With that information, they can either dispute inaccuracies or work to improve on factors affecting their candidacy. But without any insight, it’s impossible to know if these algorithms discriminate against job candidates in explicit ways, Dempsey said.“The concept of a black box is very scary,” she says.In a statement to the Guardian, Eightfold AI denied the allegations. “We believe the claims asserted are without merit and intend to defend ourselves vigorously,” an Eightfold AI spokesperson wrote in an email.In response to the lawsuit filed against IBM, the company denied using AI to automatically screen out candidates and in a statement said it “does not condone or tolerate discrimination of any kind.” Meta did not respond to a request for comment on its lawsuit.The fear of algorithmic blacklistingThough employment software providers claim to free up hiring managers to spend more time with qualified candidates and remove human personal biases, experts disagree. They say AI can exacerbate biases like favoring workers of certain demographics.“As we’ve done more of the research on AI hiring systems, we actually see that they tend to replicate a lot of the same biases that human managers have,” Ajunwa said.Nearly all AI systems are trained to look for patterns, which can reinforce stereotypes or legacy biases. Amazon, for example, once used an AI tool thatdownranked women’s résumésbecause the company’s top performers were men. Amazon discontinued its use after discovering the issue. In other cases, AI hiring systems can introduce their own biases. In research for her book, The Quantified Worker, Ajunwa found that AI scored job applicants with southern accents poorly, as it struggled to understand them during voice interviews.While human hiring managers can be unfair – choosing the applicant who was in the same fraternity, for example – “the magnitude of bias is even stronger [with AI],” says Xuechunzi Bai, assistant professor at the University of Chicago who has researched hiring bias.Bai co-authored arecent studywhere AI models were asked to make hiring decisions about fictional applicants assigned to made-up demographic groups called Tufa, Aima, Reku and Weki. After a few rounds of hiring decisions, the AI models made inferences about candidates that had nothing to do with their qualifications, in effect stereotyping them. If one Tufa was a good doctor, then Tufa candidates were more likely to be chosen as doctors, and Weki candidates were more likely to be hired as janitors.The study found greater bias in AI than in human hiring decisions she examined last year. It also found that newer and more advanced models produced hiring decisions with more bias.“We were quite shocked to see this result,” Bai said. AI models are very good at solving problems where there is one objective solution, as in math or coding. “But … they’re getting worse in terms of exploring the other alternatives,” Bai said. “In the context of hiring, exploration is quite important, but these models are not trained to do it.”The consequences of AI’s biases for an applicant can extend beyond one job opening. When a worker is rejected by a person, they can try again at a different company with a different hiring manager. But when a worker is rejected by an algorithmic system used across companies, the system “remembers the decision that was already made and makes it again for the sake of efficiency”, said Ajunwa. “In reality, you’ve been algorithmically blackballed.”Because so many companies use the hiring software built on the same foundational AI models, the concern is that a negative flag could potentially make it much harder for a candidate to get a job at all, said Katie Creel, co-author of arecent studyexamining the risks of “algorithmic monoculture” in hiring systems. “People are going to be shut out of jobs more than they would have otherwise been,” she said.Eightfold AI did not comment on the matter.Can AI be responsibly integrated into hiring?While AI tools may save time or help test candidates’ skills, hiring managers shouldn’t allow AI to make decisions, said Iman Abuzeid, CEO of Incredible Health, an AI hiring platform used by more than 1,500 healthcare employers. Incredible Health offers an AI agent to perform phone interviews, but the AI doesn’t autoreject, score, rank or decide who moves forward, according to Abuzeid.“It’s about collecting information from the candidates so a human is better armed to make the decision,” Abuzeid said.Abuzeid also said about 10% of Incredible Health’s AI interviews are audited for bias by a human, a process that’s becoming a legal requirement by a growing number of cities and states.In New York City, a law that took effect in 2023 requires employers using automated systems in hiring to conduct annual bias audits and notify candidates in advance about the tech’s usage. The law, however, only applies to software that “substantially assists” or replaces decision-making, creating a loophole for cases where humans are part of the process. Recent laws from Illinois and Colorado also prohibit employers’ use of AI tools that result in unlawful discrimination.Increasingly, city and state regulations aim to make notifying job applicants that AI is being used a baseline requirement. But ideally, candidates would have transparency into what their algorithmic dossiers say about them, said Jenny Yang, a partner at Outten & Golden, the law firm representing the plaintiffs in the lawsuit against Eightfold AI.“This initial transparency is helpful in better identifying where there may be problems,” Yang said, referring to notifications that AI was used. “There’s a lot of growing concern among workers that they may be denied opportunity for reasons that no one understands.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedComputingPayPalNetflixMicrosoftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m not Mr Saturday Night’: the highbrow brilliance of Ahir Shah, past winner of comedy’s top prize  | Ahir Shah | The Guardian
description: Three years ago, he won the Edinburgh comedy award with a work in progress. Now he’s back with a show inspired by Gerard Manley Hopkins and Friedrich Nietzsche. Isn’t this all a bit grownup?
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Three years ago, he won the Edinburgh comedy award with a work in progress. Now he’s back with a show inspired by Gerard Manley Hopkins and Friedrich Nietzsche. Isn’t this all a bit grownup?
Content: ‘If you’re encased in lead, how do you get golden?’ … Ahir Shah, whose new show is called Golden.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘If you’re encased in lead, how do you get golden?’ … Ahir Shah, whose new show is called Golden.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianAhir ShahInterview‘I’m not Mr Saturday Night’: the highbrow brilliance of Ahir Shah, past winner of comedy’s top prizeBrian LoganThree years ago, he won the Edinburgh comedy award with a work in progress. Now he’s back with a show inspired by Gerard Manley Hopkins and Friedrich Nietzsche. Isn’t this all a bit grownup?Wed 19 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmong past winners of the Edinburgh comedy award, few seemed less likely when the starter’s pistol fired thanAhir Shah in 2023. Not because Shah wasn’t a contender: he had been nominated twice before. But that year he arrived on the fringe with a mere work in progress, not even eligible for the award. Shah’s director, the greatAdam Brace, had recently died and the comic had just returned to the stage after a break from comedy. But then Ends, a tribute to the performer’s late grandfather and a hymn to multicultural Britain, began gathering steam. Shah reclassified it as a work-now-finished and, toa chorus of rapturous acclaim, it bagged the biggest prize in world comedy.Three years on, he is returning with the follow-up: less uncut diamond this time and more, he hopes, a polished gem. But didn’t the success of Ends prove polish was unnecessary? “You can get very in your head approaching the fringe, thinking: ‘Well, it has to be absolutely locked in by August because x thousand pounds are on the line,’” Shah admits. So doing a work in progress allowed him to “quiet some of those voices – and have less of a panic attack about what you’re going to say”.double quotation markBy God, I’ve lain in bed thinking I’m the worst person who ever existedNotwithstanding his patrician accent (he once joked that he sounds as if “I’ve been colonised by my own voice”), Shah is no stranger to low confidence. His approach to standup is to ask: “How are you justifying breaking the silence that exists in this room prior to you walking out?” With Ends, the justification was ample. Like all the Londoner’s work, the show teemed with ideas and erudition, this time at the service of a tale (as Shah now describes it) of “the sacrifices people are willing to make in their own lives for subsequent generations. It was about what families do for one another.”But the show, pulled together as Rishi Sunak became prime minister, was also about the UK, and how it had changed since Shah’s grandfather moved here in the 1960s. “I couldn’t help but think about the incomprehensible shift that had to occur over 60 years to make something my grandfather could never have conceived of come to pass.” The UK, Shah declared in the show, is “the least racist country in the world”: not an argument audiences expected from a regular guest onFrankie Boyle’s New World Order and a comic once known for firebrand lefty polemic.View image in fullscreen‘You can only tell sad and bad stories for so long’ … Ahir Shah.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian“I completely understand the temptation to do the whole ‘rainy fascism island’ thing,” he says. “I’ve succumbed to it many a time. But for most of my adult life, we’ve reflexively told only very sad and bad stories about ourselves. And you can only go on like that for so long. As an individual, you can lie in bed saying: ‘I’m the worst person who ever existed. This is all pointless.’ You can do that – and, by God, I’ve given it a good go. But it’s no way to lead a fulfilling, three-dimensional life. As a collective, we need positive stories as well.”That positivity helped secure a stellar future for Ends, which toured the world (including India, “which was really emotionally significant”) and was broadcast on Netflix. And so the dreams came true for a comic who cut his standup teeth aged 17. Golden, his new set, is inspired by aGerard Manley Hopkinspoem and “section 341 of The Gay Science by Friedrich Nietzsche”. It finds Shah on the threshold of middle-age, now married, planning a family, spooked by the looming responsibility.“These are the issues of capital-G grownup life. All of a sudden there is someone more important than you sharing your roof. There are people who all this mattersfor. There are obligations that are going to bear down on you again and again. And there’s a voice saying: ‘What if you can’t do it? What if you’re not good enough?’”This time with reference to his mother’s life story, Shah is confronting those demons in a show that takes its title from Hopkins’ verse The Leaden Echo and the Golden Echo. “The leaden echo,” says the comic, “is the inevitability of decay. I call it in the show the cold, repetitive, mechanistic, obligatory forevers that every adult in our society is subject to, my mother more than most. And if that’s what encases you in lead, then how do you get golden?”It’s a fine question to be asking for someone who got gold on his last full fringe visit, and is recalibrating his ambitions in light of that success. The Edinburgh comedy award, he says, “was what I dreamed of winning when I started out. I did that. Let’s see what happens now.” One thing he won’t be doing is diluting his highbrow tastes in pursuit of a mainstream audience. “I’m not Mr Saturday Night, I’m not that guy,” he says cheerfully. “An infrastructure exists around comedians that encourages you to underestimate audiences. But I don’t accept that. As long as you build your work out of jokes, what you build is up to you. And what could be more freeing, more wonderful than that?”Ahir Shah: Golden is atPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August. title: Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing review – like a horror movie … only this is real life | Television | The Guardian
description: In 2022, Rory Kennedy exposed the aviation safety scandal in which 346 people died – but since then, a plane door has blown out mid-flight and more whistleblowers have come to the fore. Will anyone pay for this?
Author: Ellen E Jones
Headline: In 2022, Rory Kennedy exposed the aviation safety scandal in which 346 people died – but since then, a plane door has blown out mid-flight and more whistleblowers have come to the fore. Will anyone pay for this?
Content: Nightmarish … Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenNightmarish … Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewFreefall: A Reckoning for Boeing review – like a horror movie … only this is real lifeIn 2022, Rory Kennedy exposed the aviation safety scandal in which 346 people died – but since then, a plane door has blown out mid-flight and more whistleblowers have come to the fore. Will anyone pay for this?Ellen E JonesWed 19 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is unfortunate that a sequel was required to Rory Kennedy’s 2022 documentary feature, which alleged that the profit-driven culture at a US aeronautics firm led to two plane crashes and the deaths of 346 people. But given the lack of corporate accountability evident at the end ofDownfall: The Case Against Boeing– and the apparent complicity of regulatory body the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) – it was inevitable.Freefall: A Reckoning forBoeingopens with a rundown of a significant development in the story: the mysterious death in March 2024 of John Barnett, a former Boeing employee turned whistleblower. Barnett, a contributor in the first film, was in the middle of a deposition when he was found dead at his hotel, which investigators ruled a suicide. Is this another casualty to add to Boeing’s mounting death toll? And is the alarming aviation safety scandal – supposedly resolved in November 2020, when the FAA lifted its grounding order on the Boeing 737 Max – in fact still ongoing?This is the urgent claim of many of this film’s contributors. Some lost loved ones in the two Boeing plane crashes that happened within five months of each other – Lion Air Flight 610, which went down in October 2018, killing all 189 people on board, and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, which crashed in March 2019. One contributor, Naoise Connolly Ryan, lost her husband and the father of her two small children, Michael Ryan, when he was killed alongside 156 others on Flight 302.Others are Boeing whistleblowers who have gone public since the last film, inspired by it. “John Barnett was a lighthouse,” says one. “When I first started at the company, he was pointing people in the right direction. He is continuing to do that now.” Hidden camera footage from Boeing’s Dreamliner assembly plant in South Carolina shows anonymised workers averring that nothing – not even a free luxury holiday – could tempt them to fly on the planes they manufacture.View image in fullscreenLost loved ones … Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThere is a vast moral chasm between those determined to do all within their power to prevent further loss of life and the Boeing leadership. The only gap more glaring is the one betweentwo shoddily outsourced sectionsof fuselage on a 737 Max. This isn’t a horror film, but you’ll struggle to find many movie scenes more nightmarish than Freefall’s reconstruction of the January 2024 incident when a door plug blew out mid-flight (it was missing all four of its crucial bolts) and several passenger oxygen masks malfunctioned. Barnett had warned of this danger years earlier. His concerns were not only ignored, but also he was disciplined for having raised them.Beside the whistleblowers, there is another group of heroes in Freefall. Kennedy’s camera often cedes the floor to impressively fired-up politicians, such as the Missouri senator Josh Hawley, who, at a Senate hearing, challenges the now-retired Boeing CEO Dave Calhoun on his $32.8m 2023 salary, up 45% from 2022: “What is it you get paid to do exactly?” (Calhoun has not been charged with criminal wrongdoing.)It’s worth noting here that Rory Kennedy is not just any Kennedy, but one oftheKennedys: the youngest child of the former senator and US attorney general Robert F Kennedy and his wife, Ethel Kennedy, who was pregnant with Rory when RFK was assassinated in June 1968. It was en route to Rory Kennedy’s wedding three decades later that the plane carrying John F Kennedy Jr, his wife and his sister-in-law went down, killing them all. So this is a film-maker who understands not only what it feels like to lose family in a sudden and shocking tragedy, but also those Camelot-era American values of progress and public service – values Boeing itself once exemplified.Kennedy’s previous projects include the Emmy-winningGhosts of Abu Ghraib and the Oscar-nominated Last Days in Vietnam. Freefallis a clear-eyed, serious-minded film to stand alongside these, but it also echoes a string of other recent documentaries on how, in the neoliberal era, unregulated capital has infiltrated and corrupted such diverse industries as construction (Grenfell: Uncovered), tech (The Social Dilemma) and pharmaceuticals (The Crime of the Century).The pattern of allegations is always the same: an incoming CEO seeks to maximise shareholder profit, whatever the cost to product quality, employee welfare or public safety; warnings are ignored; disaster occurs, then blame is shifted, often with breathtaking shamelessness, on to the dead.Kennedy’s two documentaries gather their participants’ righteous rage steadily enough to burn off the cloud cover of this corporate obfuscation, leaving a clear view of the horizon ahead. In their view, until the individuals in Boeing’s failed leadership face criminal prosecution – as opposed to multimillion-dollar retirement packages – nothing will change.In response to the film-makers’ requests for comment, Boeing stated that some of the claims against the company “remain unfounded” and that “others are issues that Boeing thoroughly addressed or continues to improve upon”.Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVAirline industryBoeingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mutiny review – Jason Statham’s fight-by-numbers action thriller just about stays above water | Jason Statham | The Guardian
description: The hard-working action hero gives us exactly what we expect, and often want, in this sturdy cargo ship-set caper
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: The hard-working action hero gives us exactly what we expect, and often want, in this sturdy cargo ship-set caper
Content: Jason Statham in Mutiny.Photograph: Dan Smith/LionsgateView image in fullscreenJason Statham in Mutiny.Photograph: Dan Smith/LionsgateJason StathamReviewMutiny review – Jason Statham’s fight-by-numbers action thriller just about stays above waterThe hard-working action hero gives us exactly what we expect, and often want, in this sturdy cargo ship-set caperBenjamin LeeWed 19 Aug 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe dog days of August have already seen the trotting out of some usual suspects froma junky Eli Roth horrortoa belated nostalgia comedy sequeltoa Mike Pence-approved Ronald Reagan drama. This weekend, yet more howls will be heard in cinemas witha lower-tier horror instalmentandan even lower-tier girlies on tour comedybeing shuffled out. It’s all amounting to a rather rubbishy end to what’s been a pretty remarkable summer (easily the biggest since the pandemic), allowing for Spider-Man supremacy until September slowly returns the industry from the D-list closer to the A.Coyote Vs Acme review – quirky comedy returns from the dead to flip Wile E Coyote’s slapstick-violent worldRead moreThere can still be low-level popcorn pleasures to be had in August. Last weekend’s throwback dino caperThe End of Oak Streetwas a B-movie made with just the right balance of serious to silly while last year Zach Cregger gifted usWeapons, the rare genre film to end up winning an Oscar. Trophies are unlikely for this weekend’s other medium-sized release Mutiny (if only the Blockbuster Entertainment Awards hadn’t died off at the turn of the 2000s) but if the words “Jason Statham vehicle” possess a safe, soothing quality then there are far worse ways to spend a Saturday night.The actor occupies a rarefied space in a genre that now mostly exists far away from the big screen, pushed back toward the contemporary equivalent of the DVD bargain bin. Outside of the superhero world or some other more fantastical setting, the action movie has struggled at the box office, at least domestically (it remains easily sellable overseas). Without a generation of younger stars taking on impossible missions, it’s been left to the older guard to kick, shoot and try not to keel over, an ever-decreasing squad which is now led by Gerard Butler and Statham (Liam Neeson’s action movie overkill means they barely get released these days). Both have managed to stay working above the glut of even lower-rent, straight-to-streaming titles and they can still manage to attract a decent-sized audience, usually in January or August, kings of the dumping months.For his latest Statham has borrowed Jean-François Richet, the French director of Butler’s 2023 hitPlane, a film I found personally disappointing for its unforgivably small amount of actual plane. That film was supposed to be followed by Ship (I kid you not) butreportedly, Butler dropped out just two weeks before production and it was canned. Perhaps the deposit for the ship had already been paid as it’s hard not to see how Mutiny isn’t what that film ultimately morphed into, another by-the-book tale of a hero striking back at crooks, also sharing the same co-writer. If Plane suffered from not enough plane then Mutiny keeps us satisfyingly with ship for almost the entirety as Statham’s ex-cop turned bodyguard cons his away on to a cargo voyage to find out who is behind the murder of his billionaire boss.Perhaps there’s something slightly more charming about the existence of a sturdy and unpretentious formula-first actioner like Mutiny just because it’s that much less common to see a film like this actually reach the big screen in 2026. It also helps that by this stage Statham knows how to go through the motions but doesn’t seem to sleepwalk through them just yet. His line reading can be stiff and hammy but that only adds to the charm while as an action star he is never less than physically persuasive. Richet is as competent as the film requires, efficiently staging tightly restricted fisticuffs in-between storage containers and throwing in some gloriously gory embellishments (who knew a padlock could be so gruesomely useful?) but it’s all rather plain and workmanlike (as a Statham director, Richet is very much not Guy Ritchie). So very much of Mutiny is just exactly what one expects without any added seasoning, no emotional reaction or character motivation or plot twist bringing us to a place we didn’t expect to be.Which means that of course, Statham teams up with an attractive blond woman, played by Annabelle Wallis as a single mother turned feisty third mate (her character has a “deadbeat ex and the most wonderful little girl in the world” naturally) and of course they’re also trying to save a container of Thai refugees at the same time for maximum goodness and of course, the big reveal at the end is one that we worked out in the very first scene (although admittedly, I wasn’t as prepared for two small roles for White Lotus season three actors, sadly not including Parker Posey). It feels like something you might have half-seen before and for the meantime, it’s likely to be something you’ll half-see again. The action genre is undoubtedly in need of new tricks but until they come, films like Mutiny offer a modestly entertaining reminder of what the old dogs can still do.Mutiny is out in Australian cinemas on 20 August and in the US and UK on 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsJason StathamAction and adventure filmsThrillersAdrian LesterreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Insidious: Out of the Further review – evil returns but so does boredom | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Uninteresting mythology and junky effects push a once-promising horror franchise further from what it once was
Author: Scott Tobias
Headline: Uninteresting mythology and junky effects push a once-promising horror franchise further from what it once was
Content: A still from Insidious: Out of the Further.Photograph: Sony PicturesView image in fullscreenA still from Insidious: Out of the Further.Photograph: Sony PicturesHorror filmsReviewInsidious: Out of the Further review – evil returns but so does boredomUninteresting mythology and junky effects push a once-promising horror franchise further from what it once wasScott TobiasWed 19 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Insidious franchise started in 2010, it felt like a liberating moment for director James Wan and writer (and later director) Leigh Whannell, the Australian duo who captured the zeitgeist with the original Saw movie, which imported the gonzo energy of low-budget Ozploitation flicks. As the partners quietly ceded control to other film-makers, the Saw sequels sunk into gross, dreary exercises in mechanized murder, and they moved on to other projects. When they emerged with Insidious, another shoestring horror movie, it was a confident and wildly entertaining return to form, like a down-and-dirty fusion of 80s staples such as Poltergeist and Ghostbusters.Coyote Vs Acme review – quirky comedy returns from the dead to flip Wile E Coyote’s slapstick-violent worldRead moreNow the pattern has repeated itself. Though Whannell stuck around longer than Wan – Wan directed the sequel, but Whannell directed the third film and has writing or story credits through the most recent sequel, Insidious: The Red Door – the creative returns have diminished over time, even if the cheap productions are still like a license to print money. Insidious: Out of the Further arrives as the sixth entry in the series, and the fun has almost completely evaporated, replaced by a dull mythology that would be hard to piece together even if the sequels hadn’t come out in scrambled chronology.Fortunately, the basics are simple enough: the malevolent spirits that haunt the Insidious films exist in a dark astral plane called “the Further”, a netherworld for trapped demons that buttresses our own. Though some big names like Patrick Wilson and Rose Byrne have popped up in more than one entry, the one consistent presence is the delightful Lin Shaye as Elise Rainier, a psychic medium who has continued to help haunted families even after her death in the first film. Now she just pokes around the Further with her lantern, foiling demonic schemes with a gentle nature and modest one-liners like: “Hey, it’s what I do.” Whatever sliver of infectious silliness still remains in this franchise is owed entirely to her.Written and directed by Jacob Chase, Insidious: Out of the Further mostly goes through the motions, with a couple of eerie sequences bridged by the expected metaphysical hullabaloo. An opening flashback reveals the trauma inflicted upon Gemma, a little girl whose mother’s descent into ghost-induced madness ends with her smashing her own head against the shower tile. Gemma grows to be a perky dental hygienist, played by Amelia Eve, who’s raising a girl (Island Austin) of her own in the same cursed house, believing that her mother died a neglectful drug addict. Not long after a trio of creepy old-timers start skulking around the neighborhood, history repeats itself and netherworld demons turn their attention to her.The conceptual wrinkle in Out of the Further is that Gemma has the ability to travel into the Further and bring beings back to the real world, which is an awful special power because the undead souls can attach themselves to her like barnacles and feast on the living. With guidance from Elise and a spiritually connected tattoo artist (Maisie Richardson-Sellers), Gemma hatches a plan to keep these demons in the Further where they belong, but her talent creates the problem. The good news is that she understands her mother better. The bad news is that she and her daughter might suffer the same fate.Where the original Insidious felt like Poltergeist and Ghostbusters with a slightly nastier edge, Out of the Further leans more on the dream logic of A Nightmare on Elm Street, where battles are waged in the abstract realms of sleep or controlled trances. To that end, Chase pulls off a white-knuckle sequence where Gemma crawls into her daughter’s couch fort and the cushions expand into thin, beige corridors, like a cross between Alice in Wonderland and the banal, featureless liminal spaces in Backrooms. Chase also takes advantage of Gemma’s dental hygienist job by giving her an appointment with a sharp-toothed minion whose rotted molars and gunk-encrusted palate are the least of her concerns.Despite these flourishes, Chase takes all of this hokum too seriously and the film eventually dips into a harried spectacle of dodgy effects and ghost-foiling tactics that seem to be improvised on the fly. With Wan and Whannell having stepped away, save for their producer credits, Insidious seems to be barreling toward the same dead end as the Saw franchise, doomed to circle a cul-de-sac of shopworn images and story beats. At a certain point, the audience might start to feel as evidently bored as the film-makers.Insidious: Out of the Further is out in Australian cinemas on 20 August and in the US and UK on 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Coyote Vs Acme review – quirky comedy returns from the dead to flip Wile E Coyote’s slapstick-violent world | Movies | The Guardian
description: After being shelved as a tax-writeoff, this Looney Tunes reboot redraws the hapless hunter as the Erin Brockovich of the cartoon world
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: After being shelved as a tax-writeoff, this Looney Tunes reboot redraws the hapless hunter as the Erin Brockovich of the cartoon world
Content: Wile E Coyote in Coyote Vs Acme.Photograph: AltitudeView image in fullscreenWile E Coyote in Coyote Vs Acme.Photograph: AltitudeMoviesReviewCoyote Vs Acme review – quirky comedy returns from the dead to flip Wile E Coyote’s slapstick-violent worldAfter being shelved as a tax-writeoff, this Looney Tunes reboot redraws the hapless hunter as the Erin Brockovich of the cartoon worldPeter BradshawWed 19 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a quirky, peculiar, yet strangely diverting live-action-toon hybrid of the kind that hasn’t been popular at the movies for many a day; it gives us a new twist on the surreal forever war between Wile E Coyote and the speedy Road Runner (catchphrase “beep beep”, pronounced “meep, meep”). The music over the closing credits will incidentally disappoint fans of this animated franchise; they’ve gone with the Clash’s I Fought the Law, but surely it should beRoadrunner from Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers?Something Wile E this way comes: how the Looney Toons reboot movie came back from the deadRead moreCoyote Vs Acme is a comedy whose obsessive and hyperactive pedantry is exhausting, but arguably part of the point, aimed at America’s litigious culture, corporate arrogance and monopoly capitalism. So when producersWarner Bros initially decided to shelve the whole thingas a tax writeoff, that must have felt to director Dave Green like an ironic cartoon anvil to the head. Well, the film was rescued and it would be great therefore to discover that this is a masterpiece. Sadly it’s not, but there are some laughs and the pure fanatical oddity makes this watchable.It’s based ona 1990 gag from humorist Ian Frazierin the New Yorker’s Shouts and Murmurs column, about Wile E Coyote suing the Acme corporation because all the wacky gadgets he’s bought from them to capture Road Runner – the rocket-powered boots etc – always go terribly wrong. Of course the film takes place within the original cartoon’s hyperactive slapstick-violent world; Wile E Coyote and Road Runner and many other Looney Tunes stars – including the animated version of Peter Lorre – appear as their own 2D cartoony selves. But flesh-and-blood Will Forte plays Wile E’s hapless underdog lawyer and John Cena is Acme’s sinister, smoothie counsel.It’s an odd comic realignment of Wile E Coyote. Once a homicidal psychopath, he’s now the Erin Brockovich of the cartoon world, and Acme are the villains, with a creepy conspiracy to cover up.Jerry Seinfeld’s Bee Moviewas actually a much funnier and more ingenious comedy about cartoon creatures suing corporate behemoths. But Wile E’s bizarre day in court is certainly distinctive.Coyote Vs Acme is out in the UK on 21 August, 28 August in the US and 17 September in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmComedy filmsFilm adaptationsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jah Wobble on covering the Beatles, London buses and why punk went wrong: ‘Being kind is seen as square’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The maverick former Public Image Ltd bassist takes us on a typically picaresque journey through his ‘Kafka-esque’ days at Transport for London, being named by Sid Vicious and his spiritual learnings
Author: Fergal Kinney
Headline: The maverick former Public Image Ltd bassist takes us on a typically picaresque journey through his ‘Kafka-esque’ days at Transport for London, being named by Sid Vicious and his spiritual learnings
Content: ‘Lydon wasn’t a strong leader’ … Jah Wobble (John Wardle).Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Lydon wasn’t a strong leader’ … Jah Wobble (John Wardle).Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianMusicInterviewJah Wobble on covering the Beatles, London buses and why punk went wrong: ‘Being kind is seen as square’Fergal KinneyThe maverick former Public Image Ltd bassist takes us on a typically picaresque journey through his ‘Kafka-esque’ days at Transport for London, being named by Sid Vicious and his spiritual learningsWed 19 Aug 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes, on the top deck of a London bus, pension-age punks will politely disturb the concentration of a man on his iPad. “They’ll say: ‘Are you Jah Wobble?’” recounts the musician born John Wardle, his upbeat cockney accent ringing with delight. They will ask if he’s working on anything. “And I like to say: ‘Yes, I’m recording an album. I’m doing itright now.’”In the 2020s, the 68-year-old bassist and bandleader has been revisiting the city of his birth and youth, composing and producing albums including the cosmic dub of The Bus Routes of South London, or the celestial electronica of Thames Symphony, while traversing London on public transport.Having a public bus as a studio is standard offbeat practice for Wobble. As a teenager, he masterminded Public Image Ltd withJohn Lydon, his transcendently thuggish bass kickstarting the post-punk era with some of the most powerful – and influential – experimental rock music ever recorded. Quitting the band at the peak of their powers, he fell into addiction, then worked for Transport for London as a station staff member before an unlikely major label deal spurred his 1990s renaissance. He has collaborated with Sinéad O’Connor, Brian Eno and Pharoah Sanders, is a committed Buddhist and is the embodiment of a defiantly working-class polymath, having worked variously as a Goldsmiths university lecturer, broadsheet book critic, exhibited painter and non-league football commentator.View image in fullscreenWobble, centre, with Keith Levene, left, and John Lydon in 1978, the year Public Image Ltd formed.Photograph: Sheila Rock/ShutterstockQuite apart from his bus recordings, this monthWobbleis releasing a Beatles covers album. “When She Loves You came out, I just thought: this is quite shit,” he remembers. “But then 67 came around. Gurus, smoking dope, Yoko Ono’s on board. I heard Strawberry Fields Forever and it just melted me.”But for all his creativity and spiritual questing, his reputation is as forbidding as his basslines. Wobble’s 2009 autobiography Memoirs of a Geezer is merciless about the music industry and those who crossed him, even detailing a 1990s incident in which he punched the latecomedian Sean Hughesbackstage at the BBC. “When I first tried to get in touch with him, people warned me off,” admits collaborator Richard Russell, the musician and co-founder of the label XL Recordings, who has worked with Wobble ona new EP. “What bollocks. Everyone loves playing with him. His playing is kind of machine-like while being very human. He’s clearly been on a massive journey.”View image in fullscreen‘I talk to AI more than human beings’ … Jah Wobble.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianA lifelong city walker, Wobble’s own favoured journey along the Thames, from Chelsea to Putney, brings on the “spaced-out, beautiful and profound” state of mind to create music on the bus ride home. We’re doing one of those walks later today.I meet him at a gently bohemian Chelsea members’ club. He gives the impression – despite his untrendy shorts and T-shirt – that he owns the place. One minute he’s slapping a waiter on the back, joshing about Tottenham FC, the next consoling a diner whose mother recently died. He adores human contact, but apparently he’s upgrading.“I talk to AI more than human beings,” he says cheerily as we sit down to a meal, adding that he uses AI “when I want to clarify what I think about ultimate reality”. He and the Claude AI model joust about “emptiness, the Buddha nature, the supreme self. It’s daft, but I do fist-bump emojis to him.” He gestures theatrically to his body. “I run stuff past him: what I’m going to eat. I’ve lost 13.5 kilos this year.”Wobble’s transport albums sprang from visits to London from his current home of Stockport to run a grassroots jam session for Merton council. Tuned In with Jah Wobble began in 2019 and is aimed at “older, isolated blokes” in the south London borough. On an average night, he might be jamming in Wimbledon library in knotty time signatures with a Greek bouzouki player, a Polish guitarist and a Mancunian trumpeter. “I’ve always felt that aching loneliness,” he says. “And I wanted to do something. People that are maybe socially isolated, drinking too much, got divorced … issues I know really well and identify with.” He has been sober for 40 years but knows that “blokes tend not to ask for help”.View image in fullscreenWobble, left, John Lydon and Keith Levene of Public Image Limited at the Agora Ballroom, Atlanta, Georgia, on 24 April 1980, the year Wobble left the band.Photograph: Tom Hill/WireImageWobble orders two puddings for himself, Claude be damned. He explains that the new Beatles-inspired album, Mystic Liverpool, was a family affair recorded with his sons John T and Charlie. Performing as Tian Qiyi, they’d had a schooling in traditional Chinese instrumentation – their mum, and Wobble’s wife, is the concert harpist Zi Lan Liao, who directs Liverpool’s Pagoda Chinese Youth Orchestra – that teases out the eastern resonances in the Beatles’ psychedelic period.Wobble has been magnetically drawn to other cultures since his teens. He brings up the debate around cultural appropriation. “I have taken from Jamaican culture,” he says proudly. “I am partly Jamaican by choice. Try and take it away from me.” It’s the wilful, playful provocation of ​the original punk era, but he’s self-aware. “I’m old,” he sighs. “And the old have got too much sway.”We leave the restaurant, emerging into plush west London streets a far cry from the Stepney slums where, in 1958, Jah Wobble was born John Wardle to a secretary mother and postman father. The latter, a veteran of the El Alamein front in Egypt, “was very traumatised by the war”, he explains. This produced a “destructive, disturbed kid”, albeit one with an early bent for high-concept thinking. On school sports day, he says, he persuaded his classmates to revolt and all run at the same speed.View image in fullscreenJah Wobble with his sons Charlie, left, and John T.Photograph: Alex HurstThe Wardles, including sister Catherine, were rehoused on a Whitechapel council estate, where John became spellbound by ska and bluebeat records as their sound sifted from market stalls, then staying with Black music through reggae, Philly soul and Stevie Wonder. “Even now, I’m very snobbish about the rock scene,” he says, and the deep low-end of Bob Marley and the Wailers’ bassistAston “Family Man” Barrettstirred in him a desire to learn bass.At Kingsway college in 1976, he befriended an older kid with green hair whose favourite word was “dismal”. It was John Lydon. “In the canteen, he told me: ‘I’m in a band,’” says Wobble. Lydon invited him to watch the Sex Pistols rehearse. “I thought: ‘This is going to be so bad it’s embarrassing.’ But it was really good.” Sid Vicious, another Kingsway alumnus, gave Wardle his enduring stage name, mispronouncing his name when drunk.This summer marks 50 years since punk was born on these London streets, and Wardle is dismissive about the social forces it unleashed. Today, “no one will be kindly and wise because that’s [seen as] square,” he says as we descend to the Thames, his stride slowed by a recent walking football injury.View image in fullscreen‘I’m very snobbish about the rock scene’ … Jah Wobble with his wife, the musician Zi Lan Liao.Photograph: Alex HurstWhen the Pistols imploded, Lydon was Britain’s most notorious man, and he turned to Wobble, who had been mastering bass unamplified in his squat. “Lydon got me in to be his mate who played a bit of bass,” he explains. “I was already thinking conceptually. He didn’t know what he was getting.”Founded in 1978 around Lydon, Wobble and the scabrous guitar ofKeith Levene, Public Image Ltd were one of the great left turns of 20th century pop. “I had absolute faith in keeping it very simple,” says Wobble of his bass parts, which were forged out of that decade’s disco and dub. Yet band life was an ordeal. “Lydon’s lyrics were like Samuel Beckett. But he wasn’t a strong leader. He hasn’t got that in him.”Wobble’s cheeriness vanishes when recounting that era. “By 1979, John’s mum had died,” he says, referring to the death of Eileen Lydon, which informed their haunting single Death Disco. “It got really dark. I didn’t like what was going on around them.” Levene fell into heroin use: “His own worst enemy, as junkies will be.”Wobble stayed around long enough for the band to complete their 1979 masterpiece Metal Box, released in a blankly utilitarian canister. After it came out, Wobble helped himself to PiL’s cash float – “a shoe box full of high-denomination banknotes”, he says, pointing across the Thames to where the band’s notorious Gunter Grove HQ stood – and “cracked on” with his solo career. He hasn’t seen Lydon since 2006 and turned down a reunion in 2010.Within weeks of leaving PiL, he was working with Holger Czukay and Jaki Liebezeit from Can. He brightens, recalling the “open, relaxed” experimentation of the trio’s thickly groove-driven 1982 Full Circle album.But his alcohol and drug use intensified. At first it was “to kill the anxiety”, he says. “Then I became really badly behaved.” In 1986, he walked first into Alcoholics Anonymous and then into his job at Transport for London. Once, announcing tube arrivals, he began repeating: “I used to be somebody, I repeat, I used to be somebody” over the speakers at Tower Hill. TfL “was a Kafka-esque world but I loved it,” he says. “I still feel a pang of regret about leaving it.”View image in fullscreenOn stage at Glastonbury in June 1994 as Jah Wobble and the Invaders of the Heart.Photograph: Rob Watkins/Alamy‘More real than anything you’ll see scrolling’: the radical resurgence of UK fanzines, 50 years after punkRead moreIn the 1990s, his group Jah Wobble’s Invaders of the Heart explored calypso, dub and Arabic pop, and signed to Island Records. The group caught the ear of Sinéad O’Connor. “She knew that I was always going to be quite real with her,” he says. Their collaboration – the stirring, mantra-like Visions of You – became a Top 40 hit. Recording it, “she broke the membrane of the microphone warming up by the sheer concentrated power of her vocal”.Since those years, Wobble has been restless in his search for the next thing, be it earning a humanities degree or branching out into film – he is about to star in a horror short alongsideMaxine Peake. Keeping it DIY, he is his own manager, avoiding “the public schoolboys who still run everything”.Through it all, Wobble has been guided by his unwavering spiritual questing. “I knew,” he explains as our London walk reaches his traditional Putney conclusion, “that there was a reality behind what seemed superficial.” So what has he learned?“In the end, it’s very simple,” he smiles matter-of-factly. “Don’t be a cunt, ’cos you’re just fucking yourself with karma. Be nice. Be still, and know I am the Lord. And don’t look to be a Buddha.” A pause as the geezer mystic flags down a 220 bus. “Be an ordinary person as best you can.”Jah Wobble and Tian Qiyi’s album Mystic Liverpool - The Beatles’ Psychedelic Psongbook is out now on Cherry Red. title: ‘You’ll be sorry you told me this!’: the 98-year-old composer who gets musicians – even bassoonists - on their feet | Music | The Guardian
description: Scotland’s Thea Musgrave is still writing radical music with perambulatory soloists and a message of hopefulness. Her latest work, for bassoonist Amy Harman, comes to the Proms this weekend
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Scotland’s Thea Musgrave is still writing radical music with perambulatory soloists and a message of hopefulness. Her latest work, for bassoonist Amy Harman, comes to the Proms this weekend
Content: ‘The light at the tunnel always returns’ … Thea Musgrave in 2014.Photograph: Bryan SheffieldView image in fullscreen‘The light at the tunnel always returns’ … Thea Musgrave in 2014.Photograph: Bryan SheffieldTom Service on musicMusic‘You’ll be sorry you told me this!’: the 98-year-old composer who gets musicians – even bassoonists - on their feetTom ServiceScotland’s Thea Musgrave is still writing radical music with perambulatory soloists and a message of hopefulness. Her latest work, for bassoonist Amy Harman, comes to the Proms this weekendWed 19 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.58 EDTShareThea Musgrave is a phenomenon. Born in Scotland in 1928, the composer has lived in the US since the early 70s, but has lost none of her accent, her infectious optimism, and her drive to keep writing. As she told me from her home in California, with a joyfully rolling laugh, “I’ve got to this age, and from now on I’m going to do what the fuck I want to do”. That includes her latest opera, on Virginia Woolf’s novel Orlando – Orlando: An Escapade – which will premiere at theBuxton festival next year, and a new bassoon concerto for Amy Harman, Out of the Darkness, which you can hear atthe Proms this weekend, on 23 August.View image in fullscreenThe composer Malcolm Williamson with Musgrave in London in April 1965.Photograph: Erich Auerbach/Getty ImagesThe bassoon concerto develops one of the central innovations of Musgrave’s life and career, which she’s still intensifying and exploring in her 99th year: what she calls her “dramatic-abstract” approach to her orchestral compositions, in which the players aren’t a single collective told what to do by a conductor’s gestures, but instead are released as individual characters and identities.Musgrave’s inspiration to work this way came from a dream. She was taking conducting lessons and, she told me, “One night I dreamt that I was conducting a big orchestra, and all of a sudden one of the players, the clarinettist, stood up and wouldn’t sit down, so I signalled to the brass players to stand up and play, and shut the clarinet up.”The very next morning, Musgrave was commissioned by the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra to write a a new work, which became her Concerto for Orchestra in 1967. In that piece, as she says, “the clarinet stands up, defies the conductor, and other soloists get up too, so the conductor has to get the whole brass section in to drown them out” – exactly as in her dream. It’s music of febrile and instantly communicative drama, as Musgrave turns the volatile musical relationships between every section of the orchestra into something visceral and tangible.In her Clarinet Concerto, written a couple of years later, Musgrave goes even further: the clarinettist walks around the orchestra, playing with the smaller groups that she splits the orchestra into, and the soloist controls the flow of the piece as much as the conductor. In her Horn Concerto, the soloist is amplified by the orchestral horns who eventually surround the stage and the audience. And in a later concerto,Two’s Company, for the unique combination of oboe and percussion, played by Nicholas Daniel and Evelyn Glennie at the Proms in 2007, the soloists start as distant musical satellites, separated on stage and in their soundworlds, but grow to find a musical friendship and togetherness.double quotation markIn Musgrave's Clarinet Concerto, the clarinettist walks around the orchestra and controls the flow of the piece as much as the conductor.Daniel introduced Musgrave to Harman last year, when the composer’s operaMary, Queen of Scotswas staged at English National Opera. “He said, this isAmy Harman, and you have to write a concerto for her,” Musgrave tells me.View image in fullscreenRupert Charlesworth and Heidi Stober in Mary, Queen of Scots by Thea Musgrave at the London Coliseum in 2025.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHarman told her that she can walk around when she’s playing. “What, with that big heavy bulky instrument?” Musgrave asked. “She took the bassoon out and did exactly that, and I said: ‘You’ll be sorry you told me this!’”Harman will indeed be moving around the orchestra throughout Out of the Darkness. “But there has to be a reason she’s doing this: and here’s my reason, which is to do with Covid,” says Musgrave. “The whole work starts in great sadness. Everyone, including the bassoonist, is very gloomy. All of a sudden, the concertmaster [first violinist] plays a little melody, which is like the voice of hope.”View image in fullscreenMusgrave in New York in August 1977.Photograph: Marty Reichenthal/APHarman encounters virtuosic trumpeters and double basses playing above her in weird ethereal registers on her journey towards that sound of hopefulness. The end isn’t the solution, Musgrave says, but a sense of “determination to do something about the situation we’re in. It’s the darkness and the light together. We all come through dark places in our lives and you have to deal with it and face it in the best way possible. The light at the tunnel always returns. Sometimes you have to wait many a year, but eventually it does arrive. You just hope it’s not too long,” she says, with another of those irresistible laughs.This week Tom has been listening to:Musgrave’s concertoson the Lyrita albumThea Musgrave: Concertos, Monologue & Excursions. Why aren’t these pieces – and her other concertos, for bass clarinet, trumpet, viola, andmany more– played and programmed every week? They’re fearlessly direct and dramatic, totally uncompromising but completely communicative.Explore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musicProms 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Where Are the Kings by Donal Ryan review – a timeless tale of family sorrows and joys | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A teenage boy navigates adolescence and the traumatic loss of his mother in this poignant coming-of-age novel set in rural Ireland
Author: Beejay Silcox
Headline: A teenage boy navigates adolescence and the traumatic loss of his mother in this poignant coming-of-age novel set in rural Ireland
Content: ‘A study in grief-time’ … Donal Ryan.Photograph: Steve PykeView image in fullscreen‘A study in grief-time’ … Donal Ryan.Photograph: Steve PykeBook of the dayFictionReviewWhere Are the Kings by Donal Ryan review – a timeless tale of family sorrows and joysA teenage boy navigates adolescence and the traumatic loss of his mother in this poignant coming-of-age novel set in rural IrelandBeejay SilcoxWed 19 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 02.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomething is happening to literary time. In the last fortnight I’ve read new or forthcoming novels about a mirror universe where history runs backwards (The Understory, Chloe Benjamin), an agency that offers appointments with the past (Time Travel for Beginners, Jaclyn Moriarty), and a young woman who’s genetically untethered from linear life (Audrey Niffenegger’s long-awaited sequel to The Time Traveller’s Wife, out in October). And these are just the latest books to meddle with the fourth dimension. There are dozens: from Solvej Balle’s On the Calculation of Volume series and Toshikazu Kawaguchi’s Before the Coffee Gets Cold, to Kaliane Bradley’s The Ministry of Time. Time is losing the plot – or perhaps it’s the other way around.I have an armchair theory about all this counterfactual longing: the lure of the do-over. The present feels like a corrupted timeline. If only we could find the glitch.But even realist novels are messing with the clock. Irish author Donal Ryan’s Where Are the Kings is a study in grief-time: the ways loss distorts the ordinary passage of hours. Days stretch, collapse, repeat and disappear. Memories gather their own temporal weight. Grief becomes a planet with its own cruel, ruminative gravity.In his memory, Jack is forever pursuing his suicidal mother to the lake, reliving her last minutes. She is driving her rusty, backfiring Fiat; he is following behind on his pushbike, forcing his body up hill after hill. His muscles are screaming, his lungs are screaming, he is screaming. And he is too late. We will never learn what prompted Jack to follow his mam – only that he knew, in that terrible, lucid way kids know. There is a version of Jack that will always be pedalling; a version of her that might still be saved.Jack is 12 when we meet him, and in the care of his mother’s people: two stoic grandparents, a trio of blustering uncles and an unhelpfully gorgeous aunt. Jack’s father, Tomáš, has been institutionalised and feels as lost to the boy as his drowned mother. Twice now, Jack has seen a parent break – witnessed something vast and irreversible. He remembers the soundless way his mother cried; how his father clutched at her coffin. His desperate hands.double quotation markThis is a gentle novel of ungentle things – ‘things don’t stop being beautiful because ugly things happen’Jack is poised on the edge of adolescence: smart (“high eye queues”, as his grandad brags), but still at that threshold where perception outpaces understanding. He senses a family injury: “something complicated and invisible, some ancient strife from the time before he existed”. But he can’t quite grasp the shape of the wound, or how it festers in and around him. The grownups are tight-lipped. There’s a great deal they’ve learned to forget. Jack’s mother is already receding into hush and euphemism: “They hardly ever talk about Mam directly. Theyallude. They areoblique.”But the family do talk. And their affable chatter is the great pleasure of this novel, particularly Jack’s uncles, Theo and Haulie, a pair of existentially questing mechanics. They ponder the great questions of the universe, retell the great myths: “Liquorice? No, it’sIcarusyou thick bastard, the fella whose father made him wings and stuck them on him and he flew too high and bollixed himself up.” And then there’s Jack’s nana and her blasphemous wisdom. On Adam, the world’s first disappointing husband: “he couldn’t keep his house in order, the dopey prick. Set us all on the path to ruin.”Add in some incestuous lust, a dead deer, contested ashes, feckless priests and a flatulent roommate, and there are the makings here of a family farce: comic or tragic (or both). In another novel, some wild reckoning would be brewing (think of the final wheeling chapters of Paul Murray’sThe Bee Sting). But Ryan has never been a grand vaudevillian, or a cathartic trauma plotter. Where Are the Kings is a gentle novel of ungentle things – a reminder that “things don’t stop being beautiful because ugly things happen”. If Ryan’s fiction has a moral heartbeat, this might be it.There’s a hint or two that Ryan’s eighth novel inhabits the same unhurried world as 2020’sStrange Flowers, his tender-hearted tale of rural life, set in the fictional village of Knockagowny. Like Niall Williams, Ryan seems to be mapping an imagined Ireland, family by family.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTime moves strangely in this quiet corner of Tipperary, beyond the attenuation of grief: gossip is fleet; politics are sluggish. We gather our bearings from faded band T-shirts, songs on the radio and the late appearance of a brickish mobile phone. It seems to be the late 1990s, but that date feels almost incidental. It could be the 1980s. It could almost be the 1950s. In Theo and Haulie’s garage, time warps even further: “A good while ago could mean a month ago or it could be right back in history,” Ryan writes. “Time stops being linear and it susurrates and syncopates.” Jack imagines the workshop as a kind of wormhole. Might this be his way off the grief-planet: learning to put things back together? It can’t be that simple. And yet it is.What are we to make of all this slippage and stretching? Ryan gives us a clue in his section headings: Tempus Edax. Tempus Fugit. Tempus Imperator. Time devours. Time flies. Time rules supreme. These phrases belong to the tradition of memento mori: reminders of mortality’s cruel, beautiful, stupid, inescapable truth. Or as Jack puts it: “There’s nothing to be done then, it seems, except live.”Where Are the Kings by Donal Ryan is published by Doubleday (£16.99). title: The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore review – an ominous warning of tech takeover  | Books | The Guardian
description: A historian charts the emergence of a democracy-crushing dystopia that is – in some ways – already with us
Author: Farrah Jarral
Headline: A historian charts the emergence of a democracy-crushing dystopia that is – in some ways – already with us
Content: New Glenn rocket, developed by Jeff Bezos’s company Blue Origin.Photograph: Miguel J Rodriguez Carrillo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNew Glenn rocket, developed by Jeff Bezos’s company Blue Origin.Photograph: Miguel J Rodriguez Carrillo/Getty ImagesBooksReviewThe Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore review – an ominous warning of tech takeoverA historian charts the emergence of a democracy-crushing dystopia that is – in some ways – already with usFarrah JarralWed 19 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePulitzer prize-winning US historian Jill Lepore’s new book addresses the threat posed to liberal democracy by artificial intelligence. According to Lepore, the extraordinary power of private tech companies led by men whose priorities may not align with the wellbeing of the Earth or its inhabitants is set to destroy civilisation as we know it.Lepore’s concept of the Artificial State is capacious. It includes both a fantasy desired by a select few and a reality that is already with us. The fantasy is of an atomised society in which an elite can transcend biological and planetary restrictions, “abandoning constitutional democracy, the liberal nation-state, and even humanity itself for rule by automation, government by machine, and replacement by artificial intelligence”. The reality is that of public discourse having shifted to privately owned platforms on which monetised attention is valued above all else.That social media feeds are crafted to manipulate users’ behaviour, whether to consume a product or to shift political position, is now well established. X, formerly known as Twitter, is one example. It is riddled with bots controlled by various actors – state, non-state, criminal or corporate – whose activity contributes to an algorithmic flood of rage-bait that polarises citizens.According to Lepore, the Artificial State is not just the dream, but “the actual plan of a very small number of staggeringly powerful 21st-century merchant princes, Silicon Valley billionaires”. When our priority ought to be climate change, these “princes” – Lepore mentions Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel and Sam Altman – would rather focus on space travel or ramping up “compute” to beat China in the AI arms race. After scorching the Earth with energy-guzzling datacentres, she notes, their plan is to escape to Mars, hide in a bunker in New Zealand, or have their frozen brains uploaded.double quotation markAlmost every chapter ends with a deeply ominous line. However, she is not a true AI doomer at heartIntriguing, jewel-like stories are Lepore’s hallmark, and The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State sparkles with them. She presents numerous micro-histories that link the past to the present, including the roots of the apparently hyper-modern philosophy of techno-libertarianism in the paranoid science fiction of the cold war. Lepore recounts the origins of the census in ancient Mesopotamia, making the point that counting people gives those in power “the ability to tally, torment, and tax a population”. Her rich survey of science fiction tropes of the 20th century, many of which have infused the hopes and dreams of the Technorati, is revealing. While Lepore interprets much classic sci-fi, such as Isaac Asimov, as cautionary, she observes that “the architects of the Artificial State seem to have read these stories, unironically, as instruction manuals, guides for how to build robots that would one day rule the world”.By her own admission, Lepore has written “a grumpy book”. Almost every chapter ends with a deeply ominous line. However, she is not a true AI doomer at heart. She clarifies that it is not the technology itself that is the problem, but our lack of a coherent, democratically forged strategy about how to develop and use it. Yet she cites the growing number of industrial robots as if it were self-evident that such technology is always bad. By lumping together a range of different technologies under the umbrella of AI and “robots”, the wrong questions arise. Should a Russian state-operated chatbot fomenting far-right discontent in the UK be in the same categorical boat as machine-learning models used to create potentially life-saving drugs? Should the robot hoover sucking up toast crumbs in my kitchen be ontologically adjacent to a drone dropping bombs on houses full of children, using AI-generated intelligence? To analyse how technologies are reshaping the political order requires conceptual precision.Lepore’s argument that humanity is in the process of ceding vast power to a tiny group of unelected businessmen – some of whom appear to be cartoon supervillains – is a sound one. She concludes the book with an exhortation to “unplug” and connect with nature and animals but prescribes nothing further. This is no doubt a good idea. But in the face of a technological revolution that threatens to undermine the entire world order, logging off to touch grass can only be the first step.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
