title: In Big Walk, players just walk and talk – and find joy along the way: ‘Some stories we’ve heard are punch-in-the-gut beautiful’ | Games | The Guardian
description: After their hit Untitled Goose Game, Australian studio House House is back with a new game where your only goal is to go exploring with friends – so we took them on a big walk inside Big Walk
Author: Alexandra Neill
Headline: After their hit Untitled Goose Game, Australian studio House House is back with a new game where your only goal is to go exploring with friends – so we took them on a big walk inside Big Walk
Content: Big Walk, the new game by Australian studio House House, which also had a hit with Untitled Goose Game. ‘A month before the game came out, I had the feeling like “this is our private little space that we’ve built for ourselves”’, says designer Nico Disseldorp.Photograph: House HouseView image in fullscreenBig Walk, the new game by Australian studio House House, which also had a hit with Untitled Goose Game. ‘A month before the game came out, I had the feeling like “this is our private little space that we’ve built for ourselves”’, says designer Nico Disseldorp.Photograph: House HouseGamesIn Big Walk, players just walk and talk – and find joy along the way: ‘Some stories we’ve heard are punch-in-the-gut beautiful’After their hit Untitled Goose Game, Australian studio House House is back with a new game where your only goal is to go exploring with friends – so we took them on a big walk inside Big WalkAlexandra NeillWed 19 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I arrive to meet with the tiny team atMelbournegame developer House House, they’re sitting in a circle under a eucalyptus tree. After introductions, the five of us set off into the scrub. Over the course of our hike we take a train to the beach, huddle on deck chairs in the sand dunes and climb a mountain as the sun rises. All without ever leaving our desks.Big Walk review – larking around with mates elevated to an artformRead moreWelcome to the world ofBig Walk: House House’s new game after the runaway global successUntitled Goose Game, which saw millions fall in love with being a naughty goose rampaging through a bucolic village. After Untitled Goose Game’s overwhelming success, House House wanted their next game to be very different and “unusual”. Despite this, Big Walk has been an immediate success, with more than 1m downloads in the first week of release.In Big Walk, your only goal is to go on a walk through sprawling bushland, solving puzzles with friends. At the centre of the game’s design is a proximity voice chat, which means you can talk clearly to someone who is right beside you but can’t hear each other when you’re separated.As we board the puttering train that winds across the game’s map, the House House team tells me how Big Walk began: during Covid lockdowns, when they started playing games online with international friends. This group was the first to test a very early version of Big Walk.“One of the first things we did was just go on a walk, from one side of this map to the other,” says Nico Disseldorp, who describes his niche within the team as “capital G game design”. “And it had this really interesting feeling of wanting to pay attention to each other, to look out for each other, make sure no one got left behind.”A turning point for House House came when sound designer Em Halberstadt suggested they bring on audio programmer Nicholas Zhang. The two had a “level of ambition” that became integral to the game; while telling me about this, the train we’re on goes through a tunnel and our voices change, echoing in the confined space.View image in fullscreenThe world of Big Walk is modelled on Wilsons Promontory, a few hours south of Melbourne.Photograph: House HouseBeyond the chunky stick figure characters, the world of Big Walk is remarkably realistic. Although they initially considered the Faroe Islands in the North Atlantic as a setting, they were drawn closer to home – specificallyWilsons Promontory, a few hours south of Melbourne. “Because of its geography, it has that kind of isolated video game level feeling that we needed,” says Jake Strasser, who worked alongside Kalonica Quigley to design the game’s intricate landscape. “And it’s just so beautiful and has all this magical, rich source material to it.”Wombats, wallabies and whales: four days walking in Wilsons Promontory national parkRead moreThe team spent time on Wilsons Promontory during development, staying in a cabin at Tidal River. They would brainstorm in the mornings and go on walks in the afternoon. Strasser and Quigley took reference photos of plants and the sound team flew out to do field recordings.Jumping off the train, we head to a secluded spot by a beach. We collect deckchairs from the surrounding bush and arrange them in a circle. The sun has set but we have a glowing orb to light the way – when the sun sets in Big Walk it is properly dark.“It seems like a tough ask for a video game audience,” animator Stuart Gillespie-Cook says of the darkness, “That sometimes it’s going to be a bit slow and sad.”View image in fullscreen‘Sometimes it’s going to be a bit slow and sad’: when the sun sets in Big Walk, it really sets.Photograph: House HouseThe team realised they needed something “to guide you through and give you a reason to go on these walks”: these are puzzles, the kind “you might play if you go camping when you don’t have much equipment, that are just about communicating with each other”, Disseldorp says.The puzzles, dotted in neon buildings across the map, force you to think about communication. Often the ability to talk is removed, so you have to find another way through. Your reward for finishing each one is a red bulbous object. I’ve seen these referred to as peanuts or gourds. My friend group calls them babies.When I ask the team what their official name is, they won’t answer.“This interview is over!” Strasser jokes, running off.Disseldorp’s answer is more diplomatic: “We have our own words for what they’re called, but it’s no more or less important than what any other group calls them. So much of the game is about creating your own lexicon for the world.”Given how intimate the game’s development process was, it makes sense that Big Walk’s release was nerve-racking for the team.“A month before the game came out, I had the feeling like ‘this is our private little space that we’ve built for ourselves’, and we’ve been playing in it for six years,” Disseldorp says, “And I don’t want to let a bunch of strangers in. They’ll get their muddy feet all over the carpet.”Untitled Goose Game review – never before have I felt so appalled by my virtual actsRead moreThis worry didn’t last long. Since its release, reception to Big Walk has been overwhelmingly positive. There is a relief that people “get it”.“Some of the stories we’ve heard are punch-in-the-gut beautiful,” Strasser says. “I’ve cried over emails of brothers feeling connected with each other in a new way; cousins who’ve never met reaching out across a family feud; people who just experienced massive loss playing together and finding joy.”We leave the deck chairs to walk along the beach. Strasser and Gillespie-Cook wander off ahead as Disseldorp and Quigley recall a time when Quigley and a small group played through an early version of the game.“We felt like we owed you an ending that didn’t really exist,” Disseldorp says, more to Quigley than me. “And then the [group] that had been playing just swam into the [ocean], as deep as you could, and we could hear bits of laughter at a distance, and we were watching, very happy that you’d enjoyed the game and you were enjoying saying goodbye. And then each of you disconnected one by one in the water and that was it. You didn’t come back and say goodbye. And it felt like such a momentous finish that was in such a stark contrast to how I normally associate winding up playing a video game.”“I think that’s my biggest feeling at the moment,” Quigley adds as we begin climbing a mountain to watch the sun rise. “I have memories like that that I really cherish. And I think of them like memories of hanging out with my friends in real life.”Big Walk is out now on Switch 2, PlayStation 5 and PCExplore more on these topicsGamesVictoriaMelbournefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Will the future of gaming be powered by upstart indie developers? | Games | The Guardian
description: As gaming’s biggest publishers retreat into safer bets, a new generation of independents are building an alternative from the ground up
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As gaming’s biggest publishers retreat into safer bets, a new generation of independents are building an alternative from the ground up
Content: The games industry’s indie scene is expanding as major publishers retreat from riskier projects, with boutique companies stepping in to back smaller studios with experimental ideas.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe games industry’s indie scene is expanding as major publishers retreat from riskier projects, with boutique companies stepping in to back smaller studios with experimental ideas.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWill the future of gaming be powered by upstart indie developers?As gaming’s biggest publishers retreat into safer bets, a new generation of independents are building an alternative from the ground upDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 19 Aug 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the 1990s, a new strata of independent film studios and distributors revitalised the Hollywood movie machine. The likes of Miramax, New Line Cinema and October Films challenged the ageing behemoths of the industry and pushed forward offbeat directors such as Quentin Tarantino, Darren Aronofsky and Jane Campion. The decade is widely considered an artistic high point for western cinema after the bloated mainstream excesses of the 1980s. Could something similar now be happening in games?Certainly, we have a comparable setup. The big players of the games business are in various states of creative disarray: Electronic Arts (EA) has beenbought out by a Saudi-led consortium, which is likely to lead to more cautious, hit-driven decisions; Microsoft bought Activision and Bethesda and thenordered waves of redundancies; Ubisoft hascancelled several titlesand is posting big losses. Those companies are also facing rising development costs, so they’re circling the wagons, focusing on legacy brands and freezing recruitment. It’s hard to imagine any left-field works of genius emerging from this imaginative quagmire.Meanwhile, smaller developers who are starved of investment through traditional routes, are quietly formulating a counter-economy. Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen the arrival of boutique publishers, set up by successful studios, and designed to support grassroots talent. Kinetic Publishing was formed by the creator of successful indie ghost-hunting game Phasmophobia to support new studios; Outersloth is the funding arm ofAmong Uscreator InnerSloth, launched in 2024 to support idiosyncratic game concepts; London-based Kepler Interactive, formed in 2020, was behindClair Obscur: Expedition 33, the most critically acclaimed title of 2025. Last week saw theannouncement of Inner Pocket, a publisher founded by industry veterans and dedicated to “intimate and engaging” experiences.View image in fullscreenCritially acclaimed and indie-made … Clair Obscur Expedition 33.Photograph: Sandfall InteractiveThere has, arguably, never been a better time for this kind of grassroots revolution in games publishing. Digital distribution via stores such as Steam and the App Store has given studios a global marketplace, while social media platforms are providing comparatively cheap marketing avenues. A decade ago, it would have been costly to show new games and strike deals at big events such as E3 – but now, most titles are revealed via online showcases or through communities of fans on Discord and Reddit. At the same time, developers are able to bypass traditional publishing deals to finance projects, seeking help from regional arts networks and funding bodies, and joining local hubs for support. At the latest Develop Conference in the UK,studio collectivescame together, combining forces and sharing expertise.This isn’t a cure-all. The games industry is still a complex and intimidating market and, with a focus on digital distribution, discoverability is still a major issue for new titles – how do you gain attention, and an audience, when there are hundreds of new titles released on Steam every week? But as mainstream publishers quietly drop more ambitious and experimental projects, there is a growing community of new companies, networks and funding bodies looking to help. As John Buckley, head of publishing at PocketPair,said recently, “We’re going to see more hit games coming from publishers you’ve never heard of.”Nineties movies such as Sex, Lies and Video Tape, Reservoir Dogs and Slacker emerged from a new Hollywood culture of film school nerds, cheap equipment and funding models only a few steps up from maxing out credit cards – and a growing independent production system was there to support them. For years, chin-stroking critics asked the now-lampooned question: when will video games have their Citizen Kane moment? Now, perhaps the more pertinent version is: what will be the industry’s Blair Witch Project?What to playView image in fullscreenSerene … Cast n Chill.Photograph: Wombat BrawlerIf you have ever enjoyed a fishing minigame in an RPG thenCast n Chillis worth a look. It’s a pixel art fishing game set in beautiful nonspecific North American lakes, rivers and coastline. As the title suggests it is fairly serene – though you have to spend time upgrading your rods and boat if you want to catch some real monsters. It’s also got two-player couch co-op, a feature I’m always looking for so I can play with my sons.Keza MacDonaldAvailable on:PC and Mac via SteamEstimated playtime:18 hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenProfit before safety ... US senators are investigating child safety on Roblox.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersUS senators areinvestigating child safetyonRoblox, accusing the game’s creator of prioritising revenue and engagement metrics over children’s wellbeing.Sneaking about in the alleyways of gaming history, open-world gangland adventureMafiais approaching its 25th year. IGN celebrates withan entertaining oral historyof the series – it’s an article you can’t refuse.As a lifelong fan of weird and divisive video games, I enjoyedthis pieceon6 out of 10 bangers –the sorts of games that score “low” but only because they’re bizarre, twisted and glitchy, which can be compelling qualities. Resident Evil Gaiden and Amiga classic Shadow of the Beast are mentioned. I’d add PS2 curioMister Mosquito(where you play as a mosquito trying to suck blood from a suburban family) and crazed PlayStation driving gameRunabout(known as Felony 11-79 in the West), where you run around a city trying to unlock as many vehicles as possible. They don’t make ‘em like that any more.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickThe Blood of Dawnwalker – save your family while becoming what you hate‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseIthaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent momentAlien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new world‘The kids were right’: 30 years of Pokémon, from school-wide bans to multimillion-dollar trading cardsThe Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high water | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenSo realistic there’s probably an eight-hour wait at Dover … Euro Truck Simulator 2.Photograph: SCS SoftwareA question this week fromJon,via email:“I love driving games, but I don’t want to compete online – or even compete at all, if I’m honest. I played Forza Horizon 4 to death without actually progressing in the festival at all and I bought GTA V just so I could hop in a car and circumnavigate San Andreas without shooting anybody.Are there any other race-free driving games I could try?”There are plenty in the indie space if you don’t mind a drop in visual fidelity.Slow Roadsis a popular browser-based driving game, where you simply select a terrain and then drive along endless roads. An upgraded version is coming to the Steam store in October with a few more road types and vehicle customisation options, and the demo is available now.The Long Driveis slightly more demanding, a vehicle-based survival game where you drive around a post-apocalyptic landscape ensuring your food, water and fuel don’t run out. It’s been stalled on Steam early access for years and has probably been abandoned, which I feel is a nice metaphor for this whole sub-genre. Elsewhere,BeamNG.driveis an in-depth vehicle physics simulator where you configure a car to your specifications and then drive it through a sandbox world – it’s in early access on PC but a PS5 version has been promised. The cheery open-world driverMotor Towndoes offer missions to carry out, but mostly it’s about whizzing about in a range of different vehicles. And there’s alwaysEuro Truck Simulator 2, which has drives long enough to feel aimless, even if you do have packages to deliver.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterIndie gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Blood of Dawnwalker – save your family while becoming what you hate | Games | The Guardian
description: Human by day, vampire by night, Coen has difficult choices to make – beginning here in the 1300s, his adventure could span centuries in upcoming sequels
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Human by day, vampire by night, Coen has difficult choices to make – beginning here in the 1300s, his adventure could span centuries in upcoming sequels
Content: Live with your choices … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel WolvesView image in fullscreenLive with your choices … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel WolvesSummer games previewsGamesThe Blood of Dawnwalker – save your family while becoming what you hateHuman by day, vampire by night, Coen has difficult choices to make – beginning here in the 1300s, his adventure could span centuries in upcoming sequelsKirk McKeandWed 19 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Blood of Dawnwalker could be the start of an epic saga. Created by some of the talent behind The Witcher 3, this dark fantasy role-playing game takes place in the 14th century in the fictional land of Vale Sangora, a Carpathian valley of wetlands, mountains and forests cut off from the rest of the world and under the rule of a vicious vampire clan.The developers envisage Dawnwalker as a trilogy. And because protagonist Coen is half vampire himself, that trilogy can skip across time, culminating in the modern day.“It’s a journey through ages, continents, and cultures,” explains game director and studio CEO Konrad Tomaszkiewicz. “Interview with the Vampire was one of the references we had in mind. We want each part of the saga to stand on its own and tell a compelling, engaging, emotive story, while together shaping an epic narrative with a grander plot gradually unravelling.”It’s a fascinating idea for a series where you play as a bloodsucker, doomed to watch those around you wither and die as you persist through centuries.View image in fullscreenSword-wielding human by day … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel WolvesPlaying with the concept of time isn’t just a plan for the sequels. When the vampire clan arrives at the start of the game, they take Coen’s family, and you have 30 days and nights to rescue them. By day, you’re a normal human, fighting with a sword. By night, you can walk on walls, teleport and claw people in half.While you can explore and talk to people at your leisure, time moves forward whenever you complete a clearly marked quest. You could always attempt to save your family on day one, but you’ll be severely unprepared. You have to manage your time while growing in power, sharpening those claws for the final showdown.View image in fullscreenClawed vampire by night … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel Wolves“It is primarily about the sense that what you do in the game carries weight,” says Tomaszkiewicz. “We were looking for something that would make this feel more real and give gamers something to be mindful of. You always remember that there is someone whose fate truly depends on your actions.”Take one quest here, and another might progress over there. The fates of Vale Sangora’s citizens are interlinked, and Dawnwalker’s true depth can only be seen after multiple playthroughs. Even your blood hunger can affect the world. Leave it too long between feeds and Coen will go into a frenzy, draining the person closest to him until they’re a limp sack of skin.“In some cases, you can judge fairly quickly that a specific NPC might be important to the story,” Tomaszkiewicz says. “But in many cases, that is something you will either discover later on or not discover until you decide to play the game again from the beginning. Everything depends on your choices, and in our game, it is not only about the decisions you make, but also whether you choose to do something or not.”It’s a brave approach for a genre where people often save and reload to see how different choices play out. Dawnwalker wants you to come at it with arms open and accept what happens, rewarding players who meet it halfway by opening up new quests and stories when you accidentally – or purposefully – snuff out a life.“My dream scenario is that gamers will say the game and its story stayed with them for years,” says Tomaszkiewicz, “That it touched their hearts, and that they will keep coming back to it to see what they can do differently and how the world reacts.”The Blood of Dawnwalker comes to PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S on 3 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesPCPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Giraffe review – sparkling one-woman show stands out from the crowd | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: An unlikely relationship blossoms in Abigail Weinstock’s compelling and touching solo drama
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: An unlikely relationship blossoms in Abigail Weinstock’s compelling and touching solo drama
Content: Touching … Abigail Weinstock in Giraffe.Photograph: Andrew PerryView image in fullscreenTouching … Abigail Weinstock in Giraffe.Photograph: Andrew PerryEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewGiraffe review – sparkling one-woman show stands out from the crowdPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghAn unlikely relationship blossoms in Abigail Weinstock’s compelling and touching solo dramaMark FisherWed 19 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt takes a brave writer/performer to make her character a sociopath. How to keep the audience on board with someone who is callous and indifferent?In Abigail Weinstock’s sparkling one-woman show, 30-year-old Eliana has been caught making clandestine recordings in her neighbour’s bedroom and cannot deny it. A court summons follows. Even then, her first thought is how to game the system.Her attempt to do so is what gives Giraffe its structure. Eliana has a fortnight until going in front of a judge who will determine whether her temporary restraining order should be made permanent. If she can drum up three letters of support in that time, she has an outside chance of avoiding homelessness (she lives too close to her victim to stay put). With no obvious advocates – her mother long dead, her stepmother intolerant and her father inscrutable – she needs extra resources of imagination to find backers.Sociopaths, of course, can be ruthless, so Eliana is prepared to bluff her way into a childminding job (reassuring the confused mother that she wishes no harm to her daughter) and mask her true nature from a therapy group in the hope of seeming like a trustworthy citizen.Everything goes wrong before it comes right in Emma Jude Harris’s production but, on the way, Weinstock gives a delicious portrayal of a physical and emotional misfit who is hopelessly and hilariously at sea with the business of human communication.What emerges is a quite different diagnosis. Touchingly, in this semi-autobiographical show, Eliana understands the psychology of the silent child she looks after unlike anyone else. It proves she is an emotionally rich human being who just happens to have her own way of interpreting – and misinterpreting – the world. Standing out from the crowd in a human zoo, she and the child are giraffes among zebras. So is this show.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra/Wilson review – white-hot intensity as Verdi Requiem shakes St Paul’s vast dome | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Elemental roars and full-frontal vocal expressivity as the UFO focuses on a mission bigger than a good performance
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Elemental roars and full-frontal vocal expressivity as the UFO focuses on a mission bigger than a good performance
Content: ‘Ukraine’s artistic heroes’ … the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra with soloists Natalya Romaniw, Natalie Lewis, René Barbera and Jongmin Park  at St Paul's Cathedral.Photograph: @fmarshallphoto/Frances Marshall‘Ukraine’s artistic heroes’ … the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra with soloists Natalya Romaniw, Natalie Lewis, René Barbera and Jongmin Park  at St Paul's Cathedral.Photograph: @fmarshallphoto/Frances MarshallClassical musicReviewUkrainian Freedom Orchestra/Wilson review – white-hot intensity as Verdi Requiem shakes St Paul’s vast domeSt Paul’s Cathedral, LondonElemental roars and full-frontal vocal expressivity as the UFO focuses on a mission bigger than a good performanceFlora WillsonWed 19 Aug 2026 08.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere were climaxes in Verdi’s Requiem that would surely have registered on a seismometer as they gathered into a thrillingly elemental roar before dissipating as a series of echoed convulsions into the vast dome above. There were choral susurrations that swept over the orchestra, exhortations delivered in crisp consonants. There were sinuous woodwind lines that took a few seconds to wend their way out of the orchestral clamour, and vocal soloists – Natalya Romaniw, Natalie Lewis, René Barbera and Jongmin Park – who cut instantly through it in a shock of full-frontal expressivity from the very front of the stage.Four years after making theirUK debut with their second ever performance, the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra is now on its fifth international summer tour. Founded by Canadian-Ukrainian conductorKeri-Lynn Wilsonin response to theRussian invasionin February 2022, this orchestra has always had a mission bigger than producing a good performance. And what counts as “good” is always shaped by circumstance, after all. As the numerous speeches that preceded the music stressed, the UFO tour as “cultural ambassadors”, their work centred on hope and resilience, solidarity and justice at what one Ukrainian diplomat called “probably the most difficult moment in our modern history”. One of the orchestra’s percussionists is away at the frontline – so too is the son of composerBohdana Frolyak, whose Gloria opened the concert, its smudgy chromaticism weighted with sadness.No wonder, in this context, that as the final notes of Verdi’s Requiem died away, the orchestra received an immediate standing ovation. Wilson hailed its members as “Ukraine’s artistic heroes” before launching into a rendition of the country’s national anthem. The fact that Wilson’s swift tempi in certain movements of the Requiem resulted in an instant, chaotic blurring of texture and ensemble in this near-impossible cathedral acoustic, that the string tone was less polished than it might have been, that many of Verdi’s finer details were lost in the melee – all of it ultimately registered less than the white-hot intensity of the performance as Wilson leaned in towards the musicians, her focus on them seemingly total, their sound overwhelming.TheUFO tourvisits Amsterdam, Hamburg, Dublin and New York (final concert 26 August)Explore more on these topicsClassical musicUkrainereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Rake’s Progress review – a young cast packed with promise do Stravinsky’s dance with the devil proud | Opera | The Guardian
description: The staging is awkward and balance is an issue at points, but the singers of British Youth Opera are consistently impressive
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The staging is awkward and balance is an issue at points, but the singers of British Youth Opera are consistently impressive
Content: Modernist games … the cast of The Rake's Progress at Battersea Arts Centre.Photograph: Julian GuideraView image in fullscreenModernist games … the cast of The Rake's Progress at Battersea Arts Centre.Photograph: Julian GuideraOperaReviewThe Rake’s Progress review – a young cast packed with promise do Stravinsky’s dance with the devil proudBattersea Arts Centre, LondonThe staging is awkward and balance is an issue at points, but the singers of  British Youth Opera are consistently impressiveAlexandra CoghlanWed 19 Aug 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClapham – home to hundreds of young Londoners crammed into sticky-floored house-shares of a weeknight and the sweaty dancefloors of Infernos at the weekend. Where better to stage The Rake’s Progress, Stravinsky and WH Auden’s 1951 fairytale-cum-morality-play about a country innocent swallowed whole by the temptations and corruptions of the capital? Add a cast and creative team in their 20s, and you’ve got immersive theatre before you even open the doors.We’ve seen Rakes before from British YouthOpera(2009’s starred a certain Nicky Spence, star attraction of this year’s Last Night of the Proms – this finishing-school for students and young professionals clearly works) but never one conceived, directed, designed and stage-managed entirely by the participants themselves. In terms of professional development it’s a gift, but it made for a bit of a bumpy show on opening night.A V-shaped stage encloses conductor Oliver Cope and Sinfonia Smith Square at its centre. Three door frames (clad in Bridgerton offcuts of wisteria for Anne Trulove’s country bower, etched out in red light for London) supply Alexandra Kay’s minimal set. It’s a tricky setup that maroons characters in narrow lines or banishes them to the very back of the theatre, further obscuring already difficult sight lines. And with no pit to tame the enthusiasm of the orchestra, balance is often an issue for the young singers.View image in fullscreenThe cast delivers on the heartbreak: British Youth Opera in The Rake's Progress at Battersea Arts Centre.Photograph: Julian GuideraCope is all crisp precision and lucidity, his Prelude launching a swift, cool account of Stravinsky’s Mozart-homage of a score. The orchestra responds intermittently, but the right angles and sharp points of Stravinsky’s score are an unforgiving architecture, and too many chords and rhythms smudge or sag.Director Tom Deazley makes no big gestures in a quiet, gently contemporary staging that’s more interested in psychology than society. His cast (the first of two) do him proud. Tenor Sam Rose’s Tom Rakewell is a brittle, suggestible creature who comes startlingly into focus in the tenderness and vulnerability of his Bedlam scene. This is a beautiful young voice, packed with promise, and his physical awkwardness sits nicely against the assurance and polished stage package of Sam Young’s Nick Shadow.Sophie Bysouth is a sweet-voiced, earnest Anne, capable of harnessing some fire in “I go, I go to him”, and deeply touching in her woman-to-woman confrontation with Rhian Davies’ confident Baba the Turk. Matthew Bawden relishes his cameo as Sellem, and Gabriel Tufail Smith catches the ear in the small role of the Keeper.Stravinsky and Auden may play modernist games with arm’s length artifice and irony, but ultimately you judge a Rake by its heartbreak. This cast delivers, even if the mechanics of staging and presentation don’t always help them do it.AtBattersea Arts Centre, Londonuntil 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicBattersea Arts CentrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ihsane review – Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui leads us from brutal tragedy to euphoric harmony | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The choreographer combines a homophobic killing from 2012 with a remembrance for his father in an often rapturous show about healing
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The choreographer combines a homophobic killing from 2012 with a remembrance for his father in an often rapturous show about healing
Content: Sharing camaraderie … the cast of Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSharing camaraderie … the cast of Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewIhsane review – Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui leads us from brutal tragedy to euphoric harmonyFestival theatre, EdinburghThe choreographer combines a homophobic killing from 2012 with a remembrance for his father in an often rapturous show about healingChris WiegandWed 19 Aug 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2019 at the Edinburgh international festival, the Swiss director Milo Rau staged an intense theatrical investigation,La Reprise: Histoire(s) du Theatre (I), recreating a homophobic killing in Belgium. The murder of Ihsane Jarfi, seven years earlier, had made headlines and the news disturbed choreographer Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui who was just a little older, also gay and had a Belgian mother and Moroccan father like Jarfi.Cherkaoui now arrives at the same festival with his own act of remembrance, every bit as engrossing as Rau’s, yet more expansive. It pays tribute, too, to the choreographer’s father who died 30 years ago and whose past is interwoven with Jarfi’s death. If that raises any qualms, Cherkaoui’s larger point is about the interconnectedness of all lives and his characters morph into each other. He takes his cue from the victim’s first name, which essentially means “benevolence”, and counters the production’s disturbing flashes of violence with a floating lightness, whether in breakdance or traditional forms, and by presenting ideals of harmonious joy and kindness.View image in fullscreenInterconnected … a scene from Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThat’s where we begin, in an Arabic class, where the script is written on a board with brush strokes that initially complement two narrators’ graceful arms and echo through much of the show’s smooth flow. The tutor encourages the audience to join in with pronunciations; we share camaraderie and knowledge with the colourfully clad students. They arrange themselves in four rows of four and their tessellating gestures add to the patterns of Amine Amharech’s set and the intricate interplay of viola d’amore, piano, oud and percussion in Jasser Haj Youssef’s compositions. It is a lovely scene of common purpose, brought to an end by the set’s huge golden doors closing.They reopen to show the death of Jarfi who was tortured and killed by a group of men he met after leaving a gay bar. Here, a solitary figure torments him, with blows that never connect yet each vicious action sends the victim twisting in agony, almost as if by telekinetic force. Much later, the scene is reversed, with the body taken into the care of a woman.View image in fullscreenSmooth flow … Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRau’s forensic production asked why the crime was committed and how performancecould ever begin to help us understand it. Cherkaoui includes a horrifying assessment of the injuries, and proves similarly interested in ritual, yet his focus is more on the aftermath, even the afterlife, and how a society heals. Jarfi’s body is reclaimed by a swaying collective under Fabiana Piccioli’s golden lighting, framed within the doors. A silky ensemble, facing outwards and joined in a circle, share a similar glow. Further spoken texts analyse different types of grief and dispel the notion of closure. Time and again the movement highlights the potential of each individual life; one chapter staged with billowing white drapes unites a blissful assembly of dancers in flesh-coloured costumes.Come Back Home review – loss and love in Palestinian artist’s intriguing fringe hourRead moreTea is served during a scene that merges the casual and ceremonial, as a football is kicked across the stage, but amid this vivacity a throat is cut and blood spills across Maxime Guislain’s startling video design. Home movies and reportage also play on screens, and there are meditations on society’s strictures and the march of technology that distract from the emotional impact.On stage are 18 dancers from Cherkaoui’s two companies, Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève and Eastman, joining four musicians and a pair of singers. A whole world is created, merging past and future, and death is met with teeming life.AtFestival theatre, Edinburgh, until 20 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalDanceTheatreSidi Larbi CherkaouireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for kd lang | Culture | The Guardian
description: As her supergroup with Neko Case and Laura Veirs celebrates the 10th anniversary of its sublime album, the Ingénue herself will answer your questions
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: As her supergroup with Neko Case and Laura Veirs celebrates the 10th anniversary of its sublime album, the Ingénue herself will answer your questions
Content: From left: Neko Case, kd lang and Laura Veirs.Photograph: Jason QuigleyView image in fullscreenFrom left: Neko Case, kd lang and Laura Veirs.Photograph: Jason QuigleyFilm & Music reader interviewCulturePost your questions for kd langAs her supergroup with Neko Case and Laura Veirs celebrates the 10th anniversary of its sublime album, the Ingénue herself will answer your questionsLaura SnapesWed 19 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdecade ago, three of the finest voices in Americana got together to make a sublime supergroup record. Case/Lang/Veirs, in case the title didn’t make it plain, brought together Neko Case of the New Pornographers, stalwart Portland songwriter Laura Veirs and kd lang, the Grammy-winning Canadian country icon. Sadly, that glorious album has remained a one-off – though a new anniversary release includes a gorgeous never-before-heard song, Accidental Tattoo – but happily, lang is joining the Guardian for a very rare interview to answer your questions.Case/Lang/Veirs: Accidental Tattoo – videoMaybe you’d like to know secrets from behind the scenes of making this record in lang’s loft and Veirs’ dining room, or about lang’s relationship withthe late, great Tony Bennett, her animal rights advocacy, what the Edmonton country-swing scene was like in the mid-80s before lang became a country star and later mainstream icon, or what she and Cindy Crawford talked about when they posed for quite possiblythe greatest magazine photoshootof all time. What was Roy Orbison like to work with, is new music on the horizon, or what her contemporaryconstant cravingsare? Or anything else indeed.Post your questions in the comments bymidday BST on 25 August 2026and the best answers will appear in a future edition of the reader interview.Explore more on these topicsCultureFilm & Music reader interviewfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Christian metal band sues Netflix over KPop Demon Hunters name | KPop Demon Hunters | The Guardian
description: 25-year-old band Demon Hunter says name of streamer’s hit movie creates ‘substantial confusion’ among consumers
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: 25-year-old band Demon Hunter says name of streamer’s hit movie creates ‘substantial confusion’ among consumers
Content: Left: Ryan Clark of the band Demon Hunter at the 2019 Louder Than Life music festival in Louisville, Kentucky. Right: KPop Demon Hunters.Composite: Getty Images, NetflixView image in fullscreenLeft: Ryan Clark of the band Demon Hunter at the 2019 Louder Than Life music festival in Louisville, Kentucky. Right: KPop Demon Hunters.Composite: Getty Images, NetflixKPop Demon HuntersChristian metal band sues Netflix over KPop Demon Hunters name25-year-old band Demon Hunter says name of streamer’s hit movie creates ‘substantial confusion’ among consumersMarina DunbarWed 19 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristian metal band Demon Hunter is suingNetflix, accusing the entertainment giant of trademark infringement and unfair competition tied to the blockbuster “KPop Demon Hunters” name.The lawsuit was filed on Tuesday by Hyde Lane, the company behind Demon Hunter, and alleges thatNetflixStudios and concert promoter AEG Presents have created “substantial confusion” among consumers.“Demon Hunter [is] a well-known and celebrated metal band. Demon Hunter was formed at the turn of the century and, in the quarter-century since, it has consistently released albums, toured, and sold merchandise to a large and dedicated audience,” the Tuesdayfilingstated, according tothe Wrap.South Korea celebrates ‘miracle’ Oscar wins for KPop Demon HuntersRead more“Unfortunately, in 2025, Netflix and Netflix Studios – despite almost certainly being aware of Demon Hunter – chose to release a movie titled ‘KPop Demon Hunters’,” the filing said, adding that the film “reached unprecedented levels of success, not only as a film on Netflix’s streaming service, but also via the ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ movie soundtrack album and merchandise”.The band, who have been releasing music and touring for 25 years, say the alleged confusion has already had real-world consequences.Among the examples included in the lawsuit is an email from someone who spent $500 on top-tier tickets for a Demon Hunter concert in Albany,New York, believing the tickets were for a KPop Demon Hunters show that they planned to attend with their five- and six-year-old girls.“Is their [sic] anyway to refund me or get me a credit or something[?]” the person asked, according toComplex. “If I dont get it refunded I will not be able to purchase tickets to the actual ‘K pop demon hunters show’.”The complaint points to other alleged mix-ups as well. A television producer reportedly approached Demon Hunter’s management under the mistaken impression that the band was connected to KPop Demon Hunters, while social media users have incorrectly tagged Demon Hunter in posts about the film.Demon Hunter is now asking a court to block Netflix from using the KPop Demon Hunters name in connection with recorded music, live performances and merchandise. The band is also seeking unspecified damages.The trademark dispute comes as both sides have pursued protections for their respective names. Demon Hunter’s company registered “Demon Hunter” as a trademark covering recorded music and merchandise in 2022 and has also applied for trademark protection related to live music.Netflix, meanwhile, has registered “KPop Demon Hunters” as a trademark for several merchandise uses, with additional applications still pending.The legal fight follows the extraordinary success of the animated adventure, which centers on Huntrix, a music trio that hunts demons. Sony Pictures originally made the film before it was released through Netflix under a first-look deal.After arriving on the streaming platform in summer 2025, the movie became a runaway hit and ultimately the most-watched original film in Netflix history.Its success has already set the stage for more. Asequel was confirmedearlier this year, while Netflix is reportedly weighing additional projects connected to the property, including a television series and stage musical.Explore more on these topicsKPop Demon HuntersNetflixPop and rockLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Tom Holland set to earn $100m from Spider-Man: Brand New Day | Spider-Man: Brand New ⁠Day | The Guardian
description: In a year that’s seen the British actor star in the season’s two biggest blockbusters – and marry his co-star from both – he is reportedly earning a huge pay packet thanks to box-office bonuses
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: In a year that’s seen the British actor star in the season’s two biggest blockbusters – and marry his co-star from both – he is reportedly earning a huge pay packet thanks to box-office bonuses
Content: Probably not checking his bank balance … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenProbably not checking his bank balance … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamySpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom Holland set to earn $100m from Spider-Man: Brand New DayIn a year that’s seen the British actor star in the season’s two biggest blockbusters – and marry his co-star from both – he is reportedly earning a huge pay packet thanks to box-office bonusesLaurence PhelanWed 19 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British actor Tom Holland is expected to “make at least $100m” for starring in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, according tothe Wrap.Unnamed sources “with knowledge of Holland’s deal” say he was paid $20m (£15m) upfront, about double what he reportedly received for his previous Spider-Man film No Way Home in 2021. But the extraordinary success of Brand New Day at the global box office means the 30-year-old is expected to earn another $80m or more in backend bonuses.In only its third week of release, Brand New Day has become the eighth highest grossing film of all time (unadjusted for inflation), and surpassed $2bn in ticket sales. And of the eight films that have reached this box office milestone, it is second-fastest to have done so. (Avengers: Endgame, released in 2019, was the fastest.)Holland’s reported salary represents a vast increase from his previous performances in the role. When he first played Spider-Man, in a relatively brief but significant appearance in Captain America: Civil War (2016), he was reportedly paid $250,000. For the next three Spider-Man films in which he starred, Homecoming (2017), Far from Home (2019), and No Way Home, he was reportedly paid $500,000, $4m and $10m respectively. But his initial contract is thought to have expired after the end of No Way Home, and the hugely increased remuneration is the result of a freshly negotiated new deal.Brand New Day’s success comes as audiences’ interest in films set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and in superhero films as a whole, had been waning. In 2023, The Marvels grossed only $206m against areported production budget(that is, not including distribution and marketing costs) of $270m. In 2024, Madame Web – about a character with direct ties to Spider-Man – madeonly $100m against an $80m budget. And in 2025,Variety reportedthat Marvel had released “three consecutive commercial duds”: Captain America: Brave New World ($415m, in contrast to the $1.15bn the previous Captain America film earned in 2016); Thunderbolts ($382m, against a $180m production cost) and The Fantastic Four: First Steps ($521m, against a production budget of $200m).The box office dominance of Spider Man: Brand New Day comes in a remarkable year for Holland, during which he also appeared as Telemachus in the second most financially successful film of 2026, Christopher Nolan’s acclaimed adaptation ofThe Odyssey($1.3bn in ticket sales), andmarried Zendaya, his co-star in both films.The Guardian has contacted Sony Pictures for comment.Explore more on these topicsSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom HollandSuperhero moviesMarvelFilm industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: David Shrigley London exhibition will find the funny side of old masters  | Dulwich Picture Gallery | The Guardian
description: Dulwich Picture Gallery show to feature British artist’s work hung next to paintings by Dutch and Flemish greats
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Dulwich Picture Gallery show to feature British artist’s work hung next to paintings by Dutch and Flemish greats
Content: David Shrigley and his installation Exhibition of Old Rope, which had a price tag of £1m.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDavid Shrigley and his installation Exhibition of Old Rope, which had a price tag of £1m.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesDulwich Picture GalleryDavid Shrigley London exhibition will find the funny side of old mastersDulwich Picture Gallery show to feature British artist’s work hung next to paintings by Dutch and Flemish greatsCaroline DaviesWed 19 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe contemporary UK artistDavid Shrigleywill apply his trademark arch humour and distinctive artistic practice “in dialogue” with old masters of Dutch and Flemish painting in a major new solo exhibition in London.The celebrated visual artist will explore the 17th-century paintings with his own new works “responding to” and hung alongside original masterpieces by artists including Jan Steen, Adriaen Brouwer, David Teniers the Younger, Adriaen van Ostade, Pieter Brueghel the Younger and Rembrandt van Rijn.The exhibition, opening at theDulwich Picture Gallerynext year,will be his first solo exhibition in a public art museum in the UK since his 2012 retrospective at the Hayward Gallery, and will bring his work into conversation with one of the most significant collections of Dutch and Flemish historical paintings in Britain, the gallery said.Take the plunge! A deep dive into New York and other great American cities – in picturesRead moreIt will present a series of brand-new, never-before-seen commissions alongside works created almost 400 years apart, and “explore the comedic side of historic painting, presenting how artists through the ages have used humour to observe everyday life, human behaviour and social interaction”, the gallery said. Key works from the gallery’s collection will be shown with loans from major UK institutions.View image in fullscreenA Peasant holding a Glass (1640s) by David Teniers the Younger.Photograph: Dulwich Picture Gallery, LondonView image in fullscreenCelebration of a Birth (1683) by Richard Brakenburgh.Photograph: Dulwich Picture Gallery, LondonView image in fullscreenA Woman with a Beer-Jug (c1670s) by Adriaen van Ostade.Photograph: Dulwich Picture Gallery, LondonHelen Hillyard, head of collection and exhibitions at the gallery, said: “We are excited for David Shrigley to bring his unique perspective to Dutch and Flemish masterpieces of the 17th century.“Shrigley – like our historic painters – has an instinct for finding the funny side of everyday life. He is the perfect artist to bring back playfulness to the old masters, and remind us that great art doesn’t always need to be serious.”Shrigley, a past Turner prize nominee, painter, illustrator, writer, film-maker and sculptor, is famed for his distinct line drawings along with his playful and humorous subject matter.His most recent installations have included the 2021 Mayfair Tennis Ball Exchange, where the gallery was filled with new tennis balls, and the 2025 installation at the Stephen Friedman gallery entitled Exhibition of Old Rope, consisting of 10 tons of used and discarded rope with a £1m price tag.The Shrigley exhibition, which will run from 25 May to 5 September 2027, is one of the headline exhibitions at theDulwich Picture Gallerywhose 2027/28 programme includes what is understood to be the first UK museum exhibition devoted to the pioneering French artist Jacqueline Marval (1866–1932).Marval is believed to have created one of the earliest female nude self-portraits in the history of painting. The exhibition (2 February to 9 May 2027) will bring together than 40 paintings and selected lithographs, many of which have never before been exhibited, to highlight her vital contribution to early French Modernism and her innovative representations of women and the female form, which helped to define the Parisian avant garde.A major retrospective will celebrate the pioneering British Pakistani postwar modernist Anwar Jalal Shemza (1928-1985) in the first UK major museum exhibition in more than 30 years. A Circle, A Square, A Puzzle (21 September to 16 January 2027) will show more than 80 works by the artist famous for Blue Blue Jazz (1967), SquareComposition (1963) and the Roots series (1977 to 1984). It will offer “a fresh appraisal of a pioneering artist whose work transcended cultural boundaries and transformed diverse artistic traditions across art forms and geographies”, the gallery said.Other landmark exhibitions in the programme include solo displays featuring new commissions by Sahara Longe and Caroline Walker.Explore more on these topicsDulwich Picture GalleryExhibitionsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Libby on fashion: a summer wedding is no time for your funeral suit – have fun with colour | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The Traitors star gives his tips on how to shine at a wedding – from mismatching jacket and trousers to rocking a man bag
Author: Stephen Libby
Headline: The Traitors star gives his tips on how to shine at a wedding – from mismatching jacket and trousers to rocking a man bag
Content: Photograph: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Sam DeamanView image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Sam DeamanThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Stephen Libby on men's fashionFashionStephen Libby on fashion: a summer wedding is no time for your funeral suit – have fun with colourThe Traitors star gives his tips on how to shine at a wedding – from mismatching jacket and trousers to rocking a man bagStephen LibbyWed 19 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a long time, I didn’t enjoy going to weddings. It wasn’t the celebration or the party that put me off – it was the clothes. I felt I had to conform and wear a suit, and yet the shape and style of what was on offer were the antithesis of what I would normally wear.Wedding guest attire for women is a whole micro-industry these days. But men are still stuck in the dark ages. It’s all grey, navy and black suits. I often see men wearing the same sort of suit they might wear to a funeral. What kind of message is that sending? It’s high time we got to experiment because a wedding is a celebration of love. You don’t want to look like you’re in mourning.If it’s a summer wedding – and given it’s August, this is why we’re here – then suit-wise you should absolutely go for a relaxed cut and a different colour than you’re used to. Try approaching things as if you were going to southern Puglia for a location wedding. Maybe a pale blue or green suit, or a jacket with a dropped shoulder and a wider leg. Loose clothing is also going to keep you cooler, so if anyone raises an eyebrow you can always just blame the heat.The jacket and trousers don’t even have to match in colour and shape. Once you understand which colours go well together – I like pale green and cream, or brown and blue – you can think about the jacket and trousers as complementary items rather than matchy matchy. As long as you’re wearing a shirt, you’ll look smart enough. Just avoid white if you can help it. A light blue or light green shirt is a great way to introduce colour without being too much.Fabric-wise, pure linen looks gorgeous, but it’s highly susceptible to creasing. If you’re going to be sitting down a lot, by the time you get to the photos you’ll look as if you’ve been through a tumble dryer. Natural fibres such as cotton or a cotton-linen mix will help keep you cool, and personally, I find cotton suits to be very robust if it’s a whole day thing. But I don’t care how hot it is, shorts are never OK.The details are where it’s at, for me – I love a vintage watch or a bold sock, or a pair of sunglasses tucked into a pocket. But I have lots of little rules about how they’re put together. If your trousers aren’t hitting your shoes, they’re too short. A sockless man is the ultimate ick for me, but at the same time, don’t be dull. Have fun with your socks. Use them as an accessory. I likeHappy SocksandUniqlobecause they come in varied colours.double quotation markI love a shoe with a tiny heel - your whole posture changes when you have a bit of heightWhat else? I love a shoe with a tiny heel. I don’t mean stilettos, just a Cuban heel, or loafers raised a centimetre. Your whole posture changes when you have a bit of height – your shoulders go back, your back straightens. No hats, unless you need to for medical reasons. Just put some SPF on, stay in the shade and wear sunglasses (remember to take them off for the photos). I’m pretty easy when it comes to wearing a tie, and prefer something vintage, but I also like a bolo tie or even a brooch where the top button is. Going tie-less might seem a bit casual to some people, but if it’s warm you can just put it down to the weather again.Finally, and this might be controversial, normalise men carrying bags. When you’re having your photos taken at a wedding, I don’t want to see your wallet bulging out your pocket, or your phone. It doesn’t have to be fancy. A small leather purse which you can leave at the table while you’re dancing is just the thing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBuying a whole new suit isn’t something everyone can do (although Vinted has great secondhand options). But you can dress the one you have in a hundred different ways if the accoutrements are right. It’s the little things that can make an outfit really sing.Styling: Sam Deaman.
