title: The men I see in therapy did everything right. So why do they feel so empty? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Many of my clients expected to find fulfillment from their career, marriage and home. Instead, they feel grief
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Many of my clients expected to find fulfillment from their career, marriage and home. Instead, they feel grief
Content: The men I see in therapy did everything right. So why do they feel so emptyWell actuallyThe men I see in therapy did everything right. So why do they feel so empty?Many of my clients expected to find fulfillment from their career, marriage and home. Instead, they feel griefMatthew WillnerWed 19 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.04 EDTShare“I have the career I wanted, but at this point I just don’t care.”“I don’t know why I’m so angry.”“I have friends, but we don’t really talk much.”Different men begin therapy circling the same problem. They arrive at my practice naming anger, numbness or isolation. But over the weeks that follow, the problem they first brought into the room is rarely where we end up.Many have achieved what they thought they wanted: a good career, a comfortable home, a partner, friends. Yet they feel restless. The new job was supposed to be fulfilling. Marriage was supposed to feel like arriving. Instead, the life they worked for leaves them cold.double quotation markThere’s no blueprint to grieve a future that was expected to bring happinessWhen a man finally reaches the future he has spent years imagining and it fails to satisfy him, disappointment can harden into bitterness. He feels trapped by the very ambitions and responsibilities he believed would make him happy.What he is feeling, but often cannot name, is grief.Many had never examined why they pursued the lives they did. They shared an unconscious belief that if they worked hard, built stable relationships and took care of themselves, they would eventually arrive at a life of meaning and ease.It’s often when that promise fails that they knock on my door.There’s no blueprint to grieve a future that was expected to bring happiness. There’s no event, no funeral – so it doesn’t get named, and often isn’t processed. The consequences of it, though, run deep – and it’s where men find themselves the loneliest and the most unhappy.I find that men who live with this are more likely to experience conflict in their relationships, and are less likely to maintain close friendships or pursue community and investment outside of work.This grief isn’t unique to men. But four patterns can make it particularly difficult for men to recognize and process.First, men don’t recognize it as such. Prof Kenneth Doka coined the term “disenfranchised grief” for losses that come with no ritual or social acceptance. Most boys are still taught that vulnerability is weakness, and stoicism is strength. They’re trained out of naming sadness long before they experience anything this large. The result is often confusion about why things don’t feel right, and anger at the feeling of powerlessness.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, 'Well Actually', then 'Read more on living a good life in a complex world,' then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say 'More from this section'Second, there’s the shame.Menreceive a linear social script that centers the provider role. The unspoken contract for many is simple: if you do what is expected of you, one day you will arrive at a life of meaning and satisfaction. Many men’s identities are still tied to their ability to achieve and produce. If they can’t for one reason or another, it leaves them feeling worthless and helpless. Shame blocks mourning, and you cannot grieve what you blame yourself for.‘An uphill battle’: why are midlife men struggling to make – and keep – friends?Read moreThird, the unnamed grief shows up sideways. For many of the men I work with, it presents like anger and numbness. Both of those responses function as protection against something that feels too big and overwhelming to face directly.To regain a sense of control or avoid feeling altogether, they may throw themselves into work, gaming, doomscrolling or substance use.Finally, men tend to go it alone. Gallup data from May 2025foundthat 25% of US men aged 15-34 report feeling lonely in the past day, compared with 18% of women. A lot of men struggle to find a support system to show up for them in their grief. Pew data from 2025foundthat while men and women experience loneliness, men are much less likely to reach out to their networks for support.For many of my clients, the loss of economic stability has made this pattern worse.Over the past five years, increasing economic inequality, career uncertainty and theaffordability crisishave made success on paper feel increasingly shaky. It often exposes a bargain passed down much earlier within their family: that achievement is how you earn security, approval and love.double quotation markWhile it’s not a man’s fault that he has been socialized into this pattern, it is his responsibility to break out of itMany clients who describe losing interest in their work often reflect on how one or both of their parents or caregivers gave all of their attention to their careers, leaving a child feeling that they had to earn the affection they always needed. These clients may pursue careers to feel worthy of appreciation, only to find that success leaves them hollow.Clients who struggle with anger and irritability toward those they care about often describe a childhood burdened by other people’s expectations, in which affection felt conditional on meeting those expectations. As adults, they may experience commitment or other people’s needs as a threat rather than a source of connection.And when they lose something central, such as their job or a partner, they don’t experience the change as a loss or something sad to miss. They see it as undermining who they are.While it’s not a man’s fault that he has been socialized into this pattern, it is his responsibility to break out of it.There’s a reason why this is a tough challenge to solve; when anger or numbness serves as a wall of self-protection, being told to “talk to someone” or that “it’s OK to cry” can feel ridiculous.‘They’re taught that showing feelings is shameful’: eight reasons men don’t go to therapy – and why they shouldRead moreWhat actually works is entering through the anger or numbness itself. I encourage clients to get curious about it, rather than trying to fight it. This is easier said than done, because many clients feel at war with their own anger or indifference.For many, therapy begins with recognizing that their anger or numbness serves a purpose. Once clients understand the self-protective role of these emotions, they can begin to ask what they fear feeling if that protection disappears. The answer is often simple and painful: helpless, weak, worthless, unlovable – or something they still cannot name.By turning towards this grief and exploring it with self-compassion, clients can allow themselves to feel less controlled by it, which leads them to feel more open, and more genuinely confident. When they are less at war with their own feelings, they are able to connect more with others and develop friendships and community. It makes reaching out for support easier and creativity more accessible, and increases their sense of belonging and satisfaction outside of work.It helps them access the sense of meaning that had eluded them, even when they did all the right things.Taking that on doesn’t mean a man becomes less successful. It means taking action for himself, out of love and not fear.Matthew Willner, LCSW, is a psychotherapist licensed in New York, New Jersey and Colorado, specializing in working with men. No individual client is depicted, and the details reflect common patterns rather than any specific person

title: ‘Sounds weird, tastes incredible’: the best seltzers for summertime refreshment, tested | Summer food and drink | The Guardian
description: Low-cal, crisp and fruity, these are our expert’s favourite non-alcoholic and hard seltzer cans to pop in your bag this summer
Author: Joanne Gould
Headline: Low-cal, crisp and fruity, these are our expert’s favourite non-alcoholic and hard seltzer cans to pop in your bag this summer
Content: Get busy with the fizzy: the choice of sparkling waters, whether alcoholic or not, is on the rise.Photograph: Nadya So/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGet busy with the fizzy: the choice of sparkling waters, whether alcoholic or not, is on the rise.Photograph: Nadya So/Getty ImagesThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSummer food and drink‘Sounds weird, tastes incredible’: the best seltzers for summertime refreshment, testedLow-cal, crisp and fruity, these are our expert’s favourite non-alcoholic and hard seltzer cans to pop in your bag this summerI tried 75 low- and no-alcohol drinks: here are my favouritesJoanne GouldWed 19 Aug 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince White Claw disrupted the drinks-in-tins category with its UK arrival in 2020, hard seltzers have continued to grow in popularity. Loved by celebrities, festival-goers and commuters alike, these alcoholic sparkling waters are known for being low in calories, sugar and with minimal ingredients, while containing roughly the same amount of alcohol as a standard lager (up to about 5% ABV).Hovering at about 100 calories a can and with a few carefully chosen (usually) natural flavourings plus spirit, it’s easy to see why seltzers have gained a reputation for being a relatively light choice when picking up a couple of cans. But what makes a good seltzer?For this piece, I tasted a range of 25 refreshing seltzers – alcoholic and non – to find those that deserve a place in your picnic. From premium ingredients to rigorous eco credentials, budget options to those to savour, there’s a drink to please everyone this summer. Happy seltzing.The best seltzers for 2026Best sustainable seltzerView image in fullscreenServed,6 x 250ml cans£10.50 at Ocado£10.50 at AmazonSinger-songwriter Ellie Goulding is known for being a keen fitness enthusiast withstrong environmental principles, so it makes sense that she co-owns this high-end, sustainable seltzer with natural flavours. Using wonky fruit, quadruple-distilled beet vodka and natural plant-based flavourings, Served comes in at 95 calories a can. The raspberry flavour tastes like just-crushed raspberries in the cleanest, clearest vodka soda and is naturally sweet; a deliciously summery vibe.Best soft seltzerView image in fullscreenDash Pink Lady apple sparkling water, 12 x 330ml cans£15.99 at Dash Water£15.99 at AmazonDash Water is fresh and naturally light, with no sugar and zero calories. It’s produced using spring water and fruit, including wonky and surplus produce collected from farmers’ fields, and natural flavourings. I love this subtly tart Pink Lady apple flavour, which is hydrating but has enough about it to feel like a treat when you don’t want to indulge in alcohol. There is little sweetness, so steer clear if you’ve a sweet tooth. Dash has lots of other delicious flavours too; I likegrapefruitandpeach– which incidentally is lovely spritzed with arosé chicken wine. It’s also nice to see it’s a B Corp, making it a healthy, feelgood choice beyond a standard soda.Best light seltzerView image in fullscreenMelleau sparkling vodka soda, 330ml£4.50 at Dead TimeAt a near-saintly 3.4% ABV, Melleau provides a sessionable drinking experience with juices and carefully selected botanicals for refreshingly adult flavours. Choose from Tahiti lime and yuzu, raspberry and calamansi (plus tarragon), passion fruit and pomelo (with cardamom), and blood orange spiked with bitters – all are just gently effervescent and with great-tasting elevated ingredients that make them moreish and enjoyable to sip. With no added sugar and up to just 95 calories a can, a few of these make for a sociable evening without the sore head.Best kombucha seltzerView image in fullscreenBuci hard kombucha, 12 x 330ml cansGinger & lemon only, £29.99 at DrinkSupermarketVariety pack, £39.99 at BuciNot strictly a seltzer, but certainly seltzer-adjacent in that it’s low in sugar with minimal ingredients. This is a hard kombucha of carbonated fermented green tea and it comes in three flavours: wild berries; ginger and lemon; and pear and elderflower. Buci uses only natural ingredients, and the drinks come in at between 110 and 115 calories, with a decent 5% ABV. The taste is crisp and clean, with that tell-tale kombucha funk. Pear and elderflower has subtle notes of juniper and pepper, making it light and complex all at once; a total antithesis to your standard sugary cocktail can.Best supermarket seltzerView image in fullscreenMarks & Spencer hard seltzer, 250ml£2 at OcadoOne of the few supermarket seltzers available at the time of writing (keep an eye out for Aldi’s elusive bargain versions reappearing), this is a low-calorie alcoholic serve, with just 75 calories per 250ml despite its relatively punchy 4.5% ABV. The lemon and lime flavour is likely to be broadly enjoyed thanks to the fresh zestiness, and although there are slightly detectable added sugars and flavourings, it tastes citrussy and clean without overt artificial sweetness. Who can argue for £2 a can?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBest savoury seltzerView image in fullscreenYew pickle sparkling water,4 x 330ml£3.95 at OcadoNow here’s something a bit different: a pickle-flavoured sparkling water. Yes, you read that correctly. The viral popularity of the pickle continues apace – and is no longer limited to dirtying up martinis. This fizzy water is spiked with a hearty splash of natural dill pickle flavour against a mellow backdrop of cucumber, plus a dose of organic kombucha for good measure. Sounds weird, tastes incredible. If your tooth is more savoury than sweet, like mine, you’ll find this to be the ultimate summer thirst-quencher. With no sugar and only trace calories (2kcal per 100ml), this is a healthy choice for anyone watching what they’re eating and drinking; if not, it’s worth trying it mixed withgin,vodkaorwhisky.Best small-batch seltzerView image in fullscreenDeap Nethergate blueberry & lime seltzer, 12 x 250ml£14 at NethergateThe Nethergate Brewery and Distillery may be better known for itsOld Growler porter, but it’s now making the most of the mineral-rich water that flows through ancient chalk beds beneath its Suffolk site to create fruity vodka seltzers. It’s available inapple and elderflower, and blueberry and lime, and the latter is a delightfully different, juicy and floral flavour that I can’t get enough of. A lovely light ABV of 3.4% and 96 calories a can make this ideal for slower daytime sessions. Finally, I had to double check the price: £1.30 seems too cheap for this independent craft can, but £1.30 a can it is.Best-tasting seltzerView image in fullscreenHigh Water hard seltzer mixed pack, 12 x 250ml£27.99 at High Water£27.99 at AmazonIn my testing, High Water’s flavours stood out as the most premium, natural and authentic-tasting – with the caveat that these are the least sweet of the bunch, so possibly not for everyone. Cucumber and mint has been designed to taste like a garden party in a glass, and it does: it’s herbaceous, refreshing and verdantly green, but best in a glass with ice and a slice. I also rated the mango and peach, which nails the tropical mango without resorting to the saccharine. All made with a hefty 5% British vodka, no sweeteners or preservatives and no more than 99 cals a can. One percent of company profits go to the Just One Ocean charity.Best craft seltzerView image in fullscreenArrowtown vodka soda, 12 x 330ml£27.95 at Arrowtown£27.95 at AmazonIf you’re a fan of the black cherry flavour White Claw – and why not – the Arrowtown black cherry and apple is like a more refined version. Both use natural flavours and no artificial sweeteners, but Arrowtown’s recipe edges ahead in terms of pure, fresh, juicy cherry flavour. The peach and raspberry is also extremely dreamy, bursting with sweet stone fruit and a luscious berry zing against triple-distilled vodka. It’s 109 calories a can and 4.5% ABV, plus each can removes two plastic bottles from oceans, so it’s definitely worth investing in the mixed pack.Best big-brand seltzerView image in fullscreenWhite Claw hard seltzer,8 x 330ml£13.75 at Tesco£14.40 at Sainsbury’sOne of the originals – and for many, still the best – White Claw remains the big hitter when it comes to hard seltzers. And for good reason. Staying true to its key selling points (natural flavours, low cal, low sugar and free from artificial sweeteners), White Claw continues to launch great flavours. I like almost all the White Claw flavour lineup, butgreen appleis my current go-to: it’s a naughtier but nicer Appletiser. Its latest foray into lower-cal cocktails (Clawtails) is successful too – thepeach daiquiriin particular.For more, read our roundup of thebest tinned cocktails and winesJoanne Gould is a food, drink and lifestyle writer with a decade of experience, taste-testing anything from South African wines to speciality coffee or scotchExplore more on these topicsSummer food and drinkThe FilterSpiritsCocktailsFoodSoft drinksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ninja Luxe Cafe review: a do-it-all espresso machine at a bargain price – but far from perfect | Coffee | The Guardian
description: Ninja’s assisted machine will make every coffee you crave at hundreds of pounds cheaper than some of its rivals, although you’ll have to put up with a few quirks
Author: Sasha Muller
Headline: Ninja’s assisted machine will make every coffee you crave at hundreds of pounds cheaper than some of its rivals, although you’ll have to put up with a few quirks
Content: Freshly brewed: the Luxe Cafe can brew everything from a single espresso to filter coffee and cold brew.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFreshly brewed: the Luxe Cafe can brew everything from a single espresso to filter coffee and cold brew.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterCoffeeReviewNinja Luxe Cafe review: a do-it-all espresso machine at a bargain price – but far from perfectNinja’s assisted machine will make every coffee you crave at hundreds of pounds cheaper than some of its rivals, although you’ll have to put up with a few quirksThe best espresso machines, testedSasha MullerWed 19 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you’re not a morning person, decision-making is best avoided before 8am. Or, at the very least, until you’ve had a cup of coffee. That is why assisted espresso machines, such as the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ES601UK, are so welcome in my kitchen. They require more effort than a fully automaticbean-to-cup machine, but the reward is a glimmer ofmanual espressoperfection – without all the faff.The Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ES601UK has been gracing my kitchen worktop on and off for over a year, and – despite some mild to moderately serious irritations – it’s a capable alternative to the similarly priced, fully automatic bean-to-cup machines found in my roundup of thebest coffee machines. The big question is whether you’re willing to put in a little more effort for your morning coffee in exchange for a tastier cup – and, in doing so, put up with some of the Luxe Cafe’s quirks.View at SharkNinjaView at AmazonWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenHidden depths: a built-in compartment keeps spare baskets and accessories close at hand.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianView at SharkNinjaView at AmazonNinja’s Luxe Cafe ES601UK is dramatically cheaper than the competition. While Sage’s assisted models – theBarista Express Impress with Cold Extraction(£1,199.95),Oracle Jet(£1,699) andOracle Dual Boiler(£2,499.95) – are eyebrow-raising at the very least, the Luxe Cafe Premier ES601 retails for £549.99. Wait for a sale such as Black Friday, and you may get it for even less.And you get a lot for your money. Ninja’s home appliances often combine multiple machines into one, and the Luxe Cafe is no exception: it’s a bean-to-cup machine that brews almost any type of coffee.You can choose between single and double shots of espresso – simply swapping between the two baskets – and its unusually tall portafilter also accommodates a third, larger basket called the Luxe. That basket holds about 40g of coffee, allowing you to make longer filter-coffee-style drinks – or a huge quad espresso.double quotation markIts design means you can squeeze ridiculously tall travel cups directly under the spoutsBlack-coffee drinkers can choose from espresso, americano, filter coffee (up to 530ml), cold brew and over-ice coffee. Those who prefer coffee with milk can use the integrated frother to whip milk into anything from a cold froth to steamed milk to dollops of hot thick froth.Up top, the 350g bean hopper has a removable rubber-sealed lid to help keep the beans fresh. If you like the idea of having two (or more) types of beans on the go, you can buy spare hoppers for£24.99 from Ninja. Choose from 25 grind sizes using the knurled wheel on the left of the machine.The two-litre water tank slots in at the rear, but it’s clearly been designed with a mind to limited clearance from kitchen cupboards above. You can just pop off the lid and fill it in situ, or lift it up by a couple of centimetres and remove it sideways.All the tools you need can be stored in or around the machine. The plastic grounds funnel and tamper slot into the left-hand side, and a little door on the right opens to reveal a holder for whichever two baskets you’re not using – and the little cleaning brush. Pop the plastic end off the brush, and you’ll reveal the little pokey tool for clearing any blockages from the tip of the steam wand.Down below, the drip tray slides out and, rather unusually, has a separate central drip tray that clips into place. This is designed so that you can squeeze ridiculously talltravel cupsdirectly under the spouts.Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ES601UK specificationsType:assisted espresso machineDimensions:37 x 33 x 37cm (WDH)Water tank:2l, removableReplaceable water filter: yesAccessories supplied: 53.5mm portafilter, spring-loaded tamper, milk jug with integrated whisk, cleaning brush, single, double and luxe baskets, funnel, cleaning kit (2 x cleaning tablets, 1 x descaling tablet), water hardness test kitTime to heat up: 35 secsTime to steam milk: 2mins 20secsGrinder included: yes, 25 settingsNoise: 48dB (brew), 58dB (steam), 63dB (grind)Weight: 11.7kgWarranty:two-year repair or replacement if you register within 28 days of purchaseWhat we loveView image in fullscreenGrounds for optimism: automatic dosing helps remove the guesswork from making espresso.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianThe Luxe Cafe makes a very decent cup of coffee, and once you’ve got used to the button layout, it’s pretty simple. The ability to make quad shots or just over half a litre of filter coffee is a real step up on rival machines, too, as it means you can serve two or three people fairly quickly.Simply slot your choice of coffee basket – single, double or luxe – into the portafilter, then place the plastic funnel over the top of the basket and place the portafilter into the grinder. The Luxe Cafe automatically recognises the basket in use, grinds the correct amount of coffee, and illuminates the relevant drink options on the control panel.double quotation markYou can choose from four preset froth levels for hot and cold milk, and there’s a setting for plant-based milksIt also tells you when you need to adjust the grind size. If you prefer a filter-style brew, the Ninja will advise you to adjust the grind to a far coarser setting, and then dutifully brew you anything from a single mug to 530ml of filter coffee in a few minutes. Pour a few espressos, and it will advise you to adjust the grind size up or down if coffee is pouring too fast or too slowly. It’s not perfect – you’ll occasionally need to nudge it a step or two in either direction when things aren’t tasting quite right – but it gets you into the ballpark with zero trial and error.The Ninja’s stainless steel milk jug has a little whisk attached at the bottom – it’s a similar design to most stand-alone milk frothers or integrated models found on capsule machines – that allows it to froth cold milk. You can also choose from four preset froth levels for hot and cold milk, and there’s a setting for plant-based milks, which did a pretty good job with the almond and oat milks I tested.You can get hot water on demand, too. Pick between very warm, just right and lip-searingly hot – the Luxe Cafe will dole out about a mug’s worth in about a minute and a half. If you want less, just press the button a second time.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenButtoned up: the controls take a little time to get your head around.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianThe Luxe Cafe ES601 cuts a slightly daunting figure on the worktop. Where pricier rivals reel in users with bright, helpful touchscreens, Ninja has kept costs down with a panel of clicky buttons, knobs, and a vista of LED lights. As a result, it’s not the most welcoming machine.Ninja admits as much, too, as the machine arrives tattooed with explanatory stickers. These explain some of the different drink sizes available and provide quick recipes for popular drinks. Another highlights the little hidden compartment where you can keep the baskets that aren’t in use.Point your phone at the sticker with a big QR code, and it takes you to the Luxe Cafe’s 3D user guide on the Bilt app. Actually getting to the user guide is very clunky, but the 3D animations and robotic female voice do a decent job of explaining everything to complete beginners.Frankly, though, most people will be far better off with the paper manual. It guides you through the setup process and also explains some handy titbits such as how to adjust the temperature of your coffee and milk via hidden menus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIf you’re used to fully automatic machines or fully assisted machines, the Luxe Cafe is much more of a faffThe far bigger issue is that the Luxe Cafe may not offer enough assistance for some. Like other cheaper assisted models I’ve reviewed – such as theDe’Longhi La Specialista Touch– the Luxe Cafe asks you to do a fair bit of the work yourself. You have to place the little plastic funnel on top of the portafilter before grinding every single time, and be careful not to drop or break it, because it won’t work without it. There’s a reason why you can buyextra funnelsfor £5.99 a pop on Ninja’s website. Then you’ll need to manually tamp down the coffee yourself using the sprung tamper, remove the dosing ring and lock it into place before brewing.It doesn’t sound like much, but if you’re used to fully automatic machines where you just press a button – or fully assisted machines that provide automatic or lever-action tamping – the Luxe Cafe is more of a faff.One option is to stretch your budget to the step-upES701UK model. This replaces the manual tamper with a big lever. Just like Sage’s fancier machines, you grind, pull the lever and the tamping is done. It also does away with the annoying dosing ring and removes just enough steps in the process to make it feel markedly slicker and seamless.Warranty and repairabilityRegister with Ninja, and you’ll get a two-year warranty. This is a normal repair or replacement policy and is at Ninja’s discretion.For repairs outside the warranty, the situation is less optimistic. Radu Bria, a coffee machine whisperer and owner ofespressorepairshop.co.uk, told me that in his experience, the quality of the Luxe Cafe’s parts suggests it’s a machine built to a budget. To compound matters, Ninja currently does not sell parts to third parties for repair purposes. Once you’re out of warranty, repair options may be limited.That’s a real shame. The external accessory parts are available directly from Ninja’s website – the drip tray, water tank, milk jug, replacement water filters and so forth – so it doesn’t make sense for Ninja not to do the same for the internal parts.I’ve found the Ninja a tad temperamental over the past six months. And I’m not alone: a quick Google search unearths users experiencing a range of issues, from minor annoyances to more serious faults. That’s not unusual for a machine that’s sold truckloads of units across the globe, but it’s worth knowing.For my part, the issues have been more irritating than terminal. One repeating problem is that the milk frother starts to overheat the milk (it goes to 72C at every temperature setting), persisting even when I go into the hidden service menu and adjust the temperature manually.Initially, I wondered whether the problem might have something to do with limescale buildup impeding the milk frothing system. Putting the machine through two 90-minute descaling cycles – one with descaler, one with fresh water – proved a temporary fix, though, and the issue returned while I was writing this review. I live in a moderately hard-water area, but I made sure to replace the internal water filter and use a water filter jug. By contrast, none of the other machines I have on rotation has experienced similar issues.Another complaint is that the grinder doesn’t provide a wide enough range of adjustments: it has tended to recommend the finest of the 25 grind settings for all the medium-roast beans I’ve tried in recent weeks. I suspect that something has come loose in the grinder, as – even at the finest grind setting – the machine no longer grinds fine enough to produce a pleasingly full-bodied espresso with the kind of medium or medium-light roast beans I tend to use. For what it’s worth, it is just about fine enough for darker roasted beans – these tend to require a coarser grind – but it’s still less than ideal. If I were a normal customer, it would have to go back to Ninja under warranty.Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ES601UK: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenWorth the effort: the Luxe Cafe rewards a little extra effort with an excellent brew to suit almost every kind of coffee drinker.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianI’m picky enough to notice and care about these issues. Some might prefer their milk superheated to 72C, and those same people may be perfectly happy with the grinding and the coffee quality because they prefer more robust-tasting dark roast beans. If the coffee is strong, fresh and easy to make, who cares, right? But if you’re buying the ES601UK expecting a super-reliable – and super-consistent – workhorse, I’d recalibrate your expectations.The riposte is that – at its best – the Ninja will brew coffee that is better than any fully automatic machine at a similar price. Nor does it fall woefully short of assisted espresso rivals at twice the price. And that’s why, despite being far from perfect, the Luxe Cafe Premier ES601UK remains a great do-it-all machine for sensible money. At this price (£549.99 at the time of writing), I’d be willing to forgive more than a few quirks for the sheer value on offer – the big question is whether you are, too.View at SharkNinjaView at AmazonNinja Cafe Luxe Pro vsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianDe’Longhi Rivelia£589.98 at John Lewis£649 at DeLonghiIf the Ninja sounds a little too much like hard work, then consider a fully automatic machine. At this price, my pick would be the superb De’Longhi Rivelia. Prod the unusually helpful touchscreen, select from the wide menu of drinks (with or without milk), customise strength and length to taste, and out comes a drink. A darn good one as it happens: it goes toe-to-toe with fully automatic models at more than twice the price.Be in no doubt, the Ninja Cafe Luxe can produce a more authentic espresso – and a stronger cup of filter-style coffee if you’re keen on filling king-sizetravel cups– but the difference isn’t as big as you might expect. Both machines make really good coffee – the Rivelia simply does it with way less faff.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianSage Bambino Plus£399 at Coffee Friend£399.95 at ArgosIf you’re spending this kind of money, then consider the two-box alternative: an espresso machine and grinder. This kind of setup will allow you to make everything from espresso to americano and cortado to cappuccino. And if it’s the ‘manual’ bit that’s scaring you off, then the Bambino Plus will lend a hand – or rather, a wand.It doesn’t help you select the right grind size or amount of coffee to use – althoughSage’s Razor toolmakes life a lot easier – but it steams milk to a creamy microfoam at the touch of a button. You can select the amount of froth and temperature, too. Partner it with a top-notch hand grinder such as the £99KingGrinder K6, or a basic mains-powered grinder such as the £159.95Baratza Encore ESP, and you’ll be rivalling your favourite coffee shops in no time.View image in fullscreenSage Barista Touch with Cold Extraction£993 at AO£999.95 at John LewisSage has to take the credit for popularising the fully assisted espresso machine. Until the Ninja came along, it was pretty much the only option for a fully assisted machine – and, despite the daunting £1,199.95 RRP, it deserved its plaudits. You get to enjoy the tactile clunk, whirr and twist of the manual espresso process, but the snazzy colour touchscreen guides you from bean to cup with ease.The results are more consistent and more refined than the Ninja, but are they worth twice the price? Probably not. What’s more, the Bambino Plus pairing above will largely match it shot for shot. Even cheaper models will, with a bit of barista skill. Still, I’ve been using one for well over a year without a single issue. Pricey, yes. But excellent also.Sasha Muller is a tech and consumer journalist, avid coffee drinker and craft beer enthusiast with more than two decades of experience in testing products and avoiding deadlines. If he’s not exploring the local woods with his kids, boring people talking about mountain bike tyres or spending ill-advised amounts on classic drum’n’bass vinyl, he’s probably to be found somewhere swearing at an inanimate objectExplore more on these topicsCoffeeThe FilterGadgetsKitchen essentialsHomesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn excess green vegetables into a vibrant Spanish soup – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A gazpacho is not only a great way to use up odds and ends in the crisper drawer, it will also surprise you with its flavour and versatility
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A gazpacho is not only a great way to use up odds and ends in the crisper drawer, it will also surprise you with its flavour and versatility
Content: Tom Hunt’s green gazpacho.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s green gazpacho.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn excess green vegetables into a vibrant Spanish soup – recipeA gazpacho is not only a great way to use up odds and ends in the crisper drawer, it will also surprise you with its flavour and versatilityTom HuntWed 19 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince readingHow Not to Die, by Michael Greger, I’m always looking for ways to include greens in every meal. He regularly pops into my mind when I’m cooking, whispering in my ear: “Add some spinach to that risotto,” say, or “Moringa powder will make your porridge much more nutritious.” So I’m sure today’s green gazpacho would make him proud. It’s a great way to clear out your crisper drawer and pack a meal with all sorts of greens. Anything goes, but if any of your chosen ingredients (eg, basil or mint) has a particularly potent flavour, just add it in moderation or to taste. Incidentally, the key to a great gazpacho is the quality of the olive oil, as is a nice, bold-but-balanced acidity, which is easily achieved with a squeeze of lemon or your best vinegar.Green gazpachoWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThis is a really vibrant recipe, and perfect for the hot summer months. It’s best served well chilled, so make it with ice so you can enjoy it immediately or/and chill in the fridge or freezer for 30 minutes to an hour. It will keep, covered, in the fridge for up to three days, but is best eaten on the day it is made. You can also add a few ice cubes to the soup bowls, if you like.Decorate the top with a selection of your favourite ingredients used in the soup: finely dice them and scatter on top, along with any delicate herbs and a final drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Serves4400g green vegetables(cucumber, courgette, celery stalks and leaves, lettuce, spinach, peas, or a mix of whatever you have to hand), finely chopped – save some of your favourites to garnish50-100g soft green herbs(parsley, basil, mint, coriander, or a mixture), leaves roughly chopped, stalks finely chopped1 handful ice cubes100ml extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to finish2 tbsp lemon juice, or white-wine, sherry or cider vinegar, plus extra to taste, if necessary1 small garlic clove(or to taste), peeledSea saltOptional spices– I used cumin, ground coriander and cayenne pepper, but experiment with what you have in the cupboardRoughly chop the green vegetables and put them in a jug blender.Add the herbs and 200ml chilled water, drop in the ice cubes, oil, garlic and a pinch of salt, then add any spices you fancy. Blend for a minute, until very smooth, then adjust the seasoning, acidity and spice to taste.Chill for at least half an hour, and serve cold, topped with the reserved green vegetables, finely diced, a few herb leaves and a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteVegetablesSoupSpanish food and drinkHerbs and spicesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jammy tomato risotto and amaretto roast peaches: Toklas chef Chris Shaw’s simple summer recipes  | Food | The Guardian
description: Make the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessert
Author: Chris Shaw
Headline: Make the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessert
Content: Chris Shaw’s risotto with datterini tomatoes, pecorino and mint.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenChris Shaw’s risotto with datterini tomatoes, pecorino and mint.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.FoodJammy tomato risotto and amaretto roast peaches: Toklas chef Chris Shaw’s simple summer recipesMake the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessertChris ShawWed 19 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Toklas, ingredients such as datterini tomatoes and ripe peaches are taking centre stage. These recipes celebrate the simplicity of summer cooking, allowing produce to shine with minimal intervention. From a risotto layered with sweet tomatoes, pecorino and mint to roast peaches finished with amaretto and mascarpone, they capture the character of the season – fresh, generous and full of flavour.Risotto with datterini tomatoes, pecorino and mint (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appA really light risotto. There’s no butter in it – just olive oil and cheese – and the richness comes predominantly from the roast tomatoes.Prep15 minCook1 hr 20 minServes4For the stock4 shallots,peeled2 sticks celery,trimmed1 vine of tomatoes2 carrotsFor the roast tomatoes500gdatterinitomatoes, washedSaltOlive oil4garlic cloves,peeledFor the risottoOlive oil2 shallots, peeled and finely diced1garlic clove, peeled and crushedSalt and black pepper350g risotto rice2 tbsp tomato puree150gpecorino romano, grated30g fresh mint, leaves picked and finely choppedTo make the stock, roughly chop all the vegetables and put them in a saucepan. Cover with two litres of cold water and bring to boil over a high heat. Turn down the heat and leave to simmer for 20 minutes.Meanwhile, heat the oven to 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½. Put the tomatoes in a roasting tray, season with salt and drizzle with olive oil. Add the garlic, then roast for about an hour, until the tomatoes are jammy.Bring a large, heavy-based pan to a medium heat. Add a generous glug of olive oil, followed by the diced shallots, crushed garlic and a pinch of salt. Once the shallots are soft, add the rice and stir well to coat. Add another pinch of salt then toast the rice for a minute or two, until the edges begin to look translucent. Add the tomato puree and cook for two to three minutes.Strain the stock and discard the vegetable solids. Add the stock to the rice one large ladleful at a time, stirring continuously and allowing each addition to be absorbed before adding the next.After about 18-20 minutes, when the rice is just cooked but still has a little bite, take the pan off the heat and stir through the roast tomatoes, roast garlic, grated pecorino and chopped mint. The tomatoes should break up nicely once incorporated into the hot rice.Season to taste, finish with a generous glug of olive oil, if desired, and serve immediately.Amaretto roast peaches with mascarponeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenChris Shaw’s amaretto roast peaches with mascarpone.Inspired by the restaurantVia Carota in New York, this is a really great summer dessert – it’s super-easy, too.Prep5 minCook25 minServes4For the mascarpone cream250g mascarpone50ml double cream¼ vanilla pod, seeds scraped out50g icing sugarFor the peaches4 good-quality (ideally yellow) peaches75g icing sugar150mlamarettoCombine all the ingredients for the mascarpone cream in a bowl, beat well with a spatula until smooth, then chill until needed. (The cream helps soften the mascarpone, which can otherwise be quite stiff and heavy.)Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6.Halve the peaches, remove the stones, then cut each half in two. Arrange the peach quarters skin side down in a roasting tray. Using a sieve, dust evenly with the icing sugar, then pour the amaretto into the tray and roast for about 15 minutes, or until the peaches are tender and lightly caramelised.Serve the warm peaches with the roasting juices spooned over and the mascarpone cream on the side.Chris Shaw is head chef atToklas, London WC2Explore more on these topicsFoodRiceSummer food and drinkTomatoesMain courseItalian food and drinkCheeserecipesShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: my husband died – and birds began behaving strangely towards me | Bereavement | The Guardian
description: I was living on my own for the first time in 35 years, walking every day. Nature reminded me how much there still is to be found in emptiness
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I was living on my own for the first time in 35 years, walking every day. Nature reminded me how much there still is to be found in emptiness
Content: ‘Everywhere I went, I looked for solace in nature’ … Helen Harris, by the River Lea in east London.Photograph: Rebecca BlackView image in fullscreen‘Everywhere I went, I looked for solace in nature’ … Helen Harris, by the River Lea in east London.Photograph: Rebecca BlackA moment that changed meBereavementA moment that changed me: my husband died – and birds began behaving strangely towards meI was living on my own for the first time in 35 years, walking every day. Nature reminded me how much there still is to be found in emptinessHelen HarrisWed 19 Aug 2026 01.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter my husband died, the birds started behaving strangely towards me. This was not my imagination; it really happened. On my daily walks, I was startled by how close they came to me – approaching, hopping alongside me and chirping. If there were a lot of them – and if there was no one else around – it felt as if they were accompanying me, maybe trying to convey something.I had walked on the heath near our home with my husband for years. But his illness meant that, during his final months, he could not walk with me any more. When he died – in January 2023 – I had been walking on my own for six months and the birds, I am sure of this, had paid no attention to me.Of course, it occurred to me that this might be a message from my husband. When you are newly bereaved, it’s easy to grasp at any sign that your loved one might somehow still be there. But, in the case of my husband, I knew this could not be. Firstly, he had told me before he died that he was certain there was no afterlife and it was totally irrational of me to think that there might be. Secondly, he would never ever have chosen to come back as a bird. He was a big man, who admired big powerful animals, and – if he was that way inclined – he might have come back as a tall, many-antlered stag, roaring at me from a misty mountainside. Or, maybe more likely, because he could be morose, he might have come back as a moose or an elk, lumbering out of a gloomy forest at dusk.One evening, a robin followed me home. I know that robins often interact with people, perching on gardeners’ spades, making eye contact. But this robin hopped along beside me for an unusually long time, watching and apparently accompanying me. In a moment of foolishness, I stopped and said quietly to the bird: “OK, if it’s you, follow me home” and at once it flew away in a big fluttering rush.Three months after my husband’s death, I went to France, to a small village in the foothills of the Alps. One evening, as I was climbing the outside stone staircase to my room, a young magpie appeared out of nowhere and perched on the banister beside me, making a tremendous fuss. He squawked and flapped his wings and bounced up and down, obviously beside himself. As he was less than two feet away from me, this was quite disconcerting. I still don’t know what was upsetting him but I do know that things like that never used to happen to me.View image in fullscreen‘Sometimes I imagine my husband laughing and rolling his eyes at me’ … Helen in the south of France, January 2024.Photograph: Rebecca BlackIt made me begin to pay much more attention to my natural surroundings than I had before. I discovered the uncomplicated pleasure to be found in a weirdly shaped mushroom, in the steady clicking noise made by gorse bushes when the sun shines on them. I was not skipping through the woods, tra-la-la; I was far too sad. But my need to walk every day – which I have always had – acquired a new and deeper meaning.Everywhere I went that first year, I looked for solace in nature. I had to keep moving, whether walking on the heath or leaving home to travel. It was in the stillness of staying put that the pain was worst.Over time, I came to see that when you walk in nature with the person you love, you observe it, you enjoy it, but you are – to a certain extent – apart from it. Your companionship is its own universe. When you walk alone, you become more fully part of the world around you. So, no doubt, I was paying more attention to the birds. But I also think they sensed that there was something wrong with me – I was a wounded creature – and maybe they really were accompanying me.Back home, there is another robin who regularly tries to catch my attention through the glass of the garden door. In the afternoons, an urban fox, always the same one – I know him from the scar on his forehead – snoozes in my garden. On many evenings, a mouse runs across the garden path at 8.30pm – always in the same direction – while, overhead, through the urban dusk, flocks of green parakeets head home along their known routes, traced in the sky. Nature reminds me continually how much there still is to be found in emptiness.I relate to the natural world differently now that I have learned to sense it as company. I do still enjoy the companionship of people but with creatures there is no need for pretence. On the most active night of the Perseid meteor shower, I got up at three in the morning and saw three shooting stars from my open bedroom window. The next day, someone told me it was a good omen – but I knew that it was nothing of the sort. It just was.This might all sound very fanciful, but it is these moments that have coloured my experience of living alone for the first time in 35 years. Still, as I walk in the woods, sometimes I imagine my husband laughing and rolling his eyes at how I told everyone that, after he died, the birds started behaving strangely towards me.Explore more on these topicsBereavementA moment that changed meMarriageFamilyRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: will social media bans for teens mean the return of grownup skincare? | Social media | The Guardian
description: Soon it will be harder for the beauty industry to aggressively market at children, hopefully spelling the end of gimmicky, ineffective kiddie makeup
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Soon it will be harder for the beauty industry to aggressively market at children, hopefully spelling the end of gimmicky, ineffective kiddie makeup
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianSali Hughes on beautySocial mediaSali Hughes on beauty: will social media bans for teens mean the return of grownup skincare?Soon it will be harder for the beauty industry to aggressively market at children, hopefully spelling the end of gimmicky, ineffective kiddie makeupSali HughesWed 19 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis summer’s announcement that under-16s will soon be banned from somesocial media platformsand, more recently, that 16- and 17-year-olds will face adigital curfew, strikes me as a good and sensible decision. It also has unignorable benefits for beauty consumers who are old enough to vote, as opposed to those receiving pocket money – with whom brands are inexplicably obsessed.A social media ban makes it harder – though not impossible – for the beauty industry to market aggressively and cynically at children, which might mean gimmicky, ineffectual kiddie makeup and skincare will stop occupying a disproportionate share of marketing spend and retail space. Will it be the end for “lip oils” in 36 shades of pink?Top of my own extinction wish list is pH colour-adjusting anything: the raft of makeup designed to adapt to the wearer’s own body chemistry to create a “personalised” shade of Pepto-Bismol pink that looks horrible in comparison to any lipstick, gloss or blusher that declares its true colour from the off.Speaking of blushers, those transparent jelly sticks of rouge made to look like Haribo are the worst. They lose slip, and dry before you can blend harsh lines, and the colours are inherently lurid – and not in a good way.double quotation markAny anti-ageing skincare packaged like fruit smoothies will now largely be hidden from vulnerable teensAfter three years when there have been few major fragrance launches that could be classed as sugar-free, perhaps perfumers will once again be permitted to create without marketing briefs that could double as the dessert menu (I could go the rest of my life without another “cotton candy” note). I’ve also had my fill of sweet, cloying, buttercream-icing body sprays, but they are at least harmless – and fun to some.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: the new crop of fig perfumes make perfect scentsRead moreAny anti-ageing skincare (all pointless with the exception of sunscreen, which social media has dangerously told kids is bad for them) packaged like fruit smoothies will now largely be hidden from vulnerable teens and their insecurities. And whitening toothpastes, bought in huge numbers on TikTok, are as pernicious, with the added disadvantage of affecting no change whatsoever.Spot patches – hygienic, picking-preventative discs of helpful ingredients – should stay. They make a cute and celebrated feature of a normal teenage flaw, while so many brands are marketing full coverage makeup for the same issue.Aside from them, none of these deserve our money or our children’s attention.Beautymay soon have little choice but to grow up.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaSali Hughes on beautyBeautyMakeupSkincarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I came to the Highlands to give something back to the hills’: a volunteering trip in Scotland | Scotland holidays | The Guardian
description: I found two days of hard graft – repairing hiking paths with a conservation trust in stunningly remote Wester Ross – a surprisingly rewarding experience
Author: Mike MacEacheran
Headline: I found two days of hard graft – repairing hiking paths with a conservation trust in stunningly remote Wester Ross – a surprisingly rewarding experience
Content: Stac Pollaidh’s ‘porcupine ridge’ summit.Photograph: Tony West Photo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStac Pollaidh’s ‘porcupine ridge’ summit.Photograph: Tony West Photo/Getty ImagesScotland holidays‘I came to the Highlands to give something back to the hills’: a volunteering trip in ScotlandI found two days of hard graft – repairing hiking paths with a conservation trust in stunningly remote Wester Ross – a surprisingly rewarding experienceMike MacEacheranWed 19 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhadn’t planned to enjoy any of this. As summer light fell on Stac Pollaidh – the summit’s teeth bared, the views stretching across the surreal emptiness of Assynt – I found myself ankle-deep in blanket bog next to a hiking path, back bent, hacking at the tough terrain with a heavy-duty mattock. Farther up the hillside, another hunched figure was cutting a deep brown scar into the moor grass and, while he worked, I stood back to look at my efforts. At my feet was a cross drain that I’d unblocked and repacked with new stonework to prevent storm damage and aid runoff from the path. A burble began to trickle, slow yet clear across the sparkling bedrock. It felt a little like appreciating a masterwork in a museum.I’d come to Wester Ross with a bucket and spade, not for a beach break at particularly gorgeous Achmelvich or Clachtoll nearby, but with the notion of giving something back to the hills. TheOutdoor Access Trust for Scotland(Oats) is a steward of many of the Highlands’ most famous mountains – developing, building and repairing paths and habitats – and I’d joined a group of volunteers for a two-day stint on the north-west Highlands’ most visited peak. Factoring in a free stay atUllapool youth hosteland the promise of a home-cooked communal meal in return, plus an acceptable midge-free forecast, I’d driven north from Edinburgh the night before in a buoyant mood.Oats’s purpose is to promote sustainable public access and these days that’s largely done through voluntourism, with helpers set to work lifting, resurfacing and filling pathways, yielding landscape-scale results. Iconic if traffic-heavy mountains such as An Teallach, Lochnagar and Braeriach are annual priorities, as are a throng of glens and estates from Skye to the Cairngorms. (Due to this summer’s devastating fires, some events in the north Cairngorms may be changed to a different location or postponed.) The trust’s volunteers even regularly get to work on the Lairig Ghru, arguably Britain’s most unforgiving mountain pass.View image in fullscreenVolunteers repairing the hiking path on Stac PollaidhIt might sound like all hard graft, but it’s not. Volunteers learn new practical skills and gain awareness of mountain path design and the causes of erosion – mostly a combination of human misuse and increasing extreme weather conditions – in settings with extraordinary views. No experience is required, but volunteers must be used to spending time outdoors, have good physical fitness and be capable of using hand tools.We started that first morning from Stac Pollaidh’s car park, a space transformed by Oats two years ago to accommodate four times more vehicles – a result of the mountain’s accessibility from the North Coast 500, which hurtles past (from Kylesku to Ullapool) only five miles east, at the end of the road. But everyone comes with the same motivation. As we climbed the open moorland, Assynt’s surrounding sea of lochans (small lochs) sparkled. Stac Pollaidh’s summit, to the north, appeared even more welcoming with its porcupine ridge under a sky as blue as a newborn’s eye.double quotation markPost-Brexit, with a lack of EU funding streams, there is a drastic need for a public fund for path maintenance and habitat restorationFrom below the hilltop to the lower forest’s edge, we worked the path – unclogging ditches, removing invasive grasses, dredging, stabilising the soil, repacking stone drains, replanting edges – all while the mountain came to life. Trail runners, dog walkers and hikers from across Europe weaved up the slopes, stopping to ask what we were doing. A French school group trooped past, the pupils plastered with blue Braveheart face paint. A Dutch couple stopped to offer biscuits. Everyone swallowed the stunning views of Suilven to the north.View image in fullscreenSuilven from Loch Druim Suardalain.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Getty ImagesOur group of seven volunteers – including two New Zealanders; three retirees, one from Inverness, one from Stirling and another from Forfar; and an Edinburgh IT worker using his annual corporate volunteer days – appreciated the smiles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Scottish explorer who fancied an adventure closer to home: hiking the Highlands’ Affric Kintail WayRead moreTo a newcomer, the Highlands’ mountain paths may appear to have always been there, as if part of the landscape’s DNA. But as Oats’s volunteer coordinator Eva Kupska said, they are “always evolving and always at risk from erosion, because of the influences of nature and man … and it is our job to conserve them”.Every volunteer is vital. Post-Brexit, with a lack of EU funding streams, Eva told me there is a drastic need for a public fund for path maintenance and habitat restoration, and the charity simply doesn’t have the manpower to tackle the deteriorating pathways or native tree planting alone. To complicate matters, some of the most popular mountain paths are on privately owned land, with no access to any public funding.There are a further 12 one-day, plus three- and five-day,maintenance and conservation eventsscheduled to take place this year, including some dedicated tree-planting trips. It’s a joyful shared experience. That first afternoon, flasks of hot tea were unscrewed and homemade fruit loaf was shared. There was the warm smell of flowering heather and the earthy stink of the bogs, along with the satisfaction of time well spent in the wild.View image in fullscreenUllapool, where Mike stayed in the youth hostel.Photograph: Eleanor Scriven/Getty ImagesThat evening, back in Ullapool, the harbour abuzz with tourists eating fish suppers and gulls circling above the trawlers, we stood in the sea-view kitchen of Ullapool youth hostel sharing life stories and the day’s experience. There are plenty of excellent dinner options, includingThe Seafood ShackandThe Dipping Lugger, but we settled on a night of each other’s company (delightful), local beers (necessary) and a giant gurgling stockpot of Eva’s courgette and tomato risotto (terrific). And boy, did I sleep well.The next day brought a gossamer mist to the hills of Wester Ross. We arrived earlier, picked up where we’d left off and, largely, never complained as the sun slowly cracked through the clouds. But best of all was seeing our progress as we worked down the mountain, step by step, always avoiding the fragile vegetation at the path’s edges, creating something better and more sustainable for tomorrow. A staycation with a purpose – and it felt good.The trip was provided byOutdoor Access Trust for Scotland, with support fromVisitScotland.To register as a volunteer and to sign up for events on the annual path maintenance days programme, visitOats’svolunteering portal. Overnight accommodation in a youth hostel or a bothy, plus evening meals and transport to and from the restoration site, are includedExplore more on these topicsScotland holidaysVolunteering holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysMountainsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: It’s hard being a vicar in a long, hot summer | Environment | The Guardian
description: Madley, Herefordshire: The cool of our churches has been welcome to many, but my polyester robes are not made for the heat
Author: Rev Simon Lockett
Headline: Madley, Herefordshire: The cool of our churches has been welcome to many, but my polyester robes are not made for the heat
Content: Hot sun shining through Madley church windows.Photograph: Simon LockettView image in fullscreenHot sun shining through Madley church windows.Photograph: Simon LockettCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: It’s hard being a vicar in a long, hot summerMadley, Herefordshire:The cool of our churches has been welcome to many, but my polyester robes are not made for the heatRev Simon LockettWed 19 Aug 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 02.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery summer, while roasting in my robes, I say to myself: “I must get a lighter set.” If I had a cotton cassock instead of a polyester cassock andalb, swaying to the singing of hymns might not raise my core temperature as much. In that regard, this year hasn’t been without its challenges.Even so, our churches have become “cool spaces”. In Madley towards the end of term I received a call from Mr Batstone, headteacher of the primary school, wondering if classes could be held in church.Madley parish churchis huge, with room in the nave for each class and a cool, subterranean crypt. I headed over later that week to find the church buzzing with children.We’ve also had our summertime pet blessing, to celebrate the more‑than-human community. After a dynamic risk assessment, a bowl of water was supplied for the dogs and the door kept wide open. Unfortunately, we cannot open the stained glass windows.View image in fullscreenMadley church pet blessing.Photograph: Simon LockettI usually bring an earthworm to the service to highlight that the least glamorous animals can be the most important, but when I dug the garden there were none – they had dived deep to find moisture. This year I was concerned that a visiting guinea pig called Pippa might be eaten by one of the attending dogs; I needn’t have worried as our canine congregation were more settled than I had ever seen them, panting with exhaustion after their morning walk.The irony is that Madley church is notoriously cold. At one midnight mass, the temperature by the altar was -15C. Even with the recent heatwaves, Felicity and Claire brought jumpers to the Saturday communion – at the door, the welcomer, Carol, said: “For the first time ever you won’t be needing those.”The conversations afterwards in the porch are about the harvest and the smoke from theBannau Brycheiniog fires. Winter barley yields are good, but the spring-sown cereals are too dry in the grain. While local farmers struggle to produce food and wildlife dies in the blazes, I lament that we appear to have failed the biblical mandate to care for the Earth. The worst of the heat has passed now, but even so, I must invest in those lighter robes.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsChristianityExtreme weatherSummerPetsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Barking mad? How people in England’s ‘least friendly’ borough feel about the ranking | Communities | The Guardian
description: Does the description from a study ranking all of England’s 296 boroughs for friendliness ring true for people in the east London town?
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Does the description from a study ranking all of England’s 296 boroughs for friendliness ring true for people in the east London town?
Content: Alice Fokuo: ‘Everyone who passes says hello.’Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlice Fokuo: ‘Everyone who passes says hello.’Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianCommunitiesBarking mad? How people in England’s ‘least friendly’ borough feel about the rankingDoes the description from a study ranking all of England’s 296 boroughs for friendliness ring true for people in the east London town?Rachel HallWed 19 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlice Fokuo is so friendly with her neighbour that they have exchanged keys to each other’s homes. The level of intimacy is such that “I call her mum, because she cooks for me”.So the market trader was surprised to learn that her borough, Barking and Dagenham, rankedthe least friendly in Englandin a new study drawing on government data from the community life survey. It measures how often people chat to neighbours, feelings of loneliness and belonging, local pride, and levels of participation in civic life in England’s 296 local authority areas.“Everyone who passes says hello, children run to me and say ‘grandma’ and hug me. It’s amazing. I don’t know about other people, because everyone is different, but to me they’re nice,” she said. “I’m very happy. I belong here.”However, she worried that the once-bustling market was losing its role as a community space as younger people make more purchases online. She values its sociable atmosphere: “Here people come, sometimes six or seven people will be standing, I won’t even have a seat to sit on. The customers are friendly to me, they bring me food.”Many people in Barking’s town centre who spoke to the Guardian shared Fokuo’s fondness for their neighbours, but expressed concerns about living in London’s most indebted borough, Barking and Dagenham, and the lack of well-cared public spaces for socialising.View image in fullscreenAdrian Stan said people in the borough ‘really listen to what you’re going through’.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianAdrian Stan, a 31-year-old cleaner, was relaxing after work on a bench designed to resemble a tree stump in Barking’s Arboretum Place. He appreciated that there was “a friendly spot” where he could mingle with friends and other local people for free, but bemoaned that there weren’t more seating options in the square, and the state of its upkeep.“There is space for improvement,” he said, noting that the square would benefit from picnic tables, or activities aimed at younger people such as a skate park. He also wanted the council to do more to support rough sleepers in the borough, which has high rates of deprivation, poverty and homelessness.But he added that he found that people in the borough, which is one of the UK’s most ethnically diverse, were “open to new people”. “They really listen to what you’re going through,” he said.View image in fullscreenRana Maybeci: ‘We have a really good community here.’Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianRana Meybeci, 33, shared Stan’s concerns about the state of Barking’s public spaces. She has two young children, and worries about spending time in areas that are visibly dirty and strewn with litter. She also feels unsafe in Barking town centre, due to the level of antisocial behaviour, drug addiction and street drinking.“Sometimes people are shouting, walking towards you,” she said. “People are so unkind, and with children, I feel always ‘come here baby, sit here.’ I always feel I should protect them.”Although she does not feel proud of Barking town centre, she is happy living in nearby Barking Riverside, a newly developed residential neighbourhood created on an ex-industrial brownfield site. “We have a really good community here,” she said, adding that she was in regular contact with parents to chat and organise playdates.View image in fullscreenGeorge Mathew: ‘All the people are quite friendly and mingle.’Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianGeorge Mathew, 69, is also a longstanding resident of Barking Riverside. “I would say my area is very calm and quiet,” he said. “All the people are quite friendly and mingle, and we update each other online. We have some close friends near my house. If you want any help, they are ready to help out. It’s a good community.”The development has faced criticism for its isolated geography and limited infrastructure, as well as a dearth of amenities, from cafes and restaurants to GP services. Mathew agrees: “The social and public spaces haven’t developed so much. At present, there are only a few shops. When you consider all the population there, there should be more.”Explore more on these topicsCommunitiesLondonEnglandLocal governmentfeaturesShareReuse this content
