title: Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya | Kenya | The Guardian
description: Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief
Content: Emergency rescue teams at the site of the crash in Samburu county on Wednesday.Photograph: Kenya Red Cross Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenEmergency rescue teams at the site of the crash in Samburu county on Wednesday.Photograph: Kenya Red Cross Handout/EPAKenyaFive Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in KenyaOfficials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chiefAssociated PressWed 19 Aug 2026 16.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 16.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northernKenya, according to local police and the state department.Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.Explore more on these topicsKenyaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn | Spain | The Guardian
description: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back
Content: Tents being set up in a public car park in Ceuta on Tuesday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenTents being set up in a public car park in Ceuta on Tuesday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersSpainSpain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turnMadrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent backEurope live – latest updatesStephen Burgenin BarcelonaWed 19 Aug 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland.The majority of the estimated70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta– a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.On 13 August, the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, had said: “Anyone who illegally enters Ceuta or Melilla [another Spanish enclave in north Africa] knows they will be sent back because Spain andMoroccowork together to this end. They will not reach the peninsula, nor the European continent and nor will they remain indefinitely in Ceuta or Melilla.”The transfer of the children to the Spanish mainland is a sensitive political topic as several regions governed jointly by the conservative People’s party and the far-right Vox are reluctant or opposed to receiving their quota.To minimise conflict, the youth ministry, in coordination with the Ceuta government, is devising an urgent plan under which NGOs and child protection agencies take charge of the most vulnerable children, girls in particular, without transferring their guardianship to Spain’s regional governments.Rubén Pérez Correa, the secretary of state for children, has been in Ceuta since Sunday in an effort to resolve a situation in which hundreds of children are living on the street and existing on handouts from Ceuta residents.News of the government’s plan came only hours after the European Commission said that under EU law all of the migrants should be returned to Morocco. Asked to clarify, the commission’s spokesperson on internal affairs, Markus Lammert, said that by law all irregular migrants remaining in Ceuta should be sent back, “including unaccompanied minors”.Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreThe People’s party has rejected the government plan, saying the best place for the children is with their families. “If Morocco has asked for the children to be returned and if Europe says the illegal immigrants should all be returned, whether children or not, what more does the government need?” the People’s party deputy finance spokesperson, Juan Bravo, said in a television interview.The mixed messages partly derive from the fact the latest European pact on immigration has not yet been incorporated into Spanish law and therefore Spain’s own legislation on the treatment of unaccompanied minors remains in force.According to Spain’s ministry of inclusion and migration, as of lastMarch21,104 people aged 16-23 were guardians of the state, of whom about 3,500 were under 17. Approximately 50% were from Morocco. Girls made up about 8% of the total.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeEuropean UnionMoroccoMigrationAfricaRefugeesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Adviser to far-right Latin American leaders arrested for allegedly plotting to kill girlfriend | Bolivia | The Guardian
description: Fernando Cerimedo, 42, arrested on suspicion of ordering shooting of Bolivian lawyer Nadia Beller
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Fernando Cerimedo, 42, arrested on suspicion of ordering shooting of Bolivian lawyer Nadia Beller
Content: Fernando Cerimedo in Buenos Aires in 2024. His most recent role was adviser to the Bolivian president, Rodrigo Paz Pereira.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersView image in fullscreenFernando Cerimedo in Buenos Aires in 2024. His most recent role was adviser to the Bolivian president, Rodrigo Paz Pereira.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersBoliviaAdviser to far-right Latin American leaders arrested for allegedly plotting to kill girlfriendFernando Cerimedo, 42, arrested on suspicion of ordering shooting of Bolivian lawyer Nadia BellerTiago RogeroSouth America correspondentWed 19 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior adviser to many of Latin America’s new wave of far-right leaders has been arrested for allegedly masterminding the attempted murder of his girlfriend.The businessman and political consultant Fernando Cerimedo, 42, had been working as an adviser to the Bolivian president, Rodrigo Paz Pereira, and was one of the main strategists behind Javier Milei’s campaign in Argentina’s 2023 presidential election.He has previously been described asMaga’s manin Latin America – a reference to Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement – and is credited with helping secure the US president’s endorsement of the rightwingNasry “Tito” Asfura, who won Honduras’s presidential election in December.On Tuesday morning, Cerimedo landed in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, in Bolivia, and was arrested before boarding another flightreportedly bound for Buenos Aires, Argentina. According to police, he was detained on suspicion of ordering a gun attack on Nadia Beller, a Bolivian lawyer wholocal media reportedhad been in a relationship with Cerimedo – who is married – since last year.View image in fullscreenCCTV footage shows the shooting of Nadia Beller by two men dressed as delivery riders in Santa Cruz de la Sierra.Photograph: Video obtained by Reuters/ReutersSurveillance footageshowedtwo men dressed as delivery riders and wearing helmets open fire on Beller on Monday night outside a hotel in Santa Cruz de la Sierra. She survived and was taken to hospital.Bellertold policeshe had been lured to the hotel after receiving anonymous messages promising to hand over evidence of alleged crimes committed by Bolivia’s leftwing former presidentEvo Morales, who is subject to two outstandingarrest warrantsand remainssheltered in a coca-growing region.Beller said she believed the attack had been a trap orchestrated by Cerimedo.The local police commander, Col David Gómez,told local mediathat investigators were working on the hypothesis that Beller and Cerimedo had been in a romantic relationship and had had “a personal dispute” in the days before the attack.Cerimedo’s lawyer, Ernesto Giraldes, said his client had not been not trying to flee toArgentinaand had travelled to Santa Cruz de la Sierra specifically to visit Beller in hospital, and denied he was behind the attack.View image in fullscreenAn evidence marker is placed next to blood stains at a hotel restaurant where Nadia Beller was shot by a man dressed as a delivery rider.Photograph: Ipa Ibanez/ReutersA presidential spokesperson, José Luis Gálvez, said Cerimedo had acted as Paz Pereira’s “personal consultant” but did not hold a government post. The Bolivian president expressed “solidarity” with Beller andposted on Xthat his administration would offer “zero interference” in the investigation.Cerimedo had a prominent role in Milei’s campaign strategy and had boasted that he had been the one to suggest the self-styled libertarian take a chainsaw to campaign rallies, but he has never held a post in the Argentinian government.In Brazil, Cerimedo was indicted by federal police over his alleged involvement in theattempted coupled by the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.In 2022, five days after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the election and Bolsonaro refused to concede andplotted waysto remain in power, Cerimedo held a live stream titled “Brazil Was Stolen”, in which he presented an anonymous dossier containing false claims about the vote.Brazil’s federal police later concluded it had been a premeditated operation coordinated with Brazilian military officers and Bolsonaro aides, who had provided Cerimedo with the report. Prosecutors, however, declined to bring charges against him, saying investigators had failed to produce evidence to show Cerimedo knew the report contained fabricated information.Explore more on these topicsBoliviaArgentinaJavier MileiThe far rightAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Activist forced out of US after criticising Trump-aligned Colombian politician | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Beto Coral held up banners in Florida warning fellow Colombians to not vote for Abelardo de la Espriella
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Beto Coral held up banners in Florida warning fellow Colombians to not vote for Abelardo de la Espriella
Content: Beto Coral said that during his 30 days in detention he was assaulted and deprived of food and water.Photograph: Courtesy of Beto CoralView image in fullscreenBeto Coral said that during his 30 days in detention he was assaulted and deprived of food and water.Photograph: Courtesy of Beto CoralColombiaActivist forced out of US after criticising Trump-aligned Colombian politicianBeto Coral held up banners in Florida warning fellow Colombians to not vote for Abelardo de la EspriellaTiago RogeroSouth America correspondentWed 19 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the week before Colombia’s presidential election, Beto Coral, a well-known activist living in the United States, travelled to Florida to persuade fellow Colombians not to vote for the far-right candidate Abelardo de la Espriella.Coral held banners outside polling stations in Miami warning that the millionaire lawyer, whose candidacy wasendorsedby Donald Trump, would “help deport all of you”.The following morning the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, issued a memo to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) alleging that the activist had used his presence in the country “to conduct political activity” against a Colombian presidential candidate, and that DHS could take steps to “facilitate his departure”.Hours later, Coral was arrested.He said that, over the following 30 days in DHS detention, he was assaulted, deprived of food and water, and held in solitary confinement before securing his voluntary departure back to Colombia in mid-July, after more than 10 years living in the US.Although other immigrants have previously been detained in the US over their political activism – most notably the Palestinian studentMahmoud Khalilfor protesting against the war in Gaza – Coral’s case isbeing seenas the first involving remarks about a foreign election.“They detained me simply because I protested against a Trump-backed candidate,” said the 40-year-old activist, whose full name is Franklin Humberto Coral Garrido.View image in fullscreenAbelardo de la Espriella won June’s Colombian presidential election.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesCoral, who has no criminal record, alleges that his detention resulted from a request by De la Espriella, who went on towin the electionand was sworn in earlier this month to replace the leftwing president Gustavo Petro, with whom Trump hadrepeatedly clashed.In early June the US deputy secretary of state, Christopher Landau,wroteon social media about Colombia’s election that those “tempted to undermine or manipulate the democratic process” were putting their visas at risk. “That’s why they call meEl Quitavisas(the visa taker)”, he added.De la Espriellareplied: “I have the list, dear deputy secretary.”On the morning of 16 June, the same day Rubio issued the memo, De la Espriellaposted: “There will be good news for Colombia and for patriotic Colombians abroad,” alongside an AI-generated image of “El Quitavisas” projected into the sky. That afternoon, Coral was arrested.“De la Espriella knew that I was going to be arrested and announced it on X,” said Coral.The US state department and De la Espriella did not respond to requests for comment.Colombia’s new president already knew the activist from hisyears as a lawyer. De la Espriella represented the former president Álvaro Uribe Vélez in a defamation lawsuit filed in Florida against Coral after the activist accused him of leading paramilitary groups. Coral lost the case and was ordered to issue a public apology.Last May, Coral filed a complaint with the FBI alleging that De la Espriella had secretly recorded a telephone conversation between them and attempted to blackmail him with it. Inhis memo, Rubio cited the activist’s alleged “use of US courts to target a Colombian presidential candidate” as one of the political activities he claimed Coral had carried out “on behalf of the Petro government”.Coral entered the US on a tourist visa in December 2015 and applied for political asylum in March 2016, saying he had received death threats in Colombia afterinvestigatingthe death of his father, Humberto Coral Caballero. A police captain who took part in the US-backed operation that brought down the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar in 1993, Caballero wasmurderedmonths later.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I had been waiting for a decision on my asylum application since 2016, but I always had legal status and a work permit,” said Coral, who, besides his work as an activist andYouTuber, held “the kinds of jobs immigrants usually have in the US: I drove for Uber, worked in construction, was a cook, a waiter, a baker”.On the day of his arrest, he was returning from the supermarket with his 12-year-old son.He was later transferred six times between detention facilities across four states. “Those journeys were extremely long, and the agents wouldn’t give me water or food,” said Coral, who estimates that he spent “24 of the 30 days” in solitary confinement. “ICE officers shoved me, threw me against the wall and kicked me in the legs,” he added.A DHS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the mistreatment Coral said he suffered, instead sending a statement describing him as “an illegal alien” who “in violation of our nation’s laws, overstayed his visa for 10 years”.Nine Democratic members of Congress sent Rubio aletteron 23 June demanding Coral’s immediate release, arguing that the US government had violated his human rights, including his right to free speech. He was released only after his lawyer, Elizabeth Shaw, secured an agreement allowing him to leave the country voluntarily.In her filing, Shaw argued that Coral had been detained despite facing no immigration charges. She sought his release before De la Espriella’s inauguration, arguing that the incoming government posed “an open, real, and substantial threat” to his life.After briefly returning to Colombia – where he warned Petro that “he could be the next” to be arrested by the US – Coral has since left the country.He said he does not know where he will live next, but even though in theory he could still try to return to the US, as he was not deported, it will not be there – because it is “the worst place in the world for any immigrant”.“I find it paradoxical that Rubio is a Latino, theson of immigrantswho came from Cuba in search of a better future for him, and now he persecutes, mistreats, detains and deports an immigrant who entered the country legally,” he said.Explore more on these topicsColombiaAmericasProtestProtest (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Trump pauses Canada tariffs threat, and hints at revival of Keystone XL pipeline | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: US president delays 50% tariffs by three days, and says contentious oil project ‘may be awoken from the grave’
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: US president delays 50% tariffs by three days, and says contentious oil project ‘may be awoken from the grave’
Content: Mark Carney and Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 7 October 2025. Trump has paused tariffs on Canada for three days.Photograph: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenMark Carney and Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 7 October 2025. Trump has paused tariffs on Canada for three days.Photograph: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/APTrump tariffsTrump pauses Canada tariffs threat, and hints at revival of Keystone XL pipelineUS president delays 50% tariffs by three days, and says contentious oil project ‘may be awoken from the grave’Uwa Ede-OsifoTue 18 Aug 2026 23.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 23.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada has temporarily avoided a bruising 50% US tariff, reaching a Tuesday-evening agreement with Trump administration officials hours before a hike that would have affected $20bn worth of goods was set to take effect.Donald Trump posted late on Tuesday on social media that he had paused the tariffs for three days “based on the fact that Canada and the USA, subject to the finalization of documents, have a DEAL!”After Trump’s announcement, the Canadian prime minister,Mark Carney, said “substantial progress” had been made towards a trade deal but more work was needed.“While we continue this work, Canada remains focused on building a stronger, more independent and more competitive economy at home,” Carney said.The duties would have affected a range of Canadian exports including wine and hockey sticks.Trump orders new 15% tariff on key material for solar panels and microchipsRead moreIn the same social media post, Trump said the controversial Keystone XL pipeline project “may be awoken from the grave” without giving further details or suggesting whether it was linked to the tariffs deal.Keystone XL, which was proposed in 2008 to bring oil from Canada’s western tar sands to US refiners, was halted in 2021 by owner TC Energy afterJoe Biden revokeda key permit needed for a US stretch of the 1,200-mile (1,930km) project. It became a flashpoint in US-Canada relations, amid opposition from US landowners, Native American tribes and environmentalists.North American oil pipelines, including Dakota Access and Enbridge Line 3, have faced steady opposition from environmental groups, amid concerns about spills.Tuesday’s 11th-hour deal comes amid a contentious past year for the two countries, with the longstanding alliance strained by tit-for-tat tariffs and online broadsides in which Trump has mused about turning Canada into a US state.In February 2025, the White House hit Canada with a 25% tariff,citingwhat it regarded as inadequate progress in curbing cross-border illegal immigration and drug trafficking.In retaliation, Canada announced a reciprocal levy, calling the US’s actions “unwarranted and unreasonable”. The country’s leadership also countered the Trump administration’s claims, maintaining that it had launched a robust border protection plan and thatlessthan 1% of fentanyl and illegal crossings came from Canada.Tensions flared again in July 2026 when the White House announced the 50% tariffs, saying that it sought to hold Canada accountable for discrimination against US-produced cars, alcohol and dairy products.In recent days, top officials from the two countries were engaged in “intense and delicate” talks, Carney told reporters on Monday.Historically, Canada and the US have been strong trading partners. In 2024, trade between the countries was estimated to be roughly $909bn, according to theofficeof the US trade representative.The latest proposed US levy has stoked concern about financial devastation and untenable export costs among Canadian business owners, the CBC reported.Certain goods formerly protected from import taxes under the Trump-negotiated United States-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) deal were not shielded from the latest round of tariffs.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpTariffsUS politicsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kim Jong-un’s sister casts doubt on Trump’s claims of secret US-North Korea talks | North Korea | The Guardian
description: President says he plans to meet dictator this year but Kim Yo-jong says US remains enemy of Pyongyang
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: President says he plans to meet dictator this year but Kim Yo-jong says US remains enemy of Pyongyang
Content: Donald Trump (right) and Kim Jong-un in 2018. On Wednesday the US leader declined to say whether or not the two were in direct contact.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump (right) and Kim Jong-un in 2018. On Wednesday the US leader declined to say whether or not the two were in direct contact.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APNorth KoreaKim Jong-un’s sister casts doubt on Trump’s claims of secret US-North Korea talksPresident says he plans to meet dictator this year but Kim Yo-jong says Washington remains Pyongyang’s enemyAndrew Rothin WashingtonWed 19 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said he is planning to meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un later this year, though the reclusive leader’s younger sister cast doubt on their communications and dampened hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough between them.Trump, who also claimed North Korea had 57 nuclear weapons, had suggested he and Kim were holding secret negotiations on Tuesday after announcing the US woulddowngrade its participation in military exercisesheld by South Korea, a US ally. Asked whether Kim had responded to his request for a conversation, Trump said: “Yeah, he has.”The Wall Street Journalreportedon Tuesday that Trump was pushing aides to set up an in-person meeting with Kim, potentially during a trip to Asia in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.In cutting joint drills, Trump has given South Korea’s president what he wants. So why is Seoul so uneasy?Read moreBut on Wednesday Kim Yo-jong, thepowerful sister of North Korea’s supreme leader, said she knew “absolutely nothing” about the supposed communications, and that while Trump and Kim had an excellent relationship, the US remained an enemy of Pyongyang.“The United States’ hostile policy toward the DPRK has not changed, and the United States and its followers are vigorously carrying out hostile military activities against the DPRK even at this very moment,” she said in a statement carried by North Korean state media.Journalists questioned Trump further about his talks with Kim in front of Marine One on Wednesday. He declined to say whether or not he was in direct contact, but asked whether he was planning to meet Kim later this year, he said: “Yeah, I will be.”“I knowKim Jong-unvery well and he’s gonna be fine,” Trump said. “As long as we have a smart president, he’s gonna be fine. If we have a dumb president, then he’s probably not going to be so fine.”Trump also made the unusual disclosure that North Korea had 57 “very powerful nuclear weapons”, revealing exact intelligence that may not ordinarily be made public. He added that Iran should not be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon.In her statement, Kim’s sister lauded the relationship between him and Trump, saying he had “personally good memories and feelings” toward the US president.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe cast doubt on whether her brother had secretly been in communication with Trump. “Perhaps it is the only matter I do not know about in relation to our supreme leadership’s foreign policy,” she said.She denied claims by Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that North Korea planned to deploy tens of thousands of troops to fight for Russia.Explore more on these topicsNorth KoreaKim Jong-unSouth KoreaDonald TrumpUS foreign policyAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Is the US actually too chicken to take on China for trade? | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: A weak yuan guarantees Beijing massive trade surplus even as the White House tries tamp down on Chinese imports
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: A weak yuan guarantees Beijing massive trade surplus even as the White House tries tamp down on Chinese imports
Content: Container ships berthed at Yantian port on 18 August 2026 in Shenzhen, China.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenContainer ships berthed at Yantian port on 18 August 2026 in Shenzhen, China.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesTrump administrationAnalysisIs the US actually too chicken to take on China for trade?Eduardo PorterA weak yuan guarantees Beijing massive trade surplus even as the White House tries tamp down on Chinese importsWed 19 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTShareSinceChinaoffered a truce in the trade war last October following its threat to deprive the United States of rare-earth magnets, theTrump administrationhas been happy to stop escalating. After all, imports from China have been falling, down by 40% in the year to June, compared with the same period in 2024. Best to declare victory and call it a day.But the US hasn’t won this battle – and there’s strong evidence to show it’s too chicken to really try.Last week the White House was forced to accept that not buying Chinese stuff from China is not equivalent to not buying Chinese stuff. While China’s share of US imports has fallen pretty dramatically, its share of the total value added in US importshas not.Trade adviser Peter Navarro wasin a huffon Thursday, furious about Chinese motors bolted on to recliners imported from Vietnam. He cited an analysis by the commerce department that concluded $67bn of goods from China were transhipped through Mexico, India and Vietnam in 2025.Donald Trump doesn’t just love billionaires, he loves multimillionaires tooRead moreThe White House released a report,The Great Transhipment Scam, which lamented that “when power supplies, control panels, aluminum sheet, valves, plastics, or furniture components are rerouted from China through Mexico, Vietnam, Malaysia, Poland, or the UAE, they destroy or reduce jobs in Milwaukee, Cleveland, Toledo, Hickory, Phoenix, Youngstown, and dozens of other American manufacturing communities”.It unveiled a new tool to engage in a globe-spanning game of Whac-A-Mole: an AI-powered border “detective” that “never sleeps, never tires, and never forgets” to scan every bill of lading and shipping manifest, ID rerouted stuff, and punish the perpetrators.It goes without saying that the new detective will not restore factory jobs to Toledo, Hickory or Phoenix. Despite strenuous efforts to boost manufacturing employment over two and a half administrations spanning 10 years, it remains roughlyin the same placeas when Trump first came into office.Cracking down on rerouted imports won’t dent the US import bill either. Despite Trump’s many tariffs, it is running higher than in 2024. And it looks unlikely to do much harm to China, whose exports havekept growingdespite US efforts to squeeze them out.But what is most perplexing about the White House’s resort to AI sleuthing, though, is that the US possesses a more straightforward tool to achieve its aims, one which directly addresses a critical driver of China’s massive exports, which are not only swamping the US but also threatening industrial development around the world: the undervalued Chinese yuan. Dealing with its undervaluation can do much to rein in China’s overwhelming exports.Some economists will complain about this take. There are fundamental reasons for China’s huge trade surplus, mainly its depressed household consumption, which means it needs foreign consumers to support economic growth. There are also fundamental reasons for the US trade deficit: notably, its extraordinarily large budget deficit, which must be funded by savings from abroad (read China).double quotation markIt’s hard to overstate how Chinese exports weigh on the economies of the rest of the worldThe yuan’s weakness, like the dollar’s comparative strength, are reflections of these dynamics. In other words, “the exchange rateis a symptom, not the disease”. If Beijing were to push up the exchange rate by fiat but did nothing else, it would slow China’s growth and reduce import prices, slow inflation (perhaps even causing deflation) and thus depress the real, after-inflation exchange rate. If, by contrast, the underlying ills were addressed, the yuan would appreciate naturally.But give us a break. The exchange rate depends on those broad economic dynamics, sure. But the call to wait for Beijing to support household spending, say by raising meager pension benefits or some such, has the taste of those old exhortations to wait for China’s multiparty democracy to flourish. On the American side of the ledger, the last time the United States seriously tried to curb its budget deficit was in the 20th century. Pressure is needed for these things to happen. And exchange rate intervention could provide it.It’s hard to overstate how Chinese exportsweigh on the economiesof the rest of the world. China’s share of global manufacturing exports has risen from 3% to 20% since 1995. It accounts for over half the global exports ofhundreds of manufacturing products. Its current account surplus – equal toperhaps 5%of its GDP – is a huge drawdown on worldwide demand.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs Gene Frieda from the London School of Economicspoints out: “The barrier to progress is not policy design; it is policy preference.” This preference is to ensure the world’s dependence on China’s products, which it achieves viamassive interventionto depress the value of the yuan.And there is evidence for the power of exchange rates. The Plaza accord that weakened the dollar in the 1980s helped reduce the US trade deficit with Japan. China’sgrowing external surpluscontracted sharply asthe yuan appreciatedfollowing the global financial crisis. By contrast, the slide in China’s currency has underpinned a rising external surplus since 2023.As Brad Setser of the Council on Foreign Relations points out, history suggests currency adjustment would drive the economic realignment needed toreduce China’s overwhelming exports.Revaluing the yuan would probably induce other policy changes to plug the world’s dramatic trade imbalances. Slowing export growth would slow theChinese economy, tempting Beijing to stimulate domestic consumption to compensate. A smaller Chinese trade surplus would shrink the pool of foreign funding for the US budget deficit, perhaps even encouraging fiscal restraint in Washington.Ideally, the US would coordinate efforts to revalue the yuan with countries in Europe and elsewhere that have also been hammered by Chinese exports. Pressure on Beijing would ideally be part of a plan to revalue other depressed east Asian currencies, like the Korean won, the Taiwanese dollar and the Japanese yen, to reduce competitive pressure on China.The US has tools to pressure Beijing – notably, authority under section 301 of the Trade Act to impose tariffs on countries that purposely undervalue their currency. While Europe doesn’t have section 301, it could also impose tariffs to stop a surge of Chinese imports, as sanctioned by theWorld Trade Organization, and then link the protection to China’s exchange rate management.Getting Beijing to change its exchange rate policy won’t be a walk in the park. Xi Jinping won’t slap his forehead and say, “Why didn’t I think of this earlier?” Washington must be smart about deploying section 301 in this way – not its forte – and offer a believable path to de-escalation as Beijing allows the yuan to rise. The US must try not to alienate allies – sigh – and bring them onboard to grant both force and legitimacy to the effort.Still, this approach is more promising than sitting back to wait for Xi’s worldview to change, or to ding weaker countries like Mexico and Vietnam for transshipping Chinese stuff because, after the rare-earth magnet fracas last year, Washington has become too chickenshit to ding China directly.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationChinese economyUS economyYuanWorld Trade OrganizationEconomicsTrump tariffsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Jaecoo owner Chery takes ‘next step’ in UK push with R&D centre | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Owner of firm behind ‘Temu Range Rover’ will open facility in Bedfordshire in autumn
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Owner of firm behind ‘Temu Range Rover’ will open facility in Bedfordshire in autumn
Content: Chery’s Jaecoo 7 became the top-selling model in the UK in March.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenChery’s Jaecoo 7 became the top-selling model in the UK in March.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersAutomotive industryJaecoo owner Chery takes ‘next step’ in UK push with R&D centreOwner of firm behind ‘Temu Range Rover’ will open facility in Bedfordshire in autumnAlex DanielWed 19 Aug 2026 11.12 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Chinese carmaker behind theirreverently nicknamed “Temu Range Rover”is plotting further UK expansion with a major research and development centre in England.Chery, which makes the Jaecoo and Omoda car brands, said the launch of a new R&D site was “the next step in our long-term plan” for Britain as it also moves towards manufacturing its cars in the UK.Chery’s sales are growing at breakneck pace in Britain. In July, the Chery, Omoda and Jaecoo brands accounted for nearly 8% of UK market share, up from 3% last year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.The China-built Jaecoo 7, known as the “Temu Range Rover” for its low price and techy add-ons, became thetop-selling model in the UK in March, but Chery currently has to bring it in from abroad.The company is part-owned by the Chinese state andhas already signed a deal with Nissanto build its cars at its Sunderland plant, in a move that would begin mass-market Chinese car production in Britain for the first time from 2027.View image in fullscreenChery’s new R&D facility at Millbrook, Bedfordshire, will give it access to test tracks to fine-tune its cars for UK roads.Photograph: Rick Noel/Sprite PhotographyThe new R&D facility would open in late autumn, Chery said on Wednesday. Gary Lan, the chief executive of its UK business, said: “We waited over 20 years for the right time to enter this market, and our ambition has always gone much further than simply bringing vehicles here.”An existing vehicle testing centre inBedfordshirethat is used by engineering and motorsport companies – as well as the Ministry of Defence – will be the site of Chery’s new R&D facility.The centre, called UTAC Millbrook, will give Chery access to more than 70km (43 miles) of purpose-built test tracks for it to fine-tune its cars for UK roads. Further down the line it will also use the site to work on self-driving cars and artificial intelligence.Chinese manufacturers’ arrival as a major force in the car industry hasput enormous pressure on traditional European rivals. Chinese companies have been able to undercut European companies in building electrified cars because of state subsidies, lower labour costs and the country’s dominance in the battery industry.Chery alsolaunched its Lepas brand– its fourth in the UK – last February, aimed at younger families in the European market.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLepas, Chery, Jaecoo and Omoda models on the Millbrook ‘bowl’ test track.Photograph: Rick Noel/Sprite PhotographyKirsty Andrew, the vice-president of UTAC UK, said the new R&D centre was “a significant commitment to engineering and vehicle development in the UK”.She added: “Creating a stand-alone engineering centre here means Chery Automobile can develop and validate vehicles against the particular demands of UK roads and UK drivers, with direct access to our engineering expertise and testing environments throughout that process.”Chery said it eventually planned to recruit local talent and create engineering jobs in the area – but did not say how much it would invest in the site or how many jobs would be created.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryChinaManufacturing sectorAsia PacificEuropeEnglandBedfordshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shares in humanoid robot firm Unitree surge 600% on Chinese stock market debut | Robots | The Guardian
description: Company’s robots have gained global fame via videos of them performing martial arts and as dancers for pop stars
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Company’s robots have gained global fame via videos of them performing martial arts and as dancers for pop stars
Content: A Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Analysts project sales of humanoid robots could rise from $2bn in 2025 to $300bn in 2035.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Analysts project sales of humanoid robots could rise from $2bn in 2025 to $300bn in 2035.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesRobotsShares in humanoid robot firm Unitree surge 600% on Chinese stock market debutCompany’s robots have gained global fame via videos of them performing martial arts and as dancers for pop starsLauren AlmeidaWed 19 Aug 2026 03.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnitree, the world’s biggest humanoid robot maker, has made a spectacular entry on to China’s stock market, with its shares surging by more than 600%.The Chinese company’s robots have gained global fame viaviral videos of them performing martial arts, running at Olympic speeds and serving as backup dancers for pop stars.View image in fullscreenTwo Unitree robots in a fighting demonstration at the World Robot Conference in Beijing on Wednesday.Photograph: Adek Berry/AFP/Getty ImagesShares in the business, officially known as Yushu Technology Co, rose to as high as 1,100 yuan (£120.39) on Wednesday, up from an IPO price of just 150.8 yuan. Its gains were later pared back to a rise of nearly 500%.Investors are searching for winners in robotics development, which has emerged as one of thekey battlegrounds in the AI race.Unitree, which was founded in 2016, shipped more than 5,500 humanoid robots last year.The market for human-like robots is expected to grow rapidly, with analysts projecting that sales could rise from around $2bn (£1.5bn) in 2025 to $300bn by 2035.There was exceptional demand from Chinese retail investors in Unitree’s IPO, with the tranche of shares dedicated to non-professional stockpickers oversubscribed by thousands.Unitree is one of the few listed humanoid robot makers in the world. Its biggest competitor, AgiBot, is private and its smaller rival UBTech is listed in Hong Kong.However, at least half a dozen other Chinese humanoid robotic businesses are preparing to go public, including Deep Robotics and Leju Robotics.Wang Xingxing, who founded Unitree in 2016 and remains its chief executive, owns about a fifth of the business. The spike in its share price means his personal wealth is now worth more than $12bn on paper, according to Reuters.Unitree’s market debut also coincided with the opening of the World Robot Conference in Bejiing on Wednesday, where hundreds of companies, mostly Chinese, will launch new products and demonstrate their technical developments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast month, the US Federal Communications Commissionbanned imports of future modelsof foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots based on national security concerns.3:48Why the US government is banning Chinese robots – video explainerThis summer the Pentagon also added Unitree to a list of Chinese military companies, describing it as a “contributor to the Chinese defence industrial base”. Unitree has previously said its robots are for civilian use.The business is backed by several big Chinese technology companies, including Tencent and Alibaba.Explore more on these topicsRobotsIPOsStock marketsTechnology sectorChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Penny Wong condemns ‘insulting’ decision to clear IDF over Gaza strikes that killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom | Australian foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Foreign affairs minister says Australia is ‘outraged’ after Israeli government decided not to pursue criminal proceedings over 2024 triple drone strike on humanitarian convoy
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Foreign affairs minister says Australia is ‘outraged’ after Israeli government decided not to pursue criminal proceedings over 2024 triple drone strike on humanitarian convoy
Content: Lalzawmi ‘Zomi’ Frankcom was one of seven World Central Kitchen aid workers who were killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza in April 2024.Photograph: World Central Kitchen/WCK.org/PAView image in fullscreenLalzawmi ‘Zomi’ Frankcom was one of seven World Central Kitchen aid workers who were killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza in April 2024.Photograph: World Central Kitchen/WCK.org/PAAustralian foreign policyPenny Wong condemns ‘insulting’ decision to clear IDF over Gaza strikes that killed Australian aid worker Zomi FrankcomForeign affairs minister says Australia is ‘outraged’ after Israeli government decided not to pursue criminal proceedings over 2024 triple drone strike on humanitarian convoyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyandJosh ButlerWed 19 Aug 2026 18.39 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 17.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s foreign affairs minister has expressed “outrage” and will call in the Israeli ambassador over theIsraelDefense Forces decision overnight not to open a criminal investigation into Gaza strikes that killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.In a statement released on Thursday,Penny Wongcalled the timing of the decision, on World Humanitarian Day, “especially insulting”.Wong said she would call in Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, for formal talks and directed Australia’s ambassador to Israel, Neil Hawkins, “to convey our views directly to Israel as the Australian government considers next steps”.The April 2024 strike hit a convoy of World Central Kitchen vehicles, killing seven humanitarian workers from the US-based aid group, which has distributed food inGazathroughout the war.Israel admits its soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killedRead moreThe aid group said at the time it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars. The vehicles, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air, were left incinerated and mangled, indicating a series of targeted strikes.TheIDF said on Wednesdayit had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the convoy deviated from the previously coordinated route. It concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOne of those killed in the strike was Frankcom, anAustralian aid worker. The Australian government has previously called the deaths a “tragedy and an outrage” and pressed for full accountability and “any appropriate criminal charges”. In February the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had made it clear to Israel and its president, Isaac Herzog, that Australia expected transparency about Israel’s then-ongoing investigation into the incident.1:09Australian aid worker killed by Israeli airstrike in Gaza – video“Australia is outraged the Israeli Government has decided not to pursue criminal proceedings against those responsible for killing Zomi Frankcom and her World Central Kitchen colleagues,” Wong said in her Thursday morning statement.“The Australian government learned of Israel’s decision late last night, moments before it was announced, on World Humanitarian Day – which is especially insulting to Zomi’s loved ones, humanitarians and all Australians.“Zomi represented the best of Australia. Her courage deserves to be celebrated. Her family deserves justice.”Wong said the move “falls far short of the accountability we expect”.“This is despite Israel Defense Forces admissions that the IDF strikes on Zomi and her colleagues’ vehicles were the result of serious failures to follow IDF procedures, mistaken identification and errors in decision-making.”This was confirmed byspecial adviser air chief marshal Mark Binskin’s report, Wong said.“Democracies seek and accept higher standards. The Australian Government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues.”World Central Kitchen said it strongly disagreed with Israeli officials’ account of the airstrikes and their decision not to pursue a criminal investigation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.“At the time of the lethal attacks,the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmedand posing a threat to nobody. It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”Human rights expert Chris Sidoti said the federal government should send Newman, the Israeli ambassador, home.Sidoti, a former human rights commissioner, was a member of the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel.Mass slaughter in Gaza stands apart from other genocides, Chris Sidoti says: ‘People cannot escape’Read more“The minister, when she sees the ambassador, should tell him that he’s going home. I don’t support breaking diplomatic relations with Israel. I don’t support the closing of embassies, but this bloke is clearly an unacceptable representative.”The Greens leader, Larissa Waters, demanded Israel’s government be hit with new sanctions.“Now, strong words are not enough,” she told ABC radio on Thursday.“The Australian government sending some strongly worded statements has meant nothing. Now it is time that the Australian government puts on sanctions against the state of Israel and stops sending weapons parts to this genocide.”In April this year, Wongpaid tribute to Frankcomon the second anniversary of her death, saying “people like Zomi are rare and their selflessness should not only be celebrated but protected”.Explore more on these topicsAustralian foreign policyIsrael-Gaza warPenny WongIsraelGazaAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Roblox commits to privacy overhaul after eSafety discovers adults can contact children via gaming platform | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Regulator says verifiable safety measures are ‘critical’ to the online service’s viability
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Regulator says verifiable safety measures are ‘critical’ to the online service’s viability
Content: Australia’s eSafety commissioner says the pressure on Roblox is about ensuring the gaming platform is a safe place for children.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s eSafety commissioner says the pressure on Roblox is about ensuring the gaming platform is a safe place for children.Photograph: Getty ImagesAustralia newsRoblox commits to privacy overhaul after eSafety discovers adults can contact children via gaming platformRegulator says verifiable safety measures are ‘critical’ to the online service’s viabilityFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterWed 19 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoblox has committed to making changes to its online gaming platform after Australia’s eSafety commissioner discovered adults were still able to see child accounts and send connection requests without parental consent.The company has provided a legal agreement to the online safety regulator after testing earlier this year also revealed children and adults could view and respond to one another’s posts on forums outside game environments without parental consent.Additionally, the regulator found children’s connections and profiles – including account names and interests – were visible to anyone on Roblox.In December last year,Roblox rolled out changesto its service to limit the ability for children to speak to adults on the platform after reports of children being groomed bothfor child abuseand extremism, as well as being exposed toinappropriate or violent content.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUnder the changes, accounts for users under 16 were private by default and included tools to prevent adult users from contacting under-16s without parental consent.Direct chat was also switched off by default until the user had gone through age estimation.Parental controls could disable chat for 13- to 15-year-old users, and voice chat was not allowed for the same age group – bringing up the restriction applied to users aged 12 and under.What is Roblox and should parents be worried about whether it’s safe for children?Read moreThe eSafety commissioner had raised concerns Roblox may not be compliant with codes and standards under the Online Safety Act, alleging the platform failed to have sufficient measures in place to prevent contact between adults and children.A Roblox spokesperson said there had been “constructive dialogue with eSafety” and the company had delivered on its safety commitments to eSafety in the past year while continuing to work towards keeping children safe online.In its announcement on Thursday, eSafety said Roblox had committed to making changes to prevent adults from contacting unknown children without parental consent, and strengthening account settings of children so they are private by default.Roblox also committed to engaging a third-party auditor to assess its safety measures, including a check of its age-estimation technology.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe company will have three months to make the changes. The eSafety commissioner has warned Roblox the regulator may apply to the federal court for an order to comply if the undertaking is breached.About 1.7 million Australian children use Roblox, the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, said in a statement, and the pressure on the company was about ensuring Roblox is a safe place.“We have been engaging with Roblox for some time at senior levels about our concerns and the company has responded, making a number of improvements to its service,” she said.“Their executives clearly understand that verifiable safety measures are critical to their long-term viability and success.”The third-party auditing would ensure Roblox cannot “mark their own homework”, Inman Grant said.Roblox was excluded from Australia’s under-16s social media ban last year, as platforms that have the dominant purpose of gaming are not covered. Inman Grant, however, did not rule out including the platform if it was later determined its social features were its dominant purpose.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsRobloxSocial mediaSocial media banDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy sacks senior aide amid Ukraine corruption crisis | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Presidential deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra dismissed day after former defence minister called for wartime election
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Presidential deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra dismissed day after former defence minister called for wartime election
Content: No official reason was given for the sacking of Iryna Mudra, a presidential deputy chief of staff.Photograph: Raj Valley/AlamyView image in fullscreenNo official reason was given for the sacking of Iryna Mudra, a presidential deputy chief of staff.Photograph: Raj Valley/AlamyUkraineVolodymyr Zelenskyy sacks senior aide amid Ukraine corruption crisisPresidential deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra dismissed day after former defence minister called for wartime electionDan Sabbaghin KyivWed 19 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has fired a senior aide amid a fresh corruption investigation – one day after a former defence minister warned the country was facing “a crisis of governance” andneeded to hold a wartime presidential election.Iryna Mudra, a presidential deputy chief of staff, was dismissed by decree after multiple reports in Ukrainian media that her house was being searched by officials investigating an alleged money-laundering scheme.Sacking turns former Zelenskyy loyalist into potent political opponentRead moreNo official reason was given for Mudra’s sacking as Zelenskyy sought to carry on as normal, despite Mykhailo Fedorov’s surprise call for an early presidential election in a video address released late on Tuesday.The president did not directly address the ousted minister’s accusations or his election demand in his initial public statements, though he did thank Ukraine’s parliament for voting to confirm Fedorov’s replacement, Yevhen Khmara, in the post.At the heart of Fedorov’s argument were accusations that corruption remained widespread under Zelenskyy and that the president had failed to get a grip. “Corruption is only a symptom. The main problem runs much deeper. We have a systemic crisis of governance,” Fedorov had said.View image in fullscreenMykhailo Fedorov has become the first major public figure to call for an election, effectively posing a direct challenge to the sitting president.Photograph: Efrem Lukatsky/APThe removal of Fedorov from his post in July triggered the mostsignificant street protests in Ukrainesince the war began.Fedorov is now considering visiting the US, possibly as soon as next week, in an apparent effort to win over American support. In the past, the US president, Donald Trump, has called for Ukraine to hold elections, though his comments were made at a time when his relationship with Zelenskyy was strained.Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Fedorov became the first major public figure to call for a presidential poll, effectively posing a direct challenge to the sitting president.“Can Russia effectively be given the right to dictate when Ukrainians can choose their government again? I am convinced that the answer is no,” Fedorov said in a nine-minute video address released on social media late on Tuesday.Zelenskyy’s term notionally expired in spring 2024, but an election during wartime is prohibited by the constitution, and had anyway been considered by most Ukrainians to be impractical and potentially divisive while Russia continues to attack on a daily basis.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy has not directly addressed Mykhailo Fedorov’s accusations of widespread corruption.Photograph: Oleksandr Magula/Suspilne Ukraine/JSC “UA:PBC”/Global Images Ukraine/Getty ImagesThe Nabu anti-corruption agency said it was conducting a special operation to expose what it said was a criminal conspiracy that involved “the participation of high-ranking officials from the office of the president” and several others.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt released a video saying those involved included a deputy head of the president’s office, a serving MP and a former MP, as well as the CEO and supervisory board head at a state-owned bank, though none were named.Nabu added that the group was accused of laundering 150m hryvinas (£2.5m) through the state-owned bank in order to post bail in June for the former energy minister Herman Haluschenko, himself facing anti-corruption charges.Haluschenko is a defendant inthe high-profile Midas corruption case, alongside the businessman Timur Mindich, who has fled the country. Mindich is a former associate of the president and former co-owner of the TV production company Kvartal 95, co-founded by Zelenskyy in the years before he went into politics.Mindich is accused of orchestrating a large-scale corruption schemethat was uncovered last Novemberin which kickbacks were demanded from companies seeking to supply the country’s state-owned nuclear power generator Energoatom.The scandal damaged Zelenskyy’s credibility. A fortnight later, his then chief aide,Andriy Yermak, resignedafter anti-corruption investigators searched his home. He was thenarrested in Mayon suspicion of money laundering. Yermak’s lawyer has dismissed the allegations as “baseless”. Mindich, who fled to Israel, also denies wrongdoing.Later on Wednesday, Zelenskyy presented 25 certificates giving housing to decorated veterans and their families. The president said Ukraine was a country that honoured its heroes and emphasised it was important to be thankful to its bravest troops.“Gratitude is what should accompany respect. It must be an integral part of a normal state, a normal society and normal people,” the president said. It was perhaps the closest he had come all day to making a comment of any kind on the crisis.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sacking turns former Zelenskyy loyalist into potent political opponent | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mykhailo Fedorov’s blistering critique comes at a time of growing pressure for democratic renewal in Ukraine
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Mykhailo Fedorov’s blistering critique comes at a time of growing pressure for democratic renewal in Ukraine
Content: Mykhailo Fedorov released a video on Tuesday in which he called for wartime elections.Photograph: Mykhailo Fedorov/ReutersView image in fullscreenMykhailo Fedorov released a video on Tuesday in which he called for wartime elections.Photograph: Mykhailo Fedorov/ReutersUkraineAnalysisSacking turns former Zelenskyy loyalist into potent political opponentLuke HardingMykhailo Fedorov’s blistering critique comes at a time of growing pressure for democratic renewal in UkraineWed 19 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareFor more than a month, demonstrators have gathered in Ivan Franko Square outside Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office. Theprotesters have been chanting a name– not that of Ukraine’s embattled president but that of the man he recentlysacked as defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov. On Sunday evening, 2,000 people marched along Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s main boulevard, waving cardboard banners in support of their ousted hero.Zelenskyy has refused to reinstate Fedorov, who during his six months in the job was widely seen as an effective and reforming figure. On Wednesday, Ukraine’s parliament, the Rada,voted to approve a successoras defence minister, Yevhen Khmara. The move shows that Fedorov has been shut out from government permanently, and confirms his transition from trusted insider and Zelenskyy loyalist to a potent political opponent.On Tuesday, Fedorov released on YouTube abombshell nine-minute video. In it, the 35-year-oldcalled for wartime electionsand reminded Zelenskyy, his former boss, that power ultimately resided with the people.“Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia,” Fedorov said. “We must find a legal, safe and ‌realistic mechanism which will allowUkraineto renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of ​a long war.”Fedorov offered a blistering critique of Zelenskyy’s administration. The country was facing a “systemic crisis of governance”,he said, in which corruption inside the defence ministry was hurting the war effort. Reforms were stymied, loyalists promoted. “The old system lives by its own rules too often. ⁠It protects itself. It is scared of change,” he said, hinting that his own attempts to root out corruption in procurement had led to his sacking.View image in fullscreenA soldier holds a sign reading ‘Fedorov only’ during a protest in Kyiv on Wednesday.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianMost civil society activists agree with this big-picture analysis. Corruption has always existed in Ukraine, in common with other countries that were once a part of the Soviet Union, including and especially Russia. During the 2010-14 presidency of Viktor Yanukovych, who was backed by the Kremlin, it reached spectacular levels. In the peaceful past, large-scale theft from the state budget left less money for schools and hospitals.As Fedorov noted, today’s schemes have “an entirely different meaning” as full-scale war rages. They represent drones not bought, “ammunition that did not reach the front” and technology that “could have been put into production but wasn’t”. The video shows a photo of Andriy Yermak, Zelenskyy’s former chief of staff, who resigned last yearamid a corruption scandalimplicating other senior figures such as Timur Mindich, Zelenskyy’s former business partner. Yermak’s lawyer has dismissed the allegations as “baseless” and Mindich, who fled to Israel, also denies wrongdoing.Orysia Lutsevych, the deputy director of the Russia and Eurasia programme and head of the Ukraine forum at Chatham House, said of Fedorov’s comments: “I think he’s right. He says the system is old-fashioned, does not run fast enough, stalls innovation and prioritises loyalty.” She said “personal and vested interests” sometimes influenced official decision making, not always in Ukraine’s interests. “This could be called corruption,” she added.At the same time, Ukrainian society – led by students, veterans, journalists and anti-corruption bodies – is politically engaged. “The street is a check on the president. It corrects,” Lutsevych said. “Parliamentarians are active too. Ukraine is a pluralistic space. There are checks and balances even under martial law.”However, she said “nervous exhaustion” and Zelenskyy’s failure to explain his actions had created a public crisis. “It’s a perfect powder box,” she observed.View image in fullscreenA banner at a march in central Kyiv on Sunday.Photograph: Serhii Okunev/AFP/Getty ImagesZelenskyy has not yet responded to Fedorov’s accusations. On Wednesday hefired his deputy chief of staff, Iryna Mudra, after the National Anti-Corruption Bureau carried out a raid on her office. The bureau said Mudra and a Rada deputy were suspected of money laundering to the tune of $3.4m. A year ago, Zelenskyy triggered protests when he tried to strip the bureau of its independence. He reversed course after criticism from activists at home and pressure from Kyiv’s European partners.Olena Tregub, a co-founder of the Independent Defence Anti-Corruption Commission, said those “from the system” frequently occupied top posts, at the expense of talented professionals. “Corruption is the symptom. It’s not the cause. The cause of the problem is bad governance,” she said. There were “shades of grey” when it came to military contracts. Outside bodies that monitored procurement were often able to stop dubious purchases, she pointed out.There is little prospect Zelenskyy will hold an election any time soon, or embrace Fedorov’s idea of voting by smartphone. Under Ukraine’s constitution, polls cannot take place during wartime. Nonetheless, pressure for some form of democratic renewal is growing.It could include consultations with government critics and a restless civil society. And when presidential elections are eventually held, Fedorov has nimbly positioned himself to challenge Zelenskyy.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Germany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverse | World news | The Guardian
description: An AfD win in ​next month’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt would shatter a decades-long political consensus and reverberate throughout the EU
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: An AfD win in ​next month’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt would shatter a decades-long political consensus and reverberate throughout the EU
Content: AfD co-leaders Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel have a lot to smile about with their party riding high in the polls.Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAfD co-leaders Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel have a lot to smile about with their party riding high in the polls.Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty ImagesThis Is EuropeWorld newsGermany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverseAn AfD win in ​next month’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt would shatter a decades-long political consensus and reverberate throughout the EUDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereJon HenleyWed 19 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn just over two weeks’ time, Saxony-Anhalt – home to historic timber-framed houses, the dramatic Harz mountains and the birthplace of Martin Luther – will hold what could prove one of the most significant state elections in Germany’s postwar history.The vote, on 6 September, could see a far-right party whose local branch is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as“confirmed rightwing extremist”appoint a state premier and govern a state alone, for the first time.That could have big consequences for both Germany andEurope. With more state elections a fortnight later in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, it could also end the consensus that, since the second world war, has kept the far right at bay in Germany.The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has led most German national polls since April last year. It is comfortably ahead in eastern Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and is even second in famously liberal Berlin.In Saxony-Anhalt, the party – which dabbles in Nazi imagery, differentiates between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and whose rhetoric and policies are often way more extreme than many other EU far-right parties – is polling at up to 42%.Under Germany’s proportional representation threshold, which excludes parties that capture less than 5% of the vote, a score in the low-to-mid 40s could quite conceivably secure AfD an absolute majority in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament.As theCentre for Strategic and International Studies points out, that would have an immediate domestic impact. Germany’s 16 states exercise constitutional authority over education, policing, public broadcasting and regional civil administration.AfD’s proposed state-level measures include revising the school history curriculum to emphasise Germany’s “achievements” over its wartime crimes, defunding anti-racism initiatives, removing pride flags and rewriting the mandates of public TV and radio.An AfD government could exploit state-level public recruitment criteria and make political appointments favouring ideologically aligned candidates, and, more broadly, create an intimidating environment where state employees prefer silence to conflict.At the federal level, winning a state government would also give the AfD seats in the Bundesrat upper house representing the states. That would not allow it to block legislation unilaterally, but it could table new policy initiatives and disrupt consensus.On the EU stage, while the party is somewhat sidelined within parliament – it heads the uber-nationalist ESN group, including France’s Reconquest and Italy’s National Future – its increased influence in Germany would weaken European unity.An increasingly fragmented German political landscape would undermine Berlin’s role as an engine of European integration, affecting decision-making in key areas such as environment policy (AfDrejects the need for climate action).In other vital areas – such as policy towards Ukraine – a more influential AfD’s hostility to further military aid for Kyiv and eagerness to normalise relations with Moscow would directly benefit Russia’s efforts to sap western unity.More broadly, an AfD victory would be a potent signal that even the EU’s biggest economy is vulnerable to the far right, boosting nativist parties in countries with crunch national elections in the next 18 months, such as France, Italy, Spain and Poland.But there’s another dimension to a possible AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt that deserves a closer look. For decades, Germany’s political parties have operated a so-called “Brandmauer”, or firewall, to prevent the normalisation of far-right extremism.A Brandmauer backfireView image in fullscreenRegional elections in Saxony-Anhalt will be a test for the ruling CDU party.Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAIn essence, the firewall shouldrule out any form of coalitionor structural cooperation with the AfD. In 2018, the centre-right CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz even codified the Brandmauer into a formal “incompatibility resolution”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe objective, of course, was to prevent support for the AfD increasing, its influence expanding, and, ultimately, the far-right party winning power. It hasn’t worked – and analysts now suggest there may be three distinct flaws with the firewall strategy.First, asThe Economist argued, by making the AfD a political pariah, the Brandmauer has in effect insulated the party from the compromises and failures of government. With no need to deliver actual results, it can promise voters whatever it likes (and it does).That, of course, has made it even more appealing. Unlike many other European far-right parties that have experienced the accountability that accompanies regional or national power, the AfD has not been obliged to moderate its language or its ideas.Second, asthe German academic Alexander Görlach observed, the firewall has “hollowed-out” the centre: to build majorities excluding the far right, the CDU has had to enter “Grand Coalitions” with its historic adversary, the centre-left SPD.Over time, this constant reliance on uncomfortable alliances and ideological compromise has blurred the distinctions between the mainstream parties, reinforcing the AfD’s line that the establishment forces are carbon-copy “cartel parties”.With the far-right party dominating polling in eastern Germany, the CDU’s rigid observance of the firewall has led it into unnatural, unstable and thus largely ineffective alliances, further frustrating voters and driving support for extremes.In 2018, four years before he became CDU leader, Merz promised to halve the AfD’s score. Since then, it has almost doubled. As elsewhere in Europe, shifting rightward, notably on immigration, has served only tovalidate the far right’s agenda.It could be, of course, that the AfD does not win an absolute majority on 6 September. But even if it does not, the CDU may be forced to ally with pretty much every other party in parliament, including the radical-left Die Linke, to keep it out.That, analysts suggest, may prove a bridge too far for some senior party figures, and could have dire, even fatal consequences for Merz’s leadership – at around 13%, his approval ratings are already among the lowest of any postwar chancellor.But the fate of Germany’s Brandmauer is worth pondering. That’s not to say it isn’t a good idea to try to isolate the far right. But if you don’t have the policies to actually beat it at the ballot box, the net result may be that the cycle of ideological compromises you are forced into merely alienates voters further – and drives them into the arms of the very far right you sought to contain.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyThe far rightnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian diver arrested in Croatia over Nord Stream pipeline bombings | Nord Stream 1 pipeline | The Guardian
description: Berlin to seek suspect’s extradition for 2022 explosions that damaged gas pipelines to Russia
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Berlin to seek suspect’s extradition for 2022 explosions that damaged gas pipelines to Russia
Content: Gas bubbles up from the damaged Nord Stream 1 pipeline after an explosion in September 2022 in the Baltic.Photograph: Swedish coast guard/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGas bubbles up from the damaged Nord Stream 1 pipeline after an explosion in September 2022 in the Baltic.Photograph: Swedish coast guard/AFP/Getty ImagesNord Stream 1 pipelineUkrainian diver arrested in Croatia over Nord Stream pipeline bombingsBerlin to seek suspect’s extradition for 2022 explosions that damaged gas pipelines to RussiaJakub KrupaWed 19 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Ukrainian man has been arrested inCroatiaas part of an investigation into the 2022 bombing of the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Germany and Russia.Undersea explosions in September 2022, just months after Russia’s full-scale invasion ofUkraine, damaged three of the four pipelines built to carry Russian fossil gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea.The man, a trained scuba diver who prosecutors allege was directly involved in the explosions, was arrested in the Croatian seaside town of Pula on Wednesday.
