Content: Live with your choices … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel WolvesView image in fullscreenLive with your choices … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel WolvesSummer games previewsGamesThe Blood of Dawnwalker – save your family while becoming what you hateHuman by day, vampire by night, Coen has difficult choices to make – beginning here in the 1300s, his adventure could span centuries in upcoming sequelsKirk McKeandWed 19 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Blood of Dawnwalker could be the start of an epic saga. Created by some of the talent behind The Witcher 3, this dark fantasy role-playing game takes place in the 14th century in the fictional land of Vale Sangora, a Carpathian valley of wetlands, mountains and forests cut off from the rest of the world and under the rule of a vicious vampire clan.The developers envisage Dawnwalker as a trilogy. And because protagonist Coen is half vampire himself, that trilogy can skip across time, culminating in the modern day.“It’s a journey through ages, continents, and cultures,” explains game director and studio CEO Konrad Tomaszkiewicz. “Interview with the Vampire was one of the references we had in mind. We want each part of the saga to stand on its own and tell a compelling, engaging, emotive story, while together shaping an epic narrative with a grander plot gradually unravelling.”It’s a fascinating idea for a series where you play as a bloodsucker, doomed to watch those around you wither and die as you persist through centuries.View image in fullscreenSword-wielding human by day … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel WolvesPlaying with the concept of time isn’t just a plan for the sequels. When the vampire clan arrives at the start of the game, they take Coen’s family, and you have 30 days and nights to rescue them. By day, you’re a normal human, fighting with a sword. By night, you can walk on walls, teleport and claw people in half.While you can explore and talk to people at your leisure, time moves forward whenever you complete a clearly marked quest. You could always attempt to save your family on day one, but you’ll be severely unprepared. You have to manage your time while growing in power, sharpening those claws for the final showdown.View image in fullscreenClawed vampire by night … The Blood of Dawnwalker.Photograph: Rebel Wolves“It is primarily about the sense that what you do in the game carries weight,” says Tomaszkiewicz. “We were looking for something that would make this feel more real and give gamers something to be mindful of. You always remember that there is someone whose fate truly depends on your actions.”Take one quest here, and another might progress over there. The fates of Vale Sangora’s citizens are interlinked, and Dawnwalker’s true depth can only be seen after multiple playthroughs. Even your blood hunger can affect the world. Leave it too long between feeds and Coen will go into a frenzy, draining the person closest to him until they’re a limp sack of skin.“In some cases, you can judge fairly quickly that a specific NPC might be important to the story,” Tomaszkiewicz says. “But in many cases, that is something you will either discover later on or not discover until you decide to play the game again from the beginning. Everything depends on your choices, and in our game, it is not only about the decisions you make, but also whether you choose to do something or not.”It’s a brave approach for a genre where people often save and reload to see how different choices play out. Dawnwalker wants you to come at it with arms open and accept what happens, rewarding players who meet it halfway by opening up new quests and stories when you accidentally – or purposefully – snuff out a life.“My dream scenario is that gamers will say the game and its story stayed with them for years,” says Tomaszkiewicz, “That it touched their hearts, and that they will keep coming back to it to see what they can do differently and how the world reacts.”The Blood of Dawnwalker comes to PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S on 3 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesPCPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid matters | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries
Content: Members of a Red Cross team carry the coffin of a suspected Ebola victim in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of a Red Cross team carry the coffin of a suspected Ebola victim in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionEbolaThe Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid mattersEditorialThe Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countriesWed 19 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareFor months health experts have warned that the scale of the Ebolaoutbreakin the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could surpass the one that swept west Africa in 2014-16. This week, the authorities in the DRCannouncedthat a grim milestone has already been passed: at least 2,325 people have died from the virus, making it the deadliest of the country’s 17 outbreaks and the fastest-growing in history.There is no effective vaccine against Bundibugyo – a rare strain of the virus that spread fatally undetected during the spring, often being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. In contrast to neighbouring Uganda, which succeeded in eliminating an outbreak, multiple factors are combining to let the disease rip through the DRC. The worst-affected region is contested by armed groups, and a context of population displacement and chronic insecurity has made monitoring and surveillance more difficult. Ebola treatment centres have beenattackedas a result of misinformation and community distrust.The impact of this dire set of circumstances has been disastrously compounded by choices made in the west and, above all, in the United States. International aid cuts have deprived the DRC of vital human and material resources with which to fight back. In 2014, as the scale of the Ebola crisis in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea became clear, Barack Obamaaddressedthe United Nations general assembly and mobilised a global response that was crucial in containing the outbreak. The US Agency for International Development (USAID)ledefforts to train local health workers, pursue contact tracing and implement an eventual vaccination programme.The contrast with the Trump administration is stark and shaming. Last year, as the de facto head of the now defunct “department of government efficiency”, Elon Musk was given licence to implement swingeing cuts that led to the eventualdismantlingof USAID. In the DRC, the direct consequence was the weakening of local health infrastructure and surveillance capacities, leaving one of the poorest countries in the world still more vulnerable. Also lost was a wealth of institutional experience and expertise gained in combating emergencies such as the one now unfolding.The US has further undermined the capacity for coordinated international action bywithdrawingfrom the World Health Organization, to which it had been one of the biggest donors. European countries, notably Britain, Germany and France, have also been viewing international aid as luxury expenditure and cutting back. Last year, Sir Keir Starmerannouncedthat from 2027 UK aid would be reduced from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3%.Against such a backdrop, the lack of diplomatic urgency over the current crisis, compared with 2014, should not perhaps come as a surprise. But that does not make it any less disappointing. The Ebola outbreak in westAfricalaid bare the risk of regional and global disruption as a result of inadequate health infrastructure. A thousand pieties were then uttered in the wake of the Covid pandemic regarding the need to invest in global health security and future preparedness.Subsequent actions by governments have belied those words, leaving the DRC exposed to an epidemic that is threatening to spiral out of control. Belatedly, the global community needs to mobilise to address the threat. More fundamentally, it needs to draw the right lessons from a case study in why international aid matters.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsEbolaOpinionDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaWorld Health OrganizationHealthUSAIDUnited NationseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Trump is full speed ahead in making money off being the US president | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: Some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more power
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: Some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more power
Content: His power is held back only by his ‘own morality’, Trump told the New York Times in January.Photograph: Samuel Corum/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHis power is held back only by his ‘own morality’, Trump told the New York Times in January.Photograph: Samuel Corum/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionDonald TrumpTrump is full speed ahead in making money off being the US presidentMargaret SullivanSome restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more powerWed 19 Aug 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 09.19 EDTShareDonald Trump is essentially unrestrained when it comes to enriching himself during his second term, with no sign of stopping. If anything, he’s ramping things up.The numbers so far are astonishing. He amassed $2.2bn in 2025 revenues, the Guardian and other news outlets havereported.And despite widespread criticism of this astonishing fact, very little is standing in the way of his reaping even more.“The Congress has decided not to commit oversight to this topic, and that’s just the fact of the matter at this point,” Eric Lipton, an investigative reporter for the New York Times,toldNational Public Radio recently.Democrats need to hammer Trump on his unprecedented corruption | Steven GreenhouseRead moreWhile his actions appall historians, academics and millions of ordinary Americans, they may be within legal boundaries.Moral or ethical boundaries? Not so much.“While Trump’s second term is less than half over, it already looks like the most openly corrupt administration in our history,” Larry Noble, a law professor and former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission,told the Guardian’sPeter Stone.Despite his loyal base of followers, much of the American public isn’t happy about it. Two-thirds of Americanspolled by CNNsaid that this president doesn’t put the good of the United States over his personal gain.His overall approval ratings have tanked to 33% – the lowest level of his presidency – with a disapproval rating at 64%, according to a newReuters/Ipsos poll.Startling as the details of his enrichment may be, his mindset – full speed ahead, don’t bother me with past practices – reflects his behavior in other realms. He glories in knowing no restraints or boundaries, and shrugs off criticism.His power is held back only by his “own morality”, hetoldthe New York Times in January. “It’s the only thing that can stop me.”He was speaking specifically about being restrained on the international stage – his freedom to use any military, economic or political power for what he sees as American supremacy.But it’s a mentality he apparently brings into feathering his and his family’s own nest. As Lipton told NPR, queries about apparent conflicts of interest are brushed off, and the party line is that the Trump family’s extracurricular businesses are building the US economy.In earlier presidencies, his actions surely would have political consequences, perhaps impeachment. (He was impeached twice, but not convicted, first in 2019 for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, then for incitement of the violent insurrection at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.)Trump has amassedat least $1.4bnlast year from his cryptocurrency ventures alone, the Guardian reported, noting that others fared less well; about a million investors in one of his crypto projects sufferednearly $4bnin losses as the value of their holdings cratered.Then there are the wealthy foreigners who have invested in the Trump family’s hotel and golf-resort projects, creating potential conflicts of interest.double quotation mark[Trump] glories in knowing no restraints or boundaries, and shrugs off criticismHis media company, Truth Social, has been another major source of wealth. Now there’sa new planto offer early access to his posts for a fee of $100,000. Those posts, of course, have the power to move markets. It’s come under heavy criticism – and prompted lawsuits from media organizations and advocacy groups such as the Freedom of the Press Foundation that argue it’s unconstitutional.But, to date, as with so much of what Trump does, it’s proceeding brazenly.Every once in a while, the courts step in to provide some restraints.Trump tried to use his already weaponized federal justice department to settle his $10bn lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. The initial result was to provide him and his family immunity from earlier audits of their tax returns, which might save the Trumps about $100m. But in a rare bit of accountability, a federal judge – one appointed by Barack Obama –nullifiedmajor parts of the agreement. The legal status is still being contested, and the stakes are high.All of this has the power to shock those paying attention to news reports. But there, too, Trump has given himself a form of protection by constantly playing on citizens’ mistrust of legacy media and to brand such investigations as “fake news”.The result, as author and journalist Craig Ungerput itrecently on Substack, is that nothing “moves the needle”. Not that long ago, he wrote, the press could “root out corruption, topple presidents, and end wars”. But now, even the biggest scoops and the most dramatic revelations seem to have little impact, Unger argues; that’s because the national citizenry doesn’t share an agreed-upon set of facts as it used to do.Trump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actions | Mohamad BazziRead moreTrump’s low approval ratings do seem to tell a different story, however, and voters will get a chance to make their voices heard soon. At the very least, some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections giveDemocratsmore power with a majority in one or both chambers of Congress.Many forecasters think the Democrats may well regain the House of Representatives but that their getting a majority of Senate seats is quite a bit less likely.For now, Trump continues to take full advantage of a situation that has so greatly benefited his personal wealth, if not his reputation or legacy.Like a greedy toddler, he keeps sticking his hand in the presidential cookie jar. And no one, so far, seems able to yank it out.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationDemocratsCryptocurrenciesUS midterm elections 2026US politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: By disparaging 2020 protests as ‘Woke 1’, liberals are following the rightwing’s lead | Andre Gee | The Guardian
description: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s co-opting of conservative language to discuss a movement against state-sanctioned killings of Black people is damning
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s co-opting of conservative language to discuss a movement against state-sanctioned killings of Black people is damning
Content: Protesters fill the streets of Brooklyn to demand justice for George Floyd on 2 June 2020.Photograph: Erik McGregor/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters fill the streets of Brooklyn to demand justice for George Floyd on 2 June 2020.Photograph: Erik McGregor/LightRocket/Getty ImagesOpinionAlexandria Ocasio-CortezBy disparaging 2020 protests as ‘Woke 1’, liberals are following the rightwing’s leadAndre GeeAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s co-opting of conservative language to discuss a movement against state-sanctioned killings of Black people is damningWed 19 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTShareAugust has brought us a referendum on “Woke 1” – a term that reductively brands 2020’s social justice movement – as prominent liberal voices reflect on that time period with disappointing hindsight. During a recent appearance on ABC’s This Week, when asked about 2020-era demands to abolish prisons and police,Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the US congresswoman from New York, abandoned her previous support of the “defund the police” movement, and instead joked: “Woke 1 was crazyyyyy.”Ocasio-Cortez, a democratic socialist, implied that the still-resounding calls for municipalities to reduce police budgets and to divert aid to poor communities were worth advocating for during the 2020 uprising, but are now “crazyyyyy”. In 2020,she notedthat “a lot of people cannot fathom what an abolitionist America looks like. Tell them it looks like a suburb. Affluent white communities already live in a world where they choose to fund youth, health, housing more than they fund police.” But she has since backtracked on that idea.Sure, ‘Woke 1’ had its issues – but we have far bigger problems on our hands | Arwa MahdawiRead moreOn 9 August, she told This Week co-host Jonathan Karl: “We all share the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible [but] rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.” Days later,Zohran Mamdani, the progressive New York mayor, echoed her sentiment by surmising: “Sometimes, what you believe can change and develop.” But their reversing course on abolition isn’t development; it’s a devolution.The backlash to Ocasio-Cortez’s comments was widespread fromleftistswho felt as if her disavowal of the abolition and “defund the police” movements was an attempt to appease the Democratic establishment at their expense. Others, however,agreed with the assertionthat “Woke 1” was defined by overly rigid radicalism, much of which occurred on social media,as with Chi Ossé’s 2021 post on Twitterdeclaring that “a cis white man should not be the next speaker of the council”. Ossé, a New York City council member, coined the term “Woke 1” after being confronted this past May with his old tweet.While everyone weighed in on “Woke 1”, though, I was more concerned with why the hell we were using brandingco-opted by conservativesto discuss a movement against state-sanctioned killings of Black people. “Woke” has long shifted from Black America’s prideful adjective to a mocking noun that has been weaponized to ridicule Black liberation movements. Progressive liberals now adopting that dismissive language while placing confines on the movement for Black lives is damning.The term “woke” originated in Black American communities, and was popularized by a 2008Erykah Badu lyric: “Even though you go through struggle and strife / To keep a healthy life, I stay woke.” The term became popular parlance in the 2010s; to “stay woke” meant you understood the components of white supremacy enough to identify them anywhere, whether in a work of art or a politician’s dog-whistling comments.double quotation markOcasio-Cortez and Ossé evoking ‘woke’ with the same pretense as these sectarian conservatives is cringeworthyBut, as with other terms that originated in Black culture (“Blexit”, “Black fatigue”), the phrase was co-opted by rightwingers who claimed that calls for progressive policy were divisive and reactionary. By 2020, as the police killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor sparked a worldwide uprising, the burning of Minnesota’s third precinct, and widespread calls for radical change, conservatives pushed back by vilifying the word “woke”.In 2022, Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, introduced theStop Woke Act(Stop Wrongs to Our Kids and Employees Act), which tried to restrict schools and businesses from discussing critical race theory, misogyny and other oppressive dynamics. The then minority leader in the Senate, Mitch McConnell, warned that corporations should stop listening to our calls for equity lest they become “a woke parallel government”. The conservative commentator Ben Shapiro held live events to discuss “how wokeness is destroying America”. And aSanta Barbara Independent op-edlauded the late far-right podcasterCharlie Kirkfor “going into the lion’s den of woke”.So Ocasio-Cortez and Ossé evoking “woke” with the same pretense as these sectarian conservatives is cringeworthy. And when they do it to scoff at a movement against the police system’s predation of Black people, it’s dangerous. These comments come at the same time that Maga-world is engaged in a full-scale assault on Black people’s past, present and future, including the rollback of diversity measures leading to mass layoffs of Black employees, the systematic erasure of Black history from schools and attempts to repeal our voting rights.The phrase “Woke 1” is also off-putting because it’s dismissive of the work that abolition advocates and social justice organizations have been doing before and after 2020. What happened at the start of the decade wasn’t momentary advocacy; it’s in lockstep with what freedom fighters have been seeking since the inception of this country. It behooves someDemocratsto realize the vitality of grassroots movement work isn’t dependent on photo ops and national headlines. The truest advocates are still on the frontlines, even if the masses have decided it’s no longer trendy.When Ocasio-Cortez was elected to Congress in 2018, the New Yorkercharacterized heras “the embodiment of anti-corporate politics”. There was hope she could help shake the party out of its moderate malaise. She initially advocated for like-minded candidates such as Cori Bush. People were excited by Ocasio-Cortez’s people-first platform: Medicare for all, raising the minimum wage to $15, the Green New Deal to mitigate the climate crisis and abolishing ICE (a stance she still holds).But some of her politics have retreated toward party orthodoxy. Today, she no longer wants to defund the police and controversially endorsed Joe Biden for president in 2024, despite him having a 42% average approval rating at the time and aiding Israel’s genocide in Palestine. And while Ocasio-Cortez still supports certain progressive candidates, she has also stopped endorsing candidates running against Democratic incumbents, helping stagnate any chance of a progressive insurgency. She’s sought to assimilate within the Democratic establishment, where the status quo outnumbers progressive voices. Some surmise that she is being pragmatic to garner more support for a 2028 White House run. But her need to do so exemplifies the hopelessness of electing progressive candidates who have to dilute themselves to rise in the party.There’s an oft-expressed belief that genuine liberation for Black people can’t come under the two-party system, with the Democratic party fixated on centrist consensus instead of radical policies that will offer marginalized groups a better material reality. For the first time in my lifetime in 2020, however brief, it seemed like Democrats understood that Black people wanted a genuinely equitable country.Officials such as Ocasio-Cortez aligned with these movements because the social current carried everyone in that direction. What happened to Floyd, Taylor and many others was too heartbreaking, too unjust to ignore. But years later, once swimming upstream became more difficult and supporting radical policy wasn’t good careerism, our demands became a “woke” fever dream to Ocasio-Cortez. I implore her and the rest of the Democrats not to find it “crazyyyyy” when droves of leftists once again express apathy toward the party in 2028.Explore more on these topicsAlexandria Ocasio-CortezOpinionDemocratsZohran MamdaniDemocratic socialismUS policingGeorge FloydRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicated | Bernie Sanders | The Guardian
description: Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged
Author: Bernie Sanders
Headline: Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged
Content: ‘The very rich get richer, while working families struggle.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The very rich get richer, while working families struggle.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersOpinionUS politicsWhy are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicatedBernie SandersPoll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is riggedWed 19 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTShareThe media pundits have written article after article desperately trying to understand why progressive candidates, despite being heavily outspent, keep defeating establishmentDemocratsin primaries around the country. Well, the answer is not complicated.Whether it is a corrupt campaign finance system, unprecedented income and wealth inequality, a broken and wildly expensive healthcare system, the enormous threats posed by AI or an immoral and destructive foreign policy, progressives are talking about the real issues facing working families. And they are providing real solutions. Establishment Democrats are not.Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged. The very rich get richer, while working families struggle. Today, while 60% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good.Trump has made our K-shaped economy even worse | Steven GreenhouseRead moreWe now have more income and wealth inequality than at any time in American history. The top 1% now own more wealth than the bottom 93% and one man, Elon Musk, owns more wealth than the bottom 50% of US households.Not surprisingly, working families are tired of status quo politics and the same old, same old establishment policies that have failed them for years. They want change, real change – and are supporting progressive candidates who are fighting for that change.In the richest country in the history of the world, Americans do not want to have to struggle every single day just to pay the bills. Working-class people do not want to die years younger than they should because of illnesses caused by the never-ending stress they experience just to survive. And, like past generations, they do not want their kids to have a lower standard of living than they do.Establishment politicians and the establishment media have described the agenda that progressive candidates are winning elections on as “radical”, “far left”, “extremist” or, in the words of Donald Trump, “communist” . All that is nonsense. On major issue after major issue, the progressive agenda is reflecting exactly what a strong majority of the American people need and want.Let me take this opportunity to share with you some of the major proposals that most progressives support. And you tell me how “extreme” they are.Campaign finance reformProgressives believe that our current campaign finance system is corrupt and is undermining democracy. It is absurd that one man, Mr Musk, can spend $290m to help elect Donald Trump as president and that billionaires in both parties can spend unlimited amounts of money in campaigns through theirSuper Pacs.We believe that we must end the disastrous US supreme court decision on Citizens United, ban Super Pacs and move to the public funding of elections. We believe that democracy means one person one vote, not billionaires buying elections.The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | EditorialRead moreHealthcareProgressives believe that our current healthcare system is broken, dysfunctional and wildly expensive. We believe that it is immoral and fiscally irresponsible for us to spend roughly twice as much per capita on healthcare as do the people of other major countries, while 85 million Americans remain uninsured or underinsured.At the same time, we pay, by far, the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs. Progressives believe that healthcare is a human right and that we should do what all other major countries on Earth do, guarantee healthcare to all people. We agree with the 64% of Americans who want a Medicare for all single payer system.Protecting American workersProgressives believe that all Americans are entitled to a decent standard of living. We regard it as outrageous that in the year 2026 millions of workers continue to earn starvation wages and that the federal minimum wage remains at a disgraceful $7.25 an hour. We believe that the federal minimum wage should be raised to a living wage of at least $20 per hour.We also believe that employers should no longer be able to deny workers their constitutional right to join unions through illegal actions. Progressives support the passage of the Pro Act which will make it easier for workers to join unions and negotiate contracts that will provide them with better wages, benefits and working conditions.Tax the richProgressives believe that, at a time of unprecedented income and wealth inequality, the wealthiest people in this country must start paying their fair share of taxes. At a time when we have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any major country on Earth and when one-third of our senior citizens are struggling economically, it is absurd that billionaires have an effective tax rate lower than truck drivers or nurses.The wealthiest people in this country and large profitable corporations must start paying their fair share of taxes so that we can adequately fund the needs of working families, the children and the elderly.Regulation of AIProgressives believe that AI and robotics, developed and pushed by the wealthiest people on Earth, are the most transformational technologies in the history of humanity and that they will impact every man, woman and child in our country.At a time when AI is threatening to displace millions of workers, eviscerate our privacy, harm our environment, undermine our democracy and negatively impact the mental health of our children, we believe that the government must play a decisive role in making sure that these revolutionary technologies are used to benefit all Americans, and not just make the big tech oligarchs even richer.Climate changeProgressives believe that Trump’s assertion that climate change is a “hoax” is not only extraordinarily ignorant, but is a real danger to the planet. The last 11 years have been the hottest 11 years on record and the last three years have been the hottest three years on record.This past year the United States and countries throughout the world have seen major heatwaves, flash floods, increased drought and horrific forest fires – and scientists tell us the worst is yet to come.The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone | EditorialRead moreProgressives believe that we must forcefully take on the greed of the fossil fuel industry. The truth is that we can create millions of good-paying union jobs by transforming our energy systems away from fossil fuels and into energy efficiency and sustainable energy. For the sake of our kids, future generations and the habitability of the planet that is what we must do.Foreign policyProgressives believe that we need to fundamentally reform our foreign and military policies. The war in Vietnam was based on a lie. The war in Iraq was based on a lie. The current war in Iran is based on a lie. We do not need to spend $1.5tn a year on the Pentagon fighting endless wars and propping up dictatorships around the world.We certainly do not have to invest tens of billions supporting the extremist Netanyahu government in Israel, which has killed 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 173,000 more – the vast majority of them women, children and the elderly.Despite what the media will have you believe, progressives are winning across this country for a simple reason: the ideas they are running on are extremely popular. It’s time for the political establishment to stop telling the American people what they should believe and start listening to what they actually want.Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of CongressExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionBernie SandersDemocratsUS economyAI (artificial intelligence)Climate crisisUS foreign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: Can anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was me | Katriona O'Sullivan | The Guardian
description: LBC’s Nick Ferrari can’t see what is stopping people buying a cheap toothbrush, but the grinding reality of living in poverty creates its own priorities, says psychologist, author and professor Dr Katriona O’Sullivan
Author: Katriona O'Sullivan
Headline: LBC’s Nick Ferrari can’t see what is stopping people buying a cheap toothbrush, but the grinding reality of living in poverty creates its own priorities, says psychologist, author and professor Dr Katriona O’Sullivan
Content: Illustration: Jess Clark/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jess Clark/The Guardian/Getty ImagesOpinionPovertyCan anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was meKatriona O'SullivanLBC’s Nick Ferrari can’t see what is stopping people buying a cheap toothbrush, but the grinding reality of living in poverty creates its own prioritiesWed 19 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTShareIdon’t listen to Nick Ferrari on LBC very often. His antagonistic way of dealing with complex problems gets me screaming at the radio far too easily. Last month was a perfect example. Someone from the Joseph Rowntree Foundation was on discussing research showing that about 7 million people arestruggling to afford basic essentials, including toothpaste and toothbrushes, because of the cost of living crisis.This did not strike me as a controversial finding. The cost of fuel, heating, food, school, clothes – everything – has gone up, while wages and benefits have not risen enough to keep pace. Ferrari, however, latched on to the toothbrushes. I found myself listening to him talk about the price of cheap toothbrushes in pound shops and at Asda. At times, it sounded like a price-comparison advert. At other times, it sounded like lazy journalism: take a complicated issue, strip it of all context and turn it into something that will generate outrage, clicks and applause.Had I been on the show, I would have brought both my lived experience and my academic knowledge to the argument. I would have explained why a person living in poverty might buy cheap wine instead of a cheap toothbrush.The first thing I would have talked to Ferrari about is decision-making. How we decide what to buy, what not to buy and where to spend our money is shaped by far more than price. One of the first questions we ask, often without realising it, is whether the thing we are buying will help us now or later.You know those people who buy 48 toilet rolls because they are on special offer? They can look ahead and think: spending more now will save me money later. Psychologists might describe this as delayed gratification. It requires the ability to resist an immediate need or reward in order to benefit in the future.Stress makes that much harder. When people are under constant pressure, they tend to focus on the here and now. What can I fix today? What problem is shouting loudest? What can make things feel slightly better for the next few hours? A toothbrush is an investment in the future. So is going for a run. So is buying healthier food that costs more and takes longer to prepare. The benefit is delayed.Poverty, on the other hand, creates urgent problems. The debt collector is knocking at your door for his money. The electricity is about to run out. The school is asking for payment for a trip. Your son is being bullied because he is wearing cheap trainers instead of Nikes. These things feel immediate. The possible dental problems caused by not replacing a toothbrush feel far away. That does not make the decision sensible. It makes it human.Long-term planning becomes more difficult during periods of stress. It is also shaped by how and where you grow up. If you are raised in an environment where life feels unstable and the future feels uncertain, it can bemuch harder to believethat sacrificing today will bring a reward tomorrow. According to some studies, growing up poor can even affect thedevelopment of your brain– the areas associated with reward are more active than those responsible for reasonable decision-making.That is part of the reason poverty is associated with higher levels of addiction and criminality. Not because poor people are naturally reckless or immoral, but because deprivation, stress and hopelessness shape our brains and our behaviour.Had I been sitting opposite Ferrari, I might have asked him whether he had ever been told to change his habits. Most of us have struggled to change something about ourselves, even when we knew exactly what we were supposed to do. If making the right choice were simply a matter of knowing what was best, we would all eat the salad, go for the run, stop smoking, drink less and buy the toothbrush.But human beings do not make decisions like machines. Our choices are influenced by stress, habit, upbringing, perceptions of self-worth, addiction, fear, exhaustion and whether we believe there is any point in planning for the future. I know this because I have made the choice not to buy toothpaste many times.I did not do that because I was stupid or a bad person. I did it because ofhow I lived, how I grew up and how I felt about myselfshaped what I believed was worth spending money on. My parents did not brush their teeth or ours. Looking after your teeth was not something I had been taught to value. I had such low self-worth that my own health was often the last thing on my mind.The same was true of sanitary products. When I was living on around £35 a week benefits in the 1990s, I sometimes bought three bottles of Diamond White rather than spending 50p on tampons. You might judge me for that. But when you live in shit, when nobody seems to care about you and you have stopped caring about yourself, a few bottles can feel like an escape. It felt easier to stuff my knickers with toilet roll from the cash-in-hand job I worked and have one night away from the misery than to sit sober with the constant belief that I was failing myself and my son. At times, it felt like the choice was three bottles or dying.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat may seem hard to understand when your life has always contained safety, options and hope. But all you have to do is ask yourself one important question – would anyone choose that type of life if they could choose another? The answer to that is simple.I am glad I stayed alive long enough to learn that poverty is not created by the bad choices of poor people. It is created and maintained by systems that leave people without security, support or genuine options – and by powerful people who reduce those lives to lazy tropes that reinforce stereotypes about irresponsibility. You cannot call something a choice when the alternatives are not equally available.Putting a 49p toothbrush on a supermarket shelf does not mean everyone has the money, the stability, the knowledge or the headspace to buy it. Availability is not the same as access, and access is not the same as capacity.Of course, people should buy toothbrushes. But repeating the price of one as though it disproves poverty is not analysis. It is ignorance dressed up as common sense. Choice is far more complicated than that. I think choice is a myth for many people; it is an idea that is inflicted on poor people by people in positions of power so they don’t have to do anything to help.Dr Katriona O’Sullivan is a psychologist, author and professor at Maynooth University. She is the author of the bestselling memoirsPoorandHungry, and is a weekly columnist for the Irish IndependentDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Reform says we need to choose between climate and economy. It’s wrong | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: The party’s deputy leader Richard Tice says we should stop worrying about extreme heat and enjoy it. This dangerous nonsense will wreck our finances and the planet, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: The party’s deputy leader Richard Tice says we should stop worrying about extreme heat and enjoy it. This dangerous nonsense will wreck our finances and the planet, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: Wheat in a field in Cheshire. Most of England and Wales is in drought, affecting harvests.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWheat in a field in Cheshire. Most of England and Wales is in drought, affecting harvests.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisReform says we need to choose between climate and economy. It’s wrongLarry ElliottThe party’s deputy leader Richard Tice says we should stop worrying about extreme heat and enjoy it. This dangerous nonsense will wreck our finances and the planetWed 19 Aug 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.23 EDTShareSo now we know: the smart response to the UK’s summer of record temperatures is to do precisely nothing.According to Richard Tice, Reform UK’s deputy leader, the climate crisis is just one of those things. Nothing can be done about it, so we should simply bask in the sunshine.It is reasonable to assume Tice would not have said anything quite as crass had he been addressing people in Stourbridge who haveseen their homes burn to the ground. Or the farmers whose crops shrivelin parched fields. Or thefirefighters exhausted from battling wildfires across Britain.Yet Tice clearly thinks he is on to something. The cost of living crisis has put the government’s commitmentto achieving net zero by 2050under the spotlight. The assumption underlying Tice’s comments is that there is a trade-off between tackling the climate emergency and raising, or even maintaining, living standards – and that for the time being, the latter should take priority.The government has certainly been acting as if it believes this is the case. While the droughtaffecting most of England and Walesmakes the strongest possible case for hastening the green transition, Andy Burnham’s focus has been on reducing prices for consumers, including bycutting VAT on electricity bills.It took the prime minister an awfully long time to use the words “climate change” to explain this summer’s heatwaves. He did so only after the devastating fires in Stourbridge and whenprodded by a letter from green groupscalling on him to end his silence.Burnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big risk | Gaby HinsliffRead moreAt one level, the emphasis on putting cash in people’s pockets makes sense. Traditionally, interest in the environment waxes during periods of strong economic growth and wanes when times are tough. Climate breakdown slips down the list of priorities for voters when they are worried about losing their jobs or struggling to pay their bills. Peaks in concern have tended to come at the end of long booms, such as the early 1970s or the late 1980s.But opinions are changing across the political spectrum. As the Conservative peer David Willettshas pointed out, 86% of Britons see climate breakdownas at least partly responsiblefor the recent heatwaves, and even 63% of net zero opponents make that connection. More than a third of Reform UK voters said tackling climate breakdownshould be more of a priorityin a recent poll.There are good reasons for the high level of public concern. The rate of food price inflation has also been coming down in recent months, but a poor harvest means that trend could well go into reverse soon.Meanwhile,a reportby the German insurance company Allianz has exploded the myth that governments have a choice between growth and the environment. The study shows that extreme heat poses structural challenges to many rich countries because, as temperatures rise above 30C, workers struggle to do their jobs and their productivity suffers. The higher the thermometer rises, the greater the losses.For the most exposed countries – especially those in continental Europe – the hit to economic activity will be considerable: over a five-year period the impact of extreme heat could knock a cumulative 5-7% off GDP.According to Allianz, the UK has hitherto been below the 30C threshold and has not been one of the countries at risk from extreme heat. But on the basis of this summer, Britain may soon become a higher-risk country alongside France and Spain.To be sure, Britain is responsible for only a small fraction of the world’s CO2 emissions, and there is a legitimate debate about how to achieve net zero. But the warning signs are flashing red. Now is not the time to go slow on tackling climate breakdown. The longer that action – global as well as domestic – is delayed, the greater the risk that the climate crisis will eventually wreck the economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA failure to invest in basic infrastructure needs to be remedied fast. People faced with hosepipe bans have the right to ask whyBritain has not built a reservoir in 30 years. The electricity grid was designed and built for fossil fuels rather than renewables, andmany green projects are held upby a lack of capacity.The UK’s housing stock is woefully inefficient. Household bills would be lower if existing homes were retrofitted with insulation. New homes should be subject to tougher building regulations to make mechanical ventilation – which keeps temperatures stable year-round – mandatory.None of this comes cheap. The state will have to invest in new infrastructure as well as making changes to the planning laws. Subsidies will be required to provide incentives for consumers to go green. No question, there are costs involved in the net zero transition, but they are outweighed by the benefits. These include cheaper running costs for electric vehicles and lower energy bills for homes where gas boilers are replaced by heat pumps.Governments can always find the money when the occasion dictates. When the security of the nation is at risk, ways to finance extra spending are found. To take one example, ministers havecommitted to raising defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035because of the perceived threat from Russia.But which is the greater threat? Is it Russia, bogged down in Ukraine after more than four years of attritional fighting, or is it the climate crisis? The answer should be obvious.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionRichard TiceReform UKEnvironment policyWildfiresGreenhouse gas emissionscommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s drop in real wages is a disaster. But the profits of major corporations are doing just fine | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: Wages are not growing out of control and the labour market is not ‘tight’
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: Wages are not growing out of control and the labour market is not ‘tight’
Content: ‘Over the past year, inflation rose faster than the wage growth in every single industry,’ writes Greg Jericho.Photograph: Jason Reed/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Over the past year, inflation rose faster than the wage growth in every single industry,’ writes Greg Jericho.Photograph: Jason Reed/ReutersGrogonomicsWages growthAustralia’s drop in real wages is a disaster. But the profits of major corporations are doing just fineGreg JerichoWages are not growing out of control and the labour market is not ‘tight’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 19 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 20.44 EDTShareExcuse me while I sadly cross off another three months on my “waiting for a wages breakout” calendar.Before I get to the wages figures, may I pause to note that this monthNAB reporteda 5% increase in its profits compared with last year,CBA reporteda 7% increase in its cash profit,BHP reportedannual profit growth of 9% andRio Tinto recordeda 47% profit increase in the first half of this year.Let’s just leave those figures there. Maybe think on them as we go on.Yesterday, the June quarter wage price index figures were released showing that in April, May and June the average growth of wages in the private sector was just 0.7% – the lowest since December 2021. If that pace continued it would equate to an annual growth of just 2.8%:If the graph does not display click hereI don’t want anyone to get too worried, but that level of wage growth is truly pathetic.You know what also happened in the June quarter? Yes, the RBA raised interest rates.One of the reasons the RBA decided to raise interest rateswas the “risk” of wages going up – even though at the time private-sector wages were growing the slowest they had for nearly six years.The annual growth in the year to June saw private-sector wages slow from 3.2% in March to 3.1% – the slowest since June 2022:If the graph does not display click hereThe only thing that kept the overall wage growth steady at 3.2% was the solid growth in public-sector wages.The ABS has helpfully provided some new data on what industries contributed the most to overall wage growth, and the public-sector driven industries of public administration and healthcare were the two biggest, followed by construction:If the graph does not display click hereOver the past year, inflation rose faster than the wage growth in every single industry, and even the construction industry – which should notionally be seeing wages taking off due to the increase in datacentre construction and also the nationwide shortage of workers – has had wages grow slower than inflation:If the graph does not display click hereIf we can’t even get a wage breakout in the industry where there is apparently so much work due to the AI datacentre boom that it was a reason the RBA gave for increasing rates, then I don’t know what more evidence we need that wages are not growing out of control and that the labour market is not “tight”.The ABS also found that in the June quarter 79% of jobs that got a change in wages had an annual wage growth of less than 4%. That is the most since 2022, and is a sign that the majority of wage growth agreements are at level more than consistent with inflation of less than 3%.If the graph does not display click hereOf course, the big problem with all these numbers is that they are currently less than inflation, and the bigger problem is they are much less than the recent increase in cost of living (which includes mortgage repayments):If the graph does not display click hereThe drop in real wages is now at such a point that, even with the RBA’s forecasts out to the end of 2028, the best workers can hope for is that in December that year their wages in real terms will be equivalent in value to what they were 17 years earlier:If the graph does not display click hereWe need to acknowledge that the loss of real wages is permanent.Efforts (or even the suggestion that it might happen) to get wages to rise faster than inflation in order to regain the loss of value are met with worries from the RBA that lead to higher interest rates.Meanwhile, the profits of major corporations rise well above inflation – and the response?Crickets. Or praise that it is a sign of a strong economy.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsWages growthGrogonomicsAustralian economyBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: A rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalism  | Hugh Muir | The Guardian
description: Amid the grief and rage at a tragic loss, it’s right to differentiate between those who fought a culture war and others who just sought the truth, says Hugh Muir, executive editor, Opinion
Author: Hugh Muir
Headline: Amid the grief and rage at a tragic loss, it’s right to differentiate between those who fought a culture war and others who just sought the truth, says Hugh Muir, executive editor, Opinion
Content: A vigil for Jason Arday in Trafalgar Square, London, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA vigil for Jason Arday in Trafalgar Square, London, 17 August 2026.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionJason ArdayA rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalismHugh MuirAmid the grief and rage at a tragic loss, it’s right to differentiate between those who fought a culture war and others who just sought the truthWed 19 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 03.06 EDTShareEven now it is very difficult to process the scale of tragedy that engulfedJason Ardayand those who loved him. The unbearable sadness at his death; the wretched knowledge that the very public onslaught against him began with the malign machinations of a self-defined “race realist” – who believes that, in an ideal world, black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. The horror that a rightwing and far-right campaign seeking a victim to fuel its nativist prejudices can now crow that it found one.There is wide and profound grief and of course there is rage, focused and unfocused. Both were on display as thousandsjoined a protest vigil in Trafalgar Squareon Monday evening.His family – in a moving statement remembering an “amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son” – has said he was “subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor atCambridge Universityby those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him”. This we know. The right and far-right desire to identify and then defenestrate anyone or anything that could be seen as symbolic of progress is virtually pathological. The rightwing media, in a quiet summer – a quarry identified – led a charge that meant Prof Arday’s face was disobligingly displayed on almost every front page, every TV screen, for weeks. His family, who knew him best, are clear about what that ultimately meant for a man who was neurodivergent and by the end – according to reports – desolate. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”This stokes high emotions. A high-profile, successful black figure is something highly prized. Many attest to the professor’s kindness and the care he lavished on those he was responsible for and, through access programmes, on others he never really knew. Many others feel the very human protective emotion of anger, having witnessed a successful but vulnerable man manoeuvred into the crosshairs. They voiced their rage in Trafalgar Square. It bristles, too, on social media.The culture-war right did what it does, but what of others in politics and other media? The right in its hostile, partisan pursuit nevertheless uncovered doubts about the professor’s academic work – accusations of plagiarism – that could not be satisfactorily dismissed. The professor himself made public claims about his life and achievements that could not be verified. Of course that was a good thing for those who, for racist and political reasons, sought to denigrate him, but wasn’t that also a legitimate concern for those who bore him no ill will – indeed cheered his ascent – but see the importance of integrity in academia and public life?Amid the pain and understandable rage in recent days, there has been invective levelled at the right, but also a deal of social-media abuse levelled at progressive journalists – notably black journalists, and especially Guardian journalists who interrogated and reported on the claims made about and by the professor. There have been attempts to load them with at least partial responsibility for his death. Suggestions that, with their actions, they have betrayed their heritage: that they personally should be for ever haunted by his fate. One can try to be understanding and frame this as part of the outpouring of grief, but that makes those attacks no less corrosive, no less hurtful to the journalists themselves.There is a particular tension to being a black or minority journalist in a white-majority culture, whether here or in the US, Europe or Australia. As a minority citizen, one shares the joys and pains and achievements of others. Very many in their work focus on the particular concerns of minorities coping and maybe thriving on challenging terrain. They are not fated to do so, but these matters interest them and many see who they are and what they know, juxtaposed with the skills they have as journalists, as an ideal way to make a contribution to society.In my reporting career, I have covered domestic politics, international politics, international conflict – the whole gamut of journalistic subjects – but I drew great pride from being the recipient of the first Commission for Racial EqualityRacein the Media award in the national newspaper category. I worked as a community affairs correspondent for the BBC for the duration of Sir William Macpherson’s landmark inquiry into the murder of Stephen Lawrence, explaining the intricacies of that historic event to millions on radio and TV. It is not a motivation exclusive to black journalists, but the vast majority I have known and worked with tend to hope that their professionalism will somehow make a positive difference to and for their communities, and to wider society’s understanding of their communities.But here’s the thing: we are journalists. We are not activists. Often we work with activists and I am very proud to have done so. Often our hopes and agendas coincide, and when they do, injustices are exposed, wrongs are righted, sometimes laws and attitudes are changed, but we are adjacent, we are not the same. Activists vary, but almost by definition they seek a means to an end. A good journalist lays out facts. Sometimes those facts push that end further away; sometimes they are unpalatable.And so, if it appears that a prominent figure – be they black or white – is being less than honest in ways that meet the test of public interest, those black journalists have a right, indeed a duty, to interrogate that. I know well some of those who did so in the case of Prof Arday, carefully and professionally, and are now, amid the anger, confusion and rage, being abused and castigated for it. They were not responsible for what Lord Chris Smith, the Cambridge University chancellor, called the “racist feeding frenzy”. They, in interrogating all the claims in a way we would expect professional, responsible, empathetic journalists to do, just did their jobs. As journalists. Even the bits that made them sad, that were unpalatable. And what if they hadn’t? Was all of the reporting and inquiry to be done by the right, by those who coveted a scalp, by culture warriors?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere will be questions to ask in the weeks to come, about the institutions involved in Prof Arday’s career, about the claims that were made for and against him, about the media coverage – all of it – in its tone and scale, about whether there could and should have been more recognition of the professor’s vulnerability under the barrage of headlines and attention. There arecalls for a public inquiry. We will all be soul-searching.Those questions should be posed – a man has died – but we cannot yet know the answers. Those who seek them are right to. Those who mourn him should have space to respectfully do so. As for those who mark his passing by arbitrarily pointing the finger at others who also grieve his loss – don’t.Hugh Muir is executive editor, OpinionIn the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The flag culture wars have come to an unlikely place: progressive Iceland | Alexander Hurst | The Guardian
description: Ahead of the Nordic nation’s EU referendum, the Icelandic flag has been co-opted by the far right, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Author: Alexander Hurst
Headline: Ahead of the Nordic nation’s EU referendum, the Icelandic flag has been co-opted by the far right, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Content: Repainting stripes of the Progressive Pride flag in Reykjavik, Iceland, last month after they were covered with an image of the national flag.Photograph: Garðaþjónusta Sigurjóns/FacebookView image in fullscreenRepainting stripes of the Progressive Pride flag in Reykjavik, Iceland, last month after they were covered with an image of the national flag.Photograph: Garðaþjónusta Sigurjóns/FacebookOpinionIcelandThe flag culture wars have come to an unlikely place: progressive IcelandAlexander HurstAhead of the Nordic nation’s EU referendum, the Icelandic flag has been co-opted by the far rightWed 19 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 04.37 EDTShareTo enter Reykjavik’s Grafarvogur Lutheran church, worshippers and visitors are invited to make their way down 16 steps painted in the rainbow stripes and the white, pink, blue, brown and black chevrons of theProgress Prideflag. The artwork, which can even be seen on satellite pictures, was originally a project of former head pastor Guðrún Karls Helgudóttir, now the bishop of Iceland, and her colleagues. The point was to show support for the LGBTQ+ community’s “need to be visible and accepted”, the church’s current head pastor,Arna Sigurðardóttir,told me.And then some time in between the barely faded midnight sun of 7 July and the early morning light of 8 July, someone painted over all those colours with just three: blue on the outside, and two thin strips of white encasing a thicker strip of red in the centre.The church’s pride flag had been defaced twice before, both times in 2022, once with black scribbling alluding to a verse from the Old Testament.This time, though, when Sigurðardóttir heard the news that it had been completely painted over with the Icelandic flag, something about it felt different. “More systematic, in a way – much more methodical,” she said. “We are experiencing everywhere this pushback against human rights, and they’re starting to envelop it in national flags.”A national flag becoming a symbol of contention and exclusion, rather than pride, is a phenomenon I know all too well. As a child, I used to sing the US national anthem to myself, in my head, to time brushing my teeth. By the time I was a teenager, in the rage and haze of the Iraq war and its dissidents, I sat for the compulsory morning pledge of allegiance, and saw the stars and stripes as a symbol of shame. This fraught relationship is why I felt such empathy, tinged with disappointment, when a young Icelander roughly my age told me, after the incident at Grafarvogur church, that for the first time in her life she was starting to feel uneasy with the Icelandic flag.I had thought, naively perhaps, that a country with such a small population might be spared from the polarisation that is tearing the US apart and increasingly affects my adopted country, France. Instead I found myself face to face with someone who was starting to feel the same sense of rupture with her country’s symbols as I had felt with mine.I didn’t want that for her, especially not for someone from a country with very little objectionable in its history. After all, Iceland, which has no army and which prosecuted its bankers for their role in the 2008 financial crisis, never colonised anyone. Even saunas and hot tubs are guilt free; the island is powered and heated almost entirely by carbon-free geothermal energy and even leads the world in capturing CO2, injecting it deep underground and turning it into rock.Why should Sigurðardóttir, or any other Icelander, suddenly feel shame about her country’s flag?View image in fullscreenAn Icelandic flag hangs outside a shop in Reykjavik.Photograph: Frank Augstein/APÁsa Berglind Hjálmarsdóttir, a representative of the Althing, Iceland’s parliament, tells me that until about a year ago she doesn’t remember the Icelandic flag ever being used in contentious ways. It remained a unifying symbol for a small country – barely 400,000 people – that only gained its independence from Denmark on 17 June 1944.A banner of ice and fire: blue for the frigid northern Atlantic waters that surround the island, white for its glaciers, red for the lava that erupts every so often from its roughly33 active volcano systems. Historically it is never flown between sundown and sunrise, or past midnight during the perpetual daylight of summer months. By tradition it was lowered to half-mast by each local community or town to announce the passing of each individual Icelander.In spring 2025, Hjálmarsdóttir, a member of the Social Democratic Alliance, encountered an anti-immigration protest outside the Althing, where what she describes as “a small group of extremists” had wrapped themselves in the flag. “I had this bad feeling in my stomach,” Hjálmarsdóttir says, “because this had never happened before.” Modern far-right politics, it seems, had finally come for Iceland too.“Our history of having the first openly gay prime minister, renewable energy, women’s rights … for me that’s what the Icelandic flag symbolises,” said Ragna Sigurðardóttir, a 33-year-old member of the Althing (no relation to Arna, the pastor). “We have to have the courage to fly it.”“It’s very important that we don’t allow the feeling of unease with the flag to grow,” Hjálmarsdóttir told me. A year ago, she called for a change in the law to ease Iceland’s restrictions on flying the flag, in the hope that more people would display it, and thereby prevent a far-right movement from appropriating it for themselves. The subsequent bill, which was adopted by the parliament and came into effect in May, means that during summer months the flag can legally be flown all day and night. Her colleague Ragna Sigurðardóttir said she had seen an increase in businesses and households doing just that.It’s a response that I find fascinating: faced with an attempt by the far right to monopolise a symbol of national unity, Hjálmarsdóttir decided that the only answer possible was to say that the flag belongs to no one and to everyone.On 29 August, Icelanders will vote on the first step in a process that could one day see another flag fly alongside theirs: also blue, but with a circle of yellow stars instead of an asymmetric cross of ice and fire. At the moment polling suggests that athin majorityof 53% supports reopening accession talks with the EU (previous negotiations were suspended over fishing rights in 2013), even if there is not yet majority support for becoming a full EU member state.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom the EU’s perspective, the benefits to welcoming Iceland as a member are clear: a wealthy, high-functioning Nordic democracy strategically located in the north Atlantic, with vast renewable energy resources and credibility when it comes to both climate and the oceans. French MEP Valérie Hayer recently argued in the Guardian that it would be in the EU’s interests toto be flexibleand offer a carve-out for Icelandic fishing – a critical component of what would be the EU’s second-smallest single economy after Malta.View image in fullscreenWaves breaking around a trawler off the Reykjanes peninsula, IcelandPhotograph: David Noton Photography/AlamyIf I were an Icelander voting, my decision would be dominated by thoughts of what it means to be a small, rule-of-law democracy in the middle of Donald Trump’s obsessive threats to annex nearby Greenland and Vladimir Putin’s imperialist aggression – one with a collection of like-minded rule-of-law democracies to its south-east.The head of Iceland’s main opposition party, Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, told Reuters recently that the country’s futuresecurity rested on Nato and the US, and that Trump’s threats to seize Greenland had not changed her position against EU membership. To an American who has spent the past 10 years observing the deterioration of the US from afar, that sounds irresponsibly optimistic. It’s not just about Greenland. The US government has been willing to gratuitously traduce its relationship with Canada, wield tariffs as coercive economic warfare against smaller countries, and pursue financial and political interference in the domestic elections of countries it is nominally allied with.Is it this context of a split over EU membership that has sparked the rise in flag-related nationalism? The Icelanders I spoke to agree that there is some convergence of beliefs among people who grasp at the flag in a nationalist way (anti-EU, anti-immigration, anti-LGBTQ+). But they are sceptical that the impending referendum is the inciting factor. That seems like a positive thing when it comes to crafting unity over EU talks, and, some day, full membership – but potentially more difficult when it comes to disentangling the flag from reactionary politics.Arna Sigurðardóttir says that conversations about the EU aren’t the most pressing in her congregation, even among those who are uncomfortable with steps painted in pride colours. Lately they’ve been discussing what’s more harmful about the flag: to make people uncomfortable with the pride colours or to harm those who need its symbolic support by removing it? In the end, the church chose torepaint the rainbow colourson its steps.The pastor told me that a few people whom she suspects had vandalised the steps had actually come out to protest when the church first removed the paint. The church was having a service outside that Sunday in a small park, and she had invited them to attend – and to bring along the Icelandic flags they were carrying. None had accepted the offer, she said. She plans to try again and organise a conversation in the autumn but makes a point of saying that her goal isn’t to change their minds. Rather, she told me: “It’s about trying to reach the people who are on the fence”.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris.
