title: As a woman who loves AFL, I feel palpable despair. Why did it take so long to put us at the centre of this story? | Jill Stark | The Guardian
description: Commentary around the Sydney Swans case has made it painfully clear that women’s safety is not valued as highly as the sporting success of its male stars
Author: Jill Stark
Headline: Commentary around the Sydney Swans case has made it painfully clear that women’s safety is not valued as highly as the sporting success of its male stars
Content: Sydney fans celebrate an AFL win against Essendon on 16 August before some Swans players were linked to an incident that led to sexual assault allegations.Photograph: Daniel Pockett/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSydney fans celebrate an AFL win against Essendon on 16 August before some Swans players were linked to an incident that led to sexual assault allegations.Photograph: Daniel Pockett/Getty ImagesOpinionAFLAs a woman who loves AFL, I feel palpable despair. Why did it take so long to put us at the centre of this story?Jill StarkCommentary around the Sydney Swans case has made it painfully clear that women’s safety is not valued as highly as the sporting success of its male starsTue 18 Aug 2026 21.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 23.53 EDTShareAs a woman who lovesAFL, the events of the last few days have left me wondering if there is a home for me in this game.It has been hard to stomach watching allegations of sexual assault that may be linked to someSydney Swansplayers being framed as an “unmitigated disaster” for the club’s finals chances.Five players havenow been sanctioned by the AFL for the rest of the season, independent of the police investigation. But since news broke on Monday, the football commentariat’s early coverage of the allegations has largely been about how the incident “threatens to derail Sydney’s season”.One senior commentator said the thing that made him most angry was that the Swans players may miss out on their last chance of winning a grand final.Women’s experiences sidelined in response to Sydney Swans sexual assault allegations | Jack SnapeRead moreAny alleged victims have largely been erased, as pundits wring their hands about how “mortifying” the allegations are for “player, club and code”.When Ispoke about this publicly, many men were quick to defend the framing, arguing that it was because commentators were constrained by what they could say legally.Frankly, that’s a cop-out.The palpable despair many women are feeling is not driven by a desire to condemn these men before police investigations are complete.We respect that legal processes should take their course and that the players deserve the presumption of innocence. We also don’t expect football journalists to be experts on Australia’s epidemic of violence against women or apportion blame before knowing the full facts.But at the very least, we expect some basic human empathy.We expect that allegations of sexual assault will not be reduced to a mere footnote in a story about missed sporting opportunities.We expect not to see them framed as inconvenient timing for the AFL finals series – as if a sexual assault investigation would have been more palatable in round three or during the off-season.We expect not to hear the club’s chief executive express disappointment that his players “have found themselves in this situation” – casting them as unfortunate victims of circumstance rather than grown men in positions of power with agency to make their own decisions.When Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich fronted media on Monday, he could have expressed compassion for the women involved without compromising the presumption of innocence.He could have made it clear that violence against women would not be tolerated at his club, and that strong action would be taken if any wrongdoing was found to have occurred.He could have acknowledged many of his club’s female players, fans and staff may be distressed, and reaffirmed the importance of a culture where women feel safe and welcome.He said none of those things.With a few exceptions, neither did most of the men in the AFL fraternity, who ordinarily have an opinion on everything.Instead, it was once again left to the women in the AFL community to speak out against a culture that has a long history of protecting its male heroes.AFL CEO Andrew Dillon has now called for care and privacy of the woman who made the report to police, and the Swans have acknowledged the allegations impacted people other than the players.Commentators are slowly starting to acknowledge the woman at the centre of these allegations, and the impact on women more broadly.But why did it take so long?As former AFLW star and Triple M commentatorKate McCarthy pointed out, when former Geelong player Sam Newman remains in the Australian Football Hall of Fame after describing the experience of a woman who was raped by AFL sports agent Ralph Carr as potentially having “buyer’s remorse”, we should be asking “serious questions about what and who we continue to celebrate as a league.”Newman’s comments came as former West Coast star Ben Cousins embarked on a press tour to promote a drug and alcohol program.Cousins was previously jailed for aggravated stalking and breaching restraining orders. He now works for Channel 7 and has been lauded for his redemption efforts.When a man is valuable to the game, football will always find a way to rehabilitate his image and protect his legacy. For the women harmed along the way, their stories are too often forgotten, or simply not believed.Journalists help frame whose experience takes centre stage, and how public perception on complex issues is shaped.As a former health journalist involved in revising guidelines for theresponsible reporting of mental illness and suicide, I’m acutely aware of how profoundly damaging careless language can be.The reporting of the Sydney Swans case has made it painfully clear that journalists, commentators and AFL leaders need training on how to talk about sexual assault in a way that doesn’t minimise violence against women or erase it entirely.Until women’s safety is valued as much as the commercial interests of the game and the sporting success of its male stars, there can be no real home for us in football.Jill Stark is a Melbourne-based writer and podcasterInformation and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse is available from the following organisations. In Australia, support is available atFull Stop Australia(1800 385 578). In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsAFLOpinionSydney SwansAustralian rules footballAustralia sportWomenViolence against women and girlscommentShareReuse this content

title: I have seen the raw grief of a family who lost a son to gambling. Labor’s stitch-up shows politics is broken | David Pocock | The Guardian
description: How is it that Australians can call so strongly for action on gambling advertising and the major parties fail so comprehensively to listen?
Author: David Pocock
Headline: How is it that Australians can call so strongly for action on gambling advertising and the major parties fail so comprehensively to listen?
Content: ‘The gambling lobby, leaning on free-to-air television and the major sporting codes, have well and truly won the day,’ writes Senator David Pocock.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The gambling lobby, leaning on free-to-air television and the major sporting codes, have well and truly won the day,’ writes Senator David Pocock.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesOpinionGamblingI have seen the raw grief of a family who lost a son to gambling. Labor’s stitch-up shows politics is brokenDavid PocockHow is it that Australians can call so strongly for action on gambling advertising and the major parties fail so comprehensively to listen?Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 18 Aug 2026 21.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 01.44 EDTShareThedeal the prime minister has cut with the Coalitionon gambling will be a huge disappointment to people across Australia.This legislation was about more than just gambling reform. It was a test of whether our parliament listens to the people over vested interests, and the clear answer to that is no. It also raises serious questions about our major party system.The prime minister had an opportunity to leave a legacy and change our country for the better, and he has instead chosen a path pushed by the gambling industry. Communities rightly feel sold out to a predatory industry that profits from people’s pain.Coalition MPs cross floor over ‘weak’ gambling crackdown as major parties strike dealRead moreThat pain was on full display during a recent Senate inquiry into the bill. We heard the raw grief from a family who lost a brother and a son. This family courageously shared their story in the hope that the government would act to prevent gambling harm, to stop other families having to experience the indescribable pain their own suffers to this day. They shared some of their son’s and brother’s last words, words that brought the committee to tears.“I am ending my life because I am so pathologically addicted to gambling and cannot get myself to stop. I can’t even get myself to stop to save my own life nor to save my loved ones from the pain of me committing suicide. I am just so disgusted and revolted with myself and want to end my life as soon as possible before my addiction ruins more people around me. I am convinced that the world will, in the long run, be better off with one less person like me. I wish I never placed that first bet. But here I am. I cannot change anything in the past, and so this is where my life will end.”Hearing testimony like this, after being pulled aside at event after event by predominantly young men over the last few years, has left me angry. I’ve heard story after story of shame, strained relationships and financial ruin as a result of gambling addiction.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHow can the prime minister hear evidence of the overwhelming harm and respond witha few tweaks to a weak package?It is damning that Australians can call so strongly for protections from the harms of gambling advertising and the major parties fail so comprehensively to listen. That we can have backbenchers on both the Labor and Coalition side defy party solidarity and speak out, calling for stronger reform, only to be ignored and forced to vote with their respective parties for inadequate legislation.What does all this say about the parliamentary process?1:58David Pocock gives furious speech saying the government has failed on gambling advertising – videoA government-led committee delivered 31 unanimously supported recommendations, a Senate inquiry heard a wealth of evidence about the need to implement those 31 recommendations. Both were ignored.This is a tragic missed opportunity – a betrayal of the people who have pushed so hard for stronger action and a betrayal of the vast majority of Australians who want an end to gambling ads. It will be a damaging legacy for the prime minister.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDespite what the PM says, this isn’t about stopping people having a punt, it’s about protecting children from being indoctrinated by what the late Labor MP Peta Murphy called a “predatory industry”.Yet again we see vested interests put ahead of community interest. The gambling lobby, leaning on free-to-air television and the major sporting codes, have well and truly won the day with this legislation. As my independent colleague, and member of the committee that handed down the Murphy report, Kate Chaney said, it shows why politics in this country is broken.Australians are angry about the way our system has lacked long-term thinking and prioritising them ahead of vested interests. They are looking for anyone who will take on the establishment and deliver for the people. We have to build a better way of doing politics in this country – that makes decisions like we plan to be here for a long time and delivers legislation in line with what is good for Australians, on everything from a gas export tax to gambling.Nordic countries have for decades operated as minority governments, which has led to a consensus culture in lawmaking that reflects the views of the community. And we seem to be pointing to their successes on everything from their sovereign wealth fund to their approach to housing. These are all things that people raise with me frequently. They also ask: how do we change this?Australians could consider this when we next go to the polls. I’ve seen the power of a government having to negotiate. In the last term of parliament, bills had to pass after negotiation with multiple independents and minor parties. It led to much better, more robust legislation. Minority government is something we need to consider embracing rather than being mugged by the major parties’ self-interested scare campaigns if we want better outcomes for the long term.David Pocockis the independent senator for the Australian Capital TerritoryIn Australia,Gambling Help Onlineis available on 1800 858 858. TheNational Debt Helplineis at 1800 007 007. The crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsGamblingOpinionDavid PocockIndependentsAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: My Edinburgh fringe odyssey: ‘The nudity is expressive, shocking – sometimes harrowing’ | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: There are 3,649 shows at the fringe this year, but how many embody its spirit of radical experimentation? I took a journey through foam, lube and gore to find out ...
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: There are 3,649 shows at the fringe this year, but how many embody its spirit of radical experimentation? I took a journey through foam, lube and gore to find out ...
Content: Arifa Akbar hunts for out-there shows.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArifa Akbar hunts for out-there shows.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026My Edinburgh fringe odyssey: ‘The nudity is expressive, shocking – sometimes harrowing’There are 3,649 shows at the fringe this year, but how many embody its spirit of radical experimentation? I took a journey through foam, lube and gore to find out ...Arifa AkbarWed 19 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomewhere in Edinburgh,a man is drinking his own urine. Elsewhere, the story of a religious sect that commands its followers touse “butt plugs”plays out as a musical. In yet another room, a comedian sings the same songover and over for an hour.It is shows like these that have sustained the welcomingly weird and ungovernable lore of theEdinburgh festivalfringe. In recent years, though, the annual jamboree has been accused of becoming an increasingly commercially savvy entity. The radical experimentalism might just be intact, but does this now sit at the fringes of the fringe, rather than its centre?Francesca Moody, one of the festival’s superproducers, says that putting on a show here has become increasingly expensive. When she producedPhoebe Waller-Bridge’s stage version of Fleabagin 2013, it cost about £10,000. By 2019, when she co-producedRichard Gadd’s Baby Reindeer, it cost about £40,000. Putting on a one-person show now, she says, costs her closer to £100,000.The reasons for this, which have beenwell reported, include soaring accommodation costs, funding cuts and rising production costs. Some have argued that this might dial down the risky spirit on which the fringe was founded. The ethos was different when the financial risks were not as high, says Moody. “It was a space for messing around and building your craft, your sense of taste. As a producer or as an artist, you’re working out what your voice is, and doing that over a number of years.”Artists and producers may now want more out of it too: to be scouted for the big-time with a transfer to London or, the ultimate dream, a television series in the mould of Fleabag or Baby Reindeer. Some high-profile productions have lined up transfers before their shows debut at the fringe. The Australian writer-performer Hannah Reilly’s showRoleplay, about a woman who becomes a “slutfluencer” – which is also produced by Moody – already has a London transfer. As doesBigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It, featuring a clown duo who cause chaos in their town after faking Bigfoot sightings. Elsewhere, the musical Bliss, which turns the traditional fairytale story on its head, will travel to London with the backing of the entertainment company ATG.Moody believes the low-budget gems are still out there though. Comedian and fellow fringe veteran Rory Bremner agrees. Although he is a big name at the festival, with his latest show, Making an Impression, playing at the 1,000-seater McEwan Hall, he still likes to test out “work-in-development” material alongside new, unknown acts. “It’s an opportunity to try stuff that I’ve written in the last couple of days,” he says. These below-the-radar gigs take place in pubs or tents, sometimes containing as few as six people in the audience and often raising money for charity.View image in fullscreenSet for the big time? Xhloe and Natasha, the clown duo in Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMoody thinks small-scale, risk-taking work will find a home at the fringe because people are “hungry” for it. “There is always going to be a weird, idiosyncratic little show in a back room or basement that people discover at the fringe. It’s just about finding it.”So off I go on my very own theatrical odyssey to discover the “fringe of the fringe” and find an interactive act with a surprising degree of danger attached. Truthmachine plays out in an upstairs room of the city’s Quaker Meeting House and is produced by the Australian company Counterpilot. A maximum of 12 people at any one time sign up to a 30-minute participatory show with a lie detector test at its heart. If that exudes Jeremy Kyle vibes, it proves much more thoughtful and transgressive than the gimmick it first appears to be. We are seated before our own voting machines for a warm-up, in which people are selected at random, put under a spotlight and asked to state “yes” or “no” to questions that range from the conceptual (“has capitalism failed?”) to the icky (“have you ever touched yourself at night?”). It has an interrogatory feel, as exposing as a game of spin the bottle, but with strangers. I find myself wondering what might come next, and where the nearest exits are.There is no time to escape because, before you can say “polygraph machine”, one of us is chosen to be strapped up to one. It is hardly coercive – the lie detector test is the basis on which we have all convened – but I still grow edgy. A young woman is chosen and begins boldly answering questions that become more intimate while her heartbeat and other biological measurements are taken, giving us the probability of her telling a lie as a percentage. “Have you ever had a sexual dream about a family member?” she is asked. I feel everyone in the room wince. Then: “Have you had a sexual experience in public?” “Did you enjoy it?” “Was it your idea?” “Did you want to get caught?” There are existential inquiries too: “Do you think you will get what you want?” “Can everyone be forgiven?”Things have turned a shade Black Mirror, it seems. This is not so much a playful game of truth or dare as a carefully orchestrated experiment around group dynamics and exposure. What are we prepared to share? What will we hide from others? What brings up shame or social inadequacy? I am surprised by how relieved I am not to be the person strapped up to the biometric sensors, but also how much my discomfort tells me about myself.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Collins in Succubus, a one-woman horror comedy.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianI come out blinking into the daylight and head to Succubus, a one-woman horror show that features a trigger warning of cannibalism. A debut written and acted by burlesque performer Georgina Collins (AKA Strawberry Duvall), it was inspired partly by her experience with doctors dismissing her medical symptoms as “hormonal issues”. The play touches on medical misogyny but in dark, satirical ways, its social commentary as sharp-fanged as the female killer at its centre. Its conspicuously low-budget set design adds to its semblance of a B-movie feminist horror gore-fest, especially its props, which include a string of fake sausages representing human intestines.Succubus is performed at the 60-seater Dexter stage at the Underbelly and is packed on the day I attend. Directed by Grainne Robson, it is not just an imaginative take on the notion of the monstrous feminine but finely crafted in its writing. Emily Ritchie and Zara Jayant, former theatre publicists, are its producers. “When we started the company, there were so many artists whose only resort was to wait for the door to open. We thought: ‘Why not build the door ourselves?’” says Jayant. Succubus was financed on a profit-share model, its £6,500 budget raised through crowdfunding, a supper-club, a horror-themed film quiz night, a burlesque cabaret night and a raffle.View image in fullscreenCraig Manson as Bunny, an aspiring theatre starlet … and a serial killerPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe night show at Summerhall Arts is another horror, in the shape of Bunny! It is the name of Craig Manson’s drag alter ego, who emerges in a blond wig and off-the-shoulder gold dress with tufts of chest hair peeping from beneath. The self-produced show is gloriously scrappy but with a serious sting. Bunny is a struggling performer, desperate for a breakthrough after a decade of rejections and living in penury. In real life, Manson has been vocal about the state of arts funding in Scotland. In a blend of comedy and song, Bunny decides that the only way to correct the inequities is to kill off her competitors, beginning with an artistic director and graduating to famous actors and artists. It is fizzy entertainment, intelligently barbed.So is Mother, Maiden and Crone at the Bedlam theatre, a loose modern-day adaptation of Macbeth by an Edinburgh-based drag troupe. Shakespeare is occasionally winched into a plotline involving the drama of a gay bar (a hen do for a bride called McBride), with a violent denouement on a dancefloor involving fatal quantities of foam and lube.View image in fullscreenModern-day take on Macbeth … Mother, Maiden and Crone.Photograph: Lou Mccurdy @Loumacphotography/Loumac PhotographyThe show had a limited run in a hotel basement at last year’s fringe and has been financed through fundraisers. The auditorium is filled this year and I feel as if I have been let in on a thrilling local secret.The fringe is famed for discovering student talent, namely through the Edinburgh University group Footlights, but the show I plump for is off the beaten-track of university comedy societies. Moth And Dog Are Dying to Get Out is a play with enormous ambition, selected for the National student drama festival at Curve theatre, in Leicester, this spring. It features two teenage boys navigating same-sex desire for each other under the oppressive forces of homophobia, peer pressure and strong-man masculinity. Written by full-time student Aidan Monks and inspired by the writings of the poet Peter Scalpello, it stars Dylan Swain as Dog and Ben Stuart as Moth. They are schoolboys, one of whom has been “outed” as gay with a graphic image stuck on his locker (a photo of his “spread arsehole” from Grindr). It plays out in flashbacks and forwards, the narrative jagged yet emotionally tender. It is a heart-rending play, as lo-fi as Succubus in its production values but full of promise and led by two brave performances.There are other shows tucked away in studio spaces that encapsulate the spirit of experiment, such as Letícia Rodrigues’s autobiographical production about body size,116 Grams: A Play to Lose Weight, which shocks with its expressive, sometimes harrowing, nudity.Thank You, F**k You and I’m Sorry(was there ever a more fringe-appropriate title?), is in the studio space at C Arts and is an intense, sung-through requiem that mourns a dead father. There is an audience of three on the night I attend but Welsh performer Jonathan Powell (also known as Jonny Forever) powers on, playing violin and guitar alongside the vocals. It is entirely self-funded and deeply personal.The fringiest shows, I realise, are visible in plain sight if you look, and often nestling in the smaller spaces of established venues. Bunny! is in the modestly sized Anatomy lecture theatre at Summerhall. Another jewel of the festival is in an even smaller basement space in the venue, the former gents locker room at Summerhall.QFWFQ, with Los Angeles performer Gregory Nussen, directed by Hannah Pilkes, is an enormously accomplished riff on Italo Calvino’s novel, If on a Winter’s Night a Traveller, with its own postmodern stops and starts, direct addresses and reflections on the construction of story. It is a small but exquisitely formed creature of the festival, full of experimental energy, intelligent inquiry and, most of all, an exciting mix of mischief and danger. Nussen leads one audience member to the toilet, makes phone calls and tells stories on stories. They are a natural comic but switch to a gripping dramatic tone when they begin their stories of coming out as non-binary, going to Jewish summer camp and then on a tour of the concentration camps in Poland. Nussen arrives at Zionism, the genocide in Gaza, the brutality of Israel’s government before they interrupt themselves with another layer of story, another voice, which states that this is too dangerous a story to be aired.As the winner of the best solo show at the 2025 Hollywood Fringe, it is not exactly an Edinburgh festival fringe discovery, but it is an amazing find from a punter’s point of view, immaculately structured, surreal and labyrinthine. The invention and imagination makes me tingle. It is better than the work I’ve seen on bigger Edinburgh stages. The best of the fringe, found in this basement room, and stumbled across before noon. This is what the festival is all about.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m not Mr Saturday Night’: the highbrow brilliance of Ahir Shah, past winner of comedy’s top prize  | Ahir Shah | The Guardian
description: Three years ago, he won the Edinburgh comedy award with a work in progress. Now he’s back with a show inspired by Gerard Manley Hopkins and Friedrich Nietzsche. Isn’t this all a bit grownup?
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Three years ago, he won the Edinburgh comedy award with a work in progress. Now he’s back with a show inspired by Gerard Manley Hopkins and Friedrich Nietzsche. Isn’t this all a bit grownup?
Content: ‘If you’re encased in lead, how do you get golden?’ … Ahir Shah, whose new show is called Golden.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘If you’re encased in lead, how do you get golden?’ … Ahir Shah, whose new show is called Golden.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianAhir ShahInterview‘I’m not Mr Saturday Night’: the highbrow brilliance of Ahir Shah, past winner of comedy’s top prizeBrian LoganThree years ago, he won the Edinburgh comedy award with a work in progress. Now he’s back with a show inspired by Gerard Manley Hopkins and Friedrich Nietzsche. Isn’t this all a bit grownup?Wed 19 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmong past winners of the Edinburgh comedy award, few seemed less likely when the starter’s pistol fired thanAhir Shah in 2023. Not because Shah wasn’t a contender: he had been nominated twice before. But that year he arrived on the fringe with a mere work in progress, not even eligible for the award. Shah’s director, the greatAdam Brace, had recently died and the comic had just returned to the stage after a break from comedy. But then Ends, a tribute to the performer’s late grandfather and a hymn to multicultural Britain, began gathering steam. Shah reclassified it as a work-now-finished and, toa chorus of rapturous acclaim, it bagged the biggest prize in world comedy.Three years on, he is returning with the follow-up: less uncut diamond this time and more, he hopes, a polished gem. But didn’t the success of Ends prove polish was unnecessary? “You can get very in your head approaching the fringe, thinking: ‘Well, it has to be absolutely locked in by August because x thousand pounds are on the line,’” Shah admits. So doing a work in progress allowed him to “quiet some of those voices – and have less of a panic attack about what you’re going to say”.double quotation markBy God, I’ve lain in bed thinking I’m the worst person who ever existedNotwithstanding his patrician accent (he once joked that he sounds as if “I’ve been colonised by my own voice”), Shah is no stranger to low confidence. His approach to standup is to ask: “How are you justifying breaking the silence that exists in this room prior to you walking out?” With Ends, the justification was ample. Like all the Londoner’s work, the show teemed with ideas and erudition, this time at the service of a tale (as Shah now describes it) of “the sacrifices people are willing to make in their own lives for subsequent generations. It was about what families do for one another.”But the show, pulled together as Rishi Sunak became prime minister, was also about the UK, and how it had changed since Shah’s grandfather moved here in the 1960s. “I couldn’t help but think about the incomprehensible shift that had to occur over 60 years to make something my grandfather could never have conceived of come to pass.” The UK, Shah declared in the show, is “the least racist country in the world”: not an argument audiences expected from a regular guest onFrankie Boyle’s New World Order and a comic once known for firebrand lefty polemic.View image in fullscreen‘You can only tell sad and bad stories for so long’ … Ahir Shah.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian“I completely understand the temptation to do the whole ‘rainy fascism island’ thing,” he says. “I’ve succumbed to it many a time. But for most of my adult life, we’ve reflexively told only very sad and bad stories about ourselves. And you can only go on like that for so long. As an individual, you can lie in bed saying: ‘I’m the worst person who ever existed. This is all pointless.’ You can do that – and, by God, I’ve given it a good go. But it’s no way to lead a fulfilling, three-dimensional life. As a collective, we need positive stories as well.”That positivity helped secure a stellar future for Ends, which toured the world (including India, “which was really emotionally significant”) and was broadcast on Netflix. And so the dreams came true for a comic who cut his standup teeth aged 17. Golden, his new set, is inspired by aGerard Manley Hopkinspoem and “section 341 of The Gay Science by Friedrich Nietzsche”. It finds Shah on the threshold of middle-age, now married, planning a family, spooked by the looming responsibility.“These are the issues of capital-G grownup life. All of a sudden there is someone more important than you sharing your roof. There are people who all this mattersfor. There are obligations that are going to bear down on you again and again. And there’s a voice saying: ‘What if you can’t do it? What if you’re not good enough?’”This time with reference to his mother’s life story, Shah is confronting those demons in a show that takes its title from Hopkins’ verse The Leaden Echo and the Golden Echo. “The leaden echo,” says the comic, “is the inevitability of decay. I call it in the show the cold, repetitive, mechanistic, obligatory forevers that every adult in our society is subject to, my mother more than most. And if that’s what encases you in lead, then how do you get golden?”It’s a fine question to be asking for someone who got gold on his last full fringe visit, and is recalibrating his ambitions in light of that success. The Edinburgh comedy award, he says, “was what I dreamed of winning when I started out. I did that. Let’s see what happens now.” One thing he won’t be doing is diluting his highbrow tastes in pursuit of a mainstream audience. “I’m not Mr Saturday Night, I’m not that guy,” he says cheerfully. “An infrastructure exists around comedians that encourages you to underestimate audiences. But I don’t accept that. As long as you build your work out of jokes, what you build is up to you. And what could be more freeing, more wonderful than that?”Ahir Shah: Golden is atPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August.
