title: ‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reunite | Music | The Guardian
description: Alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer created a feminist punk vernacular that’s still inspiring the likes of Olivia Rodrigo. They recall the clarity and conviction of their historic teenage exploits
Author: Jenn Pelly
Headline: Alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer created a feminist punk vernacular that’s still inspiring the likes of Olivia Rodrigo. They recall the clarity and conviction of their historic teenage exploits
Content: ‘I wanted people to feel what I was feeling’ … (L-R) Tracy Sawyer and Corin Tucker of Heavens to Betsy.Photograph: Chloe AftelView image in fullscreen‘I wanted people to feel what I was feeling’ … (L-R) Tracy Sawyer and Corin Tucker of Heavens to Betsy.Photograph: Chloe AftelMusicInterview‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reuniteJenn PellyAlongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer created a feminist punk vernacular that’s still inspiring the likes of Olivia Rodrigo. They recall the clarity and conviction of their historic teenage exploitsWed 19 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in June, a cut-and-paste photocopied flyer began appearing on telegraph poles around Portland, Oregon, promoting a DIY show by an apparently defunct band at an intimate community space. The band hadn’t mentioned it online, but hopeful fans bought every ticket anyway. Their bet paid off: the gig really was the first in 32 years for Heavens to Betsy, the pioneering feminist punk duo of drummer Tracy Sawyer and singer-guitarist Corin Tucker – the latter’s band beforeSleater-Kinneyunleashed her visceral vibrato unto the world. Tucker proudly made the flyer herself.Heavens to Betsy were barely out of high school when they played their very first show, 35 years ago this week, in Olympia, Washington, a two-song set as part of a now-mythical indie fest dubbed the International Pop Underground Convention. The festival also featured the likes of Fugazi, Bikini Kill and Melvins; meanwhile Heavens to Betsy had practised only a couple times. Before an audience of about 100, Sawyer was so terrified that all she could think was, “This has to be over soon.”This summer’s gig was less frightening, looking out on kids the same age that Tucker and Sawyer were when they started the band. “They were singing along to a lot of the songs,” Tucker, now 53, says on a video call from her home in Portland. “They knew all the words and were screaming them at the top of their lungs.” After the gig, Sawyer, 52, recalls from her yard in Oakland, California, “20-year-old kids came up to me and said, ‘I’m learning to play drums by listening to Heavens to Betsy records.’”View image in fullscreen‘I will decide my life’ … Sawyer (left) and Tucker.Photograph: Hannah SternsheinThose early-90s feminist-revenge songs – about body image, sexual abuse, abortion, periods, worker exploitation, defying a world that conditions women to be small – will underpin the band’s upcoming tour of the US, as well as Baby’s Gone, a new LP collecting a 1992 rare demo tape and two 7in EPs. That inventive eight-song demo was recorded by Molly Neuman of Bratmobile with a four-track she checked out of the media library from Evergreen State College in Olympia, and only circulated on around 100 cassettes dubbed by the band.Active from 1991 to 1994, Heavens to Betsy released one album, Calculated, and rounded out riot grrrl’s OG trifecta alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile (who have both reunited in recent years to rapturous crowds). Turning their spare setup into an extreme sound, Heavens to Betsy made songs that were emotional, fearsome and dead serious. “I will decide my life / No man is gonna rule my life,” they declared on Decide.Riot grrrl records and zines – which, in Tucker’s words, put academic feminist ideas into a teen-girl vernacular – have struck a chord with every subsequent generation, echoing through the DIY underground on to the 2010s defined by Tavi Gevinson’s Rookie magazine. Olivia Rodrigo claims it as an influence; Bikini Kill will play her women-led Daisy Chain Fields festival in California this month. But the enduring power of this incendiary music has always been how its rawness leaves the door open, telling fans that they could do this, too.Heavens to Betsy: Terrorist (live at Turn! Turn! Turn! in Portland) – videoHeavens to Betsy were originally signed to Kill Rock Stars. Last autumn, the label approached Tucker and Sawyer about a long-overdue wide release for the demo. “The whole thing felt like an impossible dream,” Tucker says. “I thought I had lost the physical master a long time ago.” But the label was able to make a new master from the cassette, and as they emailed back and forth, they slyly floated another idea: “And you guys could do a show, maybe?”“I think both of us were like, I don’t know!” Tucker laughs nervously.The duo had only kept in touch “a little bit”, Sawyer says, in the decades since their breakup; both are mothers of two. “I was apprehensive about the thought of playing these songs from when we were so young,” Sawyer admits. “Playing them now in our 50s felt daunting, like, does that even make sense? A whole lifetime has passed. But the more we talked, and the more I started listening to the songs again, it absolutely made sense.”Tucker hadn’t listened to some of those spartan demo recordings since the tape came out. “There’s a really particular voice with Heavens to Betsy, a way of writing a song that speaks to the clarity you have as a young person:This is wrong. This is not OK.I felt really energised and empowered by that voice coming back into my life,” she says. That invigorating clarity pierces Heavens to Betsy songs in bloodcurdling, teen-girl screams – which, Tucker concedes, she could not realistically pull off in 2026 and make it through a whole show. But she hopes her conviction will communicate that anger. “It’s really important to me that that comes across in a way that’s absolutely not softened for people,” Tucker says. “The voice of Heavens to Betsy was uncompromising, unfiltered and it never apologised for its rage and revenge-seeking.”Tucker and Sawyer first met as middle schoolers in Eugene, Oregon, bonding over REM, the Cure, and Depeche Mode at sleepovers. They saw shows constantly – the Replacements, Firehose – and watched the music documentary Athens, GA: Inside/Out relentlessly. Their fixation on the Athens scene – including REM and the likes of B-52’s and Pylon – incited what Tucker calls a “pretty bonkers” and penniless cross-country train trip in summer 1990. The pair rented an apartment for a month to “study the scene”, bought a drum kit, watched Pylon through the window of the 40 Watt Club (they were too young to enter), and dubbed themselves Heavens to Betsy.By the time Tucker arrived at Evergreen State College in Olympia that autumn, she had already crossed paths with Bratmobile singer and Girl Germs zinemaker Allison Wolfe, who hipped Tucker to the fiercely independent Oly scene. That year, Tucker made a film about local music and closely studied the bands she saw live: Beat Happening, Mecca Normal, Calamity Jane. Heavens to Betsy was still just an idea, but Tucker wrote lyrics to a song about menstruation and societal shame she called My Red Self. “I started telling people about our band when we hadn’t played a single show,” Tucker says. “Or had a practice. No songs either,” she laughs. “We had a concept.”View image in fullscreenHeavens to Betsy performing in Kentucky in 1992.Photograph: Courtesy of the bandThat’s an instructive blueprint. “You manifest it,” Sawyer offers.“And believe in it,” Tucker adds. “You have to create the world before anything else, and cling to it. That’s true about every creative idea: you need to commit to that world. And onceyoudo, then you can make it real for everyone else.”When they were asked to play “Girl Night” at the International Pop Underground Convention, they anxiously accepted and Tucker sprang into action: many of the songs on their demo were written in her childhood bedroom. Fugazi’s Ian MacKaye was so impressed by Heavens to Betsy’s live debut that he sought them out to shake their hands.“There was an openness to my voice that I think grabbed people right away,” Tucker says. “There wasn’t much filter between my emotions and my voice, so when I sang, it was really sad and angry at the same time. We kept our music really simple and focused. I wanted people to feel what I was feeling. People cried at that show. There was this movement of girls that were like,I need to talk about these things that we’re not supposed to talk about.I think my voice was just waiting for that door to open.”At the centre of Baby’s Gone is a taut, unflinching song called My Secret in which Tucker lucidly blasts an abuser. She had been influenced by the directness of Bikini Kill frontperson Kathleen Hanna’s writing. “I felt brave because of what was happening around us,” she says. “It made me realise that I needed to let out my own feelings about things that had happened to me. It put me in the position of power.” Sawyer’s minimal, pounding beat “created this shield and weapon”, Tucker adds. “I was able to harness that into a song about being sexually abused. It turned the tables on everything, and it let go of everything, and it also freaked everyone out. It was incredible. It changed my life in a way. I was able to open a door to how maybe the rest of my life was gonna go. I didn’t need to hold on to those feelings any more.”Heavens to Betsy’s songs were sometimes written in character, but informed by reality. The title track of Baby’s Gone narrates a young woman’s decision to have an abortion under conditions that leave her dead. “Back then, you couldn’t even say the word ‘abortion’, so there was a lot of euphemism around it,” Tucker says. “Young women had to deal with all of the consequences of heterosexual sex, which took all of the pressure off men in our society. I find that to be incredibly unfair.” Tucker wrote the song to ask, “What if the young woman who died having an abortion came back and wrote about her experience? What if a ghost came back and wrote the song? How would that make you feel?” She lets out a self-aware laugh.“Connecting with your rage and your anger, in a way that lets it out – it feels important,” she adds, especially in light of the current political nightmares. “The past few years have been awful, and we really don’t have a way to process it. Liking things on my phone doesn’t cut it for me.”The Baby’s Gone songs excavate trauma – “I want you to stay dead!” Tucker fumes at a memory – allowing the band’s one album, 1994’s grungier Calculated, to more explicitly claim power. “The first songs we wrote were really personal, and they were out of sheer necessity,” Tucker says. A few seem to describe vexed mother-daughter dynamics. “That relationship is always ripe for conflict,” she says. “Part of becoming a person in the world is differentiating yourself and saying, ‘No, I’m going to do things my way.’ Being a mom myself now, I’ve been on both sides of that, and it’s complicated.”View image in fullscreenTucker and Sawyer today.Photograph: Chloe AftelWe’ve spoken for an hour and a half when Sawyer has to leave for a work meeting (she has a job at a pet supply company). Tucker and I keep chatting. The Heavens to Betsy reunion has offered an opportunity to revisit the music as well as to rekindle their friendship. “Getting a second chance feels like a real gift,” she says. “I’ve really enjoyed getting to know what Tracy’s life has been like and what we have in common.” When they drifted apart after Calculated came out, something they blame on having poor communication skills at that age, Tucker had already formed Sleater-Kinney alongside Carrie Brownstein, then guitarist in queercore band Excuse 17, who Heavens to Betsy had toured with.Riot grrrl pioneer Kathleen Hanna: ‘A lot of men really get off on watching a woman get angry’Read moreTucker sounds not especially fazed by where Heavens to Betsy might fit into modern music. But I mention Wednesday’s Karly Hartzman, and she joyfully recalls a Portugal festival where she heard her scream from stage. She also brings up Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain fest: “It’s both cool and terribly sad that we’re still holding a rock show to try and talk about our needs instead of having the kind of cultural, political, and economic power that would give us full equality.”I ask about the lessons Tucker has gleaned from returning to this formative period of her life. “That courage you have as a young person to speak the truth and to find out what that means for you, that’s a really special thing to learn how to do, and it’s not always easy to maintain that when you’re becoming a mom and taking care of other people,” she says. “I do think there’s something really special about returning to Heavens to Betsy as my youngest goes off to college. I suddenly am rediscovering, what do I want, and who am I? There’s something very full circle about reconnecting with this voice that was like, ‘These are my feelings. This is my truth.’”Baby’s Gone is released via Kill Rock Stars on 16 October. Heavens to Betsy tour the US from 17 October.Explore more on these topicsMusicPunkIndieSleater-KinneyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for kd lang | Culture | The Guardian
description: As her supergroup with Neko Case and Laura Veirs celebrates the 10th anniversary of its sublime album, the Ingénue herself will answer your questions
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: As her supergroup with Neko Case and Laura Veirs celebrates the 10th anniversary of its sublime album, the Ingénue herself will answer your questions
Content: From left: Neko Case, kd lang and Laura Veirs.Photograph: Jason QuigleyView image in fullscreenFrom left: Neko Case, kd lang and Laura Veirs.Photograph: Jason QuigleyFilm & Music reader interviewCulturePost your questions for kd langAs her supergroup with Neko Case and Laura Veirs celebrates the 10th anniversary of its sublime album, the Ingénue herself will answer your questionsLaura SnapesWed 19 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdecade ago, three of the finest voices in Americana got together to make a sublime supergroup record. Case/Lang/Veirs, in case the title didn’t make it plain, brought together Neko Case of the New Pornographers, stalwart Portland songwriter Laura Veirs and kd lang, the Grammy-winning Canadian country icon. Sadly, that glorious album has remained a one-off – though a new anniversary release includes a gorgeous never-before-heard song, Accidental Tattoo – but happily, lang is joining the Guardian for a very rare interview to answer your questions.Case/Lang/Veirs: Accidental Tattoo – videoMaybe you’d like to know secrets from behind the scenes of making this record in lang’s loft and Veirs’ dining room, or about lang’s relationship withthe late, great Tony Bennett, her animal rights advocacy, what the Edmonton country-swing scene was like in the mid-80s before lang became a country star and later mainstream icon, or what she and Cindy Crawford talked about when they posed for quite possiblythe greatest magazine photoshootof all time. What was Roy Orbison like to work with, is new music on the horizon, or what her contemporaryconstant cravingsare? Or anything else indeed.Post your questions in the comments bymidday BST on 25 August 2026and the best answers will appear in a future edition of the reader interview.Explore more on these topicsCultureFilm & Music reader interviewfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’ll be sorry you told me this!’: the 98-year-old composer who gets musicians – even bassoonists - on their feet | Music | The Guardian
description: Scotland’s Thea Musgrave is still writing radical music with perambulatory soloists and a message of hopefulness. Her latest work, for bassoonist Amy Harman, comes to the Proms this weekend
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Scotland’s Thea Musgrave is still writing radical music with perambulatory soloists and a message of hopefulness. Her latest work, for bassoonist Amy Harman, comes to the Proms this weekend
Content: ‘The light at the tunnel always returns’ … Thea Musgrave in 2014.Photograph: Bryan SheffieldView image in fullscreen‘The light at the tunnel always returns’ … Thea Musgrave in 2014.Photograph: Bryan SheffieldTom Service on musicMusic‘You’ll be sorry you told me this!’: the 98-year-old composer who gets musicians – even bassoonists - on their feetTom ServiceScotland’s Thea Musgrave is still writing radical music with perambulatory soloists and a message of hopefulness. Her latest work, for bassoonist Amy Harman, comes to the Proms this weekendWed 19 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.58 EDTShareThea Musgrave is a phenomenon. Born in Scotland in 1928, the composer has lived in the US since the early 70s, but has lost none of her accent, her infectious optimism, and her drive to keep writing. As she told me from her home in California, with a joyfully rolling laugh, “I’ve got to this age, and from now on I’m going to do what the fuck I want to do”. That includes her latest opera, on Virginia Woolf’s novel Orlando – Orlando: An Escapade – which will premiere at theBuxton festival next year, and a new bassoon concerto for Amy Harman, Out of the Darkness, which you can hear atthe Proms this weekend, on 23 August.View image in fullscreenThe composer Malcolm Williamson with Musgrave in London in April 1965.Photograph: Erich Auerbach/Getty ImagesThe bassoon concerto develops one of the central innovations of Musgrave’s life and career, which she’s still intensifying and exploring in her 99th year: what she calls her “dramatic-abstract” approach to her orchestral compositions, in which the players aren’t a single collective told what to do by a conductor’s gestures, but instead are released as individual characters and identities.Musgrave’s inspiration to work this way came from a dream. She was taking conducting lessons and, she told me, “One night I dreamt that I was conducting a big orchestra, and all of a sudden one of the players, the clarinettist, stood up and wouldn’t sit down, so I signalled to the brass players to stand up and play, and shut the clarinet up.”The very next morning, Musgrave was commissioned by the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra to write a a new work, which became her Concerto for Orchestra in 1967. In that piece, as she says, “the clarinet stands up, defies the conductor, and other soloists get up too, so the conductor has to get the whole brass section in to drown them out” – exactly as in her dream. It’s music of febrile and instantly communicative drama, as Musgrave turns the volatile musical relationships between every section of the orchestra into something visceral and tangible.In her Clarinet Concerto, written a couple of years later, Musgrave goes even further: the clarinettist walks around the orchestra, playing with the smaller groups that she splits the orchestra into, and the soloist controls the flow of the piece as much as the conductor. In her Horn Concerto, the soloist is amplified by the orchestral horns who eventually surround the stage and the audience. And in a later concerto,Two’s Company, for the unique combination of oboe and percussion, played by Nicholas Daniel and Evelyn Glennie at the Proms in 2007, the soloists start as distant musical satellites, separated on stage and in their soundworlds, but grow to find a musical friendship and togetherness.double quotation markIn Musgrave's Clarinet Concerto, the clarinettist walks around the orchestra and controls the flow of the piece as much as the conductor.Daniel introduced Musgrave to Harman last year, when the composer’s operaMary, Queen of Scotswas staged at English National Opera. “He said, this isAmy Harman, and you have to write a concerto for her,” Musgrave tells me.View image in fullscreenRupert Charlesworth and Heidi Stober in Mary, Queen of Scots by Thea Musgrave at the London Coliseum in 2025.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHarman told her that she can walk around when she’s playing. “What, with that big heavy bulky instrument?” Musgrave asked. “She took the bassoon out and did exactly that, and I said: ‘You’ll be sorry you told me this!’”Harman will indeed be moving around the orchestra throughout Out of the Darkness. “But there has to be a reason she’s doing this: and here’s my reason, which is to do with Covid,” says Musgrave. “The whole work starts in great sadness. Everyone, including the bassoonist, is very gloomy. All of a sudden, the concertmaster [first violinist] plays a little melody, which is like the voice of hope.”View image in fullscreenMusgrave in New York in August 1977.Photograph: Marty Reichenthal/APHarman encounters virtuosic trumpeters and double basses playing above her in weird ethereal registers on her journey towards that sound of hopefulness. The end isn’t the solution, Musgrave says, but a sense of “determination to do something about the situation we’re in. It’s the darkness and the light together. We all come through dark places in our lives and you have to deal with it and face it in the best way possible. The light at the tunnel always returns. Sometimes you have to wait many a year, but eventually it does arrive. You just hope it’s not too long,” she says, with another of those irresistible laughs.This week Tom has been listening to:Musgrave’s concertoson the Lyrita albumThea Musgrave: Concertos, Monologue & Excursions. Why aren’t these pieces – and her other concertos, for bass clarinet, trumpet, viola, andmany more– played and programmed every week? They’re fearlessly direct and dramatic, totally uncompromising but completely communicative.Explore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musicProms 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing review – like a horror movie … only this is real life | Television | The Guardian
description: In 2022, Rory Kennedy exposed the aviation safety scandal in which 346 people died – but since then, a plane door has blown out mid-flight and more whistleblowers have come to the fore. Will anyone pay for this?
Author: Ellen E Jones
Headline: In 2022, Rory Kennedy exposed the aviation safety scandal in which 346 people died – but since then, a plane door has blown out mid-flight and more whistleblowers have come to the fore. Will anyone pay for this?
Content: Nightmarish … Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenNightmarish … Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewFreefall: A Reckoning for Boeing review – like a horror movie … only this is real lifeIn 2022, Rory Kennedy exposed the aviation safety scandal in which 346 people died – but since then, a plane door has blown out mid-flight and more whistleblowers have come to the fore. Will anyone pay for this?Ellen E JonesWed 19 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is unfortunate that a sequel was required to Rory Kennedy’s 2022 documentary feature, which alleged that the profit-driven culture at a US aeronautics firm led to two plane crashes and the deaths of 346 people. But given the lack of corporate accountability evident at the end ofDownfall: The Case Against Boeing– and the apparent complicity of regulatory body the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) – it was inevitable.Freefall: A Reckoning forBoeingopens with a rundown of a significant development in the story: the mysterious death in March 2024 of John Barnett, a former Boeing employee turned whistleblower. Barnett, a contributor in the first film, was in the middle of a deposition when he was found dead at his hotel, which investigators ruled a suicide. Is this another casualty to add to Boeing’s mounting death toll? And is the alarming aviation safety scandal – supposedly resolved in November 2020, when the FAA lifted its grounding order on the Boeing 737 Max – in fact still ongoing?This is the urgent claim of many of this film’s contributors. Some lost loved ones in the two Boeing plane crashes that happened within five months of each other – Lion Air Flight 610, which went down in October 2018, killing all 189 people on board, and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, which crashed in March 2019. One contributor, Naoise Connolly Ryan, lost her husband and the father of her two small children, Michael Ryan, when he was killed alongside 156 others on Flight 302.Others are Boeing whistleblowers who have gone public since the last film, inspired by it. “John Barnett was a lighthouse,” says one. “When I first started at the company, he was pointing people in the right direction. He is continuing to do that now.” Hidden camera footage from Boeing’s Dreamliner assembly plant in South Carolina shows anonymised workers averring that nothing – not even a free luxury holiday – could tempt them to fly on the planes they manufacture.View image in fullscreenLost loved ones … Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThere is a vast moral chasm between those determined to do all within their power to prevent further loss of life and the Boeing leadership. The only gap more glaring is the one betweentwo shoddily outsourced sectionsof fuselage on a 737 Max. This isn’t a horror film, but you’ll struggle to find many movie scenes more nightmarish than Freefall’s reconstruction of the January 2024 incident when a door plug blew out mid-flight (it was missing all four of its crucial bolts) and several passenger oxygen masks malfunctioned. Barnett had warned of this danger years earlier. His concerns were not only ignored, but also he was disciplined for having raised them.Beside the whistleblowers, there is another group of heroes in Freefall. Kennedy’s camera often cedes the floor to impressively fired-up politicians, such as the Missouri senator Josh Hawley, who, at a Senate hearing, challenges the now-retired Boeing CEO Dave Calhoun on his $32.8m 2023 salary, up 45% from 2022: “What is it you get paid to do exactly?” (Calhoun has not been charged with criminal wrongdoing.)It’s worth noting here that Rory Kennedy is not just any Kennedy, but one oftheKennedys: the youngest child of the former senator and US attorney general Robert F Kennedy and his wife, Ethel Kennedy, who was pregnant with Rory when RFK was assassinated in June 1968. It was en route to Rory Kennedy’s wedding three decades later that the plane carrying John F Kennedy Jr, his wife and his sister-in-law went down, killing them all. So this is a film-maker who understands not only what it feels like to lose family in a sudden and shocking tragedy, but also those Camelot-era American values of progress and public service – values Boeing itself once exemplified.Kennedy’s previous projects include the Emmy-winningGhosts of Abu Ghraib and the Oscar-nominated Last Days in Vietnam. Freefallis a clear-eyed, serious-minded film to stand alongside these, but it also echoes a string of other recent documentaries on how, in the neoliberal era, unregulated capital has infiltrated and corrupted such diverse industries as construction (Grenfell: Uncovered), tech (The Social Dilemma) and pharmaceuticals (The Crime of the Century).The pattern of allegations is always the same: an incoming CEO seeks to maximise shareholder profit, whatever the cost to product quality, employee welfare or public safety; warnings are ignored; disaster occurs, then blame is shifted, often with breathtaking shamelessness, on to the dead.Kennedy’s two documentaries gather their participants’ righteous rage steadily enough to burn off the cloud cover of this corporate obfuscation, leaving a clear view of the horizon ahead. In their view, until the individuals in Boeing’s failed leadership face criminal prosecution – as opposed to multimillion-dollar retirement packages – nothing will change.In response to the film-makers’ requests for comment, Boeing stated that some of the claims against the company “remain unfounded” and that “others are issues that Boeing thoroughly addressed or continues to improve upon”.Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVAirline industryBoeingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Shapes and ladders: Edinburgh fringe’s dance shows reach for the sky | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With brute strength and beauty, party tricks and personal revelations, this year’s dance and circus programme has ambition and a spirit of togetherness
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: With brute strength and beauty, party tricks and personal revelations, this year’s dance and circus programme has ambition and a spirit of togetherness
Content: Wildly impressive … Donna Carnow in Dusk/Night/Dawn.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWildly impressive … Donna Carnow in Dusk/Night/Dawn.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewShapes and ladders: Edinburgh fringe’s dance shows reach for the skyWith brute strength and beauty, party tricks and personal revelations, this year’s dance and circus programme has ambition and a spirit of togethernessLyndsey WinshipWed 19 Aug 2026 04.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 06.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you want to be wowed by technical prowess, I recommend taking a trip to see a couple of New York pole dancers, Donna Carnow and Gina Alm, in their Edinburgh fringe show Dusk/Night/Dawn. The pair are wildly impressive performers with just one piece of apparatus, a hanging pole suspended above the stage, on which they climb and spin and balance seemingly on thin air and origami their limbs into impossible shapes, swimming and spiralling through the shadows in mesmerising fashion.What they demonstrate is absolute mastery of their art, Carnow especially – a former dancer and US Pole Art champion. The movement is utterly fluid, despite the brute strength required; the physics of it is so finely tuned but you’re unaware because you’re lost in the flow. That’s what a great performer does, and Dusk/Night/Dawn is in part about performance. At one point their two bodies are writhing under flashing red light, smeared with black paint, and then suddenly the lights come up and it’s like waking up, they’re wiping themselves down, the act’s over. There are all sorts of slippery questions about the dissolving line between person and performer, the nature of fantasy, the pleasure of discovering the power of your own body, and there’s also just the awesome talent.Technical skill, of course, comes in lots of different packages, some of them unexpected. When French dancer Sofiane Chalal gets on stage, people often gasp. “They go, ‘Huh! He’s fat! He can’t dance!” Chalal tells us in his show Bigger. He knows he’s a big guy, always has been, and he’s always been a dancer too because he can move, with thrust and precision, arms flying swiftly through stop-start poses. He dances like a man with something to prove, and one who wants to entertain (beyond hip-hop, he names Charlie Chaplin and Laurel and Hardy as influences). The 35-minute piece is more like a work in progress at the moment, a series of party pieces, but there are some thoughtful voiceovers that hint it could be more – a section about how Chalal is obsessed with not spilling food on himself, because he’ll be judged in a way a slim person never would, is thought-provoking.View image in fullscreenA slow build … Border Bodies.Photograph: @adrianoescanhuela/Adriano Escanhuela PhotographyA big chunk of the fringe programme is made up of international delegations and there’s one dance show in this year’s São Paulo showcase: Border Bodies by choreographer Igor Gasparini and his company TF Cia de Dança. It’s the kind of dance you can zone in and out of – not necessarily a bad thing – contemporary, driven by mood, energy, pulse, flow and a gradually morphing percussion-driven soundtrack. It’s a slow build of a piece for eight dancers, from strained, static poses and the feeling of people under pressure, to joints being slowly oiled, into organic waves of movement. It’s not unison, but it’s unified – spurred by the same rhythm, ruled by the same centre of gravity. The theme is connection across diversity, and this company certainly shows that. The movement itself stops being interesting after a while, but it does build to something, and there is a sense of release by its sweaty, exhausted ending, a togetherness that seeps into the audience too.There’s less peaceful utopia and more unchecked anger in Everybody’s Got a Bomb, which erupts into violence partway through: a throat cut, a piercing assault of primal screams, wrestling and shoving and railing against the world in general. Elsewhere though, the dance itself is a bit polite and could do with more reckless and explosive firepower. Choreographer Riley Fitzgerald, a former dancer with SydneyDanceCompany and Ballet National de Marseille, has clearly got the ideas and ambition, but hasn’t yet quite honed the voice.View image in fullscreenGood concept, cool props … The Pieces by AloftSwedish acrobats Axel Ahl and Sara Sanchez Runsten of the company Below Zero have their own grumbles and disagreements, but they’re played out in a much quieter way in their supremely gentle show Pace, which has some lovely moments. The act they do, hand-to-hand acrobatics, is based on the simplest of connections but there’s a good bit where the couple cease to connect, plagued by petty irritations and missed communication. At one point she throws herself at him and he just doesn’t catch her. Don’t worry, though, they work it out.Exit review – a circus squad who really drive each other up the wallRead moreChicago circus company Aloft have a really good concept and some cool props for their show The Pieces. Each of the six performers has a metal ladder. The ladders can’t really stand on their own, but two ladders together? That’s more stable. And with multiple ladders slotted together you can really start to build something. The metaphor for cooperation and community is not that subtle, but it works, and there’s a great moment where all the ladders make a giant wave shape, with an acrobat riding its crest. All in all, though, the result is rather underwhelming – and not well served by its electronic score. It’s nice enough, but where’s the wow?Dusk/Night/Dawnis at Assembly Roxy until 30 August.Biggeris at French Institute in Scotland until 29 August.Border Bodiesis at Assembly @ Dance Base until 30 August.Paceis at Underbelly’s Circus Hub on the Meadows until 29 August.The Pieces by Aloftis at Underbelly’s Circus Hub on the Meadows until 29 August.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026CircusDanceTheatreEdinburgh festivalFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tom Holland set to earn $100m from Spider-Man: Brand New Day | Spider-Man: Brand New ⁠Day | The Guardian
description: In a year that’s seen the British actor star in the season’s two biggest blockbusters – and marry his co-star from both – he is reportedly earning a huge pay packet thanks to box-office bonuses
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: In a year that’s seen the British actor star in the season’s two biggest blockbusters – and marry his co-star from both – he is reportedly earning a huge pay packet thanks to box-office bonuses
Content: Probably not checking his bank balance … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenProbably not checking his bank balance … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamySpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom Holland set to earn $100m from Spider-Man: Brand New DayIn a year that’s seen the British actor star in the season’s two biggest blockbusters – and marry his co-star from both – he is reportedly earning a huge pay packet thanks to box-office bonusesLaurence PhelanWed 19 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British actor Tom Holland is expected to “make at least $100m” for starring in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, according tothe Wrap.Unnamed sources “with knowledge of Holland’s deal” say he was paid $20m (£15m) upfront, about double what he reportedly received for his previous Spider-Man film No Way Home in 2021. But the extraordinary success of Brand New Day at the global box office means the 30-year-old is expected to earn another $80m or more in backend bonuses.In only its third week of release, Brand New Day has become the eighth highest grossing film of all time (unadjusted for inflation), and surpassed $2bn in ticket sales. And of the eight films that have reached this box office milestone, it is second-fastest to have done so. (Avengers: Endgame, released in 2019, was the fastest.)Holland’s reported salary represents a vast increase from his previous performances in the role. When he first played Spider-Man, in a relatively brief but significant appearance in Captain America: Civil War (2016), he was reportedly paid $250,000. For the next three Spider-Man films in which he starred, Homecoming (2017), Far from Home (2019), and No Way Home, he was reportedly paid $500,000, $4m and $10m respectively. But his initial contract is thought to have expired after the end of No Way Home, and the hugely increased remuneration is the result of a freshly negotiated new deal.Brand New Day’s success comes as audiences’ interest in films set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and in superhero films as a whole, had been waning. In 2023, The Marvels grossed only $206m against areported production budget(that is, not including distribution and marketing costs) of $270m. In 2024, Madame Web – about a character with direct ties to Spider-Man – madeonly $100m against an $80m budget. And in 2025,Variety reportedthat Marvel had released “three consecutive commercial duds”: Captain America: Brave New World ($415m, in contrast to the $1.15bn the previous Captain America film earned in 2016); Thunderbolts ($382m, against a $180m production cost) and The Fantastic Four: First Steps ($521m, against a production budget of $200m).The box office dominance of Spider Man: Brand New Day comes in a remarkable year for Holland, during which he also appeared as Telemachus in the second most financially successful film of 2026, Christopher Nolan’s acclaimed adaptation ofThe Odyssey($1.3bn in ticket sales), andmarried Zendaya, his co-star in both films.The Guardian has contacted Sony Pictures for comment.Explore more on these topicsSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom HollandSuperhero moviesMarvelFilm industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: David Shrigley London exhibition will find the funny side of old masters  | Dulwich Picture Gallery | The Guardian
description: Dulwich Picture Gallery show to feature British artist’s work hung next to paintings by Dutch and Flemish greats
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Dulwich Picture Gallery show to feature British artist’s work hung next to paintings by Dutch and Flemish greats
Content: David Shrigley and his installation Exhibition of Old Rope, which had a price tag of £1m.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDavid Shrigley and his installation Exhibition of Old Rope, which had a price tag of £1m.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesDulwich Picture GalleryDavid Shrigley London exhibition will find the funny side of old mastersDulwich Picture Gallery show to feature British artist’s work hung next to paintings by Dutch and Flemish greatsCaroline DaviesWed 19 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe contemporary UK artistDavid Shrigleywill apply his trademark arch humour and distinctive artistic practice “in dialogue” with old masters of Dutch and Flemish painting in a major new solo exhibition in London.The celebrated visual artist will explore the 17th-century paintings with his own new works “responding to” and hung alongside original masterpieces by artists including Jan Steen, Adriaen Brouwer, David Teniers the Younger, Adriaen van Ostade, Pieter Brueghel the Younger and Rembrandt van Rijn.The exhibition, opening at theDulwich Picture Gallerynext year,will be his first solo exhibition in a public art museum in the UK since his 2012 retrospective at the Hayward Gallery, and will bring his work into conversation with one of the most significant collections of Dutch and Flemish historical paintings in Britain, the gallery said.Take the plunge! A deep dive into New York and other great American cities – in picturesRead moreIt will present a series of brand-new, never-before-seen commissions alongside works created almost 400 years apart, and “explore the comedic side of historic painting, presenting how artists through the ages have used humour to observe everyday life, human behaviour and social interaction”, the gallery said. Key works from the gallery’s collection will be shown with loans from major UK institutions.View image in fullscreenA Peasant holding a Glass (1640s) by David Teniers the Younger.Photograph: Dulwich Picture Gallery, LondonView image in fullscreenCelebration of a Birth (1683) by Richard Brakenburgh.Photograph: Dulwich Picture Gallery, LondonView image in fullscreenA Woman with a Beer-Jug (c1670s) by Adriaen van Ostade.Photograph: Dulwich Picture Gallery, LondonHelen Hillyard, head of collection and exhibitions at the gallery, said: “We are excited for David Shrigley to bring his unique perspective to Dutch and Flemish masterpieces of the 17th century.“Shrigley – like our historic painters – has an instinct for finding the funny side of everyday life. He is the perfect artist to bring back playfulness to the old masters, and remind us that great art doesn’t always need to be serious.”Shrigley, a past Turner prize nominee, painter, illustrator, writer, film-maker and sculptor, is famed for his distinct line drawings along with his playful and humorous subject matter.His most recent installations have included the 2021 Mayfair Tennis Ball Exchange, where the gallery was filled with new tennis balls, and the 2025 installation at the Stephen Friedman gallery entitled Exhibition of Old Rope, consisting of 10 tons of used and discarded rope with a £1m price tag.The Shrigley exhibition, which will run from 25 May to 5 September 2027, is one of the headline exhibitions at theDulwich Picture Gallerywhose 2027/28 programme includes what is understood to be the first UK museum exhibition devoted to the pioneering French artist Jacqueline Marval (1866–1932).Marval is believed to have created one of the earliest female nude self-portraits in the history of painting. The exhibition (2 February to 9 May 2027) will bring together than 40 paintings and selected lithographs, many of which have never before been exhibited, to highlight her vital contribution to early French Modernism and her innovative representations of women and the female form, which helped to define the Parisian avant garde.A major retrospective will celebrate the pioneering British Pakistani postwar modernist Anwar Jalal Shemza (1928-1985) in the first UK major museum exhibition in more than 30 years. A Circle, A Square, A Puzzle (21 September to 16 January 2027) will show more than 80 works by the artist famous for Blue Blue Jazz (1967), SquareComposition (1963) and the Roots series (1977 to 1984). It will offer “a fresh appraisal of a pioneering artist whose work transcended cultural boundaries and transformed diverse artistic traditions across art forms and geographies”, the gallery said.Other landmark exhibitions in the programme include solo displays featuring new commissions by Sahara Longe and Caroline Walker.Explore more on these topicsDulwich Picture GalleryExhibitionsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Irvin, British film-maker who directed Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, dies aged 86 | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director’s BBC hit opened the door to Hollywood action films including Hamburger Hill, The Dogs of War and Raw Deal
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: The director’s BBC hit opened the door to Hollywood action films including Hamburger Hill, The Dogs of War and Raw Deal
Content: John Irvin with actor Dylan McDermott on the set of Hamburger Hill. The director was known for his versatility over a 50-year career that spanned TV, documentaries and action films.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Irvin with actor Dylan McDermott on the set of Hamburger Hill. The director was known for his versatility over a 50-year career that spanned TV, documentaries and action films.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesMoviesJohn Irvin, British film-maker who directed Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, dies aged 86The director’s BBC hit opened the door to Hollywood action films including Hamburger Hill, The Dogs of War and Raw DealSian CainWed 19 Aug 2026 00.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Irvin, the British film-maker who directed the Bafta-winning BBC miniseriesTinker Tailor Soldier Spy, as well as films including Hamburger Hill, The Dogs of War and Raw Deal, has died aged 86.Irvin died “peacefully at home” on 11 August, surrounded by his family, his producer Claire Evans confirmed to the Guardian.Over a 50-year career that spanned TV, documentaries and action films, Irvin was known for his versatility, working with everyone from Fred Astaire to Arnold Schwarzenegger. His most famous work was Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, the John le Carré adaptation starringAlec Guinnessas the spy George Smiley; Guinness once wrote of his admiration of Irvin, “a director with balls behind the camera!”Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy: 40 years on, the labyrinthine thriller is still TV caviarRead moreBorn in 1940 in Wallasey, Cheshire, Irvin started out as a student at the London Film School and worked at British Movietone News. In 1963 he released his first film, the documentary Gala Day, and a documentary short, Inheritance, which was narrated by Richard Burton and won Irvin his first Bafta.After he documented the North Yemen war, Irvin said MI6 took an interest in his work but he was never formally enlisted as a spy. “I was far too left wing, for a start, but was anti-apartheid, anti-war, anti-nuclear. They were probably well aware of my leftwing activities, so I was certainly not involved in any hanky-panky,” he said in a 2021 interview.Irvin directed several short films for the BBC and ITV, including 1969’s The Peasants Revolt, starring Anthony Hopkins in his first TV role. In the 1970s he moved into TV drama, directing The Nearly Man, Hard Times starring Timothy West, and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy with Guinness, Ian Richardson, Patrick Stewart and Beryl Reid. The miniseries won two Baftas from six nominations and was nominated for an Emmy for outstanding limited series.View image in fullscreenAlec Guinness and Siân Phillips during filming of the 1979 miniseries Tinker Tailor Soldier SpyThe success of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy opened the door to Hollywood, with Irvin directing The Dogs of War (1980) starring Christopher Walken and Tom Berenger; the horror film Ghost Story (1981) starring Fred Astaire; Champions (1984) starring John Hurt; Turtle Diary (1985) starring Ben Kingsley, Glenda Jackson and Michael Gambon; Raw Deal (1986) starring Schwarzenegger; Hamburger Hill (1987) starring Don Cheadle and Dylan McDermott; and Next of Kin (1989) starring Patrick Swayze and Liam Neeson.‘The aim was to give Kevin Costner’s version a good kicking’: director John Irvin on his anti-Thatcher Robin HoodRead moreIn 1991 Irvin directed Robin Hood with Patrick Bergin and a 20-year-old Uma Thurman; the film was deliberately commissioned as a rival to Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves starring Kevin Costner. While Irvin’s film was released two months before Costner’s, the latter was a megahit at the box office. “It was very much a stand-alone film with the aim of giving Kevin Costner’s version a good kicking if we could,”Irvin told the Guardian in May. “The studio wanted to go immediately because they wanted to pre-empt the Costner … I didn’t get involved in that mess, I just put my head down. Politics were left to the producers and executives.”In the 2000s, Irvin focused on independent cinema, directing films such as Shiner (2000) with Michael Caine, The Moon And The Stars (2006) with Alfred Molina and Jonathan Pryce, and The Garden Of Eden (2008) with Jack Huston, Mena Suvari and Richard E Grant.Irvin’s final film was 2016’sMandela’s Gun, a biopic of Nelson Mandela focused on his experience as a guerrilla fighter for the African National Congress. Irvin was working on a new cut of the film at the time of his death.Irvin is survived by his three children, Emilie, Luke and Amy, and two grandchildren.Explore more on these topicsFilmJohn le CarréAlec GuinnessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tupac Shakur trial: lawyers share full account of killing as witnesses still refuse to testify | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Murder trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, former South Side Compton Crips gang leader, opens in Las Vegas
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: Murder trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, former South Side Compton Crips gang leader, opens in Las Vegas
Content: James McDonald is cross-examined by defense attorney Michael Sanft during the murder trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis in Las Vegas on Tuesday.Photograph: John Locher/ReutersView image in fullscreenJames McDonald is cross-examined by defense attorney Michael Sanft during the murder trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis in Las Vegas on Tuesday.Photograph: John Locher/ReutersTupac ShakurTupac Shakur trial: lawyers share full account of killing as witnesses still refuse to testifyMurder trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, former South Side Compton Crips gang leader, opens in Las VegasLois BeckettTue 18 Aug 2026 20.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor nearly 30 years, the unsolved murder of 25-year-old rapper Tupac Shakur has sparkedlawsuits,theoriesandconspiracies.Now, decades after his death in a September 1996 drive-by shooting inLas Vegas, local prosecutors are finally offering a detailed official account of Shakur’s killing, accusing Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a 63-year-old former South Side Compton Crips gang leader, of being the “on-the-ground, on-site commander of the effort to kill Tupac”.Davis, who described himself as playing a main role in Shakur’s killing in his 2019 memoir, has pleaded not guilty, and his lawyers are trying to convince the jury that the claims he made in his book and in other interviews were lies Davis told for clout.Thirty years after Tupac Shakur’s killing, can a murder trial offer justice?Read moreFor Shakur’s relatives, the long-delayed chance at accountability in court is bringing both relief and renewed pain. On Tuesday, the second day of the trial, prosecutors focused on the most basic elements of Shakur’s killing and their case against Davis. Witnesses authenticated surveillance footage of a fight in the MGM Grand Hotel involving Davis’s nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, which allegedly inspired the shooting, and reviewed the bullet casings police found on the street and the autopsy photos of Shakur’s body.Jurors looked intently at the photos of Shakur’s body, which was bloated and had multiple chest wounds. The nearly full courtroom was silent.The display of graphic photos of the body of the beloved hip-hop artist and activist prompted some of his family members to leave the courtroom, and some to look away. Others chose to witness the painful evidence. Seeing the photos of Shakur’s body made Zayd Akinyela, Shakur’s cousin, feel “very angry, very angry, to say the least, very sad”, he said, in explaining why he had chosen to stay in the courtroom.“I feel like the details, especially for people that are close to him, honestly for me helps, helps the grief process. I think we’ve been waiting 30 years to grieve properly,” Akinyela told the Associated Press outside the courtroom. “A lot of people don’t get to grieve until they understand what happened to their loved one and how it happened.” He added: “That’s why I wanted to stay and just see for my own personal closure.”He said he hadn’t known how many times his cousin was shot and couldn’t help but think of the ways the night could have played out differently.The investigation of Shakur’s 1996 killing continues to be affected by the refusal of some witnesses and participants to testify to law enforcement officials about who was involved in his murder.“You better treat me as a hostile witness,” James McDonald, a former associate of Marion “Suge” Knight, the Death Row Records co-founder who was in the car with Shakur when he was shot, told attorneys on the trial’s second day.“Me or anybody else bringing up the dead is wrong,” McDonald said. He emphasized that he was only appearing in court because he had been subpoenaed.“I’m aware of a lot of things, things that was going on. People ain’t talked about it in 30 years. Today ain’t one of them,” McDonald testified.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t want to send him to prison, even though we don’t like each other,” McDonald said at one point, apparently pointing to Davis, who was sitting in the courtroom directly behind his attorney. “I don’t want to send you to prison,” McDonald repeated.The courtroom live stream showed no reaction from a grim-faced Davis.During his cross-examination, McDonald berated Davis’s defense attorney Michael Sanft, telling him: “You asking something that’s going to hurt this dude,” and, later appearing to address Davis: “Talk to your lawyer, man, this dude is tripping.”“I changed my life. I’m raising my grandkids, teaching them never to be like their Pawpaw, and here I am, explaining to people what I used to be, and I’m not proud of that, I’m not proud of that at all,” McDonald said. “You’re asking me questions that can hurt him, and like I told them, I’m trying to avoid to answer the questions.”The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTupac ShakurLas VegasGun crimeNevadaHip-hopRapUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the jawdropping story of the mother who faked her son’s illness | Television | The Guardian
description: A shocking documentary about a woman who pretended her child was terminally ill. Plus: isolation and horror in Australia’s desolate outback. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: A shocking documentary about a woman who pretended her child was terminally ill. Plus: isolation and horror in Australia’s desolate outback. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Toxic fantasy … from left, Chris, Matthew, Laura and Lisa Hayden-Johnson in I Love You to Death.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenToxic fantasy … from left, Chris, Matthew, Laura and Lisa Hayden-Johnson in I Love You to Death.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the jawdropping story of the mother who faked her son’s illnessA shocking documentary about a woman who pretended her child was terminally ill. Plus: isolation and horror in Australia’s desolate outback. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hannah Verdier,Priya ElanandSimon WardellWed 19 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLove You to Death9pm, Channel 4“He seemed to be allergic to the 21st century,” said journalist Paul Levie of Matthew Hayden-Johnson, a child from Torbay who, his mother, Lisa, claimed, was unable to walk, eat or breathe without medical assistance. However, as this jawdropping documentary series shows, Matthew’s litany of disability was a fantasy maintained by Lisa. With testimony from Matthew and Lisa themselves, it tracks a toxic fantasy as it took root, then fell apart.Phil HarrisonVoices of the Valleys8pm, Sky ArtsThis uplifting series about a sometimes overlooked but enduring Welsh folk tradition concludes. The big day has arrived for our three male voice choirs as they head to the Llangollen International Eisteddfod. As the competition looms, it’s a surprisingly intense and serious business.PHProfessor T9pm, ITV1Ben Miller returns for the fourth season of Professor T, which doesn’t find him in a good place. He’s doing everything to avoid getting involved in police work after Lisa’s death, but when a young woman disappears on a boat, the whole team spring into action.Hannah VerdierGuy Montgomery’s Guy Mont Spelling Bee9.45pm, BBC ThreeThe fun fake 70s vibe of this gameshow (check out Ray’s massive kipper tie!) is eye-catching, but nostalgia takes a back seat to the genuinely laugh out loud one-liners delivered by the host and the banter with his guests, who this week include off-the-wall comic Ray Badran and flirty Josh Thomas.Priya ElanOutback Murder Highway10pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenCreepy goings-on … criminologist Louise StedingPhotograph: Ryan McCurdy/Channel 4Anyone who has seen the 2005 film Wolf Creek knows the drill: outback Australia, isolation, mystery and horror. This creepy series travels the desolate Flinders Highway along which 11 people have gone missing since 1970. First, two nurses who planned to hitchhike across Australia with fatal results. Criminologist Louise Steding explores their disappearance.PHCouples Therapy10pm, BBC TwoMore couples explore their relationship pinch-points in the soothing company of Dr Orna Guralnik. First up, a man who has been paying women for “cuddling sessions” says himself to his remarkably tolerant better half, and a man with autism struggles to control the meltdowns he experiences when challenged by his partner.PHFilm choiceThe Beast, (Bertrand Bonello, 2022) 11.40pm, Film4View image in fullscreenBack in the future … George MacKay and Léa Seydoux in The Beast.Photograph: Carole BethuelInspired by a Henry James novella, Bertrand Bonello’s anguished sci-fi romance crosses space and time to explore the loneliness, fear and desire that are all part of what makes us human. In 2044, Gabrielle (Léa Seydoux) is persuaded by the AI that controls the world to undergo a past-life regression to “purify” her DNA and rid herself of unacceptably complicated emotions. But, in each existence she discovers a deep connection with George MacKay’s Louis. In 1910, she’s a bourgeois Parisian wife with an existential dread of disaster (“the beast”) attracted to his English gentleman. In 2014 Los Angeles, she’s an actor menaced by his incel stalker. Back in the future, could he be her soulmate?Simon WardellMonkey Man (Dev Patel, 2022) 11.30pm, BBC OneYou wouldn’t necessarily expect Dev Patel’s directorial debut to be an extremely violent action thriller. But this was a passion project for the actor, and he throws himself wholeheartedly into the tale of an Indian underground fighter who wears a monkey mask and is paid to take a beating. Then he sees the police chief (Sikandar Kher) who murdered his mother when he was a kid and vows revenge. Mixing social and political commentary in with the close-quarter fisticuffs, it’s an impressive first effort.SWLive sportTest cricket, England v Pakistan10am, Sky Sports Main Event.Joe Root returns to captain England on the opening day of the first Test at Headingley.Women’s cycling, Tour of Britain10:45am, TNT Sports 1.Stage one, a 158.9km route that starts and ends in Cockermouth.Champions League Football, Celtic v LASK7.30pm, TNT Sports 1.A play-off round first-leg match.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Love You to Death review – is this all they asked the woman who faked her son’s illnesses?  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Lisa Hayden-Johnson was convicted of child cruelty, but she still insists that she didn’t do anything wrong – and barely gets a grilling about it. Her children, who speak for the first time in this documentary, deserve much more
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Lisa Hayden-Johnson was convicted of child cruelty, but she still insists that she didn’t do anything wrong – and barely gets a grilling about it. Her children, who speak for the first time in this documentary, deserve much more
Content: ‘Incomprehensible purposes’ … Lisa and her son Matthew.Photograph: Paul Levie/TNAView image in fullscreen‘Incomprehensible purposes’ … Lisa and her son Matthew.Photograph: Paul Levie/TNATV reviewTelevision & radioReviewLove You to Death review – is this all they asked the woman who faked her son’s illnesses?Lisa Hayden-Johnson was convicted of child cruelty, but she still insists that she didn’t do anything wrong – and barely gets a grilling about it. Her children, who speak for the first time in this documentary, deserve much moreLucy ManganWed 19 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s an increasingly common pattern emerging whereby documentary makers take a story that was run through the Outrage-A-Tron by the tabloids to produce headlines that warped public understanding (“Britain’s Worst/Most Evil/Most Deadly” and so on), then proceed to put back some of the lost nuance and present the more complicated original picture. Lucy Letby (“Britain’s Worst Child Killer”) has been the subject of at least two such films redressing the lost balance. Last week, the story of Rhianan Rudd (“Britain’s Youngest Terrorist”) was unpacked and its many sadder parts laid out for inspection inThe Schoolgirl Terrorist?In Love You to Death, it is the turn of Lisa Hayden-Johnson, who became known as “Britain’s Most Evil Mum” during her trial and conviction for child crueltyafter years spent fabricating her son Matthew’s apparent illnesses. He was put through more than 300 medical encounters, nine general anaesthetics, four operations by the age of nine, and endured many unnecessary constraints on his life, including using a wheelchair, feeding tube and oxygen tank, until Lisa was arrested when he was nine.Love You to Death interviews Lisa, Matthew and his older sister Laura – who has some memories of being “a trial run” for her mother’s fabrications but whose suffering is largely of the more indirect, but no less damaging, kind that comes with living in a household that revolves around an ill and disabled member, taking on caring responsibilities very young, then finding out that all of it existed only to serve another’s incomprehensible purposes.The documentary lays out the chronology first, from Matthew’s seven-week premature birth in 2001, through his early stays in hospital as Lisa insisted he was failing to thrive because he was allergic to so many foods. It goes on through his apparently accumulating conditions, his local fame as “the boy in the buggy” whom the community rallied to help, and Lisa’s insistence to their main clinician Dr Broomhall – not interviewed, though their local GP Dr Paul Johnson is – that Matthew be referred to Great Ormond Street for more thorough investigations. This was despite Broomhall’s reluctance and the increasing suspicions among ward staff that all was not well.View image in fullscreenLisa and Matthew at the Children of Courage Awards 2005.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyEventually Dr Stella Imong, who had many dealings with Matthew’s “quite demanding” mother on the ward and had noticed the increasing number of factors in his notes that weren’t quite tallying, confronted Dr Broomhall about the situation and the latter reported Lisa to the police. The working presumption was that Lisa was suffering from Munchausen’s syndrome by proxy (now known as fabricated or induced illness) and enjoying the attention gained by having a sick child.It is a glaring weakness of the programme that it does not probe further into the whys and wherefores of the medical establishment’s inertia here. Especially as GP Paul Johnson all but shuffles his feet in embarrassment as he describes how confrontation “before you’re sure” can damage doctors’ reputations and hurt anyone falsely accused of harming their child. There is also mention of nurses raising concerns much earlier than any were acted upon, and any astute viewer will surely have more questions than are answered. A film about medical ethics, arrogance, cowardice and self-protection could easily work here.But the emphasis is on Lisa and her enduring insistence – bar the occasional slight concessions – that she did nothing wrong. Matthew was ill, she says, and everything she did was to help him. The children have no contact with her now, which clearly upsets her, but there is no sign that she is willing – or perhaps able – to provide them with the acceptance of her condition and what she really did that they need to establish any kind of rapprochement. Another weakness is the lack of anything other than softball questions to Lisa. She is rarely pressed on any issue or incident and it feels like a dereliction of journalistic duty.Laura and Matthew talk about her with regret, mystification and – particularly in Laura’s case – a longing for her to accept responsibility for their suffering. They are a study in grace and compassion. They manage to see her as mentally ill rather than “evil”, despite their experience of life lived right on the border between those two states. They undoubtedly deserve better – from their mother, from the professionals involved with their childhoods, and this programme, which – though it valuably restores much of what the tabloids eschewed – fails on some of its own quite vital terms.Love You to Death is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionHealthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Where Are the Kings by Donal Ryan review – a timeless tale of family sorrows and joys | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A teenage boy navigates adolescence and the traumatic loss of his mother in this poignant coming-of-age novel set in rural Ireland
Author: Beejay Silcox
Headline: A teenage boy navigates adolescence and the traumatic loss of his mother in this poignant coming-of-age novel set in rural Ireland
Content: ‘A study in grief-time’ … Donal Ryan.Photograph: Steve PykeView image in fullscreen‘A study in grief-time’ … Donal Ryan.Photograph: Steve PykeBook of the dayFictionReviewWhere Are the Kings by Donal Ryan review – a timeless tale of family sorrows and joysA teenage boy navigates adolescence and the traumatic loss of his mother in this poignant coming-of-age novel set in rural IrelandBeejay SilcoxWed 19 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 02.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomething is happening to literary time. In the last fortnight I’ve read new or forthcoming novels about a mirror universe where history runs backwards (The Understory, Chloe Benjamin), an agency that offers appointments with the past (Time Travel for Beginners, Jaclyn Moriarty), and a young woman who’s genetically untethered from linear life (Audrey Niffenegger’s long-awaited sequel to The Time Traveller’s Wife, out in October). And these are just the latest books to meddle with the fourth dimension. There are dozens: from Solvej Balle’s On the Calculation of Volume series and Toshikazu Kawaguchi’s Before the Coffee Gets Cold, to Kaliane Bradley’s The Ministry of Time. Time is losing the plot – or perhaps it’s the other way around.I have an armchair theory about all this counterfactual longing: the lure of the do-over. The present feels like a corrupted timeline. If only we could find the glitch.But even realist novels are messing with the clock. Irish author Donal Ryan’s Where Are the Kings is a study in grief-time: the ways loss distorts the ordinary passage of hours. Days stretch, collapse, repeat and disappear. Memories gather their own temporal weight. Grief becomes a planet with its own cruel, ruminative gravity.In his memory, Jack is forever pursuing his suicidal mother to the lake, reliving her last minutes. She is driving her rusty, backfiring Fiat; he is following behind on his pushbike, forcing his body up hill after hill. His muscles are screaming, his lungs are screaming, he is screaming. And he is too late. We will never learn what prompted Jack to follow his mam – only that he knew, in that terrible, lucid way kids know. There is a version of Jack that will always be pedalling; a version of her that might still be saved.Jack is 12 when we meet him, and in the care of his mother’s people: two stoic grandparents, a trio of blustering uncles and an unhelpfully gorgeous aunt. Jack’s father, Tomáš, has been institutionalised and feels as lost to the boy as his drowned mother. Twice now, Jack has seen a parent break – witnessed something vast and irreversible. He remembers the soundless way his mother cried; how his father clutched at her coffin. His desperate hands.double quotation markThis is a gentle novel of ungentle things – ‘things don’t stop being beautiful because ugly things happen’Jack is poised on the edge of adolescence: smart (“high eye queues”, as his grandad brags), but still at that threshold where perception outpaces understanding. He senses a family injury: “something complicated and invisible, some ancient strife from the time before he existed”. But he can’t quite grasp the shape of the wound, or how it festers in and around him. The grownups are tight-lipped. There’s a great deal they’ve learned to forget. Jack’s mother is already receding into hush and euphemism: “They hardly ever talk about Mam directly. Theyallude. They areoblique.”But the family do talk. And their affable chatter is the great pleasure of this novel, particularly Jack’s uncles, Theo and Haulie, a pair of existentially questing mechanics. They ponder the great questions of the universe, retell the great myths: “Liquorice? No, it’sIcarusyou thick bastard, the fella whose father made him wings and stuck them on him and he flew too high and bollixed himself up.” And then there’s Jack’s nana and her blasphemous wisdom. On Adam, the world’s first disappointing husband: “he couldn’t keep his house in order, the dopey prick. Set us all on the path to ruin.”Add in some incestuous lust, a dead deer, contested ashes, feckless priests and a flatulent roommate, and there are the makings here of a family farce: comic or tragic (or both). In another novel, some wild reckoning would be brewing (think of the final wheeling chapters of Paul Murray’sThe Bee Sting). But Ryan has never been a grand vaudevillian, or a cathartic trauma plotter. Where Are the Kings is a gentle novel of ungentle things – a reminder that “things don’t stop being beautiful because ugly things happen”. If Ryan’s fiction has a moral heartbeat, this might be it.There’s a hint or two that Ryan’s eighth novel inhabits the same unhurried world as 2020’sStrange Flowers, his tender-hearted tale of rural life, set in the fictional village of Knockagowny. Like Niall Williams, Ryan seems to be mapping an imagined Ireland, family by family.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTime moves strangely in this quiet corner of Tipperary, beyond the attenuation of grief: gossip is fleet; politics are sluggish. We gather our bearings from faded band T-shirts, songs on the radio and the late appearance of a brickish mobile phone. It seems to be the late 1990s, but that date feels almost incidental. It could be the 1980s. It could almost be the 1950s. In Theo and Haulie’s garage, time warps even further: “A good while ago could mean a month ago or it could be right back in history,” Ryan writes. “Time stops being linear and it susurrates and syncopates.” Jack imagines the workshop as a kind of wormhole. Might this be his way off the grief-planet: learning to put things back together? It can’t be that simple. And yet it is.What are we to make of all this slippage and stretching? Ryan gives us a clue in his section headings: Tempus Edax. Tempus Fugit. Tempus Imperator. Time devours. Time flies. Time rules supreme. These phrases belong to the tradition of memento mori: reminders of mortality’s cruel, beautiful, stupid, inescapable truth. Or as Jack puts it: “There’s nothing to be done then, it seems, except live.”Where Are the Kings by Donal Ryan is published by Doubleday (£16.99). title: The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore review – an ominous warning of tech takeover  | Books | The Guardian
description: A historian charts the emergence of a democracy-crushing dystopia that is – in some ways – already with us
Author: Farrah Jarral
Headline: A historian charts the emergence of a democracy-crushing dystopia that is – in some ways – already with us
Content: New Glenn rocket, developed by Jeff Bezos’s company Blue Origin.Photograph: Miguel J Rodriguez Carrillo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNew Glenn rocket, developed by Jeff Bezos’s company Blue Origin.Photograph: Miguel J Rodriguez Carrillo/Getty ImagesBooksReviewThe Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore review – an ominous warning of tech takeoverA historian charts the emergence of a democracy-crushing dystopia that is – in some ways – already with usFarrah JarralWed 19 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePulitzer prize-winning US historian Jill Lepore’s new book addresses the threat posed to liberal democracy by artificial intelligence. According to Lepore, the extraordinary power of private tech companies led by men whose priorities may not align with the wellbeing of the Earth or its inhabitants is set to destroy civilisation as we know it.Lepore’s concept of the Artificial State is capacious. It includes both a fantasy desired by a select few and a reality that is already with us. The fantasy is of an atomised society in which an elite can transcend biological and planetary restrictions, “abandoning constitutional democracy, the liberal nation-state, and even humanity itself for rule by automation, government by machine, and replacement by artificial intelligence”. The reality is that of public discourse having shifted to privately owned platforms on which monetised attention is valued above all else.That social media feeds are crafted to manipulate users’ behaviour, whether to consume a product or to shift political position, is now well established. X, formerly known as Twitter, is one example. It is riddled with bots controlled by various actors – state, non-state, criminal or corporate – whose activity contributes to an algorithmic flood of rage-bait that polarises citizens.According to Lepore, the Artificial State is not just the dream, but “the actual plan of a very small number of staggeringly powerful 21st-century merchant princes, Silicon Valley billionaires”. When our priority ought to be climate change, these “princes” – Lepore mentions Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel and Sam Altman – would rather focus on space travel or ramping up “compute” to beat China in the AI arms race. After scorching the Earth with energy-guzzling datacentres, she notes, their plan is to escape to Mars, hide in a bunker in New Zealand, or have their frozen brains uploaded.double quotation markAlmost every chapter ends with a deeply ominous line. However, she is not a true AI doomer at heartIntriguing, jewel-like stories are Lepore’s hallmark, and The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State sparkles with them. She presents numerous micro-histories that link the past to the present, including the roots of the apparently hyper-modern philosophy of techno-libertarianism in the paranoid science fiction of the cold war. Lepore recounts the origins of the census in ancient Mesopotamia, making the point that counting people gives those in power “the ability to tally, torment, and tax a population”. Her rich survey of science fiction tropes of the 20th century, many of which have infused the hopes and dreams of the Technorati, is revealing. While Lepore interprets much classic sci-fi, such as Isaac Asimov, as cautionary, she observes that “the architects of the Artificial State seem to have read these stories, unironically, as instruction manuals, guides for how to build robots that would one day rule the world”.By her own admission, Lepore has written “a grumpy book”. Almost every chapter ends with a deeply ominous line. However, she is not a true AI doomer at heart. She clarifies that it is not the technology itself that is the problem, but our lack of a coherent, democratically forged strategy about how to develop and use it. Yet she cites the growing number of industrial robots as if it were self-evident that such technology is always bad. By lumping together a range of different technologies under the umbrella of AI and “robots”, the wrong questions arise. Should a Russian state-operated chatbot fomenting far-right discontent in the UK be in the same categorical boat as machine-learning models used to create potentially life-saving drugs? Should the robot hoover sucking up toast crumbs in my kitchen be ontologically adjacent to a drone dropping bombs on houses full of children, using AI-generated intelligence? To analyse how technologies are reshaping the political order requires conceptual precision.Lepore’s argument that humanity is in the process of ceding vast power to a tiny group of unelected businessmen – some of whom appear to be cartoon supervillains – is a sound one. She concludes the book with an exhortation to “unplug” and connect with nature and animals but prescribes nothing further. This is no doubt a good idea. But in the face of a technological revolution that threatens to undermine the entire world order, logging off to touch grass can only be the first step.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
