title: Over/Under review – beautiful coming of age story of female best friends set across five summers | Movies | The Guardian
description: There’s an astonishing naturalism about the two leads, navigating the ups and downs of adolescence, bodily changes and learning to use tampons
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: There’s an astonishing naturalism about the two leads, navigating the ups and downs of adolescence, bodily changes and learning to use tampons
Content: Summer sun … Stella (Anastasia Veronica Lee) and Violet (Emajean Bullock) in Over/Under.Photograph: Bulldog Film DistributionView image in fullscreenSummer sun … Stella (Anastasia Veronica Lee) and Violet (Emajean Bullock) in Over/Under.Photograph: Bulldog Film DistributionMoviesReviewOver/Under review – beautiful coming of age story of female best friends set across five summersThere’s an astonishing naturalism about the two leads, navigating the ups and downs of adolescence, bodily changes and learning to use tamponsLeslie FelperinWed 19 Aug 2026 06.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePractically any woman who had a best female friend in early adolescence will be able to relate to this fragile, thoughtful drama about two American children, Violet (Emajean Bullock) and Stella (Anastasia Veronica Lee), living through the ages of nine to 13, a time as packed with incident as it is simultaneously uneventful and reassuringly dull. Unlike Richard Linklater’s justly acclaimed Boyhood, which had the resources to film for over a decade and thus observe its central character grow up, this was clearly made over a more compact schedule. Violet and Stella age much more subtly here, gradually growing breasts and getting a little bit taller, but those tiny incremental changes mean so much to them. Just as in real life with girls this age, a little bit of makeup, different clothes and some flat-ironing on the hair can alter a kid’s whole presentation.As the film starts, the two are nine-year-old besties, spending their summers together in New England where they go to camp, frolic in the surf (the title refers to a game they play with waves) and try to sleep over at each other’s houses. Unfortunately, Stella can’t yet cope with sleeping through the night at someone else’s place, and every time they try she must be collected by her parents after waking up frightened in the night. But it’s still something the girls yearn for. They even wish for it when they trap morning moths in jars, hoping fairies will grant them their hearts’ desires.But when both girls go home at the end of the summer, Violet to Los Angeles and Stella to San Diego, life is not so dreamy and blissful. Violet is bullied at school by a hateful little poppet and her friends who make fun of her birthmark and fantastic head of wavy, naturally crimped hair. Plus, it looks like her parents’ marriage is on the rocks. Stella has a more stable home life at first glance, but she too has worries, especially around the survival of her mother (Madeline Wise) who copes throughout with breast cancer, while her father (Adam David Thompson) is contending with an offscreen mother with dementia.These sidelong glimpses into the travails of adulthood don’t make the youngsters any less curious about their own bodily changes. They scrutinise every underarm hair on each another, and try to work out how you’re supposed to put in tampons – a life event nearly every woman goes through but which I don’t think I’ve seen depicted in a film before. When they have a chance, they hide in the dunes and study adult bodies at the nudist beach with fascination/repulsion. In the hands of a different director this all might have come across as twee or even icky, but here the actors’ astonishing naturalism and ease in front of the camera make this an exemplary coming of age story from Sophia Silver, dramatic enough to hold interest but never veering into melodrama or patronising didacticism.Over/Under is on digital platforms from 24 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsComedy filmsChildrenWomenComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: David review – biblical Goliath-slayer animation offers upbeat boybandish worship musical | Movies | The Guardian
description: Christian kids’ movie is entertaining during the big battle, but the older bouffant hero’s lack of depth is distracting and the worship songs a weak link
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Christian kids’ movie is entertaining during the big battle, but the older bouffant hero’s lack of depth is distracting and the worship songs a weak link
Content: The boy who would be king … scene from David.Photograph: Courtesy of Angel StudiosView image in fullscreenThe boy who would be king … scene from David.Photograph: Courtesy of Angel StudiosMoviesReviewDavid review – biblical Goliath-slayer animation offers upbeat boybandish worship musicalChristian kids’ movie is entertaining during the big battle, but the older bouffant hero’s lack of depth is distracting and the worship songs a weak linkCath ClarkeWed 19 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleU2’s Bono once described King David as “the Elvis of the Bible” – but in this musical kids’ adaptation, David is more boyband than rock’n’roll, with voluminous bouffant hair and a soundtrack of upbeat worship songs. The singing is actually a weak link in what is otherwise an unexpectedly entertaining film, with better than average animation and plenty of PG-approved sword-and-sandal battles. That said, David is unquestionably Christian cinema and frequently takes a preachy tone (often in song form); how much you enjoy it will probably depend on your tolerance for a bit of God.The Bible’s inconvenient plotting means that David’s takedown of the fearsome giant Goliath (voiced by Kamran Nikhad) comes relatively early in the film. We hear Goliath before we see him, ground trembling, as shepherd boy David (voiced by Brandon Engman) steps on to the battlefield armed with an only slingshot and stone. He has already been anointed by the prophet Samuel (Brian Stivale) as the future king of Israel. David has said he doesn’t want the job, which as Samuel sagely points out, makes him an ideal candidate. After his surprise victory against Goliath, David is brought by current ruler Saul to live at the royal palace.Years pass, and David (now voiced by Phil Wickham) grows into a devastatingly handsome young man raised as son by Saul (still unaware his young charge is earmarked to be king). Meanwhile, the kingdom is under threat from the Philistines and the nomadic Amalekites, brilliantly animated as a terrifying tribe of warriors in battledress of horns and animal pelts. There’s plenty of brotherly betrayal, double-crossing and other juicy Bible stuff, but it’s let down rather by David’s woefully bland characterisation: pretty to look at, brave, and possessing the psychological depth of a daisy.David is in UK and Irish cinemas from 21 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmChristianityAction and adventure filmsReligionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ihsane review – Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui leads us from brutal tragedy to euphoric harmony | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The choreographer combines a homophobic killing from 2012 with a remembrance for his father in an often rapturous show about healing
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The choreographer combines a homophobic killing from 2012 with a remembrance for his father in an often rapturous show about healing
Content: Sharing camaraderie … the cast of Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSharing camaraderie … the cast of Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewIhsane review – Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui leads us from brutal tragedy to euphoric harmonyFestival theatre, EdinburghThe choreographer combines a homophobic killing from 2012 with a remembrance for his father in an often rapturous show about healingChris WiegandWed 19 Aug 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2019 at the Edinburgh international festival, the Swiss director Milo Rau staged an intense theatrical investigation,La Reprise: Histoire(s) du Theatre (I), recreating a homophobic killing in Belgium. The murder of Ihsane Jarfi, seven years earlier, had made headlines and the news disturbed choreographer Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui who was just a little older, also gay and had a Belgian mother and Moroccan father like Jarfi.Cherkaoui now arrives at the same festival with his own act of remembrance, every bit as engrossing as Rau’s, yet more expansive. It pays tribute, too, to the choreographer’s father who died 30 years ago and whose past is interwoven with Jarfi’s death. If that raises any qualms, Cherkaoui’s larger point is about the interconnectedness of all lives and his characters morph into each other. He takes his cue from the victim’s first name, which essentially means “benevolence”, and counters the production’s disturbing flashes of violence with a floating lightness, whether in breakdance or traditional forms, and by presenting ideals of harmonious joy and kindness.View image in fullscreenInterconnected … a scene from Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThat’s where we begin, in an Arabic class, where the script is written on a board with brush strokes that initially complement two narrators’ graceful arms and echo through much of the show’s smooth flow. The tutor encourages the audience to join in with pronunciations; we share camaraderie and knowledge with the colourfully clad students. They arrange themselves in four rows of four and their tessellating gestures add to the patterns of Amine Amharech’s set and the intricate interplay of viola d’amore, piano, oud and percussion in Jasser Haj Youssef’s compositions. It is a lovely scene of common purpose, brought to an end by the set’s huge golden doors closing.They reopen to show the death of Jarfi who was tortured and killed by a group of men he met after leaving a gay bar. Here, a solitary figure torments him, with blows that never connect yet each vicious action sends the victim twisting in agony, almost as if by telekinetic force. Much later, the scene is reversed, with the body taken into the care of a woman.View image in fullscreenSmooth flow … Ihsane.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRau’s forensic production asked why the crime was committed and how performancecould ever begin to help us understand it. Cherkaoui includes a horrifying assessment of the injuries, and proves similarly interested in ritual, yet his focus is more on the aftermath, even the afterlife, and how a society heals. Jarfi’s body is reclaimed by a swaying collective under Fabiana Piccioli’s golden lighting, framed within the doors. A silky ensemble, facing outwards and joined in a circle, share a similar glow. Further spoken texts analyse different types of grief and dispel the notion of closure. Time and again the movement highlights the potential of each individual life; one chapter staged with billowing white drapes unites a blissful assembly of dancers in flesh-coloured costumes.Come Back Home review – loss and love in Palestinian artist’s intriguing fringe hourRead moreTea is served during a scene that merges the casual and ceremonial, as a football is kicked across the stage, but amid this vivacity a throat is cut and blood spills across Maxime Guislain’s startling video design. Home movies and reportage also play on screens, and there are meditations on society’s strictures and the march of technology that distract from the emotional impact.On stage are 18 dancers from Cherkaoui’s two companies, Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève and Eastman, joining four musicians and a pair of singers. A whole world is created, merging past and future, and death is met with teeming life.AtFestival theatre, Edinburgh, until 20 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalDanceTheatreSidi Larbi CherkaouireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Giraffe review – sparkling one-woman show stands out from the crowd | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: An unlikely relationship blossoms in Abigail Weinstock’s compelling and touching solo drama
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: An unlikely relationship blossoms in Abigail Weinstock’s compelling and touching solo drama
Content: Touching … Abigail Weinstock in Giraffe.Photograph: Andrew PerryView image in fullscreenTouching … Abigail Weinstock in Giraffe.Photograph: Andrew PerryEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewGiraffe review – sparkling one-woman show stands out from the crowdPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghAn unlikely relationship blossoms in Abigail Weinstock’s compelling and touching solo dramaMark FisherWed 19 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt takes a brave writer/performer to make her character a sociopath. How to keep the audience on board with someone who is callous and indifferent?In Abigail Weinstock’s sparkling one-woman show, 30-year-old Eliana has been caught making clandestine recordings in her neighbour’s bedroom and cannot deny it. A court summons follows. Even then, her first thought is how to game the system.Her attempt to do so is what gives Giraffe its structure. Eliana has a fortnight until going in front of a judge who will determine whether her temporary restraining order should be made permanent. If she can drum up three letters of support in that time, she has an outside chance of avoiding homelessness (she lives too close to her victim to stay put). With no obvious advocates – her mother long dead, her stepmother intolerant and her father inscrutable – she needs extra resources of imagination to find backers.Sociopaths, of course, can be ruthless, so Eliana is prepared to bluff her way into a childminding job (reassuring the confused mother that she wishes no harm to her daughter) and mask her true nature from a therapy group in the hope of seeming like a trustworthy citizen.Everything goes wrong before it comes right in Emma Jude Harris’s production but, on the way, Weinstock gives a delicious portrayal of a physical and emotional misfit who is hopelessly and hilariously at sea with the business of human communication.What emerges is a quite different diagnosis. Touchingly, in this semi-autobiographical show, Eliana understands the psychology of the silent child she looks after unlike anyone else. It proves she is an emotionally rich human being who just happens to have her own way of interpreting – and misinterpreting – the world. Standing out from the crowd in a human zoo, she and the child are giraffes among zebras. So is this show.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Rake’s Progress review – a young cast packed with promise do Stravinsky’s dance with the devil proud | Opera | The Guardian
description: The staging is awkward and balance is an issue at points, but the singers of British Youth Opera are consistently impressive
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The staging is awkward and balance is an issue at points, but the singers of British Youth Opera are consistently impressive
Content: Modernist games … the cast of The Rake's Progress at Battersea Arts Centre.Photograph: Julian GuideraView image in fullscreenModernist games … the cast of The Rake's Progress at Battersea Arts Centre.Photograph: Julian GuideraOperaReviewThe Rake’s Progress review – a young cast packed with promise do Stravinsky’s dance with the devil proudBattersea Arts Centre, LondonThe staging is awkward and balance is an issue at points, but the singers of  British Youth Opera are consistently impressiveAlexandra CoghlanWed 19 Aug 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClapham – home to hundreds of young Londoners crammed into sticky-floored house-shares of a weeknight and the sweaty dancefloors of Infernos at the weekend. Where better to stage The Rake’s Progress, Stravinsky and WH Auden’s 1951 fairytale-cum-morality-play about a country innocent swallowed whole by the temptations and corruptions of the capital? Add a cast and creative team in their 20s, and you’ve got immersive theatre before you even open the doors.We’ve seen Rakes before from British YouthOpera(2009’s starred a certain Nicky Spence, star attraction of this year’s Last Night of the Proms – this finishing-school for students and young professionals clearly works) but never one conceived, directed, designed and stage-managed entirely by the participants themselves. In terms of professional development it’s a gift, but it made for a bit of a bumpy show on opening night.A V-shaped stage encloses conductor Oliver Cope and Sinfonia Smith Square at its centre. Three door frames (clad in Bridgerton offcuts of wisteria for Anne Trulove’s country bower, etched out in red light for London) supply Alexandra Kay’s minimal set. It’s a tricky setup that maroons characters in narrow lines or banishes them to the very back of the theatre, further obscuring already difficult sight lines. And with no pit to tame the enthusiasm of the orchestra, balance is often an issue for the young singers.View image in fullscreenThe cast delivers on the heartbreak: British Youth Opera in The Rake's Progress at Battersea Arts Centre.Photograph: Julian GuideraCope is all crisp precision and lucidity, his Prelude launching a swift, cool account of Stravinsky’s Mozart-homage of a score. The orchestra responds intermittently, but the right angles and sharp points of Stravinsky’s score are an unforgiving architecture, and too many chords and rhythms smudge or sag.Director Tom Deazley makes no big gestures in a quiet, gently contemporary staging that’s more interested in psychology than society. His cast (the first of two) do him proud. Tenor Sam Rose’s Tom Rakewell is a brittle, suggestible creature who comes startlingly into focus in the tenderness and vulnerability of his Bedlam scene. This is a beautiful young voice, packed with promise, and his physical awkwardness sits nicely against the assurance and polished stage package of Sam Young’s Nick Shadow.Sophie Bysouth is a sweet-voiced, earnest Anne, capable of harnessing some fire in “I go, I go to him”, and deeply touching in her woman-to-woman confrontation with Rhian Davies’ confident Baba the Turk. Matthew Bawden relishes his cameo as Sellem, and Gabriel Tufail Smith catches the ear in the small role of the Keeper.Stravinsky and Auden may play modernist games with arm’s length artifice and irony, but ultimately you judge a Rake by its heartbreak. This cast delivers, even if the mechanics of staging and presentation don’t always help them do it.AtBattersea Arts Centre, Londonuntil 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicBattersea Arts CentrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: After 25 years, I’m breaking up with The Sims. Here’s why you should, too | Jordan Erica Webber | The Guardian
description: Now that Jared Kushner and the Saudi Investment Fund have bought The Sims’ publisher, EA, it’s unlikely to remain a game celebrating diversity and inclusivity, says video games writer Jordan Erica Webber
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: Now that Jared Kushner and the Saudi Investment Fund have bought The Sims’ publisher, EA, it’s unlikely to remain a game celebrating diversity and inclusivity, says video games writer Jordan Erica Webber
Content: ‘The Sims has long been known for including and welcoming people of all races, gender identities and sexualities.’Photograph: Electronic ArtsView image in fullscreen‘The Sims has long been known for including and welcoming people of all races, gender identities and sexualities.’Photograph: Electronic ArtsOpinionGamesAfter 25 years, I’m breaking up with The Sims. Here’s why you should, tooJordan Erica WebberNow that Jared Kushner and the Saudi Investment Fund have bought The Sims’ publisher, EA, it’s unlikely to remain a game celebrating diversity and inclusivityWed 19 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 05.47 EDTShareSometimes it feels as though horrific world events and the malicious entities behind them are reaching into every aspect of our lives, from heatwaves that keep me shut away indoors, to generative AI that makes it increasingly difficult to trust what I read online. I can no longer even retreat into my favourite video game without funding human rights abuses across the world.I’ve been playing The Sims series of life-simulation games since its first release at the turn of the millennium, when I sat with my sister in the corner of the sitting room using money cheats to build mansions for our digital dolls. Over the years, these games have helped me make friends: from the schoolmate who taught me to play more efficiently with hot keys, to the local fan who watched me stream The Sims 4 online and now meets me for lunch every week. In the last quarter of a century I’ve sunk thousands of hours into these games.But all of that stopped, with the sudden snap of a clean break, when it wasrevealedlast year that a group of private investors planned to acquire Electronic Arts (EA), the publisher of some of the world’s most popular video game series: FC (previously Fifa), Battlefield, Dragon Age, and many more – including my beloved The Sims. There are several reasons why I – and many others – object to this deal, which wascompletedafter regulatory approval this month, but it mostly comes down to the who, why and how.The purchasers taking EA out of public trading are: the Saudi Public Investment Fund (chaired by the country’s de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman), Silver Lake (which has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into AI infrastructure in the US) and Affinity Partners (owned by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner).Kushner, of course, is on his father-in-law’s so-calledBoard of Peace, planning to rebuild Gaza (first step: a newmilitary base) after theatrocitiesordered by hisfamily friend, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Saudi Arabia is known forbombing Yemeni civilians(with weapons from the UK), allegedly assassinating journalistJamal Khashoggi,abusing migrant workersandgenerally violating human rights.It is enough not to want to line these particular pockets. But hypothesise the motivations behind this deal: the people leading these companies understand the soft power of video games. Those around Trump capitalised on the men swept up in the hate campaign known as“Gamergate”, and have recently usedvideo game memesto promote the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE). Saudi Arabia has been accused of“sportswashing”, spending on popular sports to distract from its more objectionable behaviour, and seems to be attempting the same with video games.This is particularly noxious because The Sims has long been known for welcoming people of all races, gender identities andsexualities; its developers have often responded to player feedback with free updates that add requested content to the game: more diverse hairstyles, sexual orientation, pronouns. Whether its new conservative owners use the platform’s existing popularity to lure in unwary fans or whether they assert creative control to insert their own propaganda, we – the players – lose.Even if that all feels irrelevant or – depressingly – unavoidable to you, consider the method. This historic $55bn (£41bn) deal is a leveraged buyout, meaning a large portion of the cost was paid for with debt (in thiscase $22bnfrom leadingfossil fuel financierJP Morgan) that EA now owes. How will it make that extra money? Soullessgenerative AI? Predatorymicrotransactions? More life-ruininglayoffs?These concerns are shared by popular Sims content creators such aslilsimsie(real name Kayla Sims), who is one of several now seeking todivest themselvesfrom the game. She even worked with her local representative, Congressman Maxwell Frost, to inform players on how they might try to block the sale. “It’s all about cutting corners to rip off consumers instead of making games,” she said in ashort videoposted after the deal was finalised, while Frost promised to use congressional oversight to demand answers from EA and protect workers and players.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s good to know there are people in power who realise the potential consequences of this deal and are willing to act against them however they can. But unless The Sims is sold off to a less objectionable owner, I no longer feel comfortable playing my lifelong favourite game. Maybe I’ll pin my hopes on new competitorParalives, or dig out my old (already paid for, offline only) physical copies of the original The Sims. In the meantime, at least there are plenty of otherinteresting gamesto play instead.Jordan Erica Webber is a freelance writer and presenter specialising in video games and digital cultureDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Will the future of gaming be powered by upstart indie developers? | Games | The Guardian
description: As gaming’s biggest publishers retreat into safer bets, a new generation of independents are building an alternative from the ground up
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As gaming’s biggest publishers retreat into safer bets, a new generation of independents are building an alternative from the ground up
Content: The games industry’s indie scene is expanding as major publishers retreat from riskier projects, with boutique companies stepping in to back smaller studios with experimental ideas.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe games industry’s indie scene is expanding as major publishers retreat from riskier projects, with boutique companies stepping in to back smaller studios with experimental ideas.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWill the future of gaming be powered by upstart indie developers?As gaming’s biggest publishers retreat into safer bets, a new generation of independents are building an alternative from the ground upDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 19 Aug 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the 1990s, a new strata of independent film studios and distributors revitalised the Hollywood movie machine. The likes of Miramax, New Line Cinema and October Films challenged the ageing behemoths of the industry and pushed forward offbeat directors such as Quentin Tarantino, Darren Aronofsky and Jane Campion. The decade is widely considered an artistic high point for western cinema after the bloated mainstream excesses of the 1980s. Could something similar now be happening in games?Certainly, we have a comparable setup. The big players of the games business are in various states of creative disarray: Electronic Arts (EA) has beenbought out by a Saudi-led consortium, which is likely to lead to more cautious, hit-driven decisions; Microsoft bought Activision and Bethesda and thenordered waves of redundancies; Ubisoft hascancelled several titlesand is posting big losses. Those companies are also facing rising development costs, so they’re circling the wagons, focusing on legacy brands and freezing recruitment. It’s hard to imagine any left-field works of genius emerging from this imaginative quagmire.Meanwhile, smaller developers who are starved of investment through traditional routes, are quietly formulating a counter-economy. Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen the arrival of boutique publishers, set up by successful studios, and designed to support grassroots talent. Kinetic Publishing was formed by the creator of successful indie ghost-hunting game Phasmophobia to support new studios; Outersloth is the funding arm ofAmong Uscreator InnerSloth, launched in 2024 to support idiosyncratic game concepts; London-based Kepler Interactive, formed in 2020, was behindClair Obscur: Expedition 33, the most critically acclaimed title of 2025. Last week saw theannouncement of Inner Pocket, a publisher founded by industry veterans and dedicated to “intimate and engaging” experiences.View image in fullscreenCritially acclaimed and indie-made … Clair Obscur Expedition 33.Photograph: Sandfall InteractiveThere has, arguably, never been a better time for this kind of grassroots revolution in games publishing. Digital distribution via stores such as Steam and the App Store has given studios a global marketplace, while social media platforms are providing comparatively cheap marketing avenues. A decade ago, it would have been costly to show new games and strike deals at big events such as E3 – but now, most titles are revealed via online showcases or through communities of fans on Discord and Reddit. At the same time, developers are able to bypass traditional publishing deals to finance projects, seeking help from regional arts networks and funding bodies, and joining local hubs for support. At the latest Develop Conference in the UK,studio collectivescame together, combining forces and sharing expertise.This isn’t a cure-all. The games industry is still a complex and intimidating market and, with a focus on digital distribution, discoverability is still a major issue for new titles – how do you gain attention, and an audience, when there are hundreds of new titles released on Steam every week? But as mainstream publishers quietly drop more ambitious and experimental projects, there is a growing community of new companies, networks and funding bodies looking to help. As John Buckley, head of publishing at PocketPair,said recently, “We’re going to see more hit games coming from publishers you’ve never heard of.”Nineties movies such as Sex, Lies and Video Tape, Reservoir Dogs and Slacker emerged from a new Hollywood culture of film school nerds, cheap equipment and funding models only a few steps up from maxing out credit cards – and a growing independent production system was there to support them. For years, chin-stroking critics asked the now-lampooned question: when will video games have their Citizen Kane moment? Now, perhaps the more pertinent version is: what will be the industry’s Blair Witch Project?What to playView image in fullscreenSerene … Cast n Chill.Photograph: Wombat BrawlerIf you have ever enjoyed a fishing minigame in an RPG thenCast n Chillis worth a look. It’s a pixel art fishing game set in beautiful nonspecific North American lakes, rivers and coastline. As the title suggests it is fairly serene – though you have to spend time upgrading your rods and boat if you want to catch some real monsters. It’s also got two-player couch co-op, a feature I’m always looking for so I can play with my sons.Keza MacDonaldAvailable on:PC and Mac via SteamEstimated playtime:18 hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenProfit before safety ... US senators are investigating child safety on Roblox.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersUS senators areinvestigating child safetyonRoblox, accusing the game’s creator of prioritising revenue and engagement metrics over children’s wellbeing.Sneaking about in the alleyways of gaming history, open-world gangland adventureMafiais approaching its 25th year. IGN celebrates withan entertaining oral historyof the series – it’s an article you can’t refuse.As a lifelong fan of weird and divisive video games, I enjoyedthis pieceon6 out of 10 bangers –the sorts of games that score “low” but only because they’re bizarre, twisted and glitchy, which can be compelling qualities. Resident Evil Gaiden and Amiga classic Shadow of the Beast are mentioned. I’d add PS2 curioMister Mosquito(where you play as a mosquito trying to suck blood from a suburban family) and crazed PlayStation driving gameRunabout(known as Felony 11-79 in the West), where you run around a city trying to unlock as many vehicles as possible. They don’t make ‘em like that any more.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickThe Blood of Dawnwalker – save your family while becoming what you hate‘The ultimate gamers’ mascot’: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchiseIthaca: a scintillating eco-thriller RPG that aims to confront our violent momentAlien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new world‘The kids were right’: 30 years of Pokémon, from school-wide bans to multimillion-dollar trading cardsThe Sinking City 2 review – Ukrainian cosmic horror, come hell or high water | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenSo realistic there’s probably an eight-hour wait at Dover … Euro Truck Simulator 2.Photograph: SCS SoftwareA question this week fromJon,via email:“I love driving games, but I don’t want to compete online – or even compete at all, if I’m honest. I played Forza Horizon 4 to death without actually progressing in the festival at all and I bought GTA V just so I could hop in a car and circumnavigate San Andreas without shooting anybody.Are there any other race-free driving games I could try?”There are plenty in the indie space if you don’t mind a drop in visual fidelity.Slow Roadsis a popular browser-based driving game, where you simply select a terrain and then drive along endless roads. An upgraded version is coming to the Steam store in October with a few more road types and vehicle customisation options, and the demo is available now.The Long Driveis slightly more demanding, a vehicle-based survival game where you drive around a post-apocalyptic landscape ensuring your food, water and fuel don’t run out. It’s been stalled on Steam early access for years and has probably been abandoned, which I feel is a nice metaphor for this whole sub-genre. Elsewhere,BeamNG.driveis an in-depth vehicle physics simulator where you configure a car to your specifications and then drive it through a sandbox world – it’s in early access on PC but a PS5 version has been promised. The cheery open-world driverMotor Towndoes offer missions to carry out, but mostly it’s about whizzing about in a range of different vehicles. And there’s alwaysEuro Truck Simulator 2, which has drives long enough to feel aimless, even if you do have packages to deliver.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterIndie gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I came to the Highlands to give something back to the hills’: a volunteering trip in Scotland | Scotland holidays | The Guardian
description: I found two days of hard graft – repairing hiking paths with a conservation trust in stunningly remote Wester Ross – a surprisingly rewarding experience
Author: Mike MacEacheran
Headline: I found two days of hard graft – repairing hiking paths with a conservation trust in stunningly remote Wester Ross – a surprisingly rewarding experience
Content: Stac Pollaidh’s ‘porcupine ridge’ summit.Photograph: Tony West Photo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStac Pollaidh’s ‘porcupine ridge’ summit.Photograph: Tony West Photo/Getty ImagesScotland holidays‘I came to the Highlands to give something back to the hills’: a volunteering trip in ScotlandI found two days of hard graft – repairing hiking paths with a conservation trust in stunningly remote Wester Ross – a surprisingly rewarding experienceMike MacEacheranWed 19 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhadn’t planned to enjoy any of this. As summer light fell on Stac Pollaidh – the summit’s teeth bared, the views stretching across the surreal emptiness of Assynt – I found myself ankle-deep in blanket bog next to a hiking path, back bent, hacking at the tough terrain with a heavy-duty mattock. Farther up the hillside, another hunched figure was cutting a deep brown scar into the moor grass and, while he worked, I stood back to look at my efforts. At my feet was a cross drain that I’d unblocked and repacked with new stonework to prevent storm damage and aid runoff from the path. A burble began to trickle, slow yet clear across the sparkling bedrock. It felt a little like appreciating a masterwork in a museum.I’d come to Wester Ross with a bucket and spade, not for a beach break at particularly gorgeous Achmelvich or Clachtoll nearby, but with the notion of giving something back to the hills. TheOutdoor Access Trust for Scotland(Oats) is a steward of many of the Highlands’ most famous mountains – developing, building and repairing paths and habitats – and I’d joined a group of volunteers for a two-day stint on the north-west Highlands’ most visited peak. Factoring in a free stay atUllapool youth hosteland the promise of a home-cooked communal meal in return, plus an acceptable midge-free forecast, I’d driven north from Edinburgh the night before in a buoyant mood.Oats’s purpose is to promote sustainable public access and these days that’s largely done through voluntourism, with helpers set to work lifting, resurfacing and filling pathways, yielding landscape-scale results. Iconic if traffic-heavy mountains such as An Teallach, Lochnagar and Braeriach are annual priorities, as are a throng of glens and estates from Skye to the Cairngorms. (Due to this summer’s devastating fires, some events in the north Cairngorms may be changed to a different location or postponed.) The trust’s volunteers even regularly get to work on the Lairig Ghru, arguably Britain’s most unforgiving mountain pass.View image in fullscreenVolunteers repairing the hiking path on Stac PollaidhIt might sound like all hard graft, but it’s not. Volunteers learn new practical skills and gain awareness of mountain path design and the causes of erosion – mostly a combination of human misuse and increasing extreme weather conditions – in settings with extraordinary views. No experience is required, but volunteers must be used to spending time outdoors, have good physical fitness and be capable of using hand tools.We started that first morning from Stac Pollaidh’s car park, a space transformed by Oats two years ago to accommodate four times more vehicles – a result of the mountain’s accessibility from the North Coast 500, which hurtles past (from Kylesku to Ullapool) only five miles east, at the end of the road. But everyone comes with the same motivation. As we climbed the open moorland, Assynt’s surrounding sea of lochans (small lochs) sparkled. Stac Pollaidh’s summit, to the north, appeared even more welcoming with its porcupine ridge under a sky as blue as a newborn’s eye.double quotation markPost-Brexit, with a lack of EU funding streams, there is a drastic need for a public fund for path maintenance and habitat restorationFrom below the hilltop to the lower forest’s edge, we worked the path – unclogging ditches, removing invasive grasses, dredging, stabilising the soil, repacking stone drains, replanting edges – all while the mountain came to life. Trail runners, dog walkers and hikers from across Europe weaved up the slopes, stopping to ask what we were doing. A French school group trooped past, the pupils plastered with blue Braveheart face paint. A Dutch couple stopped to offer biscuits. Everyone swallowed the stunning views of Suilven to the north.View image in fullscreenSuilven from Loch Druim Suardalain.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Getty ImagesOur group of seven volunteers – including two New Zealanders; three retirees, one from Inverness, one from Stirling and another from Forfar; and an Edinburgh IT worker using his annual corporate volunteer days – appreciated the smiles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Scottish explorer who fancied an adventure closer to home: hiking the Highlands’ Affric Kintail WayRead moreTo a newcomer, the Highlands’ mountain paths may appear to have always been there, as if part of the landscape’s DNA. But as Oats’s volunteer coordinator Eva Kupska said, they are “always evolving and always at risk from erosion, because of the influences of nature and man … and it is our job to conserve them”.Every volunteer is vital. Post-Brexit, with a lack of EU funding streams, Eva told me there is a drastic need for a public fund for path maintenance and habitat restoration, and the charity simply doesn’t have the manpower to tackle the deteriorating pathways or native tree planting alone. To complicate matters, some of the most popular mountain paths are on privately owned land, with no access to any public funding.There are a further 12 one-day, plus three- and five-day,maintenance and conservation eventsscheduled to take place this year, including some dedicated tree-planting trips. It’s a joyful shared experience. That first afternoon, flasks of hot tea were unscrewed and homemade fruit loaf was shared. There was the warm smell of flowering heather and the earthy stink of the bogs, along with the satisfaction of time well spent in the wild.View image in fullscreenUllapool, where Mike stayed in the youth hostel.Photograph: Eleanor Scriven/Getty ImagesThat evening, back in Ullapool, the harbour abuzz with tourists eating fish suppers and gulls circling above the trawlers, we stood in the sea-view kitchen of Ullapool youth hostel sharing life stories and the day’s experience. There are plenty of excellent dinner options, includingThe Seafood ShackandThe Dipping Lugger, but we settled on a night of each other’s company (delightful), local beers (necessary) and a giant gurgling stockpot of Eva’s courgette and tomato risotto (terrific). And boy, did I sleep well.The next day brought a gossamer mist to the hills of Wester Ross. We arrived earlier, picked up where we’d left off and, largely, never complained as the sun slowly cracked through the clouds. But best of all was seeing our progress as we worked down the mountain, step by step, always avoiding the fragile vegetation at the path’s edges, creating something better and more sustainable for tomorrow. A staycation with a purpose – and it felt good.The trip was provided byOutdoor Access Trust for Scotland, with support fromVisitScotland.To register as a volunteer and to sign up for events on the annual path maintenance days programme, visitOats’svolunteering portal. Overnight accommodation in a youth hostel or a bothy, plus evening meals and transport to and from the restoration site, are includedExplore more on these topicsScotland holidaysVolunteering holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysMountainsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn excess green vegetables into a vibrant Spanish soup – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A gazpacho is not only a great way to use up odds and ends in the crisper drawer, it will also surprise you with its flavour and versatility
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A gazpacho is not only a great way to use up odds and ends in the crisper drawer, it will also surprise you with its flavour and versatility
Content: Tom Hunt’s green gazpacho.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s green gazpacho.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn excess green vegetables into a vibrant Spanish soup – recipeA gazpacho is not only a great way to use up odds and ends in the crisper drawer, it will also surprise you with its flavour and versatilityTom HuntWed 19 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince readingHow Not to Die, by Michael Greger, I’m always looking for ways to include greens in every meal. He regularly pops into my mind when I’m cooking, whispering in my ear: “Add some spinach to that risotto,” say, or “Moringa powder will make your porridge much more nutritious.” So I’m sure today’s green gazpacho would make him proud. It’s a great way to clear out your crisper drawer and pack a meal with all sorts of greens. Anything goes, but if any of your chosen ingredients (eg, basil or mint) has a particularly potent flavour, just add it in moderation or to taste. Incidentally, the key to a great gazpacho is the quality of the olive oil, as is a nice, bold-but-balanced acidity, which is easily achieved with a squeeze of lemon or your best vinegar.Green gazpachoWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThis is a really vibrant recipe, and perfect for the hot summer months. It’s best served well chilled, so make it with ice so you can enjoy it immediately or/and chill in the fridge or freezer for 30 minutes to an hour. It will keep, covered, in the fridge for up to three days, but is best eaten on the day it is made. You can also add a few ice cubes to the soup bowls, if you like.Decorate the top with a selection of your favourite ingredients used in the soup: finely dice them and scatter on top, along with any delicate herbs and a final drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Serves4400g green vegetables(cucumber, courgette, celery stalks and leaves, lettuce, spinach, peas, or a mix of whatever you have to hand), finely chopped – save some of your favourites to garnish50-100g soft green herbs(parsley, basil, mint, coriander, or a mixture), leaves roughly chopped, stalks finely chopped1 handful ice cubes100ml extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to finish2 tbsp lemon juice, or white-wine, sherry or cider vinegar, plus extra to taste, if necessary1 small garlic clove(or to taste), peeledSea saltOptional spices– I used cumin, ground coriander and cayenne pepper, but experiment with what you have in the cupboardRoughly chop the green vegetables and put them in a jug blender.Add the herbs and 200ml chilled water, drop in the ice cubes, oil, garlic and a pinch of salt, then add any spices you fancy. Blend for a minute, until very smooth, then adjust the seasoning, acidity and spice to taste.Chill for at least half an hour, and serve cold, topped with the reserved green vegetables, finely diced, a few herb leaves and a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteVegetablesSoupSpanish food and drinkHerbs and spicesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jammy tomato risotto and amaretto roast peaches: Toklas chef Chris Shaw’s simple summer recipes  | Food | The Guardian
description: Make the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessert
Author: Chris Shaw
Headline: Make the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessert
Content: Chris Shaw’s risotto with datterini tomatoes, pecorino and mint.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenChris Shaw’s risotto with datterini tomatoes, pecorino and mint.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.FoodJammy tomato risotto and amaretto roast peaches: Toklas chef Chris Shaw’s simple summer recipesMake the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessertChris ShawWed 19 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Toklas, ingredients such as datterini tomatoes and ripe peaches are taking centre stage. These recipes celebrate the simplicity of summer cooking, allowing produce to shine with minimal intervention. From a risotto layered with sweet tomatoes, pecorino and mint to roast peaches finished with amaretto and mascarpone, they capture the character of the season – fresh, generous and full of flavour.Risotto with datterini tomatoes, pecorino and mint (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appA really light risotto. There’s no butter in it – just olive oil and cheese – and the richness comes predominantly from the roast tomatoes.Prep15 minCook1 hr 20 minServes4For the stock4 shallots,peeled2 sticks celery,trimmed1 vine of tomatoes2 carrotsFor the roast tomatoes500gdatterinitomatoes, washedSaltOlive oil4garlic cloves,peeledFor the risottoOlive oil2 shallots, peeled and finely diced1garlic clove, peeled and crushedSalt and black pepper350g risotto rice2 tbsp tomato puree150gpecorino romano, grated30g fresh mint, leaves picked and finely choppedTo make the stock, roughly chop all the vegetables and put them in a saucepan. Cover with two litres of cold water and bring to boil over a high heat. Turn down the heat and leave to simmer for 20 minutes.Meanwhile, heat the oven to 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½. Put the tomatoes in a roasting tray, season with salt and drizzle with olive oil. Add the garlic, then roast for about an hour, until the tomatoes are jammy.Bring a large, heavy-based pan to a medium heat. Add a generous glug of olive oil, followed by the diced shallots, crushed garlic and a pinch of salt. Once the shallots are soft, add the rice and stir well to coat. Add another pinch of salt then toast the rice for a minute or two, until the edges begin to look translucent. Add the tomato puree and cook for two to three minutes.Strain the stock and discard the vegetable solids. Add the stock to the rice one large ladleful at a time, stirring continuously and allowing each addition to be absorbed before adding the next.After about 18-20 minutes, when the rice is just cooked but still has a little bite, take the pan off the heat and stir through the roast tomatoes, roast garlic, grated pecorino and chopped mint. The tomatoes should break up nicely once incorporated into the hot rice.Season to taste, finish with a generous glug of olive oil, if desired, and serve immediately.Amaretto roast peaches with mascarponeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenChris Shaw’s amaretto roast peaches with mascarpone.Inspired by the restaurantVia Carota in New York, this is a really great summer dessert – it’s super-easy, too.Prep5 minCook25 minServes4For the mascarpone cream250g mascarpone50ml double cream¼ vanilla pod, seeds scraped out50g icing sugarFor the peaches4 good-quality (ideally yellow) peaches75g icing sugar150mlamarettoCombine all the ingredients for the mascarpone cream in a bowl, beat well with a spatula until smooth, then chill until needed. (The cream helps soften the mascarpone, which can otherwise be quite stiff and heavy.)Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6.Halve the peaches, remove the stones, then cut each half in two. Arrange the peach quarters skin side down in a roasting tray. Using a sieve, dust evenly with the icing sugar, then pour the amaretto into the tray and roast for about 15 minutes, or until the peaches are tender and lightly caramelised.Serve the warm peaches with the roasting juices spooned over and the mascarpone cream on the side.Chris Shaw is head chef atToklas, London WC2Explore more on these topicsFoodRiceSummer food and drinkTomatoesMain courseItalian food and drinkCheeserecipesShareReuse this content
